items.q: Do you think it is important for young people to have role models?
items.text: I believe it is absolutely vital for adolescents to have someone to look up to. Role models act as a kind of moral compass, offering guidance on how to navigate life. When a young person admires a professional, they are internalising the values of hard work and perseverance that led to that success. Without such figures, young people can feel a little unmoored, lacking any real sense of direction.

items.q: How have the types of role models changed since your grandparents' time?
items.text: There has been a rather dramatic shift, I would say. In my grandparents' era, role models tended to be figures within the immediate community, such as teachers or elders. Today, influence is increasingly dominated by celebrities and social media personalities, many of whom are famous for very little of substance. I find this shift somewhat concerning, because fame has become almost entirely disconnected from genuine merit.

items.q: How do role models affect the way people behave in a society?
items.text: They have a profound ripple effect, in my opinion. When influential figures behave ethically, they set a positive standard that others tend to emulate. Conversely, when role models behave badly, it can normalise that behaviour, particularly among impressionable young people. So I would argue they play a significant part in shaping a society's collective values.

items.q: Why do some public figures fail to remain positive role models over time?
items.text: I think the main reason is the immense pressure and scrutiny that come with public life. Constant attention can distort a person's judgement, and some become complacent once they achieve fame. There is also the temptation of wealth and power, which can gradually erode the very values that made them admirable in the first place. Sadly, staying grounded under that spotlight is genuinely difficult.

items.q: In the future, do you think AI or fictional characters could become role models?
items.text: It is quite possible, and to some extent it is already happening. Virtual influencers are becoming increasingly prevalent, and young people do form attachments to fictional heroes. However, I would be somewhat wary of this trend, because a fabricated character lacks the real struggles that make human role models relatable. I think something genuinely authentic would be lost in that shift.

items.q: What can be done to encourage young people to choose positive role models?
items.text: Education is key, I believe. Parents and schools should actively help children think critically about who they admire and why. Rather than simply banning certain influences, which rarely works, we should cultivate media literacy so young people can distinguish substance from mere celebrity. Highlighting inspiring local figures would also provide more attainable and grounded examples to follow.

items.q: Do you think people are more influenced by role models in real life or in the media?
items.text: That is an interesting question. I would argue that media figures have a wider reach, but real-life role models, like a parent or mentor, have a far deeper and more lasting impact. The influence of a media personality is often superficial and fleeting, whereas someone you interact with daily shapes your character in a much more meaningful way.

items.q: Some people say governments should promote positive role models. Do you agree?
items.text: I partly agree. Governments can certainly showcase admirable citizens, such as scientists or humanitarians, to counterbalance shallow celebrity culture. However, I am slightly cautious, because state-endorsed role models can easily become propaganda if handled poorly. So while the intention is commendable, it needs to be done transparently and without any political agenda.

items.q: Do you think family is as important today as it was in the past?
items.text: I would say family remains just as important, though its form has changed. The emotional support and sense of belonging a family provides are timeless human needs. That said, modern life has certainly strained family bonds, with people moving away for work and spending less time together. So while its importance is undiminished, sustaining it now requires more conscious effort.

items.q: How are family relationships different now compared to a generation ago?
items.text: The biggest difference is probably the shift from large, extended families to smaller, more nuclear ones. In the past, several generations often lived under one roof, which fostered close bonds. Today, families are more dispersed, and technology has, ironically, both connected and distanced us. Relationships are more equal now, but arguably less tightly knit.

items.q: Why do you think many families spend less time together nowadays?
items.text: Several factors are at play. The demands of modern careers are relentless, leaving parents exhausted and time-poor. On top of that, digital devices have become a real distraction, with family members often absorbed in their own screens even when in the same room. This gradual erosion of shared time is genuinely detrimental to close relationships.

items.q: What role does the extended family play in your culture?
items.text: In my culture, the extended family remains absolutely central. Grandparents, uncles and cousins are deeply involved in one another's lives, providing a strong support network. This interdependence means that responsibilities, from childcare to financial help, are often shared. I think this collective approach offers a real sense of security, though it can occasionally feel a little intrusive.

items.q: How do you think family structures will change in the future?
items.text: I anticipate that families will continue to become smaller and more diverse in form. We will likely see more single-parent households and blended families becoming commonplace and widely accepted. Technology may also allow far-flung relatives to stay connected more easily. Overall, I think the definition of family will grow more flexible and inclusive.

items.q: What can families do to stay close despite busy modern lives?
items.text: I think the key is being intentional about spending time together. Simple rituals, like sharing at least one meal a day without phones, can make a real difference. Families could also prioritise occasional trips or activities that create shared memories. Ultimately, closeness does not happen by accident; it has to be actively nurtured amid the busyness.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of living with extended family?
items.text: The main advantage is the constant support; there is always someone to help with childcare or during a crisis, which is invaluable. It also passes down traditions and keeps bonds strong. On the downside, it can mean a lack of privacy and occasional friction between generations with differing views. So it is really a trade-off between solidarity and personal independence.

items.q: Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?
items.text: I strongly agree, at least in principle. In my culture, caring for elderly parents is seen as a moral obligation, a way of repaying the sacrifices they made. That said, I recognise this is not always practical in modern life, so it need not mean living together. What matters is that the elderly are not neglected and retain their dignity.

items.q: Do you think it is better to have a few close friends or many acquaintances?
items.text: I firmly believe that quality trumps quantity when it comes to friendship. A few close friends who genuinely understand you provide far deeper support than a large circle of superficial acquaintances. While it is useful to have a wide network for professional reasons, the emotional intimacy of a true friendship is something that simply cannot be replicated at scale.

items.q: How has technology changed the way people make friends?
items.text: Technology has transformed it enormously. People now form friendships online with others across the globe, which was unimaginable a generation ago. This has made connection more accessible, but I would argue these digital friendships can be more fragile. Meeting through a screen sometimes lacks the depth that comes from sharing real experiences face-to-face.

items.q: Why do some childhood friendships fade over time?
items.text: I think it is largely a natural consequence of people growing and changing. As we mature, our interests, values and circumstances diverge, and friends who once had everything in common may drift apart. Physical distance, when people move for work or study, only accelerates this. It is sad, but I see it as an almost inevitable part of life.

items.q: How important are friends compared to family in a person's life?
items.text: Both are essential, though they serve different roles. Family offers unconditional support and a sense of roots, whereas friends are people we actively choose, which makes those bonds uniquely affirming. Friends often understand aspects of our lives that family cannot. I would say a fulfilling life requires a healthy balance of both, as each provides a distinct kind of companionship.

items.q: Do you think online friendships will replace face-to-face ones in the future?
items.text: I doubt they will replace them entirely, but they will certainly become more significant. Online friendships are convenient and can be genuinely meaningful. However, humans are inherently social creatures who crave physical presence, so I believe in-person connection is irreplaceable. The most likely outcome is a hybrid, where the two forms coexist and complement each other.

items.q: What can people do to maintain long-distance friendships?
items.text: Consistent effort is really the crucial ingredient. Regular video calls and messages can keep a friendship alive despite the distance. I think it also helps to be deliberate about planning occasional visits, as nothing quite replaces meeting in person. Ultimately, both parties have to be committed, because a friendship that only one person sustains rarely lasts.

items.q: What are the benefits and drawbacks of having friends from different cultures?
items.text: The benefits are considerable. Friends from other cultures broaden your perspective and challenge your assumptions, which is deeply enriching. You learn to be more tolerant and open-minded. The only real drawback might be occasional misunderstandings arising from different customs or communication styles. But in my view, these minor obstacles are easily outweighed by the rewards.

items.q: Some say social media has made friendships shallower. Do you agree?
items.text: I largely agree with that sentiment. Social media encourages us to accumulate hundreds of contacts while investing little in any of them. The constant highlight reels can also breed comparison rather than genuine connection. That said, it depends how you use it; for maintaining existing bonds it is useful. Used as a substitute for real intimacy, though, it does trivialise friendship.

items.q: What do you think are the most important qualities of a good parent?
items.text: In my view, the most important qualities are patience and consistency. Children thrive on stability, so a parent who sets clear, fair boundaries helps them feel secure. Equally vital is unconditional love balanced with the willingness to discipline when necessary. A good parent also leads by example, since children tend to absorb behaviour far more than instructions.

items.q: How is childhood today different from childhood in the past?
items.text: Childhood has changed dramatically. In the past, children spent most of their free time playing outdoors and socialising in person. Today, much of that has been supplanted by screens, which I find rather disconcerting. Children are also under far more academic pressure now. So while modern children have more opportunities, they arguably have a less carefree upbringing.

items.q: What effect does strict parenting have on children?
items.text: It can have mixed effects. On one hand, strict parenting can instil discipline and a strong work ethic. On the other, if it is excessively authoritarian, it may stifle a child's creativity and confidence, or even breed rebellion. In my opinion, the ideal lies in a balanced approach that is firm but also nurturing and understanding.

items.q: How does a person's childhood affect them as an adult?
items.text: I think childhood is profoundly formative. The experiences and relationships we have in those early years shape our personality, our self-esteem and how we relate to others. A secure, loving childhood tends to produce confident, well-adjusted adults, whereas a troubled one can leave lasting scars. In many ways, our childhood lays the foundation for everything that follows.

items.q: How do you think parenting will change in the coming decades?
items.text: I expect parenting will become increasingly intertwined with technology. Parents will likely rely more on apps and online resources for guidance, and managing children's screen time will become an even more daunting challenge. I also anticipate a move towards more egalitarian parenting, with responsibilities shared more equally. Hopefully there will also be greater awareness of children's emotional wellbeing.

items.q: How can parents help children develop good values?
items.text: The most effective way is by modelling those values themselves, since children imitate what they see. Beyond that, parents can use everyday situations as teaching moments, discussing honesty or kindness openly. Encouraging empathy, perhaps through community involvement, also helps. Ultimately, values are instilled gradually through consistent example rather than through occasional lectures.

items.q: What are the pros and cons of both parents working full time?
items.text: The clear advantage is financial; a dual income provides a higher standard of living and more opportunities for the children. It can also make both parents positive role models of independence. The downside is that it may leave less time for the children, potentially affecting the parent-child bond. It really comes down to the quality of the time spent, not just the quantity, and whether adequate childcare is in place.

items.q: Some people think children are given too much freedom today. Do you agree?
items.text: I partly agree. Modern parenting rightly encourages children's independence, but in some cases the pendulum has swung too far, and children lack clear boundaries. A total absence of limits can leave children feeling insecure rather than free. That said, the opposite extreme is equally harmful, so the goal should be freedom within a framework of sensible, loving guidance.

items.q: Do you think there is a big generation gap in your country?
items.text: Yes, I think the generation gap in my country is quite pronounced, largely because of the rapid pace of change. Older generations grew up in a very different, more traditional society, while the young have been shaped by technology and global culture. This creates differing values and expectations, which can sometimes lead to tension, though it also brings a healthy diversity of perspectives.

items.q: What are the main differences between the older and younger generations?
items.text: The differences are quite stark. The older generation generally values stability, tradition and hard-earned security, whereas young people tend to prioritise flexibility, self-expression and work-life balance. There is also a huge gap in digital fluency. However, I think these differences are often exaggerated; at their core, both generations share many of the same fundamental aspirations.

items.q: Why do older and younger generations sometimes struggle to understand each other?
items.text: The root cause is that they have lived through fundamentally different eras. Their formative experiences, technologies and social norms were worlds apart, which shapes how they see everything. This can lead to a failure to empathise, with each side viewing the other's values as alien. A lack of open, patient communication only widens that gulf.

items.q: How can different generations learn from one another?
items.text: There is enormous potential here. Younger people can help older generations navigate technology, while the elderly offer invaluable wisdom and life experience that no textbook can provide. This kind of exchange, sometimes called reverse mentoring, is mutually beneficial. When generations genuinely listen to each other, both are enriched, and society as a whole becomes more cohesive.

items.q: Do you think the generation gap will grow larger in the future?
items.text: It is a real possibility, given how quickly technology now evolves. Each new generation is being shaped by tools the previous one barely understands, which could amplify the divide. On the other hand, constant connectivity might actually help bridge it. So the outcome is uncertain, and it may depend on whether we make a deliberate effort to stay connected across ages.

items.q: What can be done to reduce conflict between generations?
items.text: Fostering genuine dialogue is essential. Creating opportunities for generations to interact meaningfully, whether in families or communities, builds mutual understanding. Both sides need to approach differences with humility rather than judgement. I also think education plays a role in teaching young people to respect their elders while encouraging older people to remain receptive to new ideas.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of a workplace with mixed age groups?
items.text: The advantages are significant. A mix of ages brings together the fresh ideas and tech-savviness of the young with the experience and prudence of older staff, which is a powerful combination. The potential disadvantage is friction arising from clashing work styles or communication preferences. But with good management, this diversity of thought is far more of an asset than a liability.

items.q: Some say younger generations have life easier than older ones. Do you agree?
items.text: I think it is more nuanced than that. In material terms, young people today certainly enjoy comforts and technology their grandparents lacked. However, they face their own distinct pressures, such as intense competition, job insecurity and a constant online spotlight. So I would not say life is simply easier; rather, the hardships have shifted in nature.

items.q: What qualities make someone a good leader?
items.text: In my opinion, a good leader combines vision with genuine integrity. They need the ability to inspire and motivate others towards a common goal, but also the humility to listen. Crucially, effective leaders lead by example and take responsibility for failures rather than shifting blame. I think this accountability, paired with genuine empathy, is what earns lasting respect.

items.q: Is it better for a leader to be respected or feared?
items.text: I firmly believe respect is far more effective than fear. A leader who rules through fear may achieve short-term compliance, but this breeds resentment and stifles honest communication. A respected leader, by contrast, inspires genuine loyalty and willing effort. People follow such a leader out of conviction rather than intimidation, which produces far better and more sustainable results.

items.q: What happens to an organisation when it has poor leadership?
items.text: The consequences can be severe. Poor leadership often results in low morale, as employees feel directionless and undervalued. This typically leads to reduced productivity and high staff turnover. Without a clear vision, an organisation can quickly stagnate or lose its way entirely. In short, weak leadership tends to permeate every level and undermine the whole enterprise.

items.q: How important is leadership in bringing about social change?
items.text: Leadership is often the decisive factor. Throughout history, major social movements have been galvanised by charismatic leaders who could articulate a shared vision and mobilise people. A strong leader gives a movement focus and momentum. That said, I think the best leaders empower others rather than dominate, ensuring the change is collective rather than dependent on one individual.

items.q: How do you think leadership styles will change in the future?
items.text: I believe we are moving away from the traditional top-down, authoritarian model towards something more collaborative. Future leaders will likely need to be more emotionally intelligent and adaptable, given how quickly the world changes. There will also be greater emphasis on transparency and inclusivity. In short, leadership is becoming less about command and more about facilitation.

items.q: How can society develop better leaders?
items.text: I think it starts with education that nurtures not just intelligence but character and empathy. Providing young people with genuine opportunities to take responsibility, through mentorship or community projects, helps cultivate leadership skills early. We should also reward ethical leadership rather than mere ambition. Essentially, good leaders are developed over time, not simply born.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of a young person becoming a leader?
items.text: The advantages include fresh energy, innovative ideas and a willingness to challenge outdated conventions. Young leaders can be genuinely dynamic. The main disadvantage is a lack of experience, which may lead to impulsive decisions or difficulty commanding respect from older colleagues. Ideally, a young leader would be paired with experienced mentors to balance their enthusiasm with wisdom.

items.q: Some say great leaders are born, not made. Do you agree?
items.text: I largely disagree with that idea. While some people may have a natural charisma or confidence, I firmly believe leadership is a set of skills that can be learned and refined through experience. History is full of leaders who grew into the role. To claim leaders are simply born undermines the value of hard work and personal development.

items.q: Why do you think so many young people want to be famous?
items.text: I think it is largely driven by social media, which has made fame appear both glamorous and easily attainable. Young people see influencers achieving wealth and adoration seemingly overnight, which is highly seductive. There is also a deeper human desire for validation and significance. Unfortunately, this often means chasing fame as an end in itself rather than as a by-product of genuine achievement.

items.q: How is fame today different from fame in the past?
items.text: The nature of fame has changed completely. In the past, fame was usually earned through exceptional talent or accomplishment, and famous people were relatively few. Today, anyone can become famous overnight through a viral video, and fame is often fleeting and detached from any real skill. Modern celebrity is also far more invasive, with stars under constant surveillance.

items.q: What effect does celebrity culture have on young people?
items.text: The effects are often detrimental, in my view. Constant exposure to celebrities' curated, idealised lives can create unrealistic expectations and fuel insecurity, especially about appearance. It can also promote materialism and a distorted sense of what matters. That said, positive celebrities who champion good causes can be a genuinely inspiring influence, so it is not entirely negative.

items.q: Do celebrities have a responsibility to be good role models?
items.text: I would argue they do, whether they like it or not. Given the enormous influence they wield over millions of impressionable fans, celebrities have a certain moral obligation to behave responsibly. Their actions can genuinely shape public attitudes. However, it is also unfair to expect them to be flawless, since they are human. The key is a basic level of accountability and awareness.

items.q: Do you think celebrity culture will become more or less influential in the future?
items.text: I suspect it will become even more influential, but also more fragmented. Rather than a few global superstars, we are likely to see countless niche influencers, each commanding devoted audiences. Technology like virtual influencers may further blur the line between real and fabricated fame. Whether this influence is healthy will depend on whether audiences become more discerning and sceptical.

items.q: How can society reduce the negative effects of celebrity obsession?
items.text: Media literacy education is crucial here. Teaching young people to critically evaluate the polished images they see online can lessen the harmful comparisons. Promoting a broader range of admirable figures, such as scientists or activists, would also help rebalance what we celebrate. Ultimately, encouraging people to derive self-worth from their own lives rather than idolising others is the real solution.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of being famous?
items.text: The obvious advantages are wealth, influence and opportunities that most people can only dream of. Fame also provides a platform to promote worthy causes. However, the disadvantages are considerable: a total loss of privacy, relentless scrutiny, and immense pressure that can take a serious toll on mental health. Many celebrities find the constant spotlight genuinely suffocating, so it is far from the idyllic life it appears.

items.q: Some people say celebrities are paid too much. Do you agree?
items.text: I have some sympathy with that view. It does seem disproportionate that an entertainer can earn more in a day than a nurse earns in a year, when the latter arguably contributes more to society. On the other hand, their pay simply reflects the market and the vast revenue they generate. So while it feels morally questionable, it is economically logical.

items.q: Why is honesty important in relationships?
items.text: Honesty is really the bedrock of any healthy relationship. Without it, trust cannot exist, and trust is what allows people to feel safe and secure with one another. Even small lies, once discovered, can erode that foundation and breed suspicion. In my view, being truthful, even when it is difficult, is what gives a relationship genuine depth and resilience.

items.q: Do you think people are more or less honest than they were in the past?
items.text: That is a difficult question. I do not think human nature has fundamentally changed, but the opportunities for deception have multiplied with technology, from online scams to fake identities. At the same time, the internet has made it much harder to hide dishonesty, since misdeeds are quickly exposed. So perhaps we are no less honest, just more transparent.

items.q: What happens to a society when trust in institutions breaks down?
items.text: The consequences are deeply damaging. When people lose faith in institutions like government or the media, it breeds cynicism and division. Cooperation becomes difficult, conspiracy theories can flourish, and social cohesion begins to unravel. Trust is essentially the glue that holds a society together, so its breakdown can lead to genuine instability and dysfunction.

items.q: Is it ever acceptable to tell a lie?
items.text: I think there are rare cases where a so-called white lie is justifiable, particularly when the truth would cause needless harm and the lie is genuinely benevolent. Sparing someone's feelings is a common example. However, this is a slippery slope, because habitual lying, even with good intentions, can undermine trust. So while not absolute, honesty should be the strong default.

items.q: Do you think it will be harder to trust information in the future?
items.text: Unfortunately, I think it will. With the rise of sophisticated technology like deepfakes and AI-generated content, distinguishing genuine information from fabricated material will become increasingly difficult. This could make people either dangerously gullible or excessively cynical. Developing strong critical-thinking skills and reliable verification tools will be absolutely essential to navigate this new landscape.

items.q: How can trust be rebuilt once it has been broken?
items.text: Rebuilding trust is a slow and difficult process. It requires the person who broke it to take full responsibility and offer a sincere apology, without excuses. More importantly, they must demonstrate changed behaviour consistently over time, since words alone are not enough. The wronged party, meanwhile, needs to be willing to gradually reconcile. Essentially, trust is rebuilt through actions, not promises.

items.q: What are the benefits and risks of being completely honest all the time?
items.text: The great benefit of total honesty is that it builds a reputation for integrity, and people know exactly where they stand with you. It fosters deep trust. The risk, however, is that unfiltered honesty can sometimes be hurtful or tactless if not delivered with care. So I think the ideal is honesty tempered with diplomacy, being truthful but also kind.

items.q: Some say honesty is always the best policy. Do you agree?
items.text: I largely agree, though I would add a small caveat. As a general principle, honesty builds trust and spares us the burden of maintaining lies, so it is almost always wise. However, I think it must be balanced with compassion; brutal honesty that needlessly wounds someone is not virtuous. So honesty is the best policy, provided it is delivered sensitively.

items.q: Do you think peer pressure is always a bad thing?
items.text: Not at all, and this is a common misconception. While peer pressure is usually associated with negative behaviour, it can be a powerful positive force too. If your peers are ambitious and disciplined, their influence can motivate you to raise your own standards. So peer pressure is really a double-edged sword; its effect depends entirely on the company you keep and how discerning you are.

items.q: Who has more influence on teenagers, their friends or their parents?
items.text: During the teenage years specifically, I would argue friends often have the greater immediate influence. Adolescents are forming their own identity and naturally seek acceptance from their peers, sometimes at the expense of parental advice. However, parents provide the deeper, underlying values that tend to resurface later in life. So peers shape day-to-day behaviour, while parents shape long-term character.

items.q: Why are young people especially vulnerable to peer pressure?
items.text: It largely comes down to their developmental stage. Adolescents have a deep psychological need to belong and fear social rejection intensely. Their sense of identity is still forming, which makes them more susceptible to conforming with the group. Additionally, the part of the brain governing impulse control is not yet fully developed, so they are more likely to act on that pressure.

items.q: How does the desire to fit in affect people's behaviour?
items.text: The desire to fit in is an extraordinarily powerful driver of behaviour. It can lead people to conform to group norms even when they privately disagree, a phenomenon that affects everything from fashion to opinions. While this social cohesion has its benefits, it can also suppress individuality and lead to poor decisions. Learning to resist this pull and think independently is a mark of real maturity.

items.q: Do you think social media has made peer pressure stronger?
items.text: Absolutely, I think it has intensified it dramatically. In the past, peer pressure was confined to your immediate social circle, but now it is constant and global. People compare themselves to countless others online, and the pressure to project a perfect image is relentless. This amplified, round-the-clock pressure is, I believe, taking a serious toll on young people's wellbeing.

items.q: How can young people be helped to resist negative peer pressure?
items.text: Building self-confidence is the most effective safeguard. A young person with a strong sense of self is far less likely to succumb to pressure. Parents and teachers can help by fostering open communication, so children feel able to discuss difficult situations. Teaching practical strategies, like how to say no gracefully, also empowers them to stand firm.

items.q: What are the positive and negative sides of wanting to be like others?
items.text: On the positive side, wanting to emulate others can inspire self-improvement; admiring successful people can push us to work harder. It also helps social integration. The negative side is that it can lead to a loss of individuality and constant, unhealthy comparison. It may cause people to suppress their true selves to fit in. The healthiest approach is to draw inspiration from others while staying true to who you are.

items.q: Some say peer pressure decreases as people get older. Do you agree?
items.text: I broadly agree, though it never disappears entirely. As people mature, they generally develop a firmer sense of identity and care less about others' approval, making them more resilient to pressure. However, the pressure simply takes on a more subtle form in adulthood, such as keeping up with colleagues' lifestyles. So it lessens, but it certainly does not vanish.

items.q: Do you think conflict between people is always negative?
items.text: Not necessarily. While conflict is uncomfortable, it can actually be constructive if handled well. Disagreements often bring underlying problems to the surface, which allows them to be addressed rather than festering. Healthy conflict can also spark better ideas and deeper understanding. The key is whether it is managed respectfully; it is unresolved or hostile conflict that is truly damaging.

items.q: Is it better to confront a problem directly or avoid it?
items.text: In most cases, I believe confronting a problem directly is far healthier. Avoidance may keep the peace temporarily, but the underlying issue tends to fester and grow worse over time. Addressing it calmly and early usually leads to genuine resolution. That said, direct confrontation should be done tactfully, choosing the right moment, so it does not escalate into a bigger dispute.

items.q: What are the main causes of conflict between people?
items.text: In my experience, most conflict stems from poor communication and misunderstanding rather than genuine malice. When people fail to express themselves clearly or make assumptions about others' intentions, friction inevitably arises. Differences in values, competition over resources and simple miscommunication are also common triggers. Interestingly, many disputes could be avoided entirely with a little more patience and clarity.

items.q: How important is emotional intelligence in resolving conflicts?
items.text: It is absolutely crucial. Emotional intelligence allows a person to understand not only their own feelings but also the perspective of the other party, which is the foundation of any resolution. Someone with high emotional intelligence can stay calm, empathise, and communicate without inflaming the situation. Without this ability, people tend to react defensively, which almost always makes the conflict worse.

items.q: Do you think people will become better at resolving conflicts in the future?
items.text: I am cautiously optimistic. There is growing awareness of the importance of emotional intelligence and communication skills, which are increasingly taught in schools and workplaces. If this trend continues, future generations may be better equipped to handle disagreements. On the other hand, online communication can sometimes make people more polarised and less willing to compromise, so it is not guaranteed.

items.q: What is the best way to resolve a serious disagreement?
items.text: The most effective approach usually involves calm, honest dialogue where both sides genuinely listen to one another. It helps to focus on the specific issue rather than attacking the person, and to seek a compromise where possible. In some cases, involving a neutral third party as a mediator can be invaluable. Ultimately, a willingness to see the other's perspective is what unlocks resolution.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of using a mediator in disputes?
items.text: The main advantage is that a neutral mediator can defuse tension and help both parties communicate objectively, often reaching a solution they could not manage alone. It is also usually cheaper and quicker than legal action. The disadvantage is that mediation relies on both parties' goodwill; if one side is uncooperative, it can fail. It also lacks the binding authority of a court ruling.

items.q: Some say avoiding conflict keeps relationships healthier. Do you agree?
items.text: I largely disagree with that. While constant conflict is obviously harmful, consistently avoiding it is not healthy either, as it allows resentment to build silently. Relationships that never address problems often suppress genuine feelings, which eventually surface in a much larger explosion. In my view, healthy relationships are not conflict-free; they simply handle disagreement maturely and constructively.

items.q: Do you think emotional intelligence is more important than academic intelligence?
items.text: I would argue they are both important but serve different purposes. Academic intelligence may get you a qualification, but emotional intelligence is often what determines success in life and work, since it governs how you deal with people. The ability to manage emotions, empathise and communicate is genuinely indispensable. So while I would not rank one above the other, emotional intelligence is arguably more underrated.

items.q: Are emotional skills valued more in some professions than others?
items.text: Definitely. In people-facing roles such as teaching, healthcare or management, emotional intelligence is arguably the most important skill of all, as success depends on connecting with others. In more technical or solitary fields, like programming, it may seem less critical, though even there teamwork requires it. So while its importance varies, I think emotional skills are becoming increasingly valued across virtually every sector.

items.q: What happens when a person lacks emotional intelligence?
items.text: A lack of emotional intelligence can cause real difficulties, both personally and professionally. Such a person may struggle to read social cues, handle criticism, or manage their own reactions, which can damage relationships. They might come across as insensitive or provoke unnecessary conflict without even realising it. Over time, this can lead to isolation and repeated interpersonal friction.

items.q: How does emotional intelligence affect a person's relationships?
items.text: It has a profound effect. People with high emotional intelligence tend to have healthier, more fulfilling relationships because they can understand and respond to others' feelings sensitively. They handle disagreements calmly and communicate their own needs clearly. This creates an atmosphere of trust and mutual understanding. In essence, emotional intelligence is the quiet skill that makes relationships genuinely harmonious.

items.q: Will emotional intelligence become more important as technology advances?
items.text: I strongly believe it will. As machines and AI take over more analytical and routine tasks, the uniquely human skills, like empathy, creativity and emotional connection, will become more valuable, not less. These are precisely the abilities that technology cannot easily replicate. So paradoxically, in an increasingly automated world, emotional intelligence may become one of our most sought-after qualities.

items.q: Can emotional intelligence be taught, and if so, how?
items.text: Yes, I firmly believe it can be developed, even if some people are naturally more gifted. Self-awareness can be cultivated through reflection and honest feedback. Skills like active listening and empathy can be practised deliberately. Schools could help by incorporating emotional learning into the curriculum from an early age. Like any skill, it improves with conscious effort and practice, so it is far from fixed.

items.q: Are there any downsides to being highly emotionally sensitive?
items.text: There can be, yes. Being highly attuned to emotions is generally a strength, but it can occasionally become a burden. Very sensitive people may absorb others' stress and feel overwhelmed, or take criticism too personally. They can also find it hard to make tough, unpopular decisions. So the ideal is emotional sensitivity balanced with healthy boundaries and enough resilience to protect oneself.

items.q: Some say schools focus too much on academics and not enough on emotional skills. Do you agree?
items.text: I strongly agree with this criticism. Traditional education has long prioritised exam results above all else, often neglecting the emotional and social skills that are equally vital for a fulfilling life. Skills like managing stress, empathising and collaborating are rarely taught explicitly. I think a more holistic education, one that develops the whole person, would produce far more well-rounded and capable adults.

items.q: Why do you think loneliness is becoming more common today?
items.text: I think it is a paradox of modern life. Despite being more digitally connected than ever, many people feel increasingly isolated. Urbanisation has weakened traditional community bonds, and busy, individualistic lifestyles leave little time for genuine connection. Ironically, social media can exacerbate the problem by replacing deep relationships with superficial online interaction, leaving a real emotional void.

items.q: Is loneliness worse in cities or in the countryside?
items.text: This is quite counterintuitive. You might assume the countryside, being less populated, would be lonelier, but often the opposite is true. Rural communities tend to be tight-knit, where everyone knows each other. Cities, by contrast, can be profoundly alienating; you can be surrounded by millions yet feel completely anonymous. So urban loneliness, born of that anonymity, is arguably the more acute problem.

items.q: What effects can long-term loneliness have on a person?
items.text: The effects can be genuinely serious. Prolonged loneliness is strongly linked to mental health problems such as depression and anxiety. It can also have physical consequences, as chronic isolation is thought to weaken the immune system and even affect longevity. Beyond that, it can trap people in a negative cycle, where low mood makes them withdraw further, deepening the isolation and their sense of despair.

items.q: Which groups of people are most at risk of social isolation?
items.text: Several groups are particularly vulnerable. The elderly are perhaps most at risk, especially those who have lost a spouse or whose family lives far away. Newcomers to a city, who lack an established network, are also susceptible, as are those with disabilities or health issues that limit their mobility. Essentially, anyone facing barriers to regular social contact is prone to becoming isolated and marginalised.

items.q: Do you think loneliness will become a bigger problem in the future?
items.text: I fear it might, if current trends continue. As societies become more individualistic and people increasingly work and socialise remotely, opportunities for spontaneous human contact may diminish. An ageing population in many countries could also worsen the situation. However, I remain hopeful that growing awareness of the issue will prompt communities and governments to take preventive action.

items.q: What can communities do to reduce loneliness?
items.text: Communities can play a powerful role. Creating accessible public spaces and organising local events, from community gardens to social clubs, gives people natural opportunities to connect. Initiatives that specifically reach out to isolated individuals, like befriending schemes for the elderly, are especially valuable. Ultimately, fostering a culture where people look out for their neighbours can rebuild the social fabric that has frayed.

items.q: Is spending time alone always a bad thing?
items.text: Certainly not; there is an important distinction between loneliness and healthy solitude. Chosen time alone can be genuinely restorative, allowing for reflection, creativity and rest. Many people find solitude essential for recharging. The problem arises only when isolation is involuntary and prolonged. So spending time alone is perfectly healthy, as long as it is balanced with meaningful connection.

items.q: Some say technology is the main cause of modern loneliness. Do you agree?
items.text: I partly agree, but I think it is too simplistic to blame technology alone. It is true that excessive screen time can replace real interaction and foster unhealthy comparison. However, technology can also connect isolated people, such as those far from family. So the technology itself is neutral; the real issue is how we use it. The deeper causes lie in broader societal changes.

items.q: What do you think is the main purpose of education?
items.text: In my view, education serves a dual purpose. On a practical level, it equips people with the knowledge and skills needed for employment. But more importantly, I believe its deeper purpose is to cultivate critical thinking and produce well-rounded, responsible citizens. Education should teach people how to think, not merely what to think. Sadly, many systems overemphasise rote learning at the expense of this broader enrichment.

items.q: How is education today different from education in the past?
items.text: The differences are considerable. In the past, education was largely teacher-centred, based on memorisation and strict discipline. Today, there is a much greater emphasis on interactive, student-centred learning, and technology has revolutionised access to information. Learning is now more collaborative and creative. However, I would argue that academic pressure and competition have also intensified, which is a rather double-edged development.

items.q: How does the quality of education affect a country's development?
items.text: The link is absolutely fundamental. A well-educated population drives economic growth through innovation and a skilled workforce. Beyond economics, quality education tends to reduce poverty, improve public health and strengthen democratic institutions. It is, in essence, the bedrock of national progress. Conversely, a country that neglects education severely limits its own potential and risks falling behind its competitors.

items.q: Why do you think exam results are given so much importance?
items.text: I think it stems from the need for a seemingly objective way to measure ability and allocate opportunities. Exams provide a convenient, quantifiable benchmark for universities and employers. However, this overreliance on results can be counterproductive, as it encourages students to memorise for tests rather than truly understand. It also fails to capture vital qualities like creativity, which are far harder to quantify.

items.q: How could education systems be improved?
items.text: There are several improvements I would suggest. Firstly, systems should place less emphasis on high-stakes exams and more on continuous, practical assessment. Secondly, curricula should be modernised to include life skills such as financial literacy and emotional intelligence. Finally, investing in teacher training and reducing class sizes would allow for more personalised learning. The goal should be a more holistic and flexible model.

items.q: How do you think education will change in the next 20 years?
items.text: I anticipate dramatic changes, largely driven by technology. Personalised, AI-assisted learning could tailor lessons to each student's pace, and online education will make quality teaching far more accessible globally. The traditional classroom may become less central. There will likely also be a stronger focus on adaptable skills, given that people will need to reskill repeatedly throughout their careers.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of a highly competitive education system?
items.text: A competitive system can certainly drive high achievement and prepare students for a demanding world, pushing them to excel. However, the disadvantages are significant. Excessive competition can cause immense stress and anxiety, and it may stifle creativity and collaboration. It can also disadvantage those who learn differently. In my view, a healthy system needs to balance ambition with student wellbeing.

items.q: Some say education should be free for everyone. Do you agree?
items.text: I strongly agree, at least regarding basic and secondary education. I see education as a fundamental right and a public good, not a privilege for those who can afford it. Free access promotes social mobility and reduces inequality. For higher education, the picture is more complex due to cost, but I believe it should at least be heavily subsidised so that talent, not wealth, determines opportunity.

items.q: What do you think is the best way to learn something new?
items.text: In my experience, the most effective way to learn is through active, hands-on practice rather than passive listening. We tend to retain information far better when we actually apply it. I am a firm believer in learning by doing, and in making mistakes, since they are often the most instructive experiences. Combining this practical approach with genuine curiosity makes learning both effective and thoroughly engaging.

items.q: Is it better to learn alone or in a group?
items.text: Both have their merits, and the ideal depends on the task. Learning alone allows for focus and lets you progress at your own pace, which suits deep, concentrated study. Group learning, on the other hand, is more dynamic; you benefit from different perspectives and can clarify doubts through discussion. Personally, I favour a blend of the two, as they complement each other nicely.

items.q: Why do some people find learning easier than others?
items.text: There are many contributing factors. Some of it comes down to natural aptitude, but I think motivation and mindset matter far more. People who are genuinely curious and believe they can improve tend to learn faster. Environment also plays a huge role; a supportive home and good teachers make an enormous difference. So learning ability is really a mix of innate talent and nurtured habits.

items.q: How has technology changed the way people learn?
items.text: Technology has transformed learning almost beyond recognition. Information that once required a library is now instantly accessible, and online platforms allow anyone to learn almost anything for free. This has democratised education enormously. That said, it has downsides; the sheer abundance of information can be overwhelming, and constant digital distraction can actually hinder deep, focused learning.

items.q: Do you think traditional classrooms will disappear in the future?
items.text: I doubt they will disappear entirely, but their role will certainly change. Online learning will keep growing, offering flexibility that classrooms cannot match. However, physical classrooms provide something valuable: social interaction, mentorship and a structured environment that many learners need. So rather than vanishing, I expect classrooms to evolve into more interactive spaces, complementing rather than being replaced by digital tools.

items.q: How can people stay motivated when learning independently?
items.text: Self-motivation is the biggest challenge in independent learning. I think the key is setting clear, achievable goals and breaking a large subject into smaller milestones, which gives a regular sense of progress. Establishing a routine helps make studying a habit rather than a struggle. Finding a community of fellow learners online can also provide accountability and encouragement, which is often what people lack.

items.q: What are the pros and cons of online learning?
items.text: Online learning offers tremendous flexibility and access; you can learn from world-class instructors anywhere, often at low cost. It is ideal for self-directed, motivated learners. The drawbacks, however, include a lack of face-to-face interaction, which can feel isolating, and it requires considerable self-discipline. Some practical subjects are also hard to teach remotely. So it is excellent for some, but not a complete substitute for every kind of learning.

items.q: Some say the internet has made memorisation unnecessary. Do you agree?
items.text: I only partly agree. It is true that we no longer need to memorise facts that we can look up instantly, so pure memorisation is less critical than before. However, I would argue that a solid base of knowledge in your own memory is still essential for reasoning and creativity, because you cannot connect ideas you do not possess. So the internet has shifted, rather than eliminated, the value of memory.

items.q: What factors do you think are most important when choosing a career?
items.text: I think the most important factor is genuine interest, because you will spend a huge portion of your life working. A job you are passionate about is far more sustainable than a purely lucrative one. That said, practical considerations like financial security, job stability and growth opportunities cannot be ignored. Ideally, people should seek a career that strikes a healthy balance between passion and pragmatism.

items.q: Is it better to choose a job you love or a job that pays well?
items.text: This is the classic dilemma. In an ideal world, you would have both. If forced to choose, I lean towards a job you love, because passion tends to lead to better performance and long-term fulfilment, and money alone rarely brings lasting contentment. However, this is somewhat a privilege; those with financial pressures may reasonably prioritise a stable income first.

items.q: Why do many people change careers during their lives now?
items.text: Several factors drive this. The job market is far more volatile than in the past, so lifelong employment in one company is increasingly rare. People also have higher expectations of finding meaningful work, and are more willing to pursue fulfilment. Additionally, rapid technological change means some jobs disappear while new ones emerge, which compels people to adapt and retrain.

items.q: How much do parents influence their children's career choices?
items.text: In many cultures, including mine, the influence is quite significant. Parents naturally want security for their children and often steer them towards prestigious or stable professions like medicine or engineering. This guidance can be helpful, but it can also become overbearing, pushing young people into careers that do not suit them. I think the ideal is for parents to advise while ultimately respecting their child's own autonomy.

items.q: What kinds of jobs do you think will be most important in the future?
items.text: I believe jobs involving skills that machines cannot easily replicate will be most valuable. This includes creative fields, healthcare, and roles requiring emotional intelligence and complex problem-solving. Careers related to technology, such as AI and data science, will obviously be in high demand, as will jobs focused on sustainability and renewable energy. Essentially, roles that are adaptable and distinctly human will thrive.

items.q: How can young people be helped to make better career decisions?
items.text: Better career guidance in schools would make an enormous difference. Too often, students choose paths with little real understanding of what the jobs actually involve. Providing internships and work experience gives them valuable exposure to different fields. Mentorship from professionals can also offer honest, first-hand insight. Essentially, we need to help young people make informed choices rather than blind ones.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of staying in one job for a long time?
items.text: The advantages include deep expertise, job security, and the trust and seniority that come with loyalty. It offers a comforting stability. The disadvantages, however, are that it can lead to stagnation and complacency, and one may miss out on the higher pay and fresh challenges that come from changing roles. So long-term employment offers security at the potential cost of growth and variety.

items.q: Some say job security is more important than job satisfaction. Do you agree?
items.text: I think it depends heavily on a person's circumstances. For someone supporting a family, security is understandably the priority, as it provides essential peace of mind. However, I personally lean towards satisfaction, because a secure but miserable job can take a serious toll on one's mental health over time. Ideally, one should not have to sacrifice one for the other, though reality often forces a compromise.

items.q: What do you think makes people happy at work?
items.text: In my opinion, job satisfaction stems from more than just a good salary. Feeling that your work is meaningful and appreciated is paramount. A positive relationship with colleagues, opportunities to grow, and a sense of autonomy all contribute significantly. Ultimately, people are happiest when they feel valued and can see the genuine purpose behind what they do.

items.q: Is money or a sense of purpose more important for job satisfaction?
items.text: While money is obviously necessary, I believe that beyond a certain point, a sense of purpose matters more. A high salary provides comfort, but it does not compensate for feeling that your work is pointless. People who find meaning in their jobs tend to be far more engaged and resilient. So money is important up to a threshold, but purpose provides the deeper, more lasting fulfilment.

items.q: What effect does job dissatisfaction have on people?
items.text: The effects can be quite serious and far-reaching. Chronic dissatisfaction often leads to stress, low morale and even burnout, which can spill over and harm a person's personal life and health. At work, it results in reduced productivity and higher staff turnover. Essentially, an unhappy workforce is detrimental to both the individuals involved and the organisation's overall performance.

items.q: How does a person's job affect the rest of their life?
items.text: A job has a profound influence on overall wellbeing. Since we spend so many hours working, a fulfilling job can boost confidence and happiness that permeate our whole life. Conversely, a stressful or unfulfilling job can cause anxiety that affects our relationships and health. Work also shapes our identity and social status, so it is deeply intertwined with our sense of self.

items.q: Do you think people will be more or less satisfied with their jobs in the future?
items.text: I am cautiously optimistic. As automation takes over tedious, repetitive tasks, workers may be freed to focus on more creative and meaningful work, which could boost satisfaction. There is also growing awareness of employee wellbeing. On the other hand, increased job insecurity and the pressure of constant connectivity could undermine satisfaction. So the outcome will likely depend on how wisely we manage these changes.

items.q: What can employers do to make their staff happier?
items.text: Employers can do a great deal. Offering fair pay and genuine recognition for good work is fundamental. Beyond that, providing opportunities for growth, some flexibility, and a supportive, respectful culture makes an enormous difference. Simply listening to employees and giving them a degree of autonomy over their work is powerful. Investing in staff wellbeing is not just ethical; it is genuinely profitable in the long run.

items.q: Are there advantages to doing a job you find challenging?
items.text: Absolutely. A challenging job keeps you engaged and constantly learning, which prevents boredom and fuels personal growth. Overcoming difficulties also builds confidence and a real sense of accomplishment. The potential disadvantage is that if the challenge becomes overwhelming or unrelenting, it can tip into stress and burnout. So the ideal is a job that stretches you without exhausting you.

items.q: Some say people today change jobs too often. Do you agree?
items.text: I do not entirely agree that it is a problem. Changing jobs frequently is often a sensible way to gain diverse experience, increase pay and find a better fit, especially in a fast-changing economy. The old model of lifelong loyalty is somewhat outdated. That said, changing too often can look unstable to employers and prevent one from developing deep expertise, so a degree of balance is wise.

items.q: How do you think work will change in the next few decades?
items.text: I believe work will become far more flexible and technology-driven. Remote and hybrid working, already common, will likely become the norm for many roles. Automation and AI will take over routine tasks, meaning humans will focus more on creative and interpersonal work. People will also need to reskill continuously, as the concept of a single lifelong career becomes increasingly obsolete and fluid.

items.q: Is working from home better or worse than working in an office?
items.text: It really depends on the person and the job. Working from home offers wonderful flexibility and eliminates the commute, which many find liberating and more productive. However, the office provides valuable social interaction, easier collaboration and a clearer boundary between work and home life. Personally, I think a hybrid model captures the best of both, though it requires real self-discipline to work remotely well.

items.q: What effects will automation have on employment?
items.text: Automation is a genuine double-edged sword. On one hand, it will inevitably displace many workers in routine and manual jobs, which is a serious concern. On the other hand, history shows that technology also creates entirely new industries and roles. The key effect is a shift in the types of jobs available, which means workforces will need to adapt and acquire new skills.

items.q: How might the changing nature of work affect society?
items.text: The societal impact could be substantial. If automation concentrates wealth, it may widen inequality, which is a real danger. The rise of the gig economy also brings flexibility but often at the cost of job security and benefits. On a positive note, more flexible work could improve work-life balance. Managing these changes fairly will be one of the great challenges of our era, requiring thoughtful policy.

items.q: Do you think people will work fewer hours in the future?
items.text: I think it is a real possibility, and one I would welcome. As automation boosts productivity, there is a strong argument that the gains could be shared through shorter working weeks. Trials of the four-day week seem to have shown promising results, with productivity maintained. However, this will not happen automatically; it will require deliberate choices by businesses and governments to prioritise wellbeing over pure output.

items.q: How can workers prepare for a rapidly changing job market?
items.text: The single most important thing is to embrace lifelong learning. Workers should continually update their skills and remain adaptable, rather than assuming their current expertise will last forever. Developing transferable skills, like communication and problem-solving, is wise, since these remain valuable across industries. Staying curious and open to change is really the best safeguard against being left behind.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of the gig economy?
items.text: The gig economy offers genuine advantages: flexibility, independence and the ability to work for multiple clients, which suits many people. However, the disadvantages are considerable, chiefly the lack of job security, steady income and benefits like sick pay or pensions. This precariousness can be very stressful. So while it offers freedom, it often shifts significant risk onto the individual worker, which needs better regulation.

items.q: Some say machines will eventually do most human jobs. Do you agree?
items.text: I think that is something of an exaggeration, at least for the foreseeable future. Machines will certainly automate many tasks, but jobs requiring creativity, empathy, complex judgement and manual dexterity in unpredictable settings are far harder to replace. Rather than making humans redundant, I believe technology will mostly augment human work, changing jobs rather than eliminating the need for people entirely.

items.q: Do you think a university degree is necessary for success?
items.text: I do not think it is strictly necessary, though it certainly helps in many fields. A degree provides knowledge, credentials and valuable connections, and for professions like medicine it is essential. However, success can absolutely be achieved through other routes, such as vocational training or entrepreneurship. In my view, a degree is a powerful tool, but it is not the only path, and it is no guarantee of success.

items.q: Is academic education or vocational training more valuable?
items.text: I believe both are equally valuable, just for different purposes, and society needs both. Academic education develops theoretical knowledge and critical thinking, suited to research and the professions. Vocational training provides practical, job-ready skills that are in high demand and often lead directly to employment. Unfortunately, vocational paths are often unfairly stigmatised, when in reality skilled trades are absolutely essential and highly rewarding.

items.q: Why do so many young people want to attend university nowadays?
items.text: There are several reasons. Firstly, a degree is often seen as a minimum requirement for many good jobs, so there is mounting pressure to obtain one. There is also considerable social prestige attached to a university education in many cultures. Additionally, university offers young people independence and a chance to grow. However, this rush has led to some devaluation of degrees, as they become more common.

items.q: How does higher education benefit society as a whole?
items.text: The societal benefits are considerable. Universities drive research and innovation, which fuel economic and medical progress. They also produce the skilled professionals a modern society depends on, from doctors to engineers. Beyond that, higher education promotes critical thinking and informed citizenship, which strengthens democracy. In essence, universities are engines of both economic and intellectual advancement.

items.q: How do you think universities will change in the future?
items.text: I expect universities to become more flexible and accessible. Online and hybrid degrees will likely become mainstream, allowing people to study while working. There may be a shift towards shorter, more modular courses focused on specific skills rather than lengthy traditional degrees. Universities will also need to work more closely with industry to ensure their qualifications remain relevant in a fast-changing economy.

items.q: University is becoming very expensive. What could be done about this?
items.text: This is a pressing issue in many countries. Governments could increase funding and subsidies to keep public universities affordable, treating education as an investment rather than a cost. Expanding scholarships and income-based repayment schemes would help ensure that talent, not wealth, determines access. Promoting quality alternatives, like online courses and apprenticeships, would also relieve pressure on the traditional, expensive model.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of studying a subject purely out of interest?
items.text: The great advantage is genuine engagement; studying something you love leads to deeper learning and personal fulfilment, and passion often breeds excellence. The potential disadvantage is practical: a subject with poor job prospects may leave you struggling financially after graduation. So ideally, one would find a field that ignites genuine interest while also offering reasonable employability, marrying passion with pragmatism.

items.q: Some say there are too many university graduates today. Do you agree?
items.text: There is some truth to this in certain fields. The rapid expansion of higher education has, in some cases, led to a surplus of graduates in particular subjects, resulting in underemployment and a mismatch with the job market. However, I would not say education itself is the problem. The real issue is the lack of alignment between what people study and what the economy actually demands.

items.q: Which is more important for a job, skills or qualifications?
items.text: While qualifications open doors, I believe practical skills ultimately matter more in the actual workplace. A degree may get you an interview, but it is your ability to actually do the job well that determines your success and progression. Employers increasingly value demonstrable competence over paper credentials. That said, in regulated professions, formal qualifications are non-negotiable, so the ideal is really a combination of both.

items.q: Are so-called soft skills or technical skills more valuable?
items.text: Both are important, but I would argue soft skills are becoming increasingly decisive. Technical skills are essential to perform specific tasks, but they can often be taught relatively quickly. Soft skills, like communication, teamwork and adaptability, are harder to acquire yet crucial for career advancement. As technology automates technical work, these uniquely human, transferable skills are likely to become even more prized and sought-after.

items.q: Why do some qualified people struggle to find jobs?
items.text: There are several reasons. Often there is a mismatch between their qualifications and the skills employers actually need, especially if their degree is too theoretical. A lack of practical experience is another common barrier, as employers value hands-on ability. In some cases, an oversupply of graduates in a particular field simply means competition is fierce. Poor soft skills can also hinder otherwise qualified candidates.

items.q: How important is work experience compared to formal education?
items.text: I think work experience is enormously valuable and, in many fields, indispensable. It teaches practical skills, professional behaviour and real-world problem-solving that no classroom can fully replicate. This is why internships and apprenticeships are so valued. That said, formal education provides the foundational knowledge upon which experience builds. The ideal candidate usually has a solid blend of both theoretical grounding and practical exposure.

items.q: Will qualifications become less important in the future?
items.text: I think their nature will change rather than their importance disappearing. Traditional degrees may become less of a strict requirement as employers increasingly focus on demonstrable skills and portfolios. We are already seeing a rise in micro-credentials and skills-based hiring. So the emphasis may shift from what certificate you hold to what you can actually demonstrate, making qualifications more practical and specific.

items.q: How can education better prepare students with practical skills?
items.text: The most effective step is to integrate more practical, real-world experience into the curriculum. This means expanding internships, project-based learning and industry partnerships so students apply what they learn. Teaching should also explicitly develop soft skills, which are often neglected. Bridging the gap between academia and industry would ensure graduates are genuinely job-ready rather than merely knowledgeable.

items.q: What are the pros and cons of learning a skill through self-teaching?
items.text: Self-teaching offers great flexibility and is often free or cheap, and it cultivates valuable discipline and independence. Many successful people are largely self-taught. The drawbacks are the lack of structured guidance and formal recognition; without a certificate, it can be harder to prove your ability to employers. You also miss out on expert feedback. So it demands real motivation and can lack external validation.

items.q: Some say too much emphasis is placed on paper qualifications. Do you agree?
items.text: I largely agree. Society has long placed excessive weight on formal certificates, sometimes overlooking genuinely talented individuals who lack them. This can create a rigid system where a piece of paper matters more than actual ability. Thankfully, this is slowly changing as employers recognise the value of skills and experience. A shift towards judging people on real competence would be a genuinely positive development.

items.q: How important is work-life balance?
items.text: I believe it is absolutely essential for long-term wellbeing. Without a healthy balance, people risk burnout, which harms both their health and, ironically, their productivity. Time for family, rest and hobbies is not a luxury; it is what makes us resilient and effective. In my view, a culture that glorifies overwork is ultimately unsustainable and counterproductive.

items.q: Do you think people had a better work-life balance in the past?
items.text: In some respects, yes. In the past, work was more clearly confined to the workplace, and once you went home, you were genuinely off duty. Today, smartphones mean we are perpetually reachable, and the boundary between work and personal life has become dangerously blurred. That said, past generations often worked longer physical hours, so it is not entirely one-sided; the nature of the imbalance has changed.

items.q: What are the consequences of a poor work-life balance?
items.text: The consequences can be severe. Chronic overwork frequently leads to stress, burnout and serious health problems, both physical and mental. It also strains personal relationships, as work encroaches on time with family and friends. Ironically, it often reduces long-term productivity too. Essentially, neglecting your personal life for work is self-defeating, taking a heavy toll that eventually undermines everything.

items.q: How does work-life balance affect society?
items.text: A society where people are chronically overworked tends to suffer from higher rates of stress-related illness and weaker family and community bonds. When people have no time or energy left, civic and social life deteriorates. Conversely, a society that values balance tends to be healthier, happier and arguably more productive in the long run. So it is genuinely a matter of collective wellbeing.

items.q: Do you think work-life balance will improve in the future?
items.text: I am hopeful, though not entirely certain. There is a growing cultural awareness of the importance of wellbeing, and flexible and remote working could, if managed well, improve balance considerably. Concepts like the four-day week are gaining traction. However, there is a risk that constant connectivity could make things worse. So improvement is possible, but it will require a deliberate cultural shift rather than happening automatically.

items.q: What can people do to achieve a better work-life balance?
items.text: On a personal level, setting firm boundaries is crucial, such as not checking work emails after hours. Learning to prioritise and, importantly, to say no to excessive demands helps enormously. Making dedicated time for rest and relationships should be treated as non-negotiable. However, individuals can only do so much; employers must also foster a culture that genuinely respects personal time and does not reward overwork.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of flexible working hours?
items.text: The advantages are considerable: flexibility allows people to work when they are most productive and to fit work around personal commitments, which greatly improves balance. The disadvantage is that without a clear structure, work can bleed into all hours, and it requires strong self-discipline. It can also complicate team coordination. So flexibility is a wonderful benefit, provided it comes with sensible boundaries and mutual trust.

items.q: Some say working hard is more important than having free time. Do you agree?
items.text: I respectfully disagree with framing it as either-or. Hard work is certainly important for achievement, and I value diligence. However, free time is not the opposite of hard work; it is what makes sustained hard work possible by preventing burnout. The two are complementary. In my view, someone who works intensely but never rests is not admirable but heading towards exhaustion, so balance is wiser.

items.q: Do you think remote working is a positive development?
items.text: On balance, I think it is largely positive. Remote work offers people tremendous flexibility, eliminates stressful commutes and can improve work-life balance significantly. It also allows companies to hire talent regardless of location. However, it is not without drawbacks, such as isolation and blurred boundaries. So while I view it favourably, its success depends on being managed thoughtfully rather than imposed without support.

items.q: Is remote work better suited to some jobs than others?
items.text: Absolutely, the suitability varies enormously. Knowledge-based, computer-centric jobs like writing, programming or design translate very well to remote work. However, roles requiring physical presence, such as healthcare, manufacturing or hospitality, simply cannot be done remotely. Even within office jobs, tasks needing intense collaboration or mentoring may suffer. So remote work is a wonderful option for some, but it is far from universally applicable.

items.q: How has remote work affected cities and communities?
items.text: The effects have been quite significant. As fewer people commute, some city centres have seen businesses that relied on office workers struggle. Conversely, remote work has allowed people to move away from expensive cities to smaller towns, potentially revitalising those areas. This redistribution of population could reshape urban planning. So it is causing a genuine, ongoing transformation of where and how people live.

items.q: How does remote work affect relationships between colleagues?
items.text: It has a notable impact. On the positive side, it can reduce office politics and let people focus on their work. However, the spontaneous, informal interactions that build genuine camaraderie are much harder to replicate remotely. Relationships can become purely transactional, and new employees in particular may struggle to feel connected. Maintaining a real sense of belonging requires deliberate effort in a distributed team.

items.q: Do you think most people will work remotely in the future?
items.text: I think hybrid working will become the dominant model rather than fully remote work. Most companies seem to be settling on a mix, valuing both the flexibility of home and the collaboration of the office. Fully remote roles will grow but remain a minority.
