So the future of work is likely to be flexible and varied, with people splitting their time according to what each task demands.

items.q: How can companies keep remote workers engaged and productive?
items.text: Clear communication is absolutely key. Companies should set clear expectations while trusting employees rather than micromanaging them. Regular virtual check-ins and occasional in-person meetups help maintain connection and morale. Providing the right technology and supporting mental wellbeing are also crucial. Ultimately, engagement comes from a culture of trust and inclusion, ensuring remote staff never feel overlooked or forgotten.

items.q: What are the main advantages and disadvantages of working from home?
items.text: The advantages are clear: no commute, greater flexibility, fewer office distractions and often improved work-life balance. Many people are genuinely more productive. The disadvantages include social isolation, difficulty separating work from home life, and potential distractions at home. Career progression can also suffer from being out of sight. So it offers real freedom, but demands strong self-discipline to manage well.

items.q: Some say working from home makes people lazy. Do you agree?
items.text: I largely disagree with that stereotype. While a lack of supervision might tempt a few, it seems that most remote workers are just as productive, if not more so, than their office counterparts. In fact, many overwork because the boundaries blur. Laziness is really a matter of individual discipline and motivation, not location. So I think this criticism is largely unfounded and rather outdated.

items.q: Why do you think so many students want to study abroad?
items.text: There are several compelling reasons. Studying abroad often provides access to higher-quality education and internationally recognised qualifications, which boost career prospects. Beyond academics, it offers an invaluable chance to experience a new culture, gain independence and broaden one's horizons. For many, it is a genuinely transformative personal journey as much as an academic one, offering exposure that home study cannot match.

items.q: Is studying abroad better than studying in one's own country?
items.text: It depends entirely on the individual and their goals. Studying abroad offers cultural immersion and independence that home study cannot, and sometimes access to better facilities. However, it is expensive, and studying at home is cheaper, closer to family, and free of the challenge of adapting to a foreign culture. So neither is universally better; it is a matter of weighing the enrichment against the cost and difficulty.

items.q: What challenges do students face when studying in another country?
items.text: They face numerous challenges. Culture shock and homesickness are extremely common, especially at first. A language barrier can make both study and daily life difficult and isolating. There are also practical hurdles, like managing finances and navigating an unfamiliar system alone. Adapting to different academic expectations can be daunting too. However, overcoming these difficulties is precisely what makes the experience so rewarding and character-building.

items.q: How does studying abroad benefit a student's home country?
items.text: The benefits can be substantial. Students who return bring back advanced knowledge, new skills and valuable international perspectives that can drive innovation and development at home. They also form global networks that can foster trade and collaboration. However, there is a risk of a brain drain if graduates choose to stay abroad. So the benefit to the home country depends heavily on repatriating that talent and expertise.

items.q: Do you think studying abroad will become more common in the future?
items.text: I think physical study abroad will remain popular but may face competition from online alternatives. Increasingly, students can access foreign universities' courses remotely, offering the academic benefits without the cost of relocating. However, the cultural and personal growth of actually living abroad is irreplaceable, so demand will persist. The future may see a mix of physical and virtual international education, making it more accessible and diverse.

items.q: How can universities better support international students?
items.text: Universities can do a great deal. Providing strong orientation programmes and language support eases the initial transition. Pairing international students with local mentors or buddy schemes helps combat isolation and homesickness. Practical guidance on visas, housing and finances is also invaluable. Essentially, creating a genuinely inclusive and welcoming environment helps international students integrate and flourish rather than feeling like outsiders.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of studying abroad?
items.text: The advantages are significant: exposure to a new culture, greater independence, improved language skills, and often a superior education, all of which boost employability. The disadvantages, however, include the high financial cost, the emotional strain of homesickness, and the difficulty of adjusting to an unfamiliar environment. So it offers immense personal and academic growth, but at a considerable price in both money and comfort.

items.q: Some say governments should fund students to study abroad. Do you agree?
items.text: I broadly agree, provided there are sensible conditions. Funding talented students to gain world-class education and skills abroad can be a smart investment in a country's future development. However, to avoid a brain drain, such funding could reasonably require graduates to return and contribute for a period. So I support it as a strategic investment, as long as the country actually reaps the eventual benefits of that investment.

items.q: Which soft skills do you think are most valuable in the workplace?
items.text: In my view, communication is the single most valuable soft skill, since almost everything at work depends on it. Closely behind it, I would place teamwork and adaptability, as modern workplaces are collaborative and constantly changing. Problem-solving and emotional intelligence are also hugely important. These interpersonal abilities often distinguish a merely competent employee from a truly exceptional and promotable one.

items.q: Are soft skills or hard skills harder to learn?
items.text: I would argue soft skills are generally harder to acquire. Hard skills, like using a software program, can be learned through structured courses relatively quickly. Soft skills, however, involve deeply ingrained habits and personality traits, so improving your communication or empathy requires sustained self-awareness and practice over years. They are more nuanced and subtle, which is precisely why they are so prized by employers.

items.q: Why are communication skills so important at work?
items.text: Communication is fundamental because it underpins almost every workplace activity. Clear communication prevents misunderstandings, which can otherwise cause costly errors and conflict. It enables effective teamwork, allows ideas to be shared persuasively, and builds strong relationships with clients and colleagues. Someone who communicates well can influence, lead and collaborate far more effectively. In essence, poor communication can derail even the most technically gifted team.

items.q: How do soft skills affect a person's career progression?
items.text: They have an enormous impact, often more than technical ability. As people advance into leadership and management, success depends less on doing the work themselves and more on inspiring, coordinating and communicating with others. Those with strong soft skills tend to be promoted faster because they can lead teams effectively. So while hard skills may get you hired, soft skills are frequently what determine how far you ultimately ascend and excel.

items.q: Will soft skills become more important as technology advances?
items.text: I firmly believe they will. As artificial intelligence automates more technical and analytical tasks, the distinctly human skills, creativity, empathy, leadership and complex communication, will become increasingly valuable. These are precisely the abilities machines struggle to replicate. So paradoxically, the more technological the world becomes, the more premium employers are likely to place on these irreplaceable human qualities.

items.q: How can people develop their soft skills?
items.text: Soft skills are developed mainly through practice and self-reflection. Seeking out situations that stretch you, like leading a project or public speaking, builds confidence and competence. Actively seeking honest feedback and observing people who excel at these skills is invaluable. Reading and formal training can help too. The key is to treat them as learnable skills that improve with deliberate effort, not fixed traits.

items.q: Are there any downsides to focusing too much on soft skills?
items.text: There can be. While soft skills are vital, an overemphasis on charm and communication at the expense of actual competence can be problematic. Someone might talk a good game but lack the substance to deliver. In technical fields especially, genuine expertise remains indispensable. So the ideal is a solid foundation of hard skills combined with strong soft skills; one without the other leaves a person incomplete.

items.q: Some say soft skills should be taught in schools. Do you agree?
items.text: I strongly agree. Given how crucial these skills are for both work and life, it seems a serious oversight that they are rarely taught explicitly. Skills like communication, teamwork and emotional regulation could be woven into the curriculum from an early age. Equipping young people with these competencies would make them far more employable and better prepared for life, so it would be a genuinely worthwhile reform.

items.q: Do you think learning should continue throughout a person's life?
items.text: Absolutely, I am a firm believer in lifelong learning. The idea that education ends when you leave school is completely outdated, especially in today's fast-changing world. Continuing to learn keeps the mind sharp, opens new opportunities and helps people adapt to change. Beyond practical benefits, I think curiosity and growth are essential to a fulfilling life. Learning should be a lifelong pursuit, not a phase.

items.q: Is it easier to learn when you are young or when you are older?
items.text: There are trade-offs at each stage. Young people generally absorb new information, especially languages, more easily, and have fewer competing responsibilities. However, adult learners bring focus, motivation and real-world experience that can make their learning more purposeful and efficient. So while children may have a biological advantage, adults compensate with discipline and context. Neither is simply easier; it depends on what is being learned.

items.q: Why is continuous learning becoming more necessary today?
items.text: It is primarily because of the breakneck pace of technological change. Skills that were valuable a decade ago can quickly become obsolete, and entirely new fields emerge constantly. To remain employable, workers must continually update their knowledge and reskill. The old model of one qualification lasting a whole career is no longer viable. In short, adaptability through learning has become a genuine necessity, not a luxury.

items.q: How does lifelong learning benefit society?
items.text: A society that embraces lifelong learning tends to be more adaptable, innovative and economically resilient, as its workforce can respond to change. It also promotes social mobility, giving people second chances to improve their prospects. On a personal level, continued learning keeps older people mentally active and engaged, which benefits public health. So it strengthens both the economy and the overall vitality of a community.

items.q: Do you think lifelong learning will become the norm in the future?
items.text: I am confident it will, out of sheer necessity. As careers become less linear and technology evolves ever faster, continuous learning and periodic reskilling will simply be part of working life. I anticipate more flexible, bite-sized courses and employer-sponsored training becoming commonplace. Society's whole conception of education will likely shift from a one-off event to an ongoing, lifelong process.

items.q: What prevents adults from continuing to learn, and how can this be solved?
items.text: The main barriers are usually time, cost and lack of confidence. Busy working adults with family commitments struggle to find the time and money for further study. To address this, flexible online and part-time courses are invaluable, as is employer support through funded training. Governments could also offer subsidies or learning accounts. Dismantling these obstacles would make lifelong learning genuinely attainable for everyone.

items.q: Are there any drawbacks to constantly having to learn new skills?
items.text: There can be. While staying current is beneficial, the constant pressure to reskill can be exhausting and stressful, creating a feeling that you can never rest on your achievements. It may also breed anxiety about becoming obsolete. For some, particularly older workers, this relentless demand can feel genuinely overwhelming. So although the principle is sound, the pace of change can make it feel like a burden rather than a joy.

items.q: Some say you are never too old to learn. Do you agree?
items.text: I wholeheartedly agree. While learning styles may change with age, the human brain remains capable of acquiring new knowledge and skills throughout life. There are countless inspiring examples of people learning languages, instruments or even new careers late in life. I think the biggest barrier is usually psychological, a self-imposed belief that it is too late. In reality, curiosity and effort transcend age entirely, keeping us youthful in spirit.

items.q: Do you think social media has a positive or negative effect on society?
items.text: I think it is genuinely a mixed blessing. On the positive side, social media connects people across distances, gives a voice to the marginalised and spreads information rapidly. However, its negative effects are equally significant, from spreading misinformation to fuelling anxiety and comparison. In my view, the platforms themselves are neutral; the real issue is how we use them. Used mindfully, the benefits can outweigh the drawbacks.

items.q: How has social media changed the way people communicate?
items.text: It has transformed communication dramatically. In the past, staying in touch required letters or calls, whereas now we can share our lives instantly with hundreds of people at once. Communication has become faster and more visual, but arguably more superficial. We interact more frequently yet often less meaningfully, replacing deep conversations with quick likes and comments. So it has widened our reach while sometimes shallowing our connections.

items.q: How does social media affect young people's mental health?
items.text: The impact can be quite concerning. Constant exposure to carefully curated, idealised images can fuel feelings of inadequacy and low self-esteem, particularly regarding appearance. The pressure to gain likes and the fear of missing out can also cause real anxiety. That said, it can also provide community and support. On balance, though, I believe excessive use is genuinely detrimental to young people's wellbeing.

items.q: Why do you think people share so much of their lives online?
items.text: I think it stems largely from a deep human desire for validation and connection. Receiving likes and comments triggers a sense of approval that can be quite addictive. Many people also enjoy documenting their lives and keeping in touch. However, this compulsion to share can tip into oversharing, where people curate an idealised image, sometimes at the expense of actually living in the moment.

items.q: How do you think social media will develop in the future?
items.text: I anticipate it will become even more immersive, possibly through virtual and augmented reality, blurring the line between online and offline life further. Artificial intelligence will make content ever more personalised, which raises concerns about echo chambers. Hopefully, there will also be a growing backlash leading to more regulation and healthier usage habits. So it will likely become more sophisticated, but not necessarily more beneficial.

items.q: What can be done to reduce the harmful effects of social media?
items.text: A multi-pronged approach is needed. On an individual level, promoting digital literacy and encouraging conscious limits on usage helps enormously. Platforms themselves should be held accountable for their algorithms and do more to combat misinformation and protect young users. Governments may also need to introduce sensible regulation. Ultimately, teaching people to engage critically rather than passively is the most sustainable solution.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of social media for businesses?
items.text: For businesses, the advantages are substantial: it offers a cheap, powerful way to reach a huge audience, build a brand and engage directly with customers. Small businesses in particular can thrive. The disadvantages include the risk of negative publicity spreading rapidly, the pressure to constantly produce content, and vulnerability to online backlash. So it is a powerful tool, but one that requires careful, strategic management.

items.q: Some say social media does more harm than good. Do you agree?
items.text: I am somewhat torn on this. There seems to be compelling evidence of harm, from mental health issues to the spread of misinformation, which I take seriously. However, I cannot ignore the genuine benefits, such as connecting isolated people and enabling social movements. So rather than declaring it simply harmful, I would say its impact is highly dependent on usage. The technology is not inherently malign; our habits determine its net effect.

items.q: Do you think artificial intelligence will benefit or harm humanity?
items.text: I believe AI has the potential to do both, and the outcome depends entirely on how we manage it. On the positive side, it could revolutionise medicine, science and productivity, solving problems beyond human capacity. On the other hand, it raises serious concerns about job displacement, privacy and even safety. So I am cautiously optimistic, but I firmly believe it requires careful ethical oversight to remain beneficial rather than harmful.

items.q: Are there things humans can do that AI never will?
items.text: I firmly believe so, at least for the foreseeable future. While AI excels at processing data and pattern recognition, it lacks genuine consciousness, emotional depth and lived experience. True creativity, empathy, moral judgement and the ability to understand context in a human way remain uniquely ours. AI can mimic these, but I do not think it can authentically replicate the human essence behind them.

items.q: What effect will AI have on employment?
items.text: The effect will be profound and disruptive. AI will inevitably automate many jobs, particularly routine and repetitive ones, which will displace some workers. However, history suggests it will also create new roles and industries we cannot yet imagine. The key challenge is managing the transition, ensuring that displaced workers can retrain. Without such support, there is a genuine risk of increased inequality and social disruption.

items.q: How is AI already changing everyday life?
items.text: AI is already deeply embedded in our daily routines, often invisibly. It powers the recommendations on our streaming services, the navigation on our phones, and the virtual assistants we speak to. It filters our emails and even helps diagnose illnesses. Most of this makes life more convenient and efficient. However, this quiet integration also raises important questions about how much of our lives we are handing over to algorithms.

items.q: Should there be limits on the development of AI?
items.text: Yes, I strongly believe sensible limits and regulation are essential. The technology is advancing so rapidly that it risks outpacing our ability to understand its consequences. Without ethical guidelines and oversight, there are real dangers regarding privacy, bias and even autonomous weapons. This does not mean stifling innovation, but rather guiding it responsibly. I think proactive governance is far wiser than trying to contain the risks after they emerge.

items.q: How can societies prepare for the widespread use of AI?
items.text: Preparation must happen on several fronts. Education systems need to adapt, focusing on the creative and interpersonal skills that AI cannot replicate, while also teaching digital literacy. Governments should invest in retraining programmes for workers whose jobs are at risk. Crucially, robust ethical frameworks and regulations must be developed proactively. A social safety net may also be needed to cushion those affected by the disruption.

items.q: What are the main benefits and risks of using AI in healthcare?
items.text: The benefits are enormous. AI can analyse medical images with incredible accuracy, help diagnose diseases early, and accelerate drug discovery, potentially saving countless lives. However, the risks include the danger of algorithmic bias leading to unequal care, concerns over patient data privacy, and the potential for errors if AI is trusted blindly. So while it is a genuinely powerful tool, human oversight remains absolutely indispensable.

items.q: Some fear AI will one day become smarter than humans. Do you share this concern?
items.text: I have measured concern rather than alarm. AI already surpasses us in narrow tasks like calculation, and it will keep improving. The idea of a general intelligence exceeding humans is more speculative, but not impossible in the long term. My concern is less about a science-fiction takeover and more about the immediate risks of misuse and lack of control. So I think a degree of vigilance is wise, but hysteria is unhelpful.

items.q: Do you think digital communication is better than face-to-face communication?
items.text: I would say it is not better, but rather different, with its own strengths. Digital communication offers unmatched convenience and lets us stay connected across any distance instantly. However, it lacks the richness of face-to-face interaction, where tone, body language and physical presence convey so much. For deep, emotional conversations, nothing beats being together in person. So digital tools are a wonderful supplement, but not a full substitute for genuine human contact.

items.q: How is the way young people communicate different from older generations?
items.text: The difference is quite marked. Young people have grown up as digital natives, so they favour instant messaging, voice notes and social media over phone calls, which many find intrusive. Older generations often prefer calls or in-person conversation. Young people also communicate more through images, emojis and memes, a kind of visual shorthand. This can lead to occasional misunderstanding between the generations, though both are simply adapting to their era.

items.q: What effect has instant messaging had on our language?
items.text: It has had a noticeable influence. Instant messaging has spawned a whole new informal language of abbreviations, emojis and slang, which allows for quick, expressive communication. Some worry this is eroding traditional writing skills and grammar, especially among the young. However, I take a more relaxed view; language has always evolved, and people generally understand when to switch between casual and formal registers. So it is evolution, not decay.

items.q: Has technology made us more or less connected to each other?
items.text: This is a fascinating paradox. On the surface, technology has made us more connected than ever, allowing instant contact with anyone worldwide. Yet many argue we are actually more isolated, replacing deep, present relationships with shallow digital interactions. We may have hundreds of online contacts but few genuine confidants. So I would say we are more connected in quantity but perhaps less connected in quality and true intimacy.

items.q: How do you think we will communicate in the future?
items.text: I imagine communication will become even more immersive and instantaneous. Technologies like virtual reality could allow us to feel genuinely present with distant people, and real-time translation may dissolve language barriers entirely. We may increasingly communicate through augmented reality overlays too. While exciting, I hope these advances enhance rather than replace human warmth, and that we do not lose the value of simple, unmediated face-to-face connection.

items.q: How can people avoid becoming too dependent on digital communication?
items.text: Being intentional is key. Setting aside device-free time, particularly during meals or when with loved ones, helps enormously. Consciously choosing to call or meet someone rather than always texting preserves deeper connection. Turning off unnecessary notifications reduces the constant pull of our devices. Essentially, we need to treat technology as a tool that serves us, rather than allowing it to dominate our attention and displace real interaction.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of communicating mainly through text?
items.text: Text communication is convenient, allowing you to reply at your own pace and keep a written record, which is useful. It is also less intrusive than a call. However, the major disadvantage is the absence of tone and body language, which makes messages easy to misinterpret. It can also feel impersonal and lead to misunderstandings that a quick conversation would avoid. So it is efficient, but emotionally limited.

items.q: Some say technology is making face-to-face conversation a dying skill. Do you agree?
items.text: I think there is a kernel of truth to this, though I would not go so far as to call it dying. It is certainly true that some young people, accustomed to texting, can feel awkward in direct conversation and may struggle to read social cues. However, humans are inherently social, and the need for real connection persists. So the skill may be underused and in need of nurturing, but I do not believe it will ever become obsolete.

items.q: How important is online privacy to you?
items.text: I consider online privacy extremely important, though I admit I do not always protect it as well as I should. In an age where our data is constantly collected, I believe people have a fundamental right to control their personal information. The erosion of privacy can lead to manipulation and surveillance, which is genuinely worrying. So while convenience often tempts us to be careless, I think safeguarding our privacy is a vital and overlooked responsibility.

items.q: Do people care about privacy more or less than they used to?
items.text: This is quite paradoxical. On one hand, awareness of privacy issues has grown enormously following major data scandals, so people claim to care more. On the other hand, our actual behaviour suggests otherwise; we readily hand over data for the sake of convenience and free services. This gap between concern and action is often called the privacy paradox. So people are more aware, yet often equally willing to compromise their privacy.

items.q: What are the consequences of companies collecting so much personal data?
items.text: The consequences are significant and often hidden. Companies use our data to target advertising with uncanny precision, which can feel manipulative. More seriously, large data collections are vulnerable to breaches, potentially exposing people to fraud and identity theft. There is also the broader concern of this information being used to influence our behaviour and opinions. Essentially, it creates a huge imbalance of power that can undermine individual autonomy.

items.q: How does the loss of privacy affect society?
items.text: A society without privacy can become one of pervasive surveillance, which can have a chilling effect on free expression. If people feel constantly watched, they may self-censor and conform, which is unhealthy for democracy. The concentration of personal data in a few powerful hands also creates opportunities for manipulation on a mass scale. So the erosion of privacy is not merely a personal issue; it has profound implications for freedom itself.

items.q: Do you think privacy will exist in the future?
items.text: I am somewhat pessimistic, though not entirely without hope. As technology becomes ever more pervasive, with smart devices and surveillance everywhere, maintaining privacy will become increasingly difficult. However, I am hopeful that growing public awareness and stronger regulations, like data protection laws, could push back against this trend. So while privacy as we once knew it may diminish, I believe the fight to preserve a meaningful degree of it will intensify.

items.q: What can be done to better protect people's online privacy?
items.text: Solutions must operate at multiple levels. Governments should enforce robust data protection laws that give people genuine control over their information, like Europe's regulations. Companies must be more transparent about how they use data. On an individual level, education about privacy settings, strong passwords and cautious sharing is vital. Ultimately, shifting the default towards protecting the user, rather than exploiting them, is the most important safeguard.

items.q: Are there any benefits to sharing personal data with companies?
items.text: Yes, there are genuine trade-offs. Sharing data allows companies to offer highly personalised and convenient services, from tailored recommendations to smoother experiences. Many valuable free services are funded this way. In healthcare, shared data can even advance medical research. The problem is the lack of transparency and consent. So the benefits are real, but they should come from an informed, voluntary exchange rather than covert exploitation.

items.q: Some say if you have nothing to hide, privacy does not matter. Do you agree?
items.text: I strongly disagree with that argument. Privacy is not about hiding wrongdoing; it is a fundamental right that protects our autonomy and dignity. We all have private thoughts and information that are simply nobody else's business, regardless of innocence. This argument also dangerously assumes those in power will always act benevolently. In my view, defending privacy is about protecting freedom itself, not concealing anything sinister.

items.q: How important is it for people to follow the news?
items.text: I believe it is quite important for people to stay reasonably informed, as it is part of being an engaged citizen. Understanding current events helps us make sense of the world and participate in democracy. However, I would add a caveat; consuming too much news, especially negative or sensational content, can be overwhelming and anxiety-inducing. So the ideal is to stay informed through reliable sources without becoming obsessed.

items.q: How has the way people get news changed over the years?
items.text: The change has been revolutionary. In the past, people relied on scheduled TV bulletins and printed newspapers, receiving curated news once or twice a day. Now, news is constant, instant and consumed largely through social media and online sources. This has made news more accessible, but also more fragmented and harder to verify. The rise of citizen journalism is a benefit, but so too is the spread of unverified, sensational content.

items.q: Why do you think fake news spreads so easily?
items.text: Several factors are at play. Social media algorithms tend to prioritise engaging content, and false or sensational stories are often more provocative than the truth. People also share things impulsively without verifying them, especially if they confirm existing beliefs. The lack of traditional editorial gatekeepers online means misinformation can spread unchecked. Combined with a general decline in media literacy, this creates the perfect conditions for falsehoods to proliferate.

items.q: How does the media influence public opinion?
items.text: The media wields enormous influence over public opinion. By choosing which stories to cover and how to frame them, it shapes what people think is important and how they interpret events. This agenda-setting power is significant. Repeated exposure to particular viewpoints can gradually shape attitudes, sometimes reinforcing bias. So while a free media is vital for democracy, its power to sway opinion also carries real responsibility.

items.q: Do you think traditional newspapers will survive in the future?
items.text: In their printed form, I think they will largely decline, as younger generations consume news almost entirely online. However, I do not believe quality journalism itself will disappear; rather, it will continue its shift to digital platforms and subscription models. The reputable news organisations behind the papers may well endure, just in a different format. So the printed page may fade, but the institution of journalism should persist.

items.q: What can be done to combat the spread of misinformation?
items.text: Tackling this requires a combined effort. Improving media literacy so people can critically evaluate sources is perhaps the most important long-term solution. Social media platforms must also take greater responsibility, using fact-checking and adjusting algorithms that reward sensationalism. Supporting quality, independent journalism is equally vital. Ultimately, an informed, sceptical public is the best defence against the tide of misinformation.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of having 24-hour news?
items.text: The advantage is that we are kept constantly informed of breaking events as they unfold, which can be valuable in a crisis. However, the disadvantages are considerable. The pressure to fill airtime often leads to speculation, repetition and sensationalism over substance. It can also foster a state of perpetual anxiety and desensitise us to serious events. So constant news offers immediacy at the cost of depth and perspective.

items.q: Some say the media focuses too much on negative news. Do you agree?
items.text: I largely agree with this. There is a well-known principle in journalism that bad news sells, so outlets tend to prioritise disasters, conflict and scandal, which are more attention-grabbing. This can give people a distorted, overly pessimistic view of the world, ignoring genuine progress. While reporting problems is important, this relentless negativity can be demoralising. A more balanced approach, including constructive news, would be healthier.

items.q: Do you think smartphones have improved people's lives?
items.text: On the whole, I think they have, though not without significant drawbacks. Smartphones have put a world of information, communication and services in our pockets, which is genuinely empowering and convenient. However, they have also introduced constant distraction and a degree of dependence that can harm our focus and relationships. So I see them as a remarkable tool that has improved life, provided we use them consciously rather than compulsively.

items.q: How was life different before smartphones?
items.text: Life was noticeably slower and, in some ways, more present. People were less contactable and more likely to be fully engaged in their immediate surroundings rather than staring at a screen. Getting lost, being bored or having to memorise information were normal. While we have gained incredible convenience, I think we have lost a certain patience and the ability to simply be idle, which had its own value.

items.q: What effects does excessive smartphone use have on people?
items.text: The effects can be quite detrimental. Excessive use seems to be linked to reduced attention spans, disrupted sleep and increased anxiety, partly due to the constant stream of notifications. It can also erode face-to-face social skills and lead to a sedentary lifestyle. There is even a recognised phenomenon of phone addiction. So while occasional use is harmless, overuse can genuinely impair both our mental and physical wellbeing.

items.q: How have smartphones changed social interactions?
items.text: They have transformed them in mixed ways. On one hand, they let us maintain connections effortlessly across distances. On the other, they often intrude on our real-world interactions; it is common to see people together physically but absorbed in their phones. This phenomenon, sometimes called phubbing, can make people feel ignored. So smartphones have expanded our virtual social lives while sometimes diminishing the quality of our present ones.

items.q: How do you think mobile technology will develop in the future?
items.text: I anticipate devices will become even more integrated into our lives, perhaps evolving beyond the handheld phone into wearables or augmented reality glasses. Artificial intelligence will make them ever more anticipatory and personalised. The line between the digital and physical worlds is likely to blur further. While this promises even greater convenience, I hope it comes with a stronger awareness of the need to remain present and in control.

items.q: How can people reduce their dependence on their phones?
items.text: There are several practical strategies. Turning off non-essential notifications immediately reduces the constant pull to check the phone. Designating device-free times and zones, such as during meals or in the bedroom, helps re-establish boundaries. Using apps that track and limit screen time can raise awareness of usage. Ultimately, consciously replacing mindless scrolling with more rewarding activities is the most sustainable way to loosen the phone's grip.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of children owning smartphones?
items.text: The advantages include safety, as parents can stay in contact, and access to educational resources. It also helps children develop digital literacy. However, the disadvantages are considerable: exposure to inappropriate content, cyberbullying, addiction and reduced physical activity. It can also hinder the development of face-to-face social skills. So while there are benefits, I believe children's phone use needs careful supervision and sensible limits.

items.q: Some say people cannot live without their phones now. Do you agree?
items.text: I think that is an exaggeration, but it contains an uncomfortable truth. Obviously, people survived perfectly well before phones, so it is not a literal dependency. However, phones have become so integral to how we work, navigate and communicate that living without one would be genuinely inconvenient and isolating in modern society. So while we could live without them, our society has become so reliant on them that it would be a difficult adjustment.

items.q: Do you think the internet has been a good thing for society?
items.text: Overwhelmingly, yes, though it is not without serious problems. The internet has democratised access to information and education, connected the world, and driven economic innovation in extraordinary ways. It has empowered individuals and given voice to the voiceless. However, it has also enabled misinformation, cybercrime and privacy violations. On balance, I consider it one of humanity's most transformative and beneficial inventions, provided we manage its downsides responsibly.

items.q: How did people find information before the internet?
items.text: It was a far more laborious process. People relied on libraries, encyclopaedias, newspapers and asking knowledgeable individuals. Finding a specific fact could take hours or even days of research. While this was slow, some argue it encouraged deeper engagement and better retention. Today, information is instant, but arguably we process it more superficially. So the internet has traded depth and effort for unprecedented speed and convenience.

items.q: What are the effects of having so much information available online?
items.text: The effects are double-edged. On the positive side, unprecedented access to information empowers learning and informed decision-making. However, this sheer abundance can lead to information overload, making it hard to focus or discern what is reliable. It can also create echo chambers, where algorithms feed us only what we already believe. So while access is empowering, navigating it wisely requires strong discernment to avoid being overwhelmed or misled.

items.q: How has the internet affected inequality between people?
items.text: It has had a complex effect. In some ways it has reduced inequality by giving people everywhere access to free education and economic opportunities. However, it has also created a new form of inequality, the so-called digital divide, between those with reliable access and skills and those without. Those lacking connectivity or literacy risk being left further behind. So the internet is a double-edged force that can either narrow or widen disparities.

items.q: Do you think everyone will have internet access in the future?
items.text: I am hopeful that access will become nearly universal, though significant gaps will likely persist for some time. Technology like satellite internet is rapidly extending connectivity to remote regions, and access is increasingly seen as a basic necessity. However, cost and infrastructure remain real barriers in poorer areas. So while I believe the digital divide will narrow considerably, achieving truly universal access will require sustained global investment.

items.q: How can people learn to tell reliable information from unreliable information online?
items.text: Developing critical thinking is essential. People should learn to check the credibility of a source, look for corroboration from multiple reputable outlets, and be wary of sensational headlines designed to provoke. Being aware of one's own biases is also important. Ideally, these media literacy skills should be taught in schools from a young age, equipping people to scrutinise information rather than accepting it uncritically.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of children using the internet for learning?
items.text: The advantages are substantial: the internet offers a vast library of educational content, interactive tools and access to knowledge that enriches learning enormously. It caters to different learning styles too. The disadvantages include exposure to unreliable or inappropriate content, distraction, and the risk of reduced deep reading. So it is a phenomenal educational resource, but children need guidance and supervision to use it safely and effectively.

items.q: Some say the internet makes people less intelligent. Do you agree?
items.text: I disagree with that as a blanket statement, though it raises a fair concern. The internet does not make us less intelligent; rather, it changes how we use our intelligence. We may memorise less, relying on it as an external memory, but we have unparalleled access to knowledge. The risk is that passive consumption and short attention spans can weaken deep thinking. So it is a tool that can either enrich or diminish the mind, depending on use.

items.q: Do you think online entertainment is better than traditional forms?
items.text: I would say it is not necessarily better, but far more convenient and personalised. Streaming and online platforms offer endless choice on demand, which is hard to beat. However, traditional forms like cinema, live theatre or reading a physical book offer a certain quality and communal experience that online consumption can lack. So I appreciate the convenience, but I do not think it fully replaces the richness of certain traditional experiences.

items.q: How is the way people are entertained today different from the past?
items.text: The difference is stark. In the past, entertainment was largely communal and scheduled; families gathered to watch a programme at a set time, or went out to the cinema. Today, entertainment is highly individualised and on-demand, consumed alone on personal devices whenever we wish. This offers wonderful freedom, but I think we have lost some of the shared, communal aspect. Entertainment has become more personalised yet arguably more solitary.

items.q: Why has streaming become so popular?
items.text: Its popularity comes down to convenience and choice. Streaming offers instant, on-demand access to an enormous library of content that you can watch anywhere, anytime, without adverts. It is also relatively affordable compared to traditional cable. The personalised recommendations keep people engaged, and binge-watching entire series has become a cultural phenomenon. Essentially, it perfectly suits the modern desire for flexibility and instant gratification.

items.q: What impact do video games have on young people?
items.text: The impact is genuinely mixed and often exaggerated. On the positive side, many games improve problem-solving, coordination and even teamwork when played socially, and they are a legitimate form of relaxation. However, excessive gaming can lead to addiction, a sedentary lifestyle and, in some cases, exposure to toxic online behaviour. So like most things, video games are beneficial in moderation but harmful to excess.

items.q: How do you think entertainment will change in the future?
items.text: I expect entertainment to become far more immersive and interactive. Virtual and augmented reality could allow us to step inside stories and games rather than merely watching them. Artificial intelligence may create personalised content tailored precisely to individual tastes. The line between passive viewing and active participation will likely blur. While thrilling, I hope this does not come at the expense of the shared, communal joys that entertainment can foster and preserve.

items.q: How can people avoid spending too much time on online entertainment?
items.text: Self-discipline and awareness are key. Setting clear time limits and using apps that track usage can prevent hours from slipping away unnoticed. Consciously scheduling other activities, like exercise, hobbies or socialising, ensures entertainment does not crowd out everything else. It also helps to remove the constant temptation, perhaps by keeping devices out of reach. Essentially, treating entertainment as a reward rather than a default keeps it in balance.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of on-demand entertainment?
items.text: The advantages are obvious: unprecedented convenience, choice and control over what and when we watch. It is tailored to our tastes and available instantly. The disadvantages, however, include the temptation to binge excessively, which can waste time and disrupt sleep. The sheer abundance of choice can also be paralysing, and it can isolate us. So it offers wonderful freedom, but demands self-control to enjoy without overindulging.

items.q: Some say people are becoming too passive in how they spend their free time. Do you agree?
items.text: I have some sympathy with this view. There is a real tendency to default to passive consumption, like endless scrolling or binge-watching, which requires little effort and can be mindless. This may come at the expense of more active, enriching pursuits like exercise, hobbies or socialising. However, I would not generalise too broadly, as many people remain active. It is more a temptation to guard against than an inevitable decline.

items.q: At what age do you think children should be allowed to use technology?
items.text: This is a difficult question with no perfect answer. I believe very young children should have extremely limited screen time, as their development depends on real-world play and interaction. As they grow, technology can be gradually introduced, ideally in an educational and supervised way. So rather than a strict age, I favour a gradual, age-appropriate approach, always emphasising quality of content over quantity of time.

items.q: How is childhood today different because of technology?
items.text: Technology has fundamentally reshaped childhood. Today's children are digital natives, growing up with screens and instant access to information their parents never had. Much of their play, learning and socialising now happens online. While this offers incredible opportunities, it also means less unstructured outdoor play and more sedentary time. So childhood is arguably more stimulating but also more screen-bound than it was a generation ago.

items.q: What effects can too much screen time have on children?
items.text: The potential effects are concerning. Excessive screen time seems to be linked to problems with sleep, attention and physical health due to inactivity. It may also hinder the development of social skills and language if it replaces real interaction. There are concerns about exposure to unsuitable content too. So while technology has benefits, an excess can genuinely impair a child's healthy development, both physically and socially.

items.q: How can technology be used positively in children's education?
items.text: Used well, technology can be a wonderful educational tool. Interactive apps and games can make learning engaging and cater to different learning styles. It gives children access to a vast world of knowledge and can help those with special needs. Educational videos can explain complex ideas vividly. The key is that it should be used purposefully as a supplement to good teaching, not as a substitute for it.

items.q: Do you think future generations will be even more dependent on technology?
items.text: Almost certainly, yes. As technology becomes ever more woven into every aspect of life, future generations will grow up with it as an inseparable part of their existence. This dependence will likely deepen, which brings both opportunities and risks. My hope is that alongside this, we will develop a stronger culture of digital wellbeing, teaching children to use technology intentionally and to maintain a healthy balance rather than being consumed by it.

items.q: How can parents keep their children safe online?
items.text: Parents can take several practical steps. Using parental controls and age-appropriate settings helps filter unsuitable content. Keeping devices in shared family spaces rather than bedrooms allows for supervision. Most importantly, maintaining open, honest communication so children feel able to report anything troubling is vital. Educating children about online risks, like strangers and scams, empowers them. Ultimately, a combination of supervision and education is the best protection.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of children learning to code at a young age?
items.text: The advantages are significant. Coding teaches logical thinking, problem-solving and creativity, and it equips children with a highly valuable skill for the future job market. It can also be genuinely fun and empowering. The potential disadvantages are that it adds to screen time and academic pressure, and it should not crowd out other essential activities like play and physical exercise. So it is a valuable skill, provided it is kept in balance and not forced.

items.q: Some say technology is robbing children of a real childhood. Do you agree?
items.text: I partly agree, though I think it is a little overstated. There is a legitimate concern that excessive screen time is replacing the outdoor play, imagination and face-to-face friendships that define a healthy childhood. However, technology also offers genuine benefits and is simply the reality of the modern world. So rather than demonising it, I believe the answer lies in moderation, ensuring children still enjoy a rich, balanced upbringing.

items.q: Do you think traditions are still important in modern society?
items.text: I believe they are more important than ever. In a rapidly changing, globalised world, traditions provide a vital sense of identity, continuity and belonging. They connect us to our history and to one another. While some outdated customs deserve to fade, I think the core traditions that bind a community together are worth preserving. They give life a certain meaning and rhythm that modernity alone cannot provide.

items.q: Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?
items.text: To some extent, yes, though it varies. Young people, being more exposed to global culture and modern lifestyles, sometimes view certain traditions as outdated or irrelevant. However, I would not say they have abandoned tradition entirely; many still take great pride in their cultural roots, just alongside a more modern outlook. So there is a shift in emphasis, but I think the connection to heritage remains, merely reinterpreted in a contemporary context.

items.q: Why do you think some traditions are disappearing?
items.text: Several forces are at work. Globalisation and the dominance of Western culture have homogenised lifestyles, making some local customs seem less relevant. Urbanisation and modern, busy lives also leave less time for elaborate traditional practices. Additionally, as older generations pass away, knowledge and skills are sometimes not passed on. So it is really a combination of cultural dilution and the practical pressures of modern life eroding them.

items.q: How do traditions help bring communities together?
items.text: Traditions play a powerful unifying role. Shared festivals, rituals and customs create a sense of collective identity and belonging, reminding people that they are part of something larger than themselves. They bring people together to celebrate or mourn collectively, strengthening social bonds. This shared heritage fosters mutual understanding and solidarity. In essence, traditions act as a kind of social glue that reinforces community cohesion.

items.q: Do you think traditions will survive in the future?
items.text: I am cautiously optimistic. While some traditions will inevitably fade, I believe the most meaningful ones will endure, perhaps in modified forms. There is actually a growing appreciation for heritage as a counterbalance to globalisation, with many people actively seeking to revive old customs. Technology can also help document and share them. So rather than vanishing, I think traditions will evolve, adapting to remain relevant in a changing world.

items.q: What can be done to preserve traditional culture?
items.text: A concerted effort is needed. Education is crucial; teaching young people about their heritage in schools fosters pride and understanding. Documenting traditions and supporting the artisans and elders who hold this knowledge is also vital. Governments and communities can organise festivals and cultural events to keep customs alive and visible. Essentially, making tradition feel relevant and engaging to the young is the key to its continuity.

items.q: Are there any disadvantages to holding on to old traditions?
items.text: Yes, tradition can have a darker side. Some customs are rooted in outdated beliefs and can perpetuate inequality or harmful practices, such as those that discriminate against certain groups. Blindly following tradition can also stifle progress and individual freedom. So while I value heritage, I think it is important to be discerning, preserving what enriches us while being willing to discard customs that are genuinely harmful or unjust.

items.q: Some say globalisation is destroying local cultures. Do you agree?
items.text: I partly agree, as it is a genuine threat. The spread of a dominant global culture can certainly overshadow and dilute local traditions, languages and customs, leading to a worrying uniformity. However, I would not say it is entirely destructive. Globalisation also allows cultures to share and celebrate their uniqueness on a world stage. So while the risk of homogenisation is real, cultures can also prove remarkably resilient and adaptive.

items.q: Why do you think festivals are important?
items.text: Festivals serve several important purposes. They provide a much-needed break from routine and an occasion for joy and celebration. More deeply, they reinforce cultural identity and bring communities and families together in shared rituals. They also pass traditions from one generation to the next. In my view, this sense of collective celebration and belonging is something people fundamentally need, which is why festivals remain so cherished across cultures.

items.q: How are festivals celebrated differently now compared to the past?
items.text: The essence remains, but the style has changed. In the past, celebrations were often simpler and more community-focused, with everyone participating directly. Today, festivals have become more commercialised, with an emphasis on spending and consumption. Technology has also changed things; people now share their celebrations on social media. So while festivals are still meaningful, some argue they have lost a degree of authenticity, becoming more about consumerism than genuine tradition.

items.q: What effect does commercialisation have on traditional festivals?
items.text: The effect is double-edged. On one hand, commercialisation can boost the economy and raise a festival's profile, making it more widely known. On the other, it can dilute the festival's original spiritual or cultural meaning, reducing it to a shopping opportunity. The genuine sentiment behind the celebration can get lost amid the advertising and pressure to spend. So it brings visibility, but often at the cost of authenticity and true significance.

items.q: How do festivals contribute to a country's economy?
items.text: Festivals can be a significant economic driver. They boost spending on food, gifts, clothing and travel, benefiting countless businesses. Major festivals also attract tourists, generating substantial revenue for the hospitality and transport sectors. They create seasonal employment too. So beyond their cultural value, festivals are a genuine economic stimulus, injecting money into local economies and showcasing a country's culture to a global audience, which is a real asset.

items.q: Do you think traditional festivals will remain popular in the future?
items.text: I believe they will, though they will continue to evolve. While the way we celebrate may change, the fundamental human need for community, joy and shared meaning will ensure festivals endure. There may even be a resurgence of interest as people seek authenticity in an increasingly digital world. So while some may become more modernised or commercial, I think the core appeal of festivals will persist and remain relevant for generations.

items.q: How can the true spirit of festivals be preserved?
items.text: Preserving the spirit requires conscious effort. Emphasising the values behind the festival, such as togetherness, gratitude or reflection, rather than just the material aspects, is important. Involving young people in traditional practices and explaining their meaning helps too. Communities can prioritise participation over consumption. Essentially, if we consciously focus on the essence of a festival rather than its commercial trappings, its true spirit can thrive.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of large public celebrations?
items.text: Large public celebrations create a wonderful, vibrant atmosphere and a powerful sense of collective joy and unity. They boost tourism and local pride. However, the disadvantages include practical issues like overcrowding, noise, litter and strain on public services. There can also be safety concerns. So while they are culturally and economically valuable, they require careful management to minimise the disruption and ensure everyone can enjoy them safely.

items.q: Some say festivals have become too commercial. Do you agree?
items.text: I largely agree with this observation. Many festivals now seem dominated by advertising, sales and pressure to spend, which can overshadow their original cultural or spiritual meaning. The focus has shifted, in some cases, from togetherness to consumerism. That said, this is not universal, and the deeper meaning often survives beneath the commercial surface for those who seek it. So it is a real trend to resist, but not an irreversible one.

items.q: How important is food to a country's culture?
items.text: Food is absolutely central to culture, in my view. It is far more than mere sustenance; it reflects a nation's history, geography, values and social customs. Sharing a meal is a universal expression of hospitality and community. Traditional dishes carry deep sentimental and cultural significance, passed down through generations. So I would say cuisine is one of the most tangible and beloved expressions of a country's identity.

items.q: How have people's eating habits changed over the years?
items.text: Eating habits have changed considerably. In the past, people mostly ate home-cooked, seasonal and local food, often together as a family. Today, busy lifestyles have led to more processed food, takeaways and eating on the go, often alone. Portion sizes have grown, and international cuisine is now widely available. While this offers more variety and convenience, I think it has come at some cost to health and the communal nature of dining.

items.q: Why do you think fast food has become so popular?
items.text: Its popularity comes down to a few key factors. Firstly, it is convenient and quick, which suits our increasingly busy, time-poor lifestyles. Secondly, it is relatively cheap and consistently tasty, engineered to appeal to our cravings. Aggressive marketing has also made it ubiquitous and aspirational. Unfortunately, this convenience comes at a cost, as many argue its popularity has contributed to rising rates of obesity and related health problems.

items.q: How does the availability of international food affect local cuisine?
items.text: It has a mixed effect. On the positive side, it enriches our culinary options and promotes cultural exchange, allowing people to enjoy dishes from around the world. This is broadening and enjoyable. However, there is a concern that the popularity of international chains could overshadow and threaten traditional local cuisine. So while it adds welcome diversity, it is important that local food traditions are also valued and preserved alongside it.

items.q: How do you think the way we eat will change in the future?
items.text: I anticipate significant changes driven by health and sustainability concerns. Plant-based diets and alternative proteins, like lab-grown meat, are likely to become far more mainstream as we address the environmental impact of food. Technology may also personalise nutrition. Hopefully, there will be a renewed appreciation for healthy, sustainable eating. So our diets may become more conscious and innovative, balancing convenience with health and the planet.

items.q: What can be done to encourage people to eat more healthily?
items.text: A range of measures could help. Education about nutrition from a young age is fundamental, so people can make informed choices. Making healthy food more affordable and accessible, while perhaps taxing unhealthy options, can shift behaviour. Clear food labelling and restrictions on junk food advertising, especially to children, would also help. Ultimately, creating an environment where the healthy choice is the easy, appealing choice is the most effective approach.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of eating out often?
items.text: Eating out offers convenience, saves time on cooking and cleaning, and provides a pleasant social experience and variety. It can be a real treat. The disadvantages, however, are that it is expensive and often less healthy, as restaurant food tends to be higher in salt, sugar and fat, with larger portions. Doing it too often can strain both your finances and your health. So it is best enjoyed in moderation.

items.q: Some say home-cooked food is always better than restaurant food. Do you agree?
items.text: I largely agree, particularly regarding health and value. Home cooking allows you to control the ingredients, ensuring meals are fresher, healthier and cheaper, and it can be a rewarding activity. There is also something uniquely comforting about a home-cooked meal. However, I would not say it is always better; skilled chefs create exquisite dishes that are hard to replicate at home. So home cooking is generally healthier, but restaurants offer expertise and occasion.

items.q: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
items.text: People travel for a wonderful variety of reasons. Fundamentally, I think it satisfies a deep human curiosity and desire to escape routine. Experiencing new cultures, landscapes and cuisines is genuinely enriching and broadens one's perspective. Travel also offers relaxation, adventure and the chance to create lasting memories. For me, the greatest value is how it makes you more open-minded and appreciative of the world's incredible diversity.

items.q: How has travel changed compared to the past?
items.text: Travel has been transformed almost beyond recognition. In the past, it was expensive, slow and largely a privilege of the wealthy. Today, budget airlines and the internet have made it far more accessible and easy to organise, leading to mass tourism. We can now reach distant corners of the globe in hours. While this democratisation is positive, it has also led to overcrowding at popular sites and a more superficial, hurried style of travel.

items.q: What effects does tourism have on local communities?
items.text: Tourism has profound and mixed effects. Economically, it can bring vital income and jobs, boosting the local economy significantly. However, it can also cause problems: it may inflate local prices, strain infrastructure, and sometimes lead to the commodification of culture, where traditions are performed purely for tourists. Environmental damage is another concern. So while tourism offers real economic benefits, it must be managed sustainably to avoid harming the very communities it supports.

items.q: How does travel affect a person's understanding of the world?
items.text: Travel is genuinely one of the best forms of education. By experiencing different cultures firsthand, people develop empathy and challenge their own assumptions and prejudices. It reveals both the vast diversity and the fundamental similarities of humanity. This tends to make people more tolerant, worldly and appreciative of what they have at home. In essence, travel broadens the mind in a way that no book or documentary can fully replicate.

items.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?
items.text: I foresee several shifts. Growing environmental awareness will likely make sustainable and eco-tourism far more popular, as people seek to minimise their impact. Technology, such as virtual reality, might offer new ways to experience places remotely. There may also be a move towards more meaningful, immersive travel over mass tourism. So I expect the future of travel to be more conscious, more personalised, and hopefully more responsible.

items.q: How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
items.text: Sustainable tourism practices are the answer. Governments can manage visitor numbers at fragile sites through limits or timed entry to prevent overcrowding. Promoting lesser-known destinations helps spread the benefits and reduce pressure on hotspots. Encouraging tourists to respect local cultures and environments, and to support local businesses, is also key. Essentially, prioritising sustainability over sheer volume can mitigate the harm while preserving the benefits.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of tourism for a country?
items.text: The advantages are considerable: tourism generates significant income and employment, funds infrastructure, and promotes cultural exchange and international understanding. It can be a real economic lifeline. The disadvantages include environmental degradation, overcrowding, the erosion of local culture and over-reliance on a volatile industry. So tourism is a powerful economic tool, but a country must balance the pursuit of revenue against protecting its environment and cultural integrity.

items.q: Some say tourism does more harm than good to destinations. Do you agree?
items.text: I think it depends entirely on how it is managed. In some over-touristed places, the harm, from environmental damage to cultural erosion and inflated living costs, is undeniable and can indeed outweigh the benefits. However, when managed responsibly and sustainably, tourism can be a tremendous force for good, funding conservation and lifting communities out of poverty. So I would not agree it is inherently harmful; the outcome hinges on responsible stewardship and planning.

items.q: Why do you think fashion is important to some people?
items.text: For many people, fashion is a genuine form of self-expression, allowing them to communicate their personality, mood and identity without words. It can boost confidence and create a sense of belonging to a particular group. For some, it is also an art form and a source of creativity. While I personally value comfort over trends, I completely understand why fashion holds such significance; it is a powerful, visual language of identity.

items.q: Do you think people care more about fashion now than in the past?
items.text: In some ways, yes. The rise of social media has made appearance more visible and, arguably, more important, with influencers constantly showcasing new trends. Fast fashion has also made trendy clothing cheap and accessible, fuelling constant consumption. However, past eras had their own strong fashion cultures too. So perhaps it is not that people care more, but that fashion has become more fast-paced, disposable and publicly displayed than ever before.

items.q: What effect does the fashion industry have on the environment?
items.text: The environmental impact is unfortunately severe, particularly from fast fashion. The industry is a major consumer of water and a significant source of pollution and carbon emissions. The culture of buying cheap, disposable clothing generates enormous textile waste, much of which ends up in landfill. So while fashion brings joy and self-expression, its current unsustainable model exacts a heavy toll on the planet that urgently needs addressing.

items.q: How does fashion influence young people?
items.text: Fashion has a powerful hold on young people. It is closely tied to identity and social acceptance, so what they wear can strongly affect their confidence and sense of belonging. Trends spread rapidly through social media, creating pressure to keep up, which can be expensive and stressful. While fashion can be a positive outlet for creativity, this relentless pressure to conform can also breed insecurity and unhealthy comparison.

items.q: How do you think fashion will change in the future?
items.text: I anticipate sustainability will become a driving force. As awareness of fast fashion's harm grows, I expect a shift towards more durable, ethical and recycled clothing, and a move away from throwaway culture. Technology may also personalise fashion, and digital or virtual clothing could even emerge. So I am hopeful the future of fashion will be more sustainable, more conscious, and perhaps less wasteful than the current model.

items.q: What can be done to make fashion more sustainable?
items.text: Several changes are needed. On the industry side, brands should adopt ethical, eco-friendly production and be more transparent. Consumers can play a huge role by buying less, choosing quality over quantity, and embracing second-hand or recycled clothing. Repairing and reusing garments rather than discarding them also helps. Ultimately, moving away from a throwaway mindset towards more durable, considered consumption is the most impactful solution.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of following fashion trends?
items.text: Following trends can be fun and allows people to feel current, confident and part of a community. It is a creative outlet and can help people fit in socially. The disadvantages, though, are that constantly chasing trends is expensive, contributes to environmental waste, and can suppress genuine individuality. It can also foster insecurity. So while there is joy in it, an obsessive pursuit of trends can become both costly and superficial.

items.q: Some say fashion is a waste of money. Do you agree?
items.text: I only partly agree. Excessive spending on constantly changing trends, particularly disposable fast fashion, can certainly be wasteful and financially imprudent. However, I would not dismiss fashion entirely, as it is a legitimate form of self-expression and creativity that brings people genuine joy and confidence. Investing in quality, lasting pieces is also sensible. So it is not inherently a waste; it becomes one only when pursued excessively and impulsively.

items.q: Why are hobbies important in people's lives?
items.text: Hobbies are far more valuable than people often realise. They provide a vital outlet for relaxation and stress relief, offering a welcome escape from the pressures of work. They also allow for personal growth, creativity and a sense of accomplishment outside our professional identity. Additionally, many hobbies foster social connections. In my view, hobbies are essential for a balanced, fulfilling life, nourishing parts of ourselves that work often neglects.

items.q: How do people's leisure activities differ between generations?
items.text: There are noticeable differences. Older generations often favour traditional pastimes like gardening, reading physical books, or socialising in person. Younger people, by contrast, spend much of their leisure time on digital activities, such as gaming, streaming and social media. That said, there is considerable overlap, and interest in older hobbies is reviving among the young. So the core need for leisure is universal, but the medium has shifted towards the digital.

items.q: What are the benefits of having a creative hobby?
items.text: Creative hobbies offer numerous benefits. They provide a productive outlet for self-expression and can be deeply therapeutic, reducing stress and improving mental wellbeing. The sense of accomplishment from creating something is genuinely rewarding and boosts confidence. They also keep the mind active and can spark skills that enrich other areas of life. Essentially, creative pursuits nourish the soul and offer a fulfilment that passive entertainment simply cannot match.

items.q: How does having free time affect people's quality of life?
items.text: Free time is essential for a good quality of life. It provides the space to rest, recharge and pursue the activities and relationships that bring us joy and meaning. Without adequate leisure, people risk burnout, stress and a diminished sense of wellbeing. Free time allows us to be more than just workers. So I would argue that leisure is not a luxury but a fundamental necessity for a healthy, rounded existence.

items.q: Do you think people will have more free time in the future?
items.text: This is uncertain. Optimistically, if automation boosts productivity and society chooses to share the gains, people could work less and enjoy more leisure, as concepts like the four-day week suggest. However, there is an opposing risk that constant connectivity and economic pressure could actually erode our free time further. So the amount of leisure we have may depend less on technology and more on the choices society makes about priorities.

items.q: Many people say they have no time for hobbies. What can they do?
items.text: It often comes down to priorities rather than an absolute lack of time. People can start by consciously carving out even small pockets of time, perhaps by reducing passive activities like scrolling on their phones. Scheduling hobby time like any other commitment helps make it happen. Choosing hobbies that fit their lifestyle is also wise. Essentially, treating leisure as essential rather than optional helps people reclaim time they did not realise they had.

items.q: Are there any downsides to spending too much time on hobbies?
items.text: There can be, if taken to an extreme. While hobbies are healthy, an obsessive devotion to one could lead to neglecting responsibilities, relationships or work. Some hobbies can also become expensive. If a hobby turns into an escape from dealing with real problems, that is unhealthy too. So like most things, hobbies are wonderful in moderation, but they should complement a balanced life rather than consume it entirely.

items.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?
items.text: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be worthwhile. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly utilitarian mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is exactly the point.

items.q: Do you think people buy more things than they actually need?
items.text: Yes, I think overconsumption is a defining feature of modern society. We are constantly bombarded with advertising designed to create desires for things we do not truly need. Cheap goods and easy credit make impulsive buying effortless. Many people also shop for emotional reasons, as a form of therapy. So I would say that a great deal of our consumption is driven by manufactured wants rather than genuine necessity, which is quite wasteful.

items.q: How has shopping changed with the rise of the internet?
items.text: Online shopping has revolutionised the experience. It offers unparalleled convenience, allowing people to buy almost anything from home at any hour, with easy price comparison. This has, however, put pressure on traditional physical shops, many of which have struggled. The experience has become more efficient but arguably less social. So while the internet has made shopping far more convenient and accessible, it has also transformed our high streets, not always for the better.

items.q: Why do you think advertising is so influential?
items.text: Advertising is influential because it is sophisticated and pervasive. It cleverly taps into our emotions, insecurities and aspirations, associating products with happiness, status or belonging rather than mere function. Its sheer ubiquity means we are exposed to it constantly, which reinforces its messages. Modern targeted advertising is especially potent, as it is tailored precisely to our interests. So it shapes our desires far more than we consciously realise, subtly steering our behaviour.

items.q: What impact does consumerism have on society?
items.text: Consumerism has a profound and mixed impact. It drives economic growth and provides jobs, which is beneficial.
