Governments should intervene to protect citizens, provide essential services and correct market failures, as some intervention is clearly necessary for a functioning society. However, excessive intervention can stifle freedom, innovation and personal responsibility. So the ideal lies somewhere in between; the government should provide a strong safety net and framework while respecting individual autonomy and avoiding becoming overbearing or paternalistic.

items.q: How do you think the role of government will change in the future?
items.text: I anticipate governments will face new and complex challenges that reshape their role. Issues like climate change, artificial intelligence, and global pandemics require unprecedented coordination and regulation. Technology may enable more direct citizen participation but also greater surveillance. Governments will likely need to become more agile and collaborative internationally. So while the fundamental role of serving citizens remains, the tools and challenges will evolve, demanding greater adaptability from those who govern.

items.q: How can governments earn the trust of their citizens?
items.text: Trust is earned through transparency, accountability and competence. Governments that are open about their decisions, deliver on their promises, and tackle corruption tend to be trusted. Actually improving people's lives through effective policy is crucial. Listening to citizens and involving them in decisions fosters a sense of ownership. So by being transparent, honest and genuinely responsive to people's needs, governments can rebuild and maintain the public trust that is so vital to good governance.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of a strong central government?
items.text: A strong central government can act decisively, implement coherent national policy, and coordinate effectively during crises, which is valuable. It can also ensure consistency and tackle large-scale problems. The disadvantages are that too much centralised power can become authoritarian, ignore local needs, and stifle regional autonomy and diversity. It may also be less responsive. So while strong central authority has clear benefits, it must be balanced with checks and local representation to avoid overreach.

items.q: Some say governments should provide free healthcare for everyone. Do you agree?
items.text: I strongly agree with this principle. I believe access to healthcare is a fundamental human right, not a privilege dependent on wealth. Universal healthcare ensures that no one is denied treatment or bankrupted by illness, which is both humane and promotes a healthier, more productive society. While it is expensive and requires efficient management, the alternative, where people suffer for lack of money, seems deeply unjust. So I consider free, universal healthcare a worthwhile and civilised investment.

items.q: Where do you think people get their moral values from?
items.text: I believe our moral values come from a combination of sources. Our upbringing and family are hugely influential, instilling early notions of right and wrong. Culture, religion and society also shape our ethics, as do our own experiences and reflection as we mature. Some argue there is even an innate, universal sense of fairness. So our values are essentially absorbed from those around us and then refined through personal reflection over time.

items.q: Are moral values the same across all cultures?
items.text: I think there is a fascinating mix of universal and culturally specific values. Certain core principles, like prohibitions against murder or valuing honesty and care for others, appear across virtually all cultures, suggesting a shared moral foundation. However, many values, such as attitudes to family, individualism or specific customs, vary considerably between cultures. So while there are some universal moral constants, ethics are also significantly shaped by cultural context.

items.q: What happens to a society when it loses its moral values?
items.text: A society that loses its shared moral compass tends to suffer serious consequences. Trust between people erodes, corruption and dishonesty can flourish, and social cohesion breaks down. Without agreed ethical standards, laws alone struggle to maintain order, and self-interest can dominate at the expense of the common good. So a strong shared morality acts as invisible social glue; its erosion can lead to division, distrust and dysfunction.

items.q: Do you think moral values are declining in modern society?
items.text: This is a common concern, but I am somewhat sceptical. Every generation seems to believe that values are declining, yet by many measures, such as the reduction of violence and expansion of rights, society has arguably become more ethical over time. What is really happening, I think, is that values are shifting rather than declining; some traditional values fade while new ones, like tolerance and environmental awareness, emerge. So I would say values are evolving, not simply deteriorating or vanishing.

items.q: How might moral values change in the future?
items.text: I expect our moral frameworks to be tested and expanded by new challenges. Advances in technology, such as artificial intelligence and genetic engineering, will raise entirely new ethical dilemmas we have never faced before. Growing awareness may also extend our moral concern further, perhaps towards animals, the environment and future generations. So I anticipate that ethics will continue to evolve, becoming broader in scope as we grapple with unprecedented moral questions.

items.q: How can strong moral values be encouraged in young people?
items.text: The most powerful way is through example, since children learn ethics primarily by observing the adults around them. Parents and teachers who model integrity, kindness and honesty have a profound influence. Open discussion of ethical issues, encouraging empathy, and involving young people in helping others also help. Rather than simply lecturing, allowing them to reason through moral situations builds genuine understanding. So values are best instilled through consistent example and guided reflection.

items.q: Is it always right to follow the rules, or are there times to break them?
items.text: While rules are generally important for order and fairness, I do not believe following them is always morally right. History shows that some laws have been deeply unjust, and challenging them, through civil disobedience, has been essential to progress. There are times when a higher moral principle justifies breaking an unjust rule. However, this is a serious matter, not an excuse for convenience. So rules should generally be respected, but blind obedience can sometimes conflict with genuine morality.

items.q: Some say people are becoming more selfish. Do you agree?
items.text: I am not entirely convinced. It is a common perception, and certain trends, like consumerism and individualism, can appear to encourage selfishness. However, I see abundant evidence of generosity, volunteering and collective action, particularly among young people concerned with social and environmental causes. Human nature contains both selfish and altruistic tendencies. So rather than people simply becoming more selfish, I think it is a mischaracterisation; both generosity and self-interest coexist as they always have.

items.q: What do you think is the biggest challenge facing the world today?
items.text: While there are many pressing issues, I believe climate change is arguably the most significant, because it threatens the very habitability of our planet and amplifies other problems like poverty and conflict. Its effects are global and potentially irreversible. That said, inequality and the risks of new technology are also profound. So although I would single out climate change as the most urgent and far-reaching, these challenges are deeply interconnected.

items.q: Should countries solve their own problems or work together on global issues?
items.text: For many modern challenges, international cooperation is not just preferable but essential. Problems like climate change, pandemics and terrorism do not respect borders, so no single country can solve them alone. While nations should certainly address their domestic issues, the great transnational challenges require collective, coordinated action. So I would argue that in an interconnected world, a spirit of cooperation and shared responsibility is indispensable for tackling our common threats.

items.q: Why is it so difficult to solve global problems?
items.text: The difficulty largely stems from competing national interests and a lack of trust. Countries are often reluctant to bear costs or make sacrifices, especially if they fear others will not do the same. Differing priorities between rich and poor nations complicate matters, and there is no single global authority to enforce agreements. Short-term political thinking also gets in the way. So global problems persist because collective action requires overcoming deep-seated self-interest and coordination failures.

items.q: How do global problems affect ordinary people?
items.text: Global problems have very real and personal impacts, even when they seem distant. Climate change brings extreme weather that destroys homes and livelihoods. A global pandemic, as we have seen, can upend everyone's daily life and health. Economic crises that originate elsewhere can cause job losses locally. So although these issues are global in scale, their consequences are felt intimately in ordinary people's livelihoods, health and security, which is why they matter to us all.

items.q: Are you optimistic that the world can solve its biggest problems?
items.text: I try to remain cautiously optimistic, despite the daunting challenges. History shows that humanity is remarkably capable of innovation and cooperation when truly pressed, and we have overcome major threats before. Growing global awareness and technological progress offer real hope. However, success is far from guaranteed and will require unprecedented political will. So while I acknowledge the risks are serious, I choose to believe in human ingenuity and our capacity to rise to the occasion.

items.q: How can international cooperation on global issues be improved?
items.text: Strengthening international institutions and agreements is essential, giving them more authority to coordinate and, where necessary, enforce collective action. Building trust between nations through dialogue and fair burden-sharing is crucial, ensuring poorer countries are supported. Aligning short-term incentives with long-term goals would help too. Ultimately, fostering a genuine sense of shared humanity and common purpose, over narrow nationalism, is the foundation of effective cooperation.

items.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of an interconnected world?
items.text: The advantages of our interconnected world are immense: the free flow of ideas, trade and technology, cultural exchange, and the ability to cooperate on shared problems. It has driven progress and lifted many from poverty. The disadvantages are that problems, whether financial crises, pandemics or misinformation, also spread rapidly across borders, making us more vulnerable. So interconnection brings both tremendous opportunity and shared vulnerability, which we must learn to manage wisely.

items.q: Some say ordinary individuals cannot influence global issues. Do you agree?
items.text: I respectfully disagree, as I find this view unduly disempowering. While it is true that individuals cannot single-handedly solve global problems, collective individual action is precisely what drives change. Our consumer choices, our activism, and above all our votes shape the policies of governments and the behaviour of corporations. Great social movements have always begun with ordinary people. So while one person's impact is small, collectively individuals wield genuine influence and should not underestimate it.

items.q: Do you work or are you a student?
items.text: I'm working at the moment, at an education consultancy, where I predominantly help students with their applications abroad. It keeps me busy, but seeing someone reach a goal they worked towards is genuinely rewarding, so the effort feels worthwhile.

items.q: Why did you choose that job?
items.text: Mainly because I went through the application process myself as a student and realised how confusing it can be. I wanted to help people navigate that uncertainty, and this role lets me do exactly that.

items.q: What do you like most about your job?
items.text: Honestly, it's the people. Every student comes with their own hopes and worries, so no two days are identical, and guiding someone through such a daunting process gives me a real sense of purpose.

items.q: Is there anything you dislike about your work?
items.text: The deadlines can be quite stressful, particularly during the main admission seasons when everything seems to arrive at once. There's a lot of paperwork too, and I'll admit the administrative side can get rather tedious.

items.q: Would you like to change your job in the future?
items.text: Not entirely, but I'd like to grow within the field. Ideally, I'll study abroad myself one day and then come back to a more senior role. For now, though, I'm happy honing my skills where I am.

items.q: What subject did you study?
items.text: I studied business administration at university, with a focus on management. It gave me a broad understanding of how organisations actually run, which has proved surprisingly invaluable in the work I do now.

items.q: Why did you choose that subject?
items.text: Partly because of my father, to be honest. Growing up around his small business, I saw how much planning goes into keeping things running, and I suppose that sparked my interest in management quite early on.

items.q: Did you enjoy your time at university?
items.text: Very much, on the whole. The coursework was demanding at times, but I made some lifelong friends and took part in a few debating events. Those years really helped me become more self-assured and independent.

items.q: What was the most useful thing you learned?
items.text: Probably how to communicate clearly in a professional setting. We did a lot of group presentations, which I dreaded at first, but they gradually made me far more articulate, and I rely on that every day at work.

items.q: Would you like to study something else in the future?
items.text: Yes, I'd love to do a master's abroad, possibly in international education or management. I feel it would deepen my understanding of the field and open doors that aren't really available to me here.

items.q: Where is your hometown?
items.text: I'm from Sirajganj, a modest town in the north of Bangladesh, right beside the Jamuna river. It's about four hours from Dhaka by road, and I've lived there most of my life, so it has a certain tranquillity that feels like home.

items.q: What do you like most about your hometown?
items.text: Without doubt, the river. In the evenings I often walk along the Jamuna embankment, and watching the sun set over the water is incredibly soothing. The people are warm and welcoming too, which gives it a real sense of community.

items.q: Is your hometown a good place for visitors?
items.text: It's not a major tourist destination, but it has its charms. Sirajganj is known for its handloom weaving, and visitors can take a boat trip on the Jamuna. It suits anyone who enjoys a slower, more laid-back pace.

items.q: Has your hometown changed much in recent years?
items.text: Quite a lot, actually. There are more shops, better roads and far more traffic than when I was younger. Some of it is welcome progress, but part of me misses how quiet and unspoilt it used to feel.

items.q: Do you prefer living in a city or the countryside?
items.text: That's a tough one. I enjoy the energy of a city, but I genuinely appreciate the calm of the countryside. Honestly, the ideal for me would be a quieter town that isn't too far from a city.

items.q: Do you live in a house or a flat?
items.text: I live in a flat, on the third floor of a building in a quiet residential area. It's a three-bedroom place I share with my family. It suits us well, though I do occasionally wish we had a bit more open space around us.

items.q: How long have you lived there?
items.text: Well over a decade now, since I was a teenager. Before that we rented a smaller place nearby, so moving there felt like a real step up, and the flat is full of fond memories for all of us.

items.q: Which room do you spend the most time in?
items.text: Definitely my bedroom, which doubles as my study, so I'm in there for most of the day when I'm home. I've arranged it to be quiet and comfortable, which makes it easy to concentrate.

items.q: Is there anything you'd like to change about your home?
items.text: I'd love a bigger balcony, to be honest. Ours is quite narrow, so there isn't much room for plants or a chair. A bit more outdoor space would make it far more inviting on pleasant evenings.

items.q: What kind of home would you like to live in in the future?
items.text: Ideally, a small house with a garden, somewhere peaceful but still within reach of the town. I'd like to grow a few vegetables and have space for bookshelves. Nothing grand, just somewhere that feels like a genuine sanctuary.

items.q: Can you tell me about your family?
items.text: It's a fairly typical family. There are five of us: my parents, my two sisters and me, although my elder sister is married now and lives in Dhaka with her husband and children. My father ran a small business until he retired recently, and my mother looks after the home. We're quite close-knit, and those of us at home usually have dinner together every night.

items.q: Do you spend much time with your family?
items.text: Quite a lot, especially in the evenings. Once work is done, we tend to gather in the living room over tea and chat about our day. Those relaxed moments help me wind down after a long day.

items.q: Who are you closest to in your family?
items.text: Probably my younger sister. She's a student and incredibly hard-working, so we often talk about her studies and plans. I feel quite protective of her, and she's usually the first person I share news with.

items.q: What do you like to do together as a family?
items.text: We love visiting my grandparents in our ancestral village, which isn't far from Sirajganj. The whole family gathers there, especially during Eid, and those visits have an unhurried warmth that I really treasure.

items.q: Has your family changed much in recent years?
items.text: Quite a bit, actually. My elder sister got married and moved to Dhaka, and my father has recently retired, so he's at home far more. It was a big adjustment at first, but it's brought us even closer.

items.q: Does your name have any special meaning?
items.text: Yes, it does actually. My name carries a meaning connected to guidance and light, which is fairly common in our culture. I quite like it, because names here are usually chosen with real deliberation behind them.

items.q: Who chose your name?
items.text: My grandfather did, actually. In our family it's customary for the eldest relative to suggest a name, and my parents were happy to go along with it. I think that's quite a touching tradition.

items.q: Do you have a nickname?
items.text: Yes, like most people in Bangladesh, I have a short nickname that my family and close friends use. My formal name is really only for official documents, so the nickname feels far more affectionate and personal.

items.q: What names are popular in your country?
items.text: Names with religious or poetic meanings are very popular here, particularly Arabic and Bengali ones. Recently, though, I've noticed parents choosing shorter, more modern names, which reflects a broader generational change in taste.

items.q: Would you ever change your name?
items.text: No, I can't imagine doing that. My name connects me to my grandfather and to my family's traditions, so changing it would feel like losing part of my heritage.

items.q: What is your typical daily routine?
items.text: It's fairly structured on weekdays. I get up around seven, have a quick breakfast, and I'm at work by nine. After work I usually study for a couple of hours, then unwind before bed. Weekends are far more relaxed.

items.q: Do you usually get up early?
items.text: Yes, on weekdays I'm up by seven. I've found I think much more clearly in the mornings, so I make the most of that quiet, uninterrupted time. On weekends, though, I happily allow myself a lie-in.

items.q: Which part of the day do you like most?
items.text: The early morning, surprisingly. It's quiet, the day hasn't got hectic yet, and I feel clear-headed. A calm start with a cup of tea genuinely sets a productive tone for everything that follows.

items.q: Do you prefer having a routine or variety?
items.text: A bit of both, ideally. A steady routine keeps me productive, but I'd get bored without some variety. So I like structure on weekdays and something a little more spontaneous at the weekend.

items.q: Has your routine changed much since you were a student?
items.text: Quite significantly. At university my days were far more flexible, and I'd often stay up late and sleep in. Now that I work full-time, I've had to become much more disciplined, which has honestly been good for me.

items.q: Do you know your neighbours well?
items.text: Reasonably well, yes. In our building people are fairly friendly, so we greet each other and occasionally chat. I wouldn't say we're close, but there's a warm, cordial relationship, which matters when you live so near people.

items.q: How often do you see your neighbours?
items.text: Almost every day, just in passing, on the stairs or near the entrance, and we usually exchange a quick greeting. During Eid, though, we visit each other properly and share food, which is a heartwarming custom.

items.q: Do you ever help your neighbours?
items.text: Now and then, yes. There's an elderly man on our floor, so I sometimes carry his shopping upstairs or help with small errands. It's only a small gesture, but I think these acts of goodwill matter in a community.

items.q: What do you think makes a good neighbour?
items.text: Someone who's respectful and considerate, really. A good neighbour keeps the noise down, says hello and is willing to lend a hand in an emergency, but also respects your privacy and doesn't pry.

items.q: Do you think people are as close to their neighbours as they used to be?
items.text: Not really, especially in bigger cities. When I was younger, neighbours would drop in unannounced for tea. Nowadays people are busier and more private, so those bonds have eroded somewhat.

items.q: Do you have many friends?
items.text: I wouldn't say many, but I have a small circle I really trust. I've always preferred a few close friendships over a wide range of acquaintances. Those are the people I can be completely myself around.

items.q: How did you meet your closest friends?
items.text: Most of them are from school and university, so we've known each other for years and share a lot of history. A couple are former colleagues too, which shows that friendships can blossom in unexpected places.

items.q: Can you describe your best friend?
items.text: Sure. He's easygoing, genuinely kind and a great listener, which is probably why we've stayed close for so long. He has this reassuring way of putting things in perspective whenever I'm stressed.

items.q: What do you usually do with your friends?
items.text: Nothing too elaborate. We usually meet at a local tea stall and chat for hours, or watch a cricket match together. Sometimes we take a walk by the river. It's the easy, unpretentious company that I value most.

items.q: Do you think it's easy to make friends as an adult?
items.text: Not as easy as it was at school. Adults are busy with work and family, so there are fewer chances to connect naturally. Friendships still form, but they take more time and deliberate effort.

items.q: Where did you grow up?
items.text: Mostly in Sirajganj, although I spent many school holidays at my grandparents' home in our village nearby. Both places shaped me, and I still feel a strong sense of belonging whenever I go back.

items.q: What did you enjoy doing as a child?
items.text: I was quite an outdoorsy kid. I'd spend hours playing cricket with the neighbourhood children until it got dark. Looking back, those were some of the most carefree times of my life.

items.q: Did you have any hobbies as a child?
items.text: Plenty. I was always outside playing cricket, and I also loved reading comics and adventure stories. Those simple hobbies kept me endlessly entertained, long before phones and screens took over.

items.q: Did you have much freedom as a child?
items.text: Quite a lot, compared to children in big cities today. As long as I was home before dark, my parents were fairly relaxed. Our neighbourhood felt safe, so I could roam around with friends quite freely.

items.q: Do you think children today have a better childhood than you had?
items.text: In some ways, yes. They have access to far more information and opportunities. However, I think they spend too much time indoors on screens and miss out on the kind of unstructured outdoor play I enjoyed.

items.q: What languages do you speak?
items.text: I speak Bengali as my mother tongue, and English fairly fluently. I picked up English mostly through school and a lot of self-study, and I use it daily at work, so it's become almost instinctive.

items.q: Is English widely spoken in your country?
items.text: It's widely understood in cities, particularly in business, universities and among younger people. In rural areas, though, Bengali is used for almost everything. English is increasingly seen as a gateway to better jobs and study opportunities.

items.q: Would you like to learn another language?
items.text: I'd love to learn Arabic, mainly so I can understand the Quran more deeply. I've also considered German, since some students I advise are interested in universities there, so it could give me a competitive edge at work.

items.q: Do you find learning languages difficult?
items.text: It can be, especially as an adult. Grammar and vocabulary take time, but the real challenge is speaking confidently without fear of mistakes. I think consistent practice and immersion matter far more than natural talent.

items.q: Do you think children should learn a foreign language at school?
items.text: Absolutely. Children pick up languages far more easily than adults, and early exposure builds confidence. In such an interconnected world, a second language gives them a real advantage later in life.

items.q: What are your plans for the future?
items.text: In the short term, I'm focused on strengthening my career and possibly studying abroad. Longer term, I'd like to reach a point where my work has real impact and I have the stability to enjoy life a little more.

items.q: Which country would you most like to study in?
items.text: Probably the UK or Canada. Both have excellent universities and a strong reputation in business and education. Having helped so many students apply there, I understand the process well, which makes the idea far less intimidating.

items.q: Where would you like to live in the future?
items.text: I'd happily spend a few years abroad for study, but eventually I'd like to settle back in Bangladesh, perhaps in Dhaka or near my hometown. My family is here, and I feel deeply rooted in this place.

items.q: Do you usually plan things carefully?
items.text: For important matters, definitely. I like to set clear goals and break them into manageable steps. That said, I've learned that life rarely goes exactly to plan, so staying adaptable is just as important.

items.q: Do you think your life will be very different in ten years?
items.text: I imagine so. Hopefully I'll have completed further studies and be in a more senior position. I might have a family of my own by then too, so my priorities will probably evolve quite a lot.

items.q: What do you usually do at the weekend?
items.text: I try to keep weekends flexible after a busy week. Usually I catch up on sleep, meet a friend or two, and maybe run some errands. If I'm lucky, I'll fit in a book or a film to properly recharge.

items.q: Who do you usually spend your weekends with?
items.text: Mostly with my family, to be honest. My younger sister and I sometimes go out for snacks, and occasionally we all visit my grandparents in the village. Evenings are usually for friends, so my weekends feel pleasantly well-rounded.

items.q: Do you prefer weekdays or weekends?
items.text: Weekends, without question. Weekdays are productive but tiring, whereas weekends give me space to rest and see people. That balance is what keeps me going through the week.

items.q: Did you do anything special last weekend?
items.text: Nothing extraordinary. On Friday I went to the mosque for Friday prayers, then spent the afternoon reading. On Saturday I met two old friends for tea, and we ended up chatting for hours, which was thoroughly enjoyable.

items.q: Are your weekends different now from when you were a child?
items.text: Completely. As a child, weekends meant endless cricket and visits to relatives. Now they're mostly about resting and catching up on things I couldn't do during the week, so they feel less adventurous but more precious.

items.q: How many hours do you usually sleep?
items.text: Usually around seven hours on weeknights, which seems to be enough for me. At weekends I sometimes sleep a little longer to make up for the week, although I try not to overdo it.

items.q: Do you usually sleep well?
items.text: Mostly, yes, though it varies. When my mind is calm I fall asleep quickly, but on stressful days it takes a while to switch off. I've learned that avoiding my phone before bed is remarkably effective.

items.q: Do you take naps during the day?
items.text: Rarely on workdays, since there simply isn't time. On Fridays, though, I sometimes have a short nap after lunch. Even twenty minutes leaves me feeling refreshed and noticeably sharper for the rest of the day.

items.q: What do you do when you can't fall asleep?
items.text: I usually get up and read something light for a while rather than lying there frustrated. Sometimes a cup of warm milk helps too. Once my mind settles, I tend to drift off fairly quickly.

items.q: Do you think people get enough sleep nowadays?
items.text: Not really, particularly young people. Many stay up late on their phones or working, then wake early for work or classes. I think sleep is often treated as a luxury rather than a necessity these days.

items.q: Are you a punctual person?
items.text: I'd like to think so, yes. I genuinely dislike keeping people waiting, so I usually aim to arrive a little early. To me, being on time is a simple way of showing consideration for others.

items.q: How do you feel when other people are late?
items.text: It depends on the situation. If it's a friend and only a few minutes, I don't mind at all. But if someone is repeatedly late for professional meetings, I find it quite exasperating, because it wastes everyone's time.

items.q: Are you good at managing your time?
items.text: Mostly, yes. I rely a lot on a simple to-do list, which keeps me on track. I'm not perfect, and things occasionally slip, but planning ahead stops me feeling overwhelmed.

items.q: Do you usually wear a watch?
items.text: Not anymore. I used to wear one my father gave me, but now I just check the time on my phone. I still keep that watch safely in a drawer, though, because it has real sentimental value.

items.q: Do you think people are busier today than in the past?
items.text: I'd say so. With smartphones, we're always reachable, so work often spills into our personal time. Our parents seemed to have clearer boundaries, whereas now life feels far more fast-paced and demanding.

items.q: Who does most of the cooking in your family?
items.text: My mother, without a doubt. She's an excellent cook and takes real pride in it. My younger sister and I help occasionally, but honestly, nobody can replicate her fish curry, no matter how hard we try.

items.q: Do you enjoy cooking?
items.text: I do, actually, though I only really cook at the weekend. During the week I'm too busy, but on a lazy Saturday I quite enjoy trying a new recipe. I find the whole process rather therapeutic after a hectic week.

items.q: What dishes can you cook?
items.text: Nothing too ambitious. I can make a decent chicken curry, khichuri and simple fried fish. Lately I've been trying to master a proper biryani, although my first attempts were fairly disappointing, to put it kindly.

items.q: Do you find cooking relaxing?
items.text: Surprisingly, yes. When I'm not rushed, following a recipe and getting fully immersed in it takes my mind off everything else. And of course there's the reward of a good meal at the end.

items.q: Do you think children should learn to cook?
items.text: Definitely. Cooking is a basic life skill, and it teaches children about nutrition and independence. If they learn early, they're far less likely to fall back on fast food when they eventually live on their own.

items.q: What do you usually have for breakfast?
items.text: Usually something simple, like paratha with egg or a bit of vegetable curry, along with a cup of tea. It's not elaborate, but it's wholesome and keeps me going until lunch.

items.q: What is your favourite meal of the day?
items.text: Definitely dinner. It's the one meal where the whole family sits down together and actually talks, so it's as much about the company as the food. It's become a small daily ritual I really value.

items.q: Do you prefer eating at home or in restaurants?
items.text: Mostly at home, to be honest. Home-cooked food is healthier and more comforting. That said, I do enjoy dining out now and then, especially when it's a chance to socialise with friends over a meal.

items.q: Is there a traditional dish from your country you'd recommend?
items.text: I'd definitely recommend hilsa fish, especially cooked in mustard sauce. It's our national fish, and it has a rich, distinctive flavour. During Pohela Boishakh, many families eat it with panta bhat.

items.q: Have your eating habits changed in recent years?
items.text: Somewhat, yes. I used to eat a lot of fried street food, but now I try to cut back on oily snacks and eat more vegetables. I haven't given them up completely, but I'm certainly more health-conscious than before.

items.q: Where do you usually go shopping?
items.text: For everyday things, I go to the local market near our home, which is always bustling. For larger purchases, I'd rather order online or visit one of the bigger shopping centres, where there's more choice.

items.q: Do you enjoy shopping?
items.text: It depends what I'm shopping for, honestly. I like buying books or a bit of tech, but clothes shopping drains me quickly. These days I do most of it online, which saves me a lot of time.

items.q: Do you prefer shopping alone or with others?
items.text: Alone, usually, because I like to get in and out quickly. When I go with my sister, it turns into an afternoon of browsing every single shop, which is fun occasionally but exhausting.

items.q: Do you ever buy things on impulse?
items.text: Occasionally, especially books. If I see an interesting title, I find it hard to resist, even if I already have a pile waiting to be read. Otherwise, I'm fairly prudent with what I spend.

items.q: Has the way people shop in your country changed?
items.text: Dramatically. Not long ago almost everyone shopped at markets, but now online shopping and home delivery are extremely common, especially in cities. Still, traditional markets remain resilient, because people enjoy bargaining and seeing products in person.

items.q: What kind of clothes do you like to wear?
items.text: I tend to keep it simple and comfortable, mostly casual shirts and jeans. I'm not one for chasing trends. As long as something is neat and versatile, I'm perfectly happy with it.

items.q: Do you wear different clothes at work and at home?
items.text: Yes, quite different. At work I wear formal shirts and trousers, since a polished appearance matters when meeting students and parents. At home, though, I change straight into something loose and comfortable.

items.q: Do you ever wear traditional clothes?
items.text: Yes, mostly on special occasions. For Eid and weddings I always wear a panjabi, which is a long traditional shirt. I really enjoy it, because it feels festive and connects me to our cultural roots.

items.q: Do you spend a lot on clothes?
items.text: Not really. I buy new clothes mainly before Eid or when something wears out. I'd rather invest in a few good-quality items than lots of cheap ones that quickly lose their shape, as it's more economical in the long run.

items.q: Have clothing styles in your country changed much?
items.text: Considerably, especially among young people. Western styles like jeans and T-shirts are now everyday wear in towns and cities. Even so, traditional clothing remains deeply ingrained, particularly during festivals and family celebrations.

items.q: When did you get your first mobile phone?
items.text: I got my first one when I started college, at around sixteen. It was a basic model that could only make calls and send texts, but I was absolutely thrilled with it, even though it seems ancient by today's standards.

items.q: How often do you use your mobile phone?
items.text: Far too often, if I'm honest. It's become almost indispensable for work and staying in touch, so it's rarely out of my hand. Lately I've been trying to set limits, because it's easy to lose track of time.

items.q: What do you mainly use your phone for?
items.text: Mostly for work, to be honest. I reply to students' messages, check emails and join video calls. Outside work, I read the news and keep in touch with my elder sister in Dhaka, so it's become a real lifeline.

items.q: Do you prefer phone calls or text messages?
items.text: For quick things, texting, since it's fast and doesn't interrupt anyone. But for anything important, I much prefer a call. You can hear the tone of someone's voice, which makes the exchange feel far more genuine.

items.q: Do you think young children should have smartphones?
items.text: Not at a very young age. A basic phone for emergencies is sensible, but unrestricted internet access can be harmful. I think parents should introduce smartphones gradually and keep an eye on how they're used.

items.q: What technology do you use most often?
items.text: My laptop, without question. I use it all day at work for applications, emails and research, and in the evenings for studying. My phone is a close second, but the laptop is really the backbone of my working day.

items.q: How does technology help you in your work?
items.text: Enormously. Almost every application is submitted online now, and I can hold video meetings with universities abroad. Tasks that once took days can be done in hours, which has streamlined our work considerably.

items.q: Do you think you rely too much on technology?
items.text: To some extent, yes. It makes life easier, but I've noticed I reach for my phone out of habit rather than need. I'm trying to be more mindful, especially in the evenings when I should be relaxing.

items.q: Is there any piece of technology you'd like to buy?
items.text: I'd quite like a good e-reader. I read a lot, and carrying several books around isn't very practical. An e-reader would be lighter and easier on the eyes than my phone, so it seems a worthwhile investment.

items.q: Do older people in your country find technology difficult?
items.text: Many do, although it's improving. My grandfather, for instance, now makes video calls to my elder sister, but it took a lot of patience to teach him. Once they see the benefits, older people can be surprisingly receptive.

items.q: Do you do any sports or exercise?
items.text: I try to, though not as consistently as I should. I go for a brisk walk most evenings, and occasionally I play badminton. I always feel rejuvenated afterwards, so I really ought to do more of it.

items.q: Did you play any sports at school?
items.text: Yes, cricket was my main sport, and I played for my school team for a couple of years. I wasn't the most talented player, but I made up for it with sheer enthusiasm, and it taught me a lot about teamwork.

items.q: Do you prefer exercising alone or with other people?
items.text: It depends. For walking, I prefer being alone, because it gives me time to think. For something like badminton, though, company makes it far more enjoyable and keeps me accountable, so I'm less likely to skip it.

items.q: Do you have a healthy lifestyle?
items.text: Reasonably, I'd say. I eat home-cooked food most of the time and try to stay active, but my sleep could be better. It's an ongoing effort, but I think I'm gradually cultivating better habits.

items.q: Are people in your country becoming more health-conscious?
items.text: Gradually, yes. You now see many people walking or jogging in parks early in the morning, which was rare before. There's a heightened awareness of diet too, although fast food is still hugely popular among young people.

items.q: Do you prefer tea or coffee?
items.text: Tea, without a doubt. It's a bit of a ritual here, and I probably have three or four cups a day. Coffee is fine occasionally, but nothing quite beats a hot cup of tea in the morning.

items.q: How do you take your tea?
items.text: I like it strong, with milk and just a little sugar. My mother sometimes adds ginger or cardamom, especially in winter, which gives it a lovely aromatic quality. Plain black tea is fine too, but milk tea is my favourite.

items.q: Do you often drink tea outside the home?
items.text: Quite often, yes. Roadside tea stalls are everywhere here, and meeting friends at one is a big part of our social life. There's a convivial atmosphere at those stalls that you simply can't find in a café.

items.q: Is coffee becoming more popular in your country?
items.text: Definitely, especially among young people in cities. New coffee shops keep opening in Dhaka, and they've become trendy places to study or meet friends. Tea is still far more common, though, particularly outside the big cities.

items.q: Do you think you drink too much tea?
items.text: Possibly, yes. Three or four cups a day may be a bit much, especially in the evening, as it sometimes keeps me awake. I've been trying to cut back after dinner, though with mixed results so far.

items.q: Do you do much housework?
items.text: A fair amount, yes. I take care of my own room and help out at the weekend. I can't say I enjoy it, but there's a certain satisfaction in a tidy, well-organised space.

items.q: Which household chore do you dislike the most?
items.text: Washing dishes, without a doubt. After a big family meal there's always a mountain of them, and it seems to take forever. I'd much rather sweep the floor or do the shopping than face that seemingly endless pile.

items.q: Did you help with housework as a child?
items.text: A little. My mother expected us to make our beds and keep our school things in order. At the time I grumbled about it, but looking back, those small responsibilities taught me to look after my own space.

items.q: Is housework shared equally between men and women in your country?
items.text: Not yet, honestly. Traditionally, women have done most of it, and that's still common. However, younger couples, especially in cities, are increasingly sharing chores, which I see as a welcome shift.

items.q: Do you think children should do housework?
items.text: Yes, within reason. Simple chores like tidying their room or setting the table teach responsibility. It also stops them from taking for granted how much work goes into running a home.

items.q: Did you get pocket money when you were a child?
items.text: Yes, a small amount each week from my father. I usually spent it on snacks or comics, but occasionally I'd save up for a new cricket bat. That was probably my first lesson in delayed gratification.

items.q: Are you good at saving money?
items.text: I'm getting better at it. I used to spend fairly carelessly, but now I set aside a fixed amount each month before anything else. Being frugal in small ways gives me real peace of mind.

items.q: What do you spend most of your money on?
items.text: Apart from contributing to household expenses, mostly books, transport and the occasional meal out with friends. I'm also putting money aside for studying abroad, so I try not to splash out on anything unnecessary.

items.q: Do you prefer paying in cash or by mobile?
items.text: Mostly by mobile these days. Mobile banking apps are hugely popular in Bangladesh, and they've revolutionised everyday payments here. Rickshaw fares and small market purchases are still usually paid in cash, though.

items.q: Do you think schools should teach children about money?
items.text: Absolutely. Many young people finish school without knowing how to budget or save properly. Basic financial lessons would help them avoid debt and make informed decisions once they start earning.

items.q: What good habits do you have?
items.text: I'd say reading before bed is my best habit. I also keep a to-do list and try to walk most evenings. None of these are dramatic, but together they make my days feel more purposeful.

items.q: Do you have any habits you would like to change?
items.text: One or two, definitely. I spend too long on my phone, and I sometimes procrastinate. I'm slowly working on both, though old habits are surprisingly hard to break.

items.q: How do you usually develop a new habit?
items.text: I start small and attach it to something I already do. For example, I read ten pages right after my evening tea. Keeping it manageable like that makes a new habit much easier to sustain.

items.q: Did you have any bad habits as a child?
items.text: Oh yes, I used to bite my nails constantly, especially before exams. My mother tried everything to stop me. Eventually I simply outgrew it, although I still catch myself doing it when I'm nervous.

items.q: Do you think we learn our habits from our family?
items.text: To a large extent, yes. I got my love of tea and my habit of rising early from my parents. Children absorb a great deal simply by watching the adults around them, both good and bad.

items.q: What do you usually do in your free time?
items.text: It varies with my mood. Often I'll read or listen to music, and if I have more time I'll meet friends or watch a film. I try to spend it on things that genuinely relax me rather than mindless scrolling.

items.q: Do you prefer spending your free time alone or with others?
items.text: A mixture, really. After a long day with students, I often need some quiet time alone to recover. But at weekends I actively seek out friends, because I'd feel quite isolated without them.

items.q: How do you relax after a busy day?
items.text: Usually with something simple. I'll read, listen to music, or watch an episode of a show. Anything that lets me properly decompress from work does the trick.

items.q: Do you have enough free time?
items.text: Not really, if I'm honest. Between work and study, my weekdays fill up fast. I safeguard my weekends fiercely, but I do wish I had a little more downtime during the week.

items.q: Do you think people have less free time today than in the past?
items.text: In a sense, yes. People work longer hours and are constantly connected, so leisure time gets squeezed. Ironically, though, much of our free time is now spent on screens rather than genuinely fulfilling activities.

items.q: How do you usually travel around?
items.text: Mostly by bus and rickshaw for daily trips, and occasionally a ride-share app when I'm in a hurry. It works well enough, though the traffic can turn even a short journey into a real ordeal.

items.q: Do you often use public transport?
items.text: Quite often, yes, mainly buses and the occasional rickshaw for shorter trips. It's affordable and saves the stress of parking, although it can get congested during peak hours, which is the main downside.

items.q: How do you usually get to work?
items.text: Usually by rickshaw, since the office is only a short ride from home. On pleasant mornings I sometimes walk instead. It's a fairly stress-free commute compared to what my elder sister faces in Dhaka traffic.

items.q: Is traffic a problem where you live?
items.text: Very much so, especially in the bigger cities. Congestion during rush hour is genuinely frustrating and eats into everyone's day. I think better public transport is really the only viable long-term solution.

items.q: Would you like to own a car one day?
items.text: Perhaps eventually, mainly for family trips to our village. For now, though, it isn't really necessary, and the running costs are quite high. A motorbike might be a more sensible compromise in the meantime.

items.q: Do you like walking?
items.text: I do, more than I expected to. A slow evening walk is one of my favourite ways to unwind, and it's good for my health too. It clears my head far more effectively than sitting in front of a screen.

items.q: How often do you go for a walk?
items.text: Almost every evening, weather permitting. I usually walk for around half an hour after work. During the monsoon it's harder, but I try to keep it up, because skipping it leaves me feeling restless.

items.q: Where do you like to go for a walk?
items.text: My favourite spot is the embankment along the Jamuna. The breeze off the river is lovely, and the view at sunset is breathtaking. It's quite popular too, so I often bump into people I know.

items.q: Did you walk a lot as a child?
items.text: Constantly. I walked to school every day with my friends, and we'd often take the long way home just to dawdle and chat. Those walks were a highlight of the day rather than a chore.

items.q: Do you think people walk less nowadays than in the past?
items.text: Definitely. With rickshaws, motorbikes and ride-share apps so readily available, many people won't even walk short distances. It's a pity, because walking is such a simple way to stay fit and clear-headed.

items.q: What's the weather like where you live?
items.text: Hot and humid for much of the year. We have a long summer, then a heavy monsoon from around June, and a short, pleasant winter. The monsoon rain can be torrential, and flooding is common near the river.

items.q: What kind of weather do you like?
items.text: I'm fondest of mild, sunny weather, the kind you get here in winter. It's warm enough to be comfortable but not stifling, so you can actually enjoy being outside. The intense summer heat I find rather oppressive.

items.q: What is your favourite season?
items.text: Winter, easily. It's short here but lovely, with cool, pleasant days and clear skies. It's the season when I feel most energetic and want to be out and about, so I always look forward to it.

items.q: Does the weather affect your daily plans?
items.text: Quite a bit, actually. The rainy season here can be relentless, so I often check the forecast before heading out. On a pleasant, sunny day I'm far more likely to go out and do something active.

items.q: Has the weather in your country changed in recent years?
items.text: People certainly feel it has. Summers seem hotter and longer, and the rains are less predictable than they used to be. My grandfather often says the seasons have become far more erratic than in his youth.

items.q: Do you like reading?
items.text: Yes, very much. I've been a keen reader since childhood. I mostly read non-fiction these days, especially business or self-improvement, since I enjoy the feeling of broadening my knowledge with each book.

items.q: What kind of books do you enjoy?
items.text: I lean towards non-fiction, particularly psychology and personal growth. Occasionally I'll pick up a good novel to switch off, but generally I prefer something that offers a genuine insight or two.

items.q: Do you prefer printed books or e-books?
items.text: Printed books, definitely. I love the feel of paper and being able to see my progress through the pages. That said, e-books are handy for travelling, so I can see myself embracing both eventually.

items.q: What did you read as a child?
items.text: Mostly comics and adventure stories, which I borrowed from friends or bought with my pocket money. I remember being completely engrossed in them, often reading late into the night by torchlight.

items.q: Do you think young people read less than they used to?
items.text: In terms of books, probably yes, as phones and social media compete for their attention. But they actually read a great deal online. The problem is that it's often fragmented content rather than anything in depth.

items.q: Do you like listening to music?
items.text: I do, it's part of my daily life really. I listen while I work, travel and relax. My taste is fairly eclectic, from mellow acoustic tracks to a bit of classical when I need to concentrate.

items.q: What kind of music is popular in your country?
items.text: Traditional folk music is still hugely popular, especially Baul songs and the classics of Tagore and Nazrul. Younger people also love modern Bangla bands and Western pop, so there's a fascinating fusion of old and new.

items.q: Can you play a musical instrument?
items.text: Not properly, unfortunately. I dabbled with the guitar as a teenager but never persevered. It's one of those things I'd genuinely love to return to one day, when I finally have the time.

items.q: Do you like singing?
items.text: I enjoy it, though only in private or among close friends. I wouldn't sing in front of a crowd, but humming along to a favourite song is one of life's simple pleasures.

items.q: Do you think children should learn music at school?
items.text: I really think they should. Learning an instrument teaches discipline and patience, and it gives children a creative outlet that other subjects don't always offer. I sometimes wish I'd had more encouragement myself when I was younger.

items.q: What sports do you like?
items.text: Cricket, above all, which is almost a national obsession here. I enjoy playing casually, but I love watching it even more. I also play a bit of badminton, which is a fun way to stay active with friends.

items.q: Did you play much sport as a child?
items.text: All the time. After school, my friends and I would play cricket in any open field we could find, often until it got dark. Those makeshift matches, with a taped tennis ball and a wooden bat, are some of my happiest memories.

items.q: Do you enjoy watching sports?
items.text: Absolutely, especially cricket. There's a real buzz when the national team is playing, and the whole country seems to stop and watch. Even people who aren't usually into sport get caught up in the excitement.

items.q: Is there a sport you would like to try in the future?
items.text: I'd love to learn to swim properly, which might sound surprising given that I grew up beside a huge river. I can just about stay afloat, but I'd like to improve, partly for fitness and partly because it's such a vital life skill.

items.q: Do you think sport is important for young people?
items.text: Definitely. Beyond keeping them fit, sport teaches young people how to cope with losing, cooperate with others and stay disciplined. At a time when so many kids are glued to their screens, getting them outside matters more than ever.

items.q: Do you like taking photos?
items.text: I do, casually at least. I mostly take photos on my phone when I travel or see something striking. I'm no expert, but I love the idea of preserving a moment so I can look back on it later.

items.q: What do you usually take photos of?
items.text: Mostly landscapes and family moments. The Jamuna at sunset is a favourite subject, because the light on the water is just breathtaking. I also take lots of pictures of my nephew whenever we visit my sister in Dhaka.

items.q: Do you like keeping photos of special events?
items.text: Definitely. I love looking back at photos from trips and celebrations, because they bring the feelings of that day rushing back. They're some of my most treasured possessions, honestly.

items.q: Do you prefer printed photos or keeping them on your phone?
items.text: Practically, I keep almost everything on my phone, but I have a real soft spot for printed photos. My mother still has old albums from her wedding, and flicking through them together has a nostalgic charm that scrolling never quite matches.

items.q: Do you think people take too many photos nowadays?
items.text: I think so, yes. Because it costs nothing, people snap hundreds of pictures and hardly ever look at them again. Sometimes I feel we're so busy capturing a moment that we forget to actually enjoy it.

items.q: Are you interested in art?
items.text: I appreciate it, though from a distance. I enjoy visiting exhibitions and admiring how much emotion an artist can convey in a single piece, even if I can't create anything like it myself.

items.q: What kind of art do you like?
items.text: I'm most drawn to traditional Bangladeshi art, particularly the colourful rickshaw paintings you see everywhere here. They're bold, cheerful and full of detail, and I love that such intricate work decorates something so ordinary.

items.q: Are you good at drawing or painting?
items.text: Not really, I'll admit. I enjoy looking at art far more than creating it. My drawing skills are fairly rudimentary, so I happily leave that to more talented people.

items.q: Did you do art at school when you were a child?
items.text: We had art classes in primary school, and I remember enjoying them even though my pictures were fairly clumsy. It was a nice break from memorising facts, and it let us be a bit more imaginative than usual.

items.q: Do you think art is important in education?
items.text: Absolutely. Art encourages children to think creatively and express feelings they might not have words for yet. Sadly, it's often sidelined here in favour of subjects seen as more practical, which I think is a real missed opportunity.

items.q: Do you collect anything?
items.text: Books, if that counts. I find it hard to give any away, so my collection just keeps growing. There's something comforting about a shelf full of books you've read, or still intend to read one day.

items.q: Did you collect anything as a child?
items.text: Stamps and coins, like lots of children back then. My father would sometimes bring home old coins that customers had given him at the shop, and I kept them in a tin box as if they were priceless treasures.

items.q: What kinds of things do people in your country collect?
items.text: Stamps and coins used to be the classic choices, though they're less common now. These days younger people are more likely to collect cricket memorabilia, like signed bats or team jerseys, which says a lot about how much the sport means here.

items.q: Why do you think people like collecting things?
items.text: I think it gives people a sense of purpose and achievement, slowly building something over time. There's also the thrill of the hunt, that excitement of finally finding the one missing piece you've been searching for.

items.q: Would you like to start a new collection in the future?
items.text: Maybe, if I ever get to study abroad. I'd love to collect something small from every city I visit, nothing expensive, just a modest memento that brings the experience back whenever I look at it.

items.q: Do you play any video games?
items.text: Occasionally, mostly simple ones on my phone to pass the time. I'm not a serious gamer by any means. For me it's more of a light distraction during a break than a proper hobby.

items.q: What games did you play when you were a child?
items.text: Mostly outdoor games with the neighbourhood kids, like hide and seek, kabaddi and, of course, cricket. We spent long, carefree afternoons outside, and nobody needed a screen to have a good time.

items.q: Do you enjoy playing board games?
items.text: I do, especially carrom, which is hugely popular in Bangladesh. My family sometimes plays after dinner, and it gets surprisingly cut-throat, particularly between me and my younger sister, who absolutely hates losing.

items.q: Do adults in your country play games?
items.text: Quite a lot, actually. Older men often gather at tea stalls to play cards or chess in the evenings, and ludo on mobile phones has become a national pastime for people of all ages.

items.q: Do you think video games are good for children?
items.text: In moderation, they can be. Some games genuinely improve problem-solving and reaction speed. The real issue is when children play for hours on end, because it can become quite addictive and take time away from studying and being outdoors.

items.q: Do you enjoy outdoor activities?
items.text: Yes, whenever I get the chance. I love being outdoors, whether it's a walk by the river or a short trip somewhere green. Being in nature is easily the best way for me to rejuvenate.

items.q: What outdoor activities are popular in your country?
items.text: Cricket is the obvious one, played in every field and alley. Apart from that, people enjoy fishing, boating on the rivers and family picnics, which are a cherished winter tradition here.

items.q: Did you spend a lot of time outdoors as a child?
items.text: Almost constantly. My mother had a hard time getting me inside before dark. I was either playing cricket, climbing trees or wandering along the riverbank, so I was perpetually covered in mud when I finally came home.

items.q: Do you prefer being indoors or outdoors?
items.text: Given the choice, outdoors, though the weather here decides a lot. In the height of summer the heat can be sweltering, so I stay in, but on a cool winter morning nothing beats being outside.

items.q: Do you think people spend less time outdoors than in the past?
items.text: Sadly, yes. Cities are more crowded, open spaces are disappearing, and screens keep people indoors. I think we're gradually becoming disconnected from nature, which probably affects our mood and health more than we realise.

items.q: Are you interested in gardening?
items.text: A little, yes. We keep a few potted plants at home, and I quite enjoy tending to them. There's something calming about nurturing something and watching it grow because of the small effort you put in.

items.q: What kind of plants do you have at home?
items.text: Mostly small, low-maintenance ones on our balcony, like aloe vera, a money plant and a couple of chilli plants. My mother also grows a few herbs, which she proudly uses in her cooking.

items.q: Does anyone in your family enjoy gardening?
items.text: My grandmother, without a doubt. At the village home she grows beans, pumpkins and all sorts of vegetables. Her understanding of soil and seasons is completely instinctive, built up over decades rather than learned from books.

items.q: Did you do any gardening as a child?
items.text: A little, at my grandparents' house. My grandfather would let me help plant seeds, and I remember checking every morning to see if anything had sprouted. That kind of patience didn't come naturally to me back then.

items.q: Would you like to have a garden of your own one day?
items.text: I'd love that. Living in a flat, a proper garden isn't really possible, but in the future I'd like a small plot where I could grow vegetables. Eating something you've grown yourself must be incredibly rewarding.

items.q: Do you like writing?
items.text: I do, actually. My work involves a fair bit of writing, and I've grown to enjoy shaping ideas into clear, coherent sentences. I sometimes jot down thoughts in a notebook too, just for myself.

items.q: Did you enjoy writing when you were at school?
items.text: Not especially, to be honest. Essay writing felt like a chore because we mostly had to memorise model answers. It was only at university that I started to enjoy it, once I could articulate my own ideas rather than copying someone else's.

items.q: Do you often write emails or letters?
items.text: Emails, yes, mostly for work. Handwritten letters have almost disappeared, which is a shame. There's a personal warmth to a letter that a quick email just can't quite replicate.

items.q: Have you ever written a poem or a story?
items.text: Only a few short poems in Bengali when I was a teenager, mostly about the river and the monsoon. They were fairly sentimental, looking back, but I still keep them in an old notebook at home.

items.q: Do you think handwriting will still be important in the future?
items.text: Less than before, certainly, since so much is typed now. Still, I think it will always matter to some degree. A handwritten note has a personal touch, and writing by hand helps ideas sink in far better than typing does.

items.q: Can you dance?
items.text: Not particularly well. I'll join in at weddings and celebrations, which is impossible to avoid here, but I'd never call myself a dancer. I do it purely for the fun of the moment rather than any real flair.

items.q: Is dancing popular in your country?
items.text: Very much so, especially at weddings and cultural festivals. Classical and folk dance are also taught formally, and during Pohela Boishakh you often see groups performing in vibrant traditional costumes.

items.q: Did you learn to dance when you were a child?
items.text: No, dance lessons were more common for girls where I grew up. My younger sister took classical dance classes for a few years, though, and she was genuinely graceful, unlike her brother.

items.q: Do you enjoy watching other people dance?
items.text: Definitely, especially skilled performers. I once watched a Manipuri dance performance at a cultural event, and the control and precision were mesmerising. It's a completely different experience from watching relatives dance at a wedding.

items.q: Do you think dancing is a good way to keep fit?
items.text: I'd say it's one of the best, because people forget they're exercising. It works the whole body and lifts your mood at the same time, so it's far easier to stick with than a dull gym routine.

items.q: What hobbies do you have?
items.text: Reading is my main one, usually with a cup of tea in the evening. I also enjoy long walks by the river and watching cricket, which becomes something of an obsession during big tournaments.

items.q: Did you have any hobbies as a child?
items.text: Plenty. I collected stamps, flew kites on the rooftop and played cricket whenever I could. Kite flying was my favourite, and I'd spend hours trying to outmanoeuvre the neighbours' kites and cut their strings.

items.q: Do you prefer doing hobbies alone or with others?
items.text: It depends on the hobby. Reading and writing I much prefer in solitude, in a quiet corner. But sport and travel are far better shared, because the fun is really in the company.

items.q: Is there a new hobby you would like to try?
items.text: Yes, I'd love to learn photography properly. I already enjoy taking casual shots, so mastering the technical side, like lighting and composition, feels like a natural and exciting progression.

items.q: Do you think it's important to have hobbies?
items.text: I really do. Hobbies give you a break from the pressure of work and let you do something purely for enjoyment. Without them, life can easily become a monotonous cycle of working, eating and sleeping.

items.q: Do you like watching films?
items.text: I do, very much. It's my go-to way to unwind at the weekend. I enjoy a good thriller or a thoughtful drama, and I especially like films that are genuinely thought-provoking long after they've ended.

items.q: What kind of films are popular in your country?
items.text: Commercial action films and romantic dramas have always been popular here, along with Indian and Hollywood blockbusters. Recently, though, some Bangladeshi directors have made critically acclaimed films that are attracting a younger, more discerning audience.

items.q: Do you prefer watching films at home or at the cinema?
items.text: Both have their charm, but I usually watch at home for the comfort. That said, for a big, visually spectacular film, the cinema experience is hard to beat, so I save those for the big screen.

items.q: What was the last film you watched?
items.text: It was a historical drama about the Liberation War, which I watched with my father. It was quite heavy in places, but it was beautifully shot, and it sparked a long conversation between us about what my grandparents lived through at that time.

items.q: Do you think films can help people learn a language?
items.text: Without a doubt. My English listening improved a lot through watching films with subtitles. You pick up natural expressions, intonation and slang that textbooks rarely teach, and it's far more enjoyable than studying grammar.

items.q: Do you watch much television?
items.text: Not traditional TV, no. Like a lot of people my age, I've shifted almost entirely to streaming, so I watch what I want, when I want. It gives me far more control over my viewing.

items.q: Do you use streaming services?
items.text: All the time. They've completely transformed how I watch things. Having a huge library available whenever I want is incredibly convenient, and I honestly can't imagine going back to fixed TV schedules.

items.q: What kind of programmes do you like?
items.text: I gravitate towards documentaries and the occasional gripping drama. Documentaries in particular appeal to me, because I get to relax and gain a bit of insight at the same time, which feels like time well spent.

items.q: Did you watch much TV when you were a child?
items.text: Quite a lot, especially cartoons after school and cricket matches with my father. Back then the whole family gathered around one television, so watching something together was a real communal experience, which I sometimes miss.

items.q: Do you think people watch too much TV nowadays?
items.text: I think screen time in general is the issue now rather than TV itself. With streaming, it's so easy to binge-watch an entire series in one weekend, and many people, including me occasionally, lose track of time completely.

items.q: Which social media apps do you use most?
items.text: Facebook, mainly, because it's by far the most widely used platform in Bangladesh. It's where my family and friends share news, and for many local businesses it's become indispensable for reaching customers.

items.q: Do you often post things online?
items.text: Not very often. I'm more of a passive user, scrolling and reading rather than sharing. When I do post, it's usually photos from a trip or a family occasion, just to keep relatives in the loop.

items.q: Do you use social media a lot?
items.text: More than I'd like to admit. I use it to stay in touch and follow the news, but I've noticed how easily an hour vanishes. I'm trying to use it more intentionally rather than out of pure habit.

items.q: Do you think social media is good for young people?
items.text: It's a double-edged sword. It helps them learn, connect and express themselves, but it can also fuel anxiety and constant comparison with others. I think the key is teaching young people to use it wisely rather than banning it.

items.q: Has social media changed the way people communicate?
items.text: Enormously. People message constantly but talk face to face less, and conversations have become much shorter and more fragmented. On the positive side, it's much easier for me to stay in touch with friends who've moved abroad.

items.q: What festivals do you celebrate?
items.text: The two Eids are the biggest for us, along with cultural events like Pohela Boishakh, the Bengali New Year. They're wonderful occasions, full of food, family and colour, and the whole community becomes vibrant.

items.q: Which festival do you enjoy the most?
items.text: Eid-ul-Fitr, without a doubt. After a month of fasting, there's a wonderful sense of relief and joy, and the whole family comes together, often at our village home. The jubilant mood lasts for days.

items.q: How do you usually celebrate special occasions?
items.text: Usually with family and a large meal, which is really at the heart of any celebration here. We dress up, visit relatives, and the day is loud, lively and warm. Food is always the centrepiece.

items.q: How did you celebrate festivals when you were a child?
items.text: Eid was the highlight of my year. I'd get new clothes, and older relatives would give us salami, a small gift of money. My cousins and I would compare how much we'd collected, which was fiercely competitive.

items.q: Do you think festivals have changed over the years?
items.text: In some ways, yes. People now send greetings online instead of visiting everyone in person, and celebrations have become more commercialised, with lots of shopping. But the core of it, family and food, has stayed exactly the same.

items.q: Are there many museums in your hometown?
items.text: Not really. Sirajganj is a modest town, so there's nothing major. The best known is Tagore's old family estate at Shahzadpur, which has been turned into a museum and is quite atmospheric.

items.q: Do you like visiting museums?
items.text: Yes, actually. I find them fascinating, especially history museums, because they bring the past to life in a way books can't. I don't go nearly often enough, but each visit is genuinely enlightening.

items.q: When did you last visit a museum?
items.text: About a year ago, I went to the Liberation War Museum in Dhaka while visiting my sister. It was an incredibly moving experience, and some of the personal letters on display were genuinely harrowing to read.

items.q: Did you go to museums on school trips?
items.text: Only once or twice, as school trips weren't very common where I grew up. I remember being captivated by the old coins and weapons, though, and asking the guide far too many questions.

items.q: Do you think museums will still be popular in the future?
items.text: I think so, as long as they adapt. Young people expect interactive displays and digital content now, so museums that feel dull and static may struggle. But seeing real historical objects in person will always have its appeal.

items.q: Have you ever been to a concert?
items.text: A few times, yes, mostly local ones. There's a special energy to live music that a recording just can't capture. Being surrounded by a crowd who love the same songs is genuinely exhilarating.

items.q: What kind of events are held in your town?
items.text: Mostly local fairs, religious gatherings and cultural programmes on national days. The Baishakhi fair is probably the biggest, with stalls selling handicrafts and snacks, and it draws a sizeable crowd from the surrounding villages.

items.q: Do you enjoy going to public events?
items.text: I do, in moderation. Cultural fairs and festivals have a wonderful atmosphere, and I like being part of the crowd. Very large, chaotic events can be a bit much for me, though, so I pick and choose.

items.q: Do you prefer watching events live or online?
items.text: Live, if possible, because the atmosphere is half the experience. Watching online is convenient, but it feels a bit detached, as if you're looking in from the outside rather than actually taking part.

items.q: Is there an event you would love to attend in the future?
items.text: I'd love to watch a cricket World Cup match in a big stadium, ideally with Bangladesh playing. Being among thousands of passionate fans would be a once-in-a-lifetime experience, and I'd happily travel abroad for it.

items.q: What traditions are important in your family?
items.text: Respecting elders is central, so we greet older relatives formally and seek their blessings at Eid. We also make pitha, traditional rice cakes, in winter, which is a time-honoured ritual my mother learned from my grandmother.

items.q: Do you think traditional culture is important?
items.text: Very much so. It gives people a sense of identity and connects generations. In a fast-changing world, I think preserving our traditions, our language and festivals especially, matters more than ever.

items.q: Did your grandparents teach you about traditions?
items.text: Very much so, especially my grandmother. She has little formal education, but she's a treasure trove of folk tales, proverbs and old customs. Listening to her stories as a child gave me a real sense of where I come from.

items.q: Do you ever wear traditional clothes?
items.text: Quite often, actually. I wear a panjabi at Eid, at weddings and on Pohela Boishakh. It's comfortable and elegant, and wearing it gives me a quiet sense of belonging to something bigger than myself.

items.q: Do you think young people are losing interest in traditional culture?
items.text: To some extent, yes, mainly because of global influences and social media. But I don't think it's diminishing entirely. Many young people still take great pride in their roots, just alongside a more modern lifestyle.

items.q: What is a typical meal in Bangladesh?
items.text: Rice is the foundation of almost every meal, usually with fish curry, lentils and some vegetables. There's even a saying that fish and rice make a Bengali, so it's deeply rooted in our identity.

items.q: Is food an important part of your culture?
items.text: Enormously. In Bangladesh, food is at the centre of almost every gathering. Sharing a meal is how we express hospitality, so it's really far more than just eating.

items.q: What's your favourite local dish?
items.text: Hilsa cooked in mustard sauce, without question. Hilsa is our national fish, and my mother's version is unrivalled in my opinion. Coming from a river town, fresh fish is something I'd miss terribly if I lived abroad.

items.q: Can you cook any local dishes?
items.text: Only a few basic ones, like dal and a simple egg curry. My mother is an excellent cook, so I've never really had to fend for myself in the kitchen, which I know will have to change if I study abroad.

items.q: Has the food in your country changed in recent years?
items.text: Quite noticeably. Fast food outlets and cafés have mushroomed in towns as well as cities, and young people love burgers and pizza. Still, when it comes to family gatherings, traditional home cooking always wins.

items.q: Do you follow the news?
items.text: Yes, I like to stay informed, mostly through news apps and a bit of online reading. I try not to overdo it, though, because too much news can be draining. A quick daily catch-up is usually enough.

items.q: What kind of news are you most interested in?
items.text: Mostly education and international news, since both relate to my job. Changes to student visa rules abroad, for example, directly affect the students I advise, so I keep a close eye on them.

items.q: How do you usually get your news?
items.text: Almost entirely online, through my phone. It's quick and I can check headlines whenever I have a spare moment. I rarely watch the news on television any more, which feels outdated to me now.

items.q: Did your family watch the news together when you were young?
