items.text: Every evening, yes. My father religiously watched the eight o'clock news, and we all had to stay quiet until it finished. As a child I found it boring, but now I realise how much I picked up just by listening.

items.q: Do you trust the news you read online?
items.text: Not everything, no. There's a lot of misleading content online, especially on social media, so I try to cross-check stories with reliable sources before believing them. I think media literacy should really be taught in schools now.

items.q: Who makes you laugh the most?
items.text: My grandfather, surprisingly. He's in his eighties but still incredibly sharp, and he has a wonderfully dry sense of humour. He'll say something outrageous with a completely straight face, and the whole family ends up in fits of laughter.

items.q: Do you like watching comedy shows?
items.text: Yes, I love a good laugh at the end of a long day. Comedy is the easiest way for me to switch off. I especially enjoy clever, observational humour that plays on everyday situations.

items.q: Are you good at telling jokes?
items.text: Not especially. I always rush the punchline or start laughing before I finish. I'm much better at witty remarks in the moment, reacting to what's happening around me, than at telling a prepared joke.

items.q: What did you find funny when you were a child?
items.text: Mostly slapstick, like cartoons where characters fell over or got chased. My sister and I used to watch Mr Bean together and laugh until our stomachs hurt. That kind of physical comedy is universally funny, I think.

items.q: Do you think humour is different in different cultures?
items.text: Definitely. A lot of humour depends on wordplay and shared references, so it often gets lost in translation. I've noticed that some Bengali jokes simply don't work in English, however carefully I try to explain them.

items.q: Do you like making plans?
items.text: I do, generally. Having a rough plan gives me direction and stops me wasting time. That said, I try not to over-plan, because some of the best moments come from being a little spontaneous.

items.q: Do you usually plan your weekends?
items.text: Loosely. I'll usually have one or two things in mind, like visiting relatives or catching up on reading, but I leave plenty of room for rest. After a busy week, a laid-back weekend is exactly what I need.

items.q: Are you good at making decisions?
items.text: I'd say I'm decisive with small things, but I take my time over big ones, weighing up the options carefully. Occasionally I deliberate for too long, but I'd rather be thorough than rush and regret it.

items.q: Who do you ask for advice when you have an important decision to make?
items.text: Usually my father. He ran his own business for over thirty years, so he has a very practical, level-headed way of looking at things. For more personal matters, though, I often talk to my elder sister.

items.q: Is it better to plan for the future or live in the moment?
items.text: I think you need a balance. Planning ahead gives you security, especially with things like careers and savings. But if you're fixated on the future all the time, you can easily miss the joy of what's happening right now.

items.q: Are you an organised person?
items.text: Fairly, yes. I like to keep things in order, both my space and my schedule, because clutter genuinely stresses me out. A little organisation up front spares me a lot of hassle later.

items.q: How do you keep track of your tasks?
items.text: I rely mostly on my phone's calendar and a simple to-do list. At work I'm handling applications for lots of students with different deadlines, so writing everything down is non-negotiable for me.

items.q: Are you more productive in the morning or the evening?
items.text: Definitely the morning. My mind is sharpest then, so I tackle my hardest tasks early. By the evening my focus fades, so I save lighter activities for later in the day.

items.q: Were you organised when you were a child?
items.text: Not at all, I'm afraid. My school bag was always a mess and I was forever losing pencils. My mother despaired of me at times, so being organised is definitely something I learned later in life.

items.q: Do you think it's important for students to be organised?
items.text: Absolutely, and I see it every day in my job. The students who stay organised tend to meet deadlines calmly, while the others end up scrambling at the last minute and making careless mistakes on their applications.

items.q: Do you often change your daily routine?
items.text: Not much during the week, as my working hours are fairly fixed. I do try to vary my weekends, though, because doing exactly the same thing every day can make life feel a bit stale.

items.q: Do you welcome change in your life?
items.text: Cautiously, yes. I'm comfortable with routine, but I've learned that a bit of change usually leads to growth. So even when it feels daunting at first, I try to see it as an opportunity rather than a threat.

items.q: Has anything changed in your life recently?
items.text: Yes, my father retired recently after running his business for over thirty years. It's been a real period of adjustment for the whole family, since he's at home all day now, but it's lovely to see him finally relaxing.

items.q: Is there anything you would like to change about your life?
items.text: I'd like to study abroad at some point, which would be a big change. After years of helping other students do it, I feel ready to step out of my own comfort zone and experience it myself.

items.q: Do you think older people find change harder than young people?
items.text: Generally, yes, though not always. My grandfather is in his eighties and still remarkably adaptable, and he even video calls my sister in Dhaka. But many older people understandably feel more secure with familiar routines.

items.q: Are you a patient person?
items.text: Reasonably, yes, though it depends on the situation. I'm quite patient with people, but I can get restless when I'm stuck waiting, in traffic for instance. It's something I'm consciously working on.

items.q: Is patience important in your job?
items.text: Hugely important. Visa and admission processes can take months, and students naturally get anxious. Part of my role is reassuring them and staying calm and composed, even when they call me for the tenth time about the same thing.

items.q: Were you patient as a child?
items.text: Not in the slightest. I wanted everything immediately, whether it was my food, a new toy or my turn at batting. My parents constantly told me to wait, which I found completely infuriating at the time.

items.q: Who is the most patient person you know?
items.text: My mother, without question. She looks after our home, helps care for my grandparents and still finds time for everyone. I've never seen her lose her temper, which is honestly admirable given how much she juggles.

items.q: Do you think people are less patient nowadays than in the past?
items.text: I'd say so. We're used to instant gratification now, with fast internet, quick deliveries and endless entertainment on our phones. As a result, waiting even a few minutes can feel unbearable to many people.

items.q: Do you have a favourite colour?
items.text: I do, it's blue. I find it calming and easy on the eye, so a lot of my clothes and even my room lean towards it. It has a soothing quality that I'm naturally drawn to.

items.q: What colours do you usually wear?
items.text: Mostly understated shades like navy, grey and white for everyday wear, since they look smart for work. On festival days, though, I'm happy to wear something brighter to match the mood.

items.q: Is there a colour you don't like?
items.text: Not strongly, but I'm not keen on very bright orange or neon shades. They feel a bit loud and garish to me, especially on clothes, although I can see why some people love them.

items.q: Do colours have special meanings in your country?
items.text: Yes, quite a few. Red and white are strongly associated with Pohela Boishakh, and the green and red of our flag are symbolic too, representing the land and the sacrifice of those who fought for independence.

items.q: Do you think colours can affect people's mood?
items.text: I really believe they can. Soft blues and greens make a room feel calm, while warm colours tend to be more energising. That's probably why hospitals and offices choose their colour schemes so deliberately.

items.q: Are you good with numbers?
items.text: Reasonably good, I'd say. My business studies involved plenty of accounting and statistics, and I often helped my father with his shop accounts, so I'm fairly proficient with everyday calculations and budgets.

items.q: Did you enjoy maths at school?
items.text: I did, mostly. I liked that there was always a clear answer, unlike essay questions. Geometry was my weak point, though, and some of those proofs left me utterly baffled.

items.q: Is there a number you consider lucky?
items.text: Not really, to be honest. I'm not very superstitious about numbers. I know many people have a lucky one, but I've never felt that any particular number has made a difference in my life.

items.q: Do people in your country believe in lucky numbers?
items.text: Some do, though it's not as big a thing as in some other countries. You'll occasionally hear of people paying extra for a phone number with a distinctive pattern, but most people don't take it too seriously.

items.q: Do you think people remember numbers less than they used to?
items.text: Definitely. I remember knowing dozens of phone numbers by heart as a child, but now I barely know my own sister's. We've outsourced our memory to our phones, which is convenient but slightly worrying.

items.q: Do you enjoy giving gifts?
items.text: I really do. I love the challenge of finding something that suits the person perfectly, and their reaction when they open it is the best part. A thoughtful gift means far more than an expensive one.

items.q: What was the last gift you bought for someone?
items.text: A set of picture books for my four-year-old nephew. He's at that age where he wants stories read to him constantly, so I chose ones with vivid illustrations. My sister says he takes them to bed every night.

items.q: Do you like receiving gifts?
items.text: Of course, who doesn't? But what I appreciate most is the thought behind it. A small, meaningful present from someone who knows me well means much more than something lavish given without much care.

items.q: When do people give gifts in your country?
items.text: Mainly at Eid, weddings and birthdays, although birthdays are a more recent custom in many families. At weddings especially, gift-giving is quite an elaborate affair, and relatives sometimes feel pressure to give something impressive.

items.q: Do you think it's better to give money or a gift?
items.text: It depends on the person. Money is practical, especially for newly married couples, and Eid salami is a much-loved custom. But a carefully chosen gift shows real consideration, so for close friends I'd always choose something personal.

items.q: Do you enjoy helping other people?
items.text: I really do. My whole job is essentially about helping people reach their goals, and I find that deeply fulfilling. Even small acts of help brighten my day, and they usually come back around in some form.

items.q: How do you usually help people in your family?
items.text: Mostly with practical things. I sort out bills and online forms for my parents, and I help my younger sister with her English. It's nothing heroic, but it takes a bit of pressure off everyone.

items.q: Did your parents teach you to help others?
items.text: Very much so. My father often let struggling customers pay later, and my mother always shares food with the neighbours. Growing up around that kind of generosity, helping others just became second nature to me.

items.q: Do people in your country often help their neighbours?
items.text: Traditionally, yes, especially in villages and small towns like mine. If someone's ill or there's a wedding, neighbours rally round without being asked. In big cities like Dhaka, though, people tend to keep themselves to themselves more.

items.q: Do you think people are less helpful than they used to be?
items.text: Not less helpful, just busier. When there's a flood, I've seen people raise money and deliver supplies remarkably quickly, often mobilising through social media. The kindness is still there, it simply looks different now.

items.q: Do you find it easy to talk to strangers?
items.text: It depends on the setting, but generally yes. I'm fairly comfortable striking up a conversation, and you often learn something interesting. A little friendliness goes a long way in putting people at ease.

items.q: In what situations do you talk to strangers?
items.text: Most often while travelling, on long bus journeys to Dhaka, for instance. Four hours is a long time, so chatting to the person beside you is almost inevitable. I've had some surprisingly deep conversations that way.

items.q: Were you told not to talk to strangers as a child?
items.text: Yes, my mother was quite strict about it, especially in crowded places like markets. Looking back, it was a perfectly reasonable rule, although in our small neighbourhood almost nobody was really a stranger.

items.q: Are people in your country friendly towards strangers?
items.text: Generally, very. Bangladeshis are known for their warmth, and it's quite normal for someone to invite a traveller for tea or walk them somewhere rather than just pointing. Foreign visitors often mention how welcoming people are.

items.q: Do you think it's safe to talk to strangers online?
items.text: It can be, but you have to be cautious. It's very easy for people to misrepresent themselves online, so I'd never share personal details with someone I hadn't met. Young people especially need to be careful.

items.q: Would you say you're a happy person?
items.text: I'd say so, yes. I have a supportive family, a job that feels meaningful and good health. I've learned not to take things for granted, and that alone makes me feel quite fortunate most days.

items.q: What kinds of things make you happy?
items.text: Simple things, mostly. Time with people I love, a good book, a quiet evening after a productive day. I've realised over time that lasting contentment rarely comes from big events, but from small, everyday moments.

items.q: What made you happy when you were a child?
items.text: Very simple pleasures, honestly. Flying kites on the roof, visiting my grandparents in the village and eating mangoes straight from their trees. Life felt blissfully uncomplicated back then, with no deadlines or responsibilities to worry about.

items.q: Do you think money can buy happiness?
items.text: Only up to a point. Having enough to live comfortably certainly reduces stress, but beyond that, relationships and purpose matter far more. Some of the most cheerful people I know, like my grandmother, live very frugally indeed.

items.q: Do you think people are happier now than in the past?
items.text: It's hard to say. Life is certainly more comfortable, but people seem more stressed and constantly compare themselves with others online. My grandparents had far less, yet they seem more at peace than many young people I know.

items.q: Do you have a pet?
items.text: Not at the moment. We had a cat for years when I was growing up, but in a rented flat with a strict landlord it's just not practical right now.

items.q: What's your favourite animal?
items.text: Elephants. There's something calming about how slowly and deliberately they move, and I've read they have incredible memories, which I find fascinating.

items.q: Are pets popular in your country?
items.text: More than they used to be, especially cats, which are seen as easier to keep in apartments. Dogs are still less common in cities, partly for cultural reasons and partly because there's nowhere to walk them.

items.q: Do you often go to parks?
items.text: Not as often as I'd like. There's one decent park about twenty minutes from my flat, and I try to go early on Friday mornings before it fills up. The rest of the week I rarely see anything green.

items.q: Do you prefer the countryside or the city?
items.text: For living, the city — I need the jobs, the internet, the convenience. For a break, the countryside, no question. Two days by a river does more for my head than a month of weekends in town.

items.q: Did you spend much time outdoors as a child?
items.text: All the time. Our neighbourhood was much less built-up then, so there were fields to play in and ponds to swim in. Children today in the same area have a playground the size of a car park.

items.q: Do you mind noise?
items.text: It depends on the kind. Background noise — a café, traffic — I can tune out. What I can't stand is someone's phone speaker on a bus; that gets under my skin instantly.

items.q: Is your area noisy?
items.text: Very. There's construction on two sides of our building and a main road on the third, so the only quiet hour is between four and five in the morning.

items.q: Do you think cities are noisier than they used to be?
items.text: Undoubtedly. My parents talk about hearing birds from their window in the same area where I now hear only horns. More people, more vehicles, more construction — the noise is just the sum of all that.

items.q: Describe a person who has influenced you
items.text: I would like to talk about someone very close to home. The person who has influenced me most is my father, who ran a small business in Sirajganj for over thirty years and has only recently retired. Obviously I have known him all my life, but I think I only really started to understand him as a teenager, when I began helping out in his shop after school. Growing up, I watched him deal with setbacks that would have discouraged most people, yet he always stayed calm and kept going. There were slow seasons, especially during the monsoon, when hardly anyone came in, but he never let his worries spill over into family life. What shaped me was not any single piece of advice, but the quiet example he set day after day. He treated every customer, however difficult, with the same integrity, and he taught me that a good reputation is built slowly and lost quickly. When I was struggling to choose a career, he never pushed me in one direction; instead he encouraged me to be self-reliant and make my own decisions. Looking back, almost everything I value about hard work and honesty can be traced to him, and I try to bring the same patience to my job at the consultancy, especially with anxious students. His influence has been profound, and I still catch myself asking what he would do in a tricky situation. In many ways he remains my quiet role model, even now that I am an adult, and I suspect he always will be.

items.q: Do you still ask your father for advice?
items.text: Yes, quite often, especially about money or big decisions. Since he retired he has more time to talk, so we usually chat over tea in the evening, and his advice is still remarkably level-headed.

items.q: Would you like to be like him in the future?
items.text: In many ways, yes. I would love to have his patience and honesty, although I probably will not run a shop. I just hope people eventually see me as someone as trustworthy as he is.

items.q: Describe a time when you spent time with a child
items.text: I would like to describe a lovely afternoon I spent with my nephew. Not long ago, during the winter, my elder sister paid us a surprise visit from Dhaka with her four-year-old son, and I ended up spending a whole afternoon with him. My sister had some errands to run in town with my mother, so I happily volunteered to keep him entertained. I had always found him endearing, but this was the first time we had really had a proper day together, just the two of us. He was remarkably inquisitive for his age, firing off questions about almost everything, some of which genuinely stumped me, like why the river never runs out of water. We built a fort out of cushions, drew a few clumsy animals, and I read him a couple of stories, putting on silly voices that he found hilarious. Later we walked down to the bank of the Jamuna to watch the boats, which he absolutely loved. What struck me most was how perceptive children are: he picked up on my mood instantly and kept trying to cheer me up. By evening I was exhausted, but it was the most rewarding kind of tiredness. It reminded me that spending time with a child forces you to slow down and be fully present, something adults rarely manage. Honestly, that afternoon was a welcome escape from my usual routine, and I have made a point of seeing him more often since, even if that means a long bus journey to Dhaka.

items.q: Do you enjoy spending time with children in general?
items.text: Yes, I do, although I find it quite tiring. Children are so honest and unfiltered that you cannot pretend around them, and I think that is rather refreshing compared with the adult world.

items.q: Would you like to have children of your own one day?
items.text: I think so, but not for a few years. I would like to be settled in my career first, and perhaps finish studying abroad, so that I can give them proper time and attention.

items.q: Describe someone you know who has a lot of responsibilities
items.text: When I think about someone with a lot on their plate, one person immediately stands out. The person who comes to mind is my mother, who somehow manages to juggle an enormous number of duties without ever seeming overwhelmed. Besides running the entire household, she helps look after my elderly grandparents in our ancestral village, which means travelling back and forth quite often, and she still finds time to help neighbours during any crisis. On top of that, she manages the household budget and keeps a close eye on my younger sister's studies. As for how she handles it all, what amazes me is how methodical she is; she plans her days carefully so nothing important slips through the cracks. She is usually up before everyone else, and by the time we sit down to breakfast half her list is already done. I have often seen her handle a sick relative, a household emergency and a family gathering all in the same week, yet she rarely complains. She has this quiet resilience that I deeply admire, and she genuinely believes that looking after others is a privilege rather than a burden. Whenever I feel stretched by my own comparatively minor workload, I think of her and feel slightly embarrassed. She has taught me that carrying responsibility gracefully is a skill in itself. Honestly, I consider her the most dependable person I know, and the whole family leans on her more than we probably realise. I really should tell her that more often.

items.q: Do you help your mother with her responsibilities?
items.text: I try to, although not as much as I should. I do the shopping at the weekend and sometimes go with her to the village, but she still shoulders most of the work herself.

items.q: Do you think you will have more responsibilities in the future?
items.text: Almost certainly. As my parents get older, I expect to take on more at home, and my career will bring its own pressures. I just hope I can cope with them as calmly as she does.

items.q: Describe a person you admire
items.text: Someone I genuinely admire is a former teacher of mine who went far beyond what his job required. I knew him through secondary school in Sirajganj, where he taught mathematics, but his real gift was noticing students who were quietly struggling. I was one of them for a while, because I found algebra completely baffling in my first year with him. In terms of his qualities, he was endlessly patient, staying behind after class to help anyone who asked, and he never made you feel foolish for not understanding. What I admired most was his humility; despite being extremely knowledgeable, he always spoke to us as equals. He had a way of making difficult ideas feel accessible, often using examples from the local market or cricket scores, and he clearly cared about the person, not just the grade. Years later, I still remember specific things he said that shaped how I think. As for why I admire him, I think what sets people like him apart is that they are motivated by a genuine desire to help rather than any reward. He was never well paid, and he could easily have earned more from private coaching, but he chose to help struggling students for free instead. He left a lasting impression on hundreds of students, and I count myself lucky to have been one of them. In fact, in my own job I often try to explain things to students the way he once explained things to me.

items.q: Are you still in touch with him?
items.text: Not regularly, but I bump into him now and then in town. He is retired now, and he always asks about my work. It is quite touching that he still remembers me after all these years.

items.q: Would you ever like to become a teacher?
items.text: Perhaps in some form. My job already involves a lot of guiding and explaining, and I find that side of it deeply fulfilling, but I am not sure I have the patience for a classroom of teenagers.

items.q: Describe an intelligent person you know
items.text: I would like to talk about a friend whose mind I have always found slightly intimidating. One of the most intelligent people I know is a close friend from university who studied physics, while I was doing business administration. We met because we lived in the same student hostel, and we have stayed close ever since, even though he now lives in Rajshahi. What sets him apart is not just how much he knows, but how quickly he grasps complicated ideas that leave the rest of us bewildered. He has this analytical mind that breaks any problem into neat, logical steps. I remember him explaining a statistics concept I had struggled with for weeks in about five minutes, and suddenly it made perfect sense. Yet he is never arrogant about it, which makes his intelligence all the more impressive. He is also intellectually curious, always reading about subjects far outside his field, from history to economics. I think real intelligence is exactly this combination of sharpness and open-mindedness, rather than simply getting top marks. As for how I feel about him, talking to him is genuinely stimulating, because he challenges your assumptions without ever making you feel small. I will admit that I sometimes feel a little slow beside him, but mostly I just feel grateful. Honestly, I always come away from our conversations having learned something, and that is rare. I suspect he will end up doing research abroad one day, and I will be very proud of him when he does.

items.q: Do you think intelligence is something people are born with?
items.text: Partly, but I think curiosity and effort matter just as much. My friend was clearly gifted, but he also read constantly, so his intelligence was nurtured as much as it was inherited.

items.q: Do you often ask him for help?
items.text: Now and then, mostly when I need to make sense of numbers at work. He is always happy to help, although he usually ends up teaching me far more than I actually asked for.

items.q: Describe a famous person you would like to meet
items.text: If I could meet any famous person, it would probably be a well-known entrepreneur whose story I find genuinely inspiring. He is famous for building a huge technology company from almost nothing, starting out with a handful of friends and very little money. What fascinates me, though, is not the wealth but the perseverance behind it. I have read a great deal about him, in interviews and in a biography I borrowed from a friend, and I know how many times he failed before succeeding, which I find strangely reassuring. Several of his early ventures went bankrupt, and at one point even people close to him thought he should give up. What draws me to him is his reputation for thinking in genuinely unconventional ways, seeing opportunities others dismiss. As for why I would like to meet him, I would love to ask how he stayed motivated during the years when everything seemed to be collapsing. I imagine he would be surprisingly down-to-earth, because people who have struggled tend to be. Since I studied business administration, I would also be curious to hear what he thinks young people in a country like Bangladesh should focus on. I think a single conversation with someone like that could be more enlightening than any book. Realistically it will never happen, but if it did, I would come prepared with a long list of questions and simply listen. Even a few minutes with him would give me a story to tell my family for years.

items.q: Would you like to be famous yourself?
items.text: Not really. I think fame brings a lot of pressure and very little privacy. I would much rather be respected by the people around me than recognised by strangers in the street.

items.q: Do you think famous people are good role models?
items.text: Some are, especially those who worked hard and stayed humble. But many are admired for the wrong reasons, so young people need to be quite discerning about whose example they follow.

items.q: Describe a friend you have known for a long time
items.text: I would like to talk about my closest friend, whom I have known since our very first week at university, so roughly seven years now. We were both studying business administration and were placed in the same project group, and something just clicked almost immediately, probably because we were both from small towns and slightly overwhelmed by the big campus. By the end of that first term we were sharing notes, meals and far too many cups of tea. Over the years our lives have taken very different directions, yet the friendship has proved remarkably durable. He now works for a bank in Dhaka, while I am still in Sirajganj, so we do not actually see each other often, but whenever we meet it feels as though no time has passed. When we do manage to meet, we usually go for long walks by the river or watch a cricket match together, and in between we talk on the phone most weekends. I think what has kept us close is a shared sense of humour and a kind of unspoken understanding that we will always be there for each other. He is the one person I can be completely candid with, without fear of judgement. What I value most is that our friendship has never felt like hard work; it is genuinely effortless. Honestly, in a world where people drift apart so easily, having one friendship that has lasted this long feels like something worth protecting, and I hope we are still arguing about cricket when we are old men.

items.q: Do you think you will stay friends in the future?
items.text: I am fairly sure we will. We have already survived distance and busy jobs, so I cannot imagine much that would pull us apart now. If anything, the friendship keeps deepening as we get older.

items.q: How do you usually keep in touch?
items.text: Mostly through phone calls and messages. We have a habit of calling each other on Friday evenings, and even if it is only for ten minutes, it keeps us up to date with each other's lives.

items.q: Describe a stranger who helped you
items.text: I would like to describe a small act of kindness that has stayed with me for years. A few years ago I was travelling alone to Chattogram for a job interview, and on my first evening I got hopelessly lost, with a dying phone and no idea where my hotel was. The streets all looked the same in the dark, and I was starting to panic. A middle-aged stranger, who turned out to be a local schoolteacher, noticed me looking anxious and stopped to ask if I needed help. What struck me was how genuinely considerate he was; not only did he give me directions, he actually walked me halfway there. He could easily have ignored me, as most people would have, so his kindness felt almost remarkable. Along the way we chatted, and he told me a little about the area, which turned a stressful moment into a pleasant one. He even recommended a small tea stall near my hotel, which I went back to every day that week. I was incredibly grateful, and I remember trying to offer him something in return, which he politely refused. That small act of kindness has genuinely stayed with me, and it made me more willing to help strangers myself, especially students who come into our office looking lost and nervous. It was a reminder that a little compassion costs nothing but can mean a great deal. I never even learned his name, but I still think of him fondly.

items.q: Do you often help strangers?
items.text: I try to, in small ways. If someone looks lost or needs directions, I usually stop. After my own experience, I know how disorienting it feels to be alone somewhere completely unfamiliar.

items.q: Do you think people are less helpful to strangers nowadays?
items.text: In big cities, perhaps a little, because everyone is in a hurry and slightly suspicious. But in smaller towns like mine, people still stop to help, and I find that very reassuring.

items.q: Describe a family member you are close to
items.text: I would like to talk about someone I see every single day. The family member I am closest to is my younger sister, despite the fact that we argue like any siblings do. She is a few years younger than me and still a student, and she is easily the most hard-working person in our house. In many ways she feels more like a friend than a sibling. We share almost everything, from silly jokes to serious worries, and she is the first person I turn to when something is bothering me. What makes our bond so strong is that we are brutally honest with each other, even when the truth is uncomfortable. As for what we do together, we enjoy simple things, like watching films, walking along the Jamuna in the evening, or just talking late into the night over cups of tea. Sometimes I help her with her English, and in return she tells me when my ideas are ridiculous. She has this ability to make me laugh no matter how miserable I am feeling, which is a real gift, especially after a long, tiring day at work. I think the reason we get along so well is that siblings who grow up together develop an almost intuitive understanding of one another. We can often tell what the other is thinking from a single look across the dinner table. Honestly, I feel incredibly fortunate to have her, because not everyone is lucky enough to be close to their family.

items.q: Do you think you will stay close as you get older?
items.text: I really hope so. She may move away for work or marriage one day, but I think our bond is strong enough to survive the distance, just as it has with my elder sister.

items.q: Do you ever argue with her?
items.text: Of course, usually about trivial things like the television remote. But our arguments never last long, and by dinner time we have normally forgotten what we were squabbling about in the first place.

items.q: Describe a good leader you know or have heard about
items.text: I would like to describe my first manager at the education consultancy where I work, who I think embodies what good leadership really means. She has since moved to our head office in Dhaka, but I worked under her for almost two years. She led a fairly large team of counsellors, and what set her apart was that she led by example rather than by giving orders. If we had a queue of anxious students, she would sit down and help with applications herself. In terms of her qualities, she was genuinely approachable, so people felt comfortable bringing problems to her before they escalated. Rather than taking credit, she was quick to acknowledge everyone's contribution, which made the whole team want to work harder. She also had a talent for staying calm under pressure, which was reassuring during stressful periods, such as the frantic weeks before university application deadlines. What I admired most was her fairness; she treated everyone equally, regardless of seniority. As for why I think she was a good leader, too many leaders confuse authority with respect, but she understood that respect has to be earned. Under her, the team was noticeably more motivated and loyal, and hardly anyone left, which is unusual in our industry. Honestly, she set a standard for how I would want to lead people myself one day, and whenever I help a new colleague settle in, I try to remember how she treated me as a nervous beginner.

items.q: Would you like to be a leader yourself?
items.text: Yes, eventually. I would like to lead a small team one day, but I know I still need more experience. Leadership is not just about giving instructions, it is about earning people's trust.

items.q: Are you still in contact with her?
items.text: Yes, we message occasionally, and she still gives me advice about my career. She was the one who first encouraged me to think seriously about studying abroad myself, which I really appreciate.

items.q: Describe a creative person you admire
items.text: I would like to talk about someone whose imagination I find quite amazing. A creative person I really admire is a friend of mine who works as a graphic designer for an advertising agency in Dhaka. We were in the same year at university, although she was always more interested in art than in accounting. She designs logos, posters and packaging for all kinds of local brands, and she also paints in her spare time. What amazes me is how she can take a dull, ordinary brief and turn it into something genuinely striking. She seems to see possibilities that the rest of us simply miss. I have watched her sketch ideas that at first look random, then slowly come together into something clever and original. She is also fearless about experimenting, which I think is the heart of real creativity; she is not afraid to fail. Talking to her about her process is fascinating, because she draws inspiration from the most unlikely places, like the painted rickshaws in our town or old films. Her work has this distinctive style that you can recognise instantly, which is quite an achievement in a crowded field. Honestly, spending time around her makes me want to be more imaginative in my own work, even if that only means designing a slightly better presentation for students. I think creativity like hers is partly a gift and partly relentless practice, and she has plenty of both. I genuinely believe she will have her own studio one day.

items.q: Do you consider yourself a creative person?
items.text: Not especially, at least not artistically. I am more creative with words and ideas than with pictures. I would love to learn to draw, but I suspect I have no flair for it whatsoever.

items.q: Would you like to have some of her work at home?
items.text: Definitely. She once gave me a small painting of the Jamuna at sunset, and it hangs in my room. I would happily buy more of her work if she ever decided to sell it.

items.q: Describe a polite person you know
items.text: I would like to talk about someone at my office whose manners I have always admired. The most polite person I know is an older colleague of mine, whose manners are almost old-fashioned in the best possible way. I got to know him when I joined the education consultancy, because he was the one who showed me how everything worked in my first week, when I was nervous and constantly making small mistakes. No matter how busy or stressed he is, he always greets everyone warmly and remembers small details about their lives, like a colleague's child's exams or someone's sick parent. What makes his politeness feel genuine rather than forced is that it is completely consistent; he treats the office cleaner with exactly the same respect as the director. He is also a wonderful listener, never interrupting, which is a rarity these days. With students and parents, he stays unfailingly respectful, even when they are rude or impatient on the phone. I have noticed that his courtesy has a ripple effect, making the whole team more considerate towards one another. In meetings, even when he disagrees, he does so tactfully, so no one ever feels attacked. As for how I feel about him, I genuinely think politeness is an underrated quality, and he is living proof of how much smoother it makes everyday interactions. Honestly, being around him quietly reminds me to mind my own manners, and I think I have become a slightly better person for working beside him.

items.q: Do you think people are less polite nowadays?
items.text: In some ways, yes, particularly online, where people say things they would never say face to face. But I still see plenty of everyday courtesy in my town, especially towards older people.

items.q: Were you taught to be polite as a child?
items.text: Very much so. My parents were quite strict about greeting elders properly and saying thank you, and I am grateful now, because good manners have helped me a great deal at work.

items.q: Describe a person who is good at their job
items.text: I would like to talk about someone whose work I have seen at close quarters for many years. The person is our family doctor, who is genuinely excellent at what he does. He runs a small practice near our home in Sirajganj and has looked after my family since I was a child. Beyond his obvious medical knowledge, what makes him stand out is how he treats patients as people rather than cases. He is incredibly thorough, always taking the time to explain things clearly instead of rushing you out of the door. I have noticed that he has a calming presence, which is invaluable when you are worried about your health. He also keeps himself up to date, so his advice always feels current and trustworthy. What impresses me most is his dedication; he clearly sees medicine as a vocation, not just a job. I remember him coming to our flat late one night during the monsoon when my father had a high fever, which he certainly did not have to do. Because of this, the entire community trusts him completely, and appointments are always fully booked. I think being good at a job like his requires both skill and genuine empathy, and he has both in abundance. As for how I feel about him, I have enormous respect for him. Honestly, he has set my expectations of what a good professional should be, and I try to bring some of his patience to my own work.

items.q: Would you like to have a job like his?
items.text: Not really. I admire doctors enormously, but I do not think I could cope with the pressure or the sight of blood. I am much happier helping people in a less high-stakes way.

items.q: Do you think doctors are well respected in your country?
items.text: Generally yes, especially good ones like him. Doctors are highly regarded in Bangladesh, and many parents dream of their children becoming one, although the profession is extremely demanding.

items.q: Describe an older person you respect
items.text: I would like to talk about a man my whole family looks up to. The older person I respect most is my grandfather, who is now in his eighties but still remarkably sharp. He lives with my grandmother in our ancestral village home not far from Sirajganj, and we visit them as often as we can. He worked the family land for most of his life, and he lived through some genuinely difficult times, and yet he has never become bitter or cynical about life. In terms of what he is like, he is gentle and quick-witted, and he still wakes up at dawn to walk around the fields. He is also incredibly humble about his own achievements, rarely talking about the hardships he overcame. I love listening to his stories, because each one seems to carry a subtle lesson without ever being preachy. Despite his age, he remains genuinely open-minded, curious about new technology and interested in what young people think. He even asks me to show him cricket highlights on my phone, and he has strong opinions about every player. What I respect most is his wisdom; whenever the family faces a problem, he has this quiet way of putting things in perspective. I also think there is something we can all learn from his contentment; he seems at peace with his life in a way that is rare. Honestly, I hope I can grow old with even half of his grace and good humour.

items.q: Do you spend a lot of time with him?
items.text: Not as much as I would like, because of work. But whenever we visit the village, I make sure to sit with him for a while, usually in the courtyard with tea, just listening to him reminisce.

items.q: Do you think older people are respected enough in your country?
items.text: Mostly, yes. Respect for elders is deeply rooted in Bangladeshi culture, and grandparents often live with their families. However, I think that tradition is weakening slightly in the big cities.

items.q: Describe a businessperson you admire
items.text: When I think about business, one success story from my own country always comes to mind. A businessperson I really admire is the founder of a local company that started as a tiny shop and grew into a respected national brand. The business makes food products, things like biscuits and snacks that you can find in almost every corner shop in Bangladesh. What I find inspiring is not just the commercial success, but the way he treated his employees like family throughout. He was known for reinvesting profits into his staff and community rather than simply maximising his own wealth. In terms of what he achieved, I have read that he took real risks in the early years, when the venture could easily have collapsed. Over time, though, he turned a single shop into several factories, providing jobs for a great many people, including in rural areas where work is scarce. That kind of courage, combined with a clear vision, is what separates genuine entrepreneurs from the rest. He also stayed grounded despite his success, which earned him enormous loyalty. As for why I admire him, it is partly personal, because my father ran a small business for over thirty years, so I know how hard it is simply to survive. What I admire most is that he proved you can build something profitable while remaining ethical. Honestly, in an age when many businesses cut corners, his example is refreshing, and it has shaped how I think about running a company myself one day.

items.q: Would you like to start your own business?
items.text: Possibly, one day. With my background in business administration, it is tempting, but I would want some experience abroad first. Starting a company without proper preparation seems far too precarious to me.

items.q: Do you think successful businesspeople should give back to society?
items.text: Yes, I do. Businesses depend on their communities, so it seems fair that they share some of their success, whether through charity, fair wages or supporting local education.

items.q: Describe a teacher who influenced you
items.text: I would like to talk about a teacher who, in a way, is part of the reason I can speak English today. The teacher who influenced me most was my secondary school English teacher, who genuinely changed how I saw the subject. Before her class, I found English dull and mechanical, just grammar rules to memorise for exams. She taught us English language and literature for two years, and she had this gift for making lessons feel engaging, often using stories, songs and debates instead of dry exercises. Sometimes she would ask us to act out scenes from short stories, which felt terrifying at first but was great fun, and it made the language feel alive for the first time. What set her apart was her genuine belief in her students; she could spot potential we could not see in ourselves. She was also endlessly encouraging, praising effort rather than just results, which built my confidence enormously. As for how she influenced me, I still remember how she pushed me to enter a writing competition I would never have attempted alone. I did not win, but I was shortlisted, and that small success meant the world to me. That single act of faith in me changed my relationship with the language completely. Honestly, a large part of why I am comfortable using English today is attributable to her, including in my job, where I use it every single day. I think great teachers do exactly this: they light a spark that keeps burning long after the classroom.

items.q: Are you still in touch with her?
items.text: Sadly not directly, as she moved to another district some years ago. But I heard through a friend that she is still teaching, and I like to think she is still igniting that same spark in her students.

items.q: Do you think teachers are more important than textbooks?
items.text: Definitely. A textbook gives you information, but a good teacher gives you the motivation to use it. I think most people remember a great teacher far longer than any book they studied.

items.q: Describe a person who gave you good advice
items.text: I would like to talk about a conversation that genuinely changed the direction of my life. A person who gave me really good advice was an uncle of mine, my father's younger brother, at a point when I was feeling completely lost about my future. It was just after I had finished my studies, and I was paralysed by the number of choices in front of me. Some friends were preparing for government jobs, others were going abroad, and I had no idea which way to turn. He sat me down one evening after dinner and told me something simple but profound: that it is better to try and fail than to spend your life wondering. What made his advice so valuable was that he spoke from experience, having left a safe job himself to try something new in his thirties. He encouraged me to stop overthinking and take the plunge, even if the first step was a small one. That conversation was genuinely pivotal, because it shifted me from fear to action. I ended up making a decision I had been putting off for months, and it turned out well: the following week I applied for a position at an education consultancy, and I have been working there ever since. Looking back, his words were exactly what I needed at that crucial moment. Honestly, I still repeat that advice to friends who find themselves stuck, and to nervous students too, because I have seen for myself how much difference it can make.

items.q: Do you usually take advice from other people?
items.text: Yes, but I try to be selective. I listen to people who have real experience of the situation, and then I weigh up their views before deciding. In the end, the decision has to be mine.

items.q: Have you ever given someone advice that helped them?
items.text: I hope so. In my job I advise students every day about universities and courses, and a few have come back to thank me, which is one of the most satisfying parts of the work.

items.q: Describe a talented person you know
items.text: I would like to talk about someone whose talent never stops surprising me. A genuinely talented person I know is a school friend who is an extraordinary musician, particularly on the guitar. We grew up in the same neighbourhood in Sirajganj, and he still plays at local weddings and cultural events. What makes him special is that he seems to play almost instinctively, as though the instrument is an extension of himself. He can pick up a song after hearing it once and play it back perfectly, whether it is an old Bengali folk song or a modern pop hit. I know for a fact, though, that this apparent ease is the result of years of relentless practice. He started as a child on a cheap second-hand guitar and was so dedicated that he would play for hours until his fingers were sore. He never had formal lessons; he learned by listening to recordings and copying older musicians, sometimes slowing the songs down so he could catch every note. Watching him perform is genuinely mesmerising; he can shift from a gentle melody to something powerful in seconds. What I respect most is that despite his obvious gift, he remains humble and is always eager to learn from others. I think raw talent only gets you so far, and his discipline is what turned potential into real mastery. Honestly, seeing someone so devoted to their craft is inspiring, and it reminds me that excellence is rarely accidental.

items.q: Have you ever tried to learn the guitar?
items.text: Once, briefly. He gave me a few lessons, but I gave up after about a month because my fingers hurt and I clearly had no aptitude for it. I am much better at listening.

items.q: Do you think he could become a professional musician?
items.text: I think he easily could, if he wanted to. The problem is that music is a risky career here, so he treats it as a passion alongside his regular job, at least for now.

items.q: Describe a person who often helps others
items.text: I would like to talk about someone who lives just one floor below us. The most helpful person I know is a neighbour of ours who seems to spend half her life looking after other people. She is a retired schoolteacher, and she has lived in our building for as long as we have. Whether it is checking on the elderly residents, collecting parcels, or cooking for a family going through a hard time, she is always the first to step in. She also helps younger children in the building with their homework for free. As for how she helps, what strikes me is that her generosity is completely selfless; she never expects anything in return. She has this natural warmth that makes people feel comfortable asking her for help, which many are too proud to do. During a difficult period in our own family, when my mother had to stay in the village for weeks to look after my grandparents, she quietly supported us in ways we did not even ask for, sending over meals almost every evening and checking whether my sister needed anything. As for why she does it, I genuinely think some people are simply wired to be altruistic, and she is one of them. I also suspect it gives her a sense of purpose since she retired. Her kindness has a way of bringing the whole neighbourhood closer together. Honestly, she is a living reminder that small, consistent acts of generosity matter far more than grand gestures.

items.q: Do you help your neighbours too?
items.text: I try to. I carry heavy shopping up the stairs for older neighbours and help with anything technical, like setting up phones. It is a small contribution compared with hers, but it all adds up.

items.q: Do you think people help each other less than in the past?
items.text: Somewhat, especially in cities where people barely know their neighbours. In smaller towns like mine, though, that community spirit is still quite strong, and I really hope it lasts.

items.q: Describe a neighbour you like
items.text: Our building is full of friendly people, but one neighbour really stands out. I would like to talk about an elderly gentleman who lives in the flat opposite ours on the third floor and has been there for as long as we have, which is well over a decade now, so I have practically grown up around him. Despite the age gap, we have always got on remarkably well. He is the sort of neighbour everyone wishes they had: friendly, respectful and never intrusive. He is a retired government officer who lives alone now that his children have moved abroad, so he enjoys a bit of company. He keeps an eye on our flat when we visit my grandparents in the village, and in return we help him with anything that requires climbing a ladder or heavy lifting, like carrying his shopping up the stairs. What I like most is his endless supply of fascinating stories from his younger years, which are genuinely captivating. He is also incredibly considerate, always mindful of noise and careful never to overstep. On Friday evenings he sometimes invites me in for tea, and we end up discussing cricket and politics for hours. I think good neighbours are a kind of quiet blessing that people underestimate until they lose them. Over the years he has become almost like extended family, and the building would feel noticeably emptier without him. Honestly, his presence is a big part of what makes our neighbourhood feel like home.

items.q: Do you think it is important to have good neighbours?
items.text: Absolutely. Neighbours are often the first people who can help in an emergency, long before family arrives. Living near people you trust also gives you real peace of mind every day.

items.q: Do you know most of your neighbours well?
items.text: Most of the ones in our building, yes. We greet each other on the stairs and exchange food during Eid, although I know the newer families less well than those who have been here for years.

items.q: Describe a person who speaks a foreign language well
items.text: I would like to talk about a friend whose language skills I find genuinely impressive. A person who speaks a foreign language impressively well is a friend of mine who is almost fluent in Japanese, despite never having lived there. We met at university, and she is now preparing to apply for a master's degree in Japan, which is partly how we reconnected, since I helped her with her application at the consultancy where I work. Before that, we had not spoken properly for a couple of years. As for how she learned it, what amazes me is that she taught herself largely through films, music and online conversation, which shows extraordinary discipline. She practised every single day for years, even writing short diary entries in Japanese script. Her pronunciation is so authentic that native speakers are often surprised she is not from Japan. I think what makes her so good is that she was never afraid of making mistakes, which is where most learners get stuck. She immersed herself completely, treating the language as a passion rather than a chore. Watching her switch effortlessly between Bengali and Japanese is genuinely admirable, and it makes me slightly envious. She often says that learning a language opens a window into a whole culture, and I think she is right. Honestly, her commitment is inspiring, and it has motivated me to be more serious about improving my own English, especially since I hope to study abroad myself one day.

items.q: Would you like to learn another foreign language?
items.text: Yes, I would love to learn Arabic properly, since I can already read it a little from studying the Quran as a child. Understanding it fully would make my prayers feel far more meaningful.

items.q: Is learning English important in your country?
items.text: Very important. English opens doors to higher education and better jobs, and in my work I see every day how much students' futures hinge on their English test scores.

items.q: Describe a hardworking person you know
items.text: I would like to talk about a friend whose energy honestly puts me to shame. The hardest-working person I know is a close friend who is building his own small business from scratch. He runs a little café near the college in Sirajganj, which he opened about two years ago with his savings and a small loan. His work ethic is genuinely relentless; he is often up before dawn and still working late into the night. As for how he shows it, what impresses me is that he never seems to cut corners, no matter how exhausted he is. He handles everything himself in these early stages, from serving customers to doing the accounts, and he does it all with a smile. He even cleans the café himself at night so that he does not have to hire extra staff yet. I think what drives him is a deep sense of determination to build something of his own rather than work for someone else. There have been moments when I worried he was pushing himself too hard, especially when he stopped seeing friends for months, but his energy is remarkable. Watching his effort slowly pay off has been genuinely inspiring to witness, and the café is now busy most evenings. As for how I feel about him, I am enormously proud of him. Honestly, he has completely changed my idea of what commitment looks like, and he reminds me that success is usually far less glamorous than people imagine.

items.q: Do you consider yourself a hard-working person?
items.text: Fairly, yes, although not to his extreme. I work long hours during application season, but I also try to protect my evenings, because I think rest is essential if you want to sustain your effort.

items.q: Do you think hard work always leads to success?
items.text: Not always. Hard work is essential, but luck, timing and opportunities matter too. Still, people who work consistently hard give themselves a much better chance than those who do not.

items.q: Describe a person who made you laugh
items.text: I would like to talk about someone who has made me laugh more than anyone else I know. The funniest person I know is an old school friend who has an incredible talent for making people laugh. We sat next to each other for most of secondary school, and we still meet up whenever he is back in Sirajganj, usually at our old favourite tea stall. What makes him special is that his humour is completely spontaneous; he does not tell rehearsed jokes but reacts to whatever is happening in the moment. I remember one particularly dull afternoon during our final exams when the stress was unbearable, and within minutes he had the whole group in stitches. He did a perfect impression of a nervous exam invigilator, complete with a dramatic search for a missing pencil. His timing is impeccable, and he has a gift for finding the funny side of even the most awkward situations. What I appreciate most is that his jokes are never malicious; he laughs with people, not at them. As for how I felt, I laughed so much that my stomach hurt, and for the first time in weeks I completely forgot about the exams. Honestly, he has lifted my mood on countless bad days, which is a genuine gift. I think people who can make others laugh so easily are quietly valuable, because laughter is such good medicine. Being around him is always uplifting, and I feel lucky to count him as a friend.

items.q: Do you think you have a good sense of humour?
items.text: I think so, although mine is drier and quieter than his. I enjoy wordplay and gentle teasing more than big jokes, and my family says I am funniest when I do not mean to be.

items.q: Is laughter important in your life?
items.text: Very much. After a stressful day at work, a good laugh with my family over dinner helps me unwind more than anything else. I think it keeps us close as well.

items.q: Describe a sportsperson you admire
items.text: As a big cricket fan, I did not have to think very long about this one. A sportsperson I genuinely admire is a famous cricketer from my country, who is something of a national hero. He has played for Bangladesh for many years, and he has been part of some of the team's most memorable victories against much bigger cricketing nations. Beyond his obvious talent, what I admire is the humility he shows despite enormous fame. He came from a modest background and worked his way up through sheer perseverance, which makes his story relatable to ordinary people. On the field he is famous for staying calm under pressure, a quality that separates good players from truly great ones. What impresses me most is his consistency; he performs at a high level year after year, which requires incredible discipline. Off the field, he is known for his charity work, which shows real character. I think athletes like him are role models precisely because of how they carry themselves, not just their statistics. His dignity in both victory and defeat is something young people can genuinely learn from. I still remember watching one of his match-winning innings with my father and younger sister, all of us shouting at the television and my mother rushing in from the kitchen to see what had happened. Honestly, he makes the whole nation proud, and rightly so, and whenever he walks out to bat, the entire country seems to hold its breath.

items.q: Have you ever watched him play live?
items.text: Not yet, unfortunately. Tickets for big matches in Dhaka sell out quickly, and it is a long journey from Sirajganj. But watching him in a stadium is definitely on my bucket list.

items.q: Do you play cricket yourself?
items.text: Only casually these days. I played a lot as a child with friends in the neighbourhood, but now I mostly watch it, usually with my father, who is an even bigger fan than I am.

items.q: Describe a person you would like to work with
items.text: I would like to talk about someone who taught me a great deal in a very short time. A person I would love to work with is a former mentor of mine who now runs a successful consultancy in Dhaka, advising small businesses on strategy. I got to know him during an internship in my final year of business administration, and even in those three months I learned an enormous amount. What makes him an ideal colleague is that he is both brilliant and genuinely collaborative; he treats junior people as partners rather than subordinates. He has a way of bringing out the best in a team by giving people real ownership of their work. I remember him letting me present part of a report to a client, which was terrifying but hugely valuable. As for why I would like to work with him, I think working alongside him again would be incredibly stimulating, because he constantly pushes those around him to think bigger. He is also refreshingly honest, offering feedback that is direct but never harsh. As for how I feel about the idea, it excites me, although I know I would need more experience before I could keep up with him. Honestly, I believe the people you work with shape your career more than the job itself, and he is exactly the kind of person who makes you better. Being part of a team he leads would be a genuine privilege, and perhaps one day, after studying abroad, I will get that chance.

items.q: Do you prefer working alone or in a team?
items.text: It depends on the task, but generally I prefer teamwork. Other people spot mistakes I miss and bring ideas I would never think of. Working alone can feel quite isolating after a while.

items.q: Are you in touch with him now?
items.text: Yes, occasionally. We connected on a professional networking site, and he sometimes comments on my posts. Last year he even offered to write me a reference if I apply for a master's abroad.

items.q: Describe a confident person you know
items.text: I would like to talk about someone whose confidence I have always slightly envied. A strikingly confident person I know is a former classmate who now works in sales for a mobile phone company. We studied business administration together, and we were often in the same group for presentations, so I had plenty of chances to watch her in action. From the day I met her, she had this natural self-assurance that drew people to her. What I find interesting is that her confidence never tips over into arrogance; she is genuinely comfortable in her own skin. As for how she shows it, she can walk into a room full of strangers and start a conversation without the slightest hesitation, which I have always envied. In class presentations, while the rest of us were shaking, she spoke clearly and even enjoyed the difficult questions. I think a lot of her confidence comes from thorough preparation, so she rarely feels caught off guard. She is also unafraid of failure, treating setbacks as short-lived rather than devastating. Watching her handle difficult situations calmly has taught me a great deal. As for how I feel about her, I admire her enormously. Honestly, I think confidence like hers is partly a personality trait and partly a skill you can build. Being around her is genuinely empowering, because her belief in herself somehow rubs off on the people nearby. I certainly became a better presenter just by watching her, and I still borrow some of her techniques at work.

items.q: Are you a confident person?
items.text: More than I used to be. I was quite shy at university, but my job forces me to speak to students and parents every day, and that has gradually helped me come out of my shell.

items.q: Do you think confidence can be learned?
items.text: Yes, I believe so. Practice and preparation make a huge difference. The more often you face something that frightens you, like public speaking, the less frightening it becomes over time.

items.q: Describe a person who apologised to you
items.text: I would like to talk about an apology that actually made a friendship stronger. I remember an occasion when a close friend apologised to me after a misunderstanding that had strained our friendship for weeks. It happened about two years ago, and the friend was someone I had known since school. We had fallen out over something fairly trivial, a comment he made about me in a group chat, which both of us had blown out of proportion. For a few weeks we barely spoke, and it felt strange not having him around, because we used to talk almost every day. Then one evening he turned up at our flat unannounced and asked if we could go for a walk by the river. What made his apology memorable was how sincere it was; he did not make excuses or try to shift the blame. He admitted openly that he had been in the wrong, which takes real humility. I think apologising properly is genuinely difficult, because it requires swallowing your pride. His honesty completely disarmed me, and any lingering resentment melted away almost instantly. In the end I apologised too, for my own stubbornness. We ended up talking for hours and our friendship actually became stronger than before. Honestly, that experience taught me how powerful a genuine apology can be in repairing a relationship. It also reminded me that admitting fault is a sign of strength, not weakness, something many people never seem to learn.

items.q: Do you find it easy to apologise?
items.text: Not always, to be honest. Like most people, I can be a bit proud, but I have learned that a quick, genuine apology usually defuses a situation far better than defending myself.

items.q: Do you think people apologise less nowadays?
items.text: Perhaps a little. People often send a quick sorry by message instead of saying it in person, which feels less meaningful. A face-to-face apology still carries much more weight, I think.

items.q: Describe a well-dressed person you know
items.text: I would like to talk about a colleague whose sense of style everyone in our office notices. A person whose style I genuinely admire is a colleague of mine who always manages to look effortlessly elegant. She joined our consultancy about a year ago as a senior counsellor, and we often work together on university applications, so I see her almost every day. She never seems to be trying too hard, yet every outfit looks carefully considered. What I find impressive is how versatile her wardrobe is; she can look professional at work and stylish at a social event with equal ease. At the office she usually wears a simple salwar kameez or a sari in muted colours, and at weddings she looks even more graceful, without ever seeming overdressed. She favours simple, classic pieces over loud trends, which gives her a timeless, sophisticated look. I think what makes her stand out is her attention to small details, like how well things fit and the way colours complement one another. She once told me that dressing well is less about money and more about knowing what suits you, which struck me as genuinely wise. As for how I feel about her style, I find it quietly inspiring. Honestly, being around her has made me a little more thoughtful about my own appearance, and I now iron my shirts rather more carefully. I think the way you present yourself quietly shapes how others perceive you, and she understands that instinctively.

items.q: Do you care much about fashion?
items.text: Not a great deal. I like to look neat and presentable, especially for work, but I rarely follow trends. I prefer understated clothes that are comfortable and will not go out of style quickly.

items.q: What do people in your country usually wear on special occasions?
items.text: Traditional clothes, mostly. Men wear a panjabi, especially at Eid, and women often wear colourful saris. Weddings are the most formal occasions, and people dress very elaborately for them.

items.q: Describe a person who encouraged you to achieve a goal
items.text: I would like to talk about someone who, quite honestly, stopped me from giving up. A person who encouraged me to achieve an important goal was my elder cousin, at a time when I was preparing for a major exam and had almost lost faith in myself. The goal was to get into a good public university to study business administration, and the admission test was extremely competitive. After a disappointing mock test, I had convinced myself that I was not capable, and I was ready to give up. She refused to let me quit, and her belief in me was genuinely unwavering. Rather than just offering empty words, she sat with me, helped me plan, and kept me accountable week after week. She made me a detailed timetable and called every Friday to check my progress. What I appreciated most was that her support was practical, not just emotional. Whenever I felt demoralised, she would remind me how far I had already come. Thanks largely to her, I stayed disciplined and eventually achieved a result I am still proud of, and I got a place on the course I wanted. As for how I felt, I was overjoyed and hugely relieved, but above all grateful. Honestly, I am not sure I would have managed it without her constant encouragement. That experience taught me how much difference one supportive person can make, and I try to be that encouraging presence for others now, especially the nervous students I work with.

items.q: Do you still set goals for yourself?
items.text: Yes, although they are different now. At the moment my main goal is to strengthen my profile so I can study abroad. I find that breaking a goal into small steps makes it feel within reach.

items.q: Do you think encouragement is more important than talent?
items.text: In many cases, yes. Plenty of talented people give up because nobody believes in them, while ordinary people achieve a lot with the right support. Ideally, of course, you need both.

items.q: Describe a childhood friend
items.text: When I think back to my childhood, one face always comes to mind. I would like to talk about my best friend from childhood, who lived just a few houses down from us in Sirajganj. We met when we were barely five years old, on the very first day of primary school, and quickly became inseparable. Almost every afternoon was spent playing cricket in the lane, exploring the neighbourhood or getting into harmless mischief. During the monsoon we used to race paper boats in the flooded streets, and in the dry season we flew kites from the rooftops until our mothers called us in for dinner. Those years were wonderfully carefree, with none of the responsibilities that come later. What made our friendship special was how easily we understood each other, without any of the awkwardness that adults sometimes have. As for whether we are still in touch, sadly his family moved to Rajshahi when we were teenagers, and we gradually drifted apart, which I still find a little melancholy. We do reconnect occasionally, usually by phone around Eid, and it is lovely how quickly the old bond resurfaces. The last time we met, we spent the whole evening laughing about the things we had done as boys. Honestly, childhood friendships have a special kind of innocence that is hard to recreate later in life. I look back on those days with enormous fondness, and I feel grateful to have had such a good companion growing up.

items.q: Would you like to spend more time with him?
items.text: Definitely. I have been meaning to visit him in Rajshahi for ages, but work always gets in the way. This year I am determined to finally make the trip and spend a proper weekend together.

items.q: Do children today have as much freedom as you did?
items.text: Probably not. Many parents worry more about safety now, and children spend more time indoors on screens. I think they miss out on the kind of outdoor adventures we took for granted.

items.q: Describe a person you recently met and want to know more about
items.text: I would like to talk about someone I met only a few weeks ago but have not stopped thinking about. Recently I met someone at a friend's gathering who genuinely intrigued me, and I have been hoping to get to know her better. The gathering was a small dinner at a friend's home in Dhaka, when I was there visiting my elder sister. She works in an unusual field, environmental research, which immediately made her stand out in a room full of bankers and engineers. She studies how river erosion is affecting farming communities in the north of the country. What struck me was how articulate she was; she could explain complex ideas in a way that was easy to follow and genuinely interesting. We talked about climate change, the Jamuna swallowing land near my grandparents' village, and even her plans to do a PhD abroad. We ended up talking for over an hour, and the conversation never once felt tedious. She has clearly travelled widely and has a very broad-minded outlook, which I found refreshing. As for why I want to know her better, it is because she has a rare combination of intelligence and warmth. Too often first meetings feel superficial, but this one felt genuinely meaningful. We exchanged contacts, so I am hopeful we will meet again the next time I am in Dhaka. Honestly, it is quite unusual to feel an instant rapport with someone, and I do not want to let it fade.

items.q: Do you find it easy to talk to new people?
items.text: It depends on the situation. At work I am comfortable because I know my role, but at social events I can be a bit hesitant at first. Once a conversation gets going, though, I usually warm up quickly.

items.q: How do you usually make new friends?
items.text: Mostly through people I already know, like friends of friends or colleagues. I have made a few friends through work as well, since I meet so many different people at the consultancy.

items.q: Describe a person who is a good parent
items.text: I would like to talk about someone in my own family whose parenting I genuinely admire. A person I consider an excellent parent is my elder sister, and watching her raise her two children has been a real education. She lives in Dhaka with her husband and children, including a lively four-year-old son, and we see them whenever they visit Sirajganj or I go to stay with them. As for how she raises them, what impresses me is how she balances warmth with discipline; she is affectionate but never lets her children become spoiled. She listens to them genuinely, treating even their small worries as important, which I think builds real trust. Rather than simply giving orders, she explains the reasons behind rules, so her children grow up thinking for themselves. She limits their screen time, reads to them every night and makes sure they spend plenty of time with their grandparents, which I think matters enormously. She is also remarkably patient, even on the difficult days when most people would lose their temper. As for why I think she is a good parent, what I admire most is that she leads by example, modelling the values she wants them to absorb. I think parenting is one of the hardest jobs in the world, and she makes it look almost effortless.
