Honestly, her children are turning out kind and confident, which is the clearest possible proof of her nurturing approach. I suspect our mother taught her more than she realises.

items.q: Do you think you would be a good parent?
items.text: I hope so. I think I would be patient and fair, like my sister, but I would probably struggle with discipline because I tend to give in too easily. I would definitely ask her for guidance.

items.q: Do parents today have an easier job than in the past?
items.text: In some ways yes, with more information and support available. But they also face new pressures, like managing screen time and intense competition in education, which makes parenting quite demanding.

items.q: Describe a generous person you know
items.text: I would like to talk about a man whose kindness is known throughout our neighbourhood. The most generous person I know is an old family friend who seems to find genuine joy in giving. For many years he ran a shop next to my father's in the market, so I have known him since I was a small boy, and he still calls me by my childhood nickname. His generosity is not just about money, though he is quietly charitable; it is more about his time and attention. Whenever anyone is in trouble, he is the first to offer help, often before being asked. What makes his kindness so genuine is that he never seeks recognition for it; in fact, he prefers to help discreetly. I remember him supporting a struggling family in our neighbourhood for months without anyone knowing, paying their children's school fees until the father found work again. I only found out years later, through my father. During Ramadan, he also quietly sends food to families who cannot afford much for iftar. I think true generosity like his is increasingly uncommon in a world that often prizes self-interest. As for how I feel about him, I have enormous respect for him, and being around him is a gentle reminder to be more giving myself. He genuinely believes that we are all better off when we look after one another, and he lives by that principle. Honestly, his benevolence has left a lasting impression on everyone who knows him.

items.q: Do you think people in your country are generous?
items.text: Generally, yes. Charity is an important part of our culture and religion, especially during Ramadan and Eid, when people make a real effort to share food and money with those who are less fortunate.

items.q: Is it better to give money or time?
items.text: Both matter, but I think time is often more valuable. Money solves immediate problems, whereas giving someone your time and attention shows that you genuinely care about them as a person.

items.q: Describe a person who has an interesting job
items.text: I would like to talk about a friend whose job I find almost unbelievably exciting. A person with a genuinely interesting job is a friend of mine who works as a wildlife photographer. We met through a mutual friend a few years ago, and he now works freelance for magazines and conservation groups. His work takes him to remote corners of the world, capturing animals in their natural habitats, although his favourite place is still the Sundarbans, closer to home. What makes his job so fascinating is the unpredictability; no two days are ever the same, and patience is everything. He once spent nearly a week waiting quietly to photograph a single rare bird, which shows extraordinary dedication. He has also told me about spending nights on a boat in the mangrove forest, hoping for a glimpse of a tiger, which he finally saw on his third trip. I find the combination of adventure, artistry and science in his work genuinely enviable. Of course, he is quick to point out that it is far less glamorous than it looks, involving long hours in harsh conditions, from heat and mosquitoes to heavy rain. Still, I think there is something wonderful about a job that keeps you so connected to nature. As for how I feel about it, listening to his stories always makes my own routine feel a little dull. Honestly, he has one of the few careers that I think I could happily do myself, provided someone else carried the heavy equipment.

items.q: Would you like to try wildlife photography yourself?
items.text: I would love to try it once, perhaps on a short trip to the Sundarbans with him. But I suspect I lack the patience to sit still for days, so it would probably remain a hobby at best.

items.q: Do you think interesting jobs are more important than well-paid jobs?
items.text: For me, balance matters. A fascinating job that barely pays is hard to sustain, but a well-paid job you find soul-destroying is worse. Ideally, you find work that offers both.

items.q: Describe a person from a different culture you know
items.text: I would like to talk about a friendship that has taught me a lot about the wider world. A person from a different culture whom I know well is a friend from university who grew up in Turkey. She came to our university in Bangladesh for a year as an exchange student, and we were in several of the same classes. Her home town is Izmir, on the Aegean coast, and she has shown me so many photos that I feel I almost know it. Getting to know her has been genuinely eye-opening, because our backgrounds are quite different in some ways yet surprisingly similar in others. She has taught me a great deal about her country's food, festivals and customs, which I find fascinating. What I appreciate most is how her perspective has broadened my own; she often challenges assumptions I did not even realise I held. Our conversations are always enriching, and we enjoy comparing how our two cultures approach things like family and hospitality. We even discovered that our families celebrate Eid in quite similar ways. As for how I feel about the friendship, I think friendships across cultures are especially valuable, because they quietly break down stereotypes. She is warm, curious and completely without prejudice, which makes her wonderful company, and we still video call every couple of months. Honestly, knowing her has made me more open-minded, and it has confirmed my belief that people everywhere have far more in common than we tend to assume.

items.q: Would you like to visit her country?
items.text: Very much. She has invited me to Istanbul and Izmir many times, and I would love to see the historic mosques and try the food she always talks about. Hopefully I can go within the next few years.

items.q: Is it easy to make friends with people from other cultures?
items.text: It can take a little more effort at first, because of language and different customs. But once you get past that initial awkwardness, I think those friendships are often especially close and rewarding.

items.q: Describe a wise older relative
items.text: I would like to talk about the person our whole family turns to in difficult times. The wisest person in my family is undoubtedly my grandmother, who despite having little formal education has an extraordinary understanding of people and life. She lives with my grandfather in our ancestral village home not far from Sirajganj, and we visit them often, especially during Eid, when the whole family gathers in the old house. What makes her so wise is not book knowledge but decades of hard-won experience, raising a large family through floods and lean years. She has this uncanny ability to sense when something is wrong, often before anyone says a word. Whenever the family faces a difficult decision, we instinctively turn to her, because her judgement is remarkably sound. She rarely tells you what to do; instead she asks the right questions and lets you reach your own conclusion. I think that is the mark of genuine wisdom, and it means you actually learn something. Her advice is always grounded in common sense rather than emotion, which is why it is so reliable. As for how she has helped me, over the years she has helped me through several tough moments simply by putting things in perspective. When I was nervous about starting my first job, she reminded me that everyone is a beginner once, and that honesty matters more than cleverness. Honestly, I treasure my conversations with her, and I know I will miss her counsel enormously one day.

items.q: Do you visit her often?
items.text: Fairly often, usually once or twice a month with my parents. The village is not far, so we can go for the day. Sitting with her on the veranda is one of the most tranquil parts of my month.

items.q: Do you think older people are wiser than younger people?
items.text: Often, but not always. Age gives people experience, but wisdom depends on whether they reflect on it. Some young people are remarkably wise, and some older people never seem to learn.

items.q: Describe a person who solved a problem in a clever way
items.text: I would like to describe a former colleague who once solved a tricky problem at work in a genuinely clever way. He worked with me at the education consultancy until last year, when he left to do a master's degree in Australia. Our team was stuck on a project because of a scheduling conflict that seemed impossible to resolve. We had organised a university fair, but two of the most popular universities could only send representatives at exactly the same time, and we had only one hall big enough for the crowds we were expecting. While the rest of us were arguing, he calmly suggested a completely different approach that none of us had considered. He proposed dividing the hall with screens and running both sessions side by side. What impressed me was how resourceful he was; he found a simple solution hidden in plain sight. His thinking was refreshingly lateral, approaching the problem from an angle nobody else had tried. Within an hour, something that had frustrated us for days was neatly sorted out, and the fair went smoothly. As for how I felt, I was relieved but also slightly embarrassed that I had not thought of it myself. I think his real strength is staying calm and rational when everyone else is panicking. That episode taught me that the best solutions are often surprisingly simple, once someone ingenious points them out. Honestly, I still think about his approach whenever I feel stuck on a difficult problem myself.

items.q: Are you good at solving problems?
items.text: Reasonably good, I think, especially practical ones. I tend to be methodical rather than creative, so I break problems into steps. I have learned, though, that stepping away for a while often brings a breakthrough.

items.q: Do you think problem-solving skills can be taught?
items.text: Yes, to some extent. Schools can encourage it by giving students open-ended tasks instead of memorisation. But experience is the best teacher, because real problems rarely come with clear instructions.

items.q: Describe a person you enjoy talking to
items.text: I would like to talk about the friend whose company I probably enjoy most. A person I always enjoy talking to is a close friend of mine who has a genuinely curious mind. We met at a book club at the local library about four years ago, and since then we have met for tea almost every week, usually at a small café near the river. Our conversations can start with something trivial and end up exploring philosophy, travel or politics, which I find endlessly stimulating. Last week, for instance, we started talking about a cricket match and somehow ended up debating whether ambition really makes people happy. What makes talking to him so enjoyable is that he actually listens, rather than just waiting for his turn to speak. He is also wonderfully open-minded, so I can share half-formed thoughts without fear of being judged. I think good conversation is a bit of an art, and he is a master of it, although he would never admit that. He knows when to be serious and when to be playful, which keeps things from ever feeling heavy. Honestly, I always come away from our chats feeling energised and having learned something new. In a world where so much communication happens through screens, having someone you can talk to for hours is genuinely precious. I never take those conversations for granted, and I think they have made me a far better listener and a slightly more thoughtful person as well.

items.q: Do you prefer talking face to face or online?
items.text: Face to face, definitely. You can read someone's expressions and tone properly, and the conversation flows more naturally. Online chats are convenient, but they often feel rather stilted by comparison.

items.q: Are you a talkative person?
items.text: It depends on who I am with. With close friends and family I can talk for hours, but in large groups of strangers I tend to be quieter and listen more than I speak.

items.q: Describe a patient person you know
items.text: I would like to talk about someone whose calm I still try to copy. The most patient person I know is a former teacher of mine, whose calm never seemed to break no matter how testing the situation. She taught us Bengali literature at my higher secondary college in Sirajganj, so I was in her class for two years. Teaching a class of restless teenagers is difficult enough, but she handled even the most disruptive students with remarkable composure. As for how she showed patience, rather than raising her voice, she would pause, take a breath and respond calmly, which was far more effective. I remember one boy who constantly interrupted her lessons; instead of punishing him, she gave him small responsibilities, and by the end of the year he was one of her best students. What I admired was that her patience was not passive; it came from genuine understanding of why students behaved as they did. She gave people time to learn at their own pace, never making anyone feel rushed or stupid. I think patience like hers is genuinely underrated, because it requires enormous self-control. Watching her, I realised how much damage impatience can do and how much trust patience can build. Honestly, she has made me consciously try to be more tolerant in my own daily interactions, though I still have a long way to go. At work, when a student asks me the same question for the fifth time, I often think of her.

items.q: Are you a patient person?
items.text: Moderately. I am patient with students and older relatives, but I get rather irritable in traffic or long queues. It is something I am actively working on, with mixed results so far.

items.q: Why do you think people are less patient nowadays?
items.text: Mainly because technology has made everything instant. We are used to fast deliveries and immediate replies, so waiting for anything now feels frustrating, even when the delay is perfectly reasonable.

items.q: Describe a younger person you admire
items.text: I would like to talk about someone much younger than me who really inspires me. A younger person I genuinely admire is my teenage cousin, who is remarkably mature for her age. She is my uncle's daughter and lives in Bogura, not far from us, so we see each other at family gatherings and during Eid. Despite being only sixteen, she has a level of determination that puts many adults to shame. As for what she has done, alongside her studies she has started a small online venture selling her own handmade crafts, such as embroidered bags and jewellery, which she runs entirely by herself. She takes the photos, manages the orders and even arranges the deliveries, all from her bedroom desk after school. What impresses me is how disciplined she is with her time, balancing school, hobbies and her little business without ever seeming stressed. She is also refreshingly self-aware, knowing exactly what she wants and unafraid to pursue it. As for why I admire her, I think her generation faces a lot of pressure, yet she handles it with a calm confidence I did not have at her age. At sixteen, I was mainly worried about cricket scores and exam results, and I certainly could not have run a business. Watching her, I feel genuinely optimistic about the future. Honestly, she reminds me that age has little to do with wisdom or drive, and I sometimes catch myself learning from her rather than the other way around.

items.q: Do you think young people today are more mature than in the past?
items.text: In some ways, yes. They have access to so much information and opportunity that many grow up faster. However, they also face more pressure, which can be quite overwhelming for some of them.

items.q: Would you like to start a small business like hers?
items.text: Possibly, as a side project. With my business background it would be interesting, but at the moment my job keeps me very busy, and my priority is preparing to study abroad.

items.q: Describe a person who is good at cooking
items.text: I would like to talk about the person whose food I would choose over any restaurant's. The best cook I know is my mother, whose food has a reputation among everyone who has ever tasted it. She cooks almost every meal for our family, and her specialities are traditional Bengali dishes like hilsa in mustard sauce, beef curry and, at Eid, a rich biryani that relatives talk about for weeks. She never followed formal recipes; instead she learned from her own mother as a girl and refined everything through years of practice. What makes her cooking special is her intuitive sense of flavour; she seems to know exactly how much of each spice to add without measuring. Her traditional dishes are genuinely exquisite, and guests often ask for the recipes, which she happily shares. I think part of what makes her food so good is the care she puts into it; cooking for her is an act of love, not a chore. Whenever the family gathers, her kitchen becomes the beating heart of the house. As for how I feel about her cooking, it is simply the taste of home to me, and even a plain bowl of dal tastes better when she makes it. Honestly, no restaurant has ever quite matched the comfort of a meal she has prepared. I only wish I had paid closer attention over the years, because her skill feels almost irreplaceable, and if I do study abroad one day, it is the thing I will miss most.

items.q: Can you cook yourself?
items.text: Only a few basic dishes, like rice, dal and an omelette. I really need to learn more before I study abroad, so I have started asking my mother to teach me, though I am a rather clumsy pupil.

items.q: Do you prefer home-cooked food or eating out?
items.text: Home-cooked food, without a doubt. Eating out is enjoyable occasionally, but restaurant food is often too oily for me, and nothing beats sitting down to dinner with my family.

items.q: Describe a person who kept a promise to you
items.text: I would like to talk about a friend who once kept a promise to me under genuinely difficult circumstances. He is a university friend who lives in a nearby town, and we have been close for years, ever since we shared a desk in our first accounting class. A few years ago, my family moved into the flat where we live now, and it was a stressful period because my father was still busy with his business and we had very little help. My friend had promised to help me move everything on a particular weekend. As it happened, that same weekend he was offered something far more appealing, a free trip to Cox's Bazar with his colleagues, yet he turned it down without a second thought. What struck me was how reliable he proved to be, when it would have been easy to make an excuse. He showed up early, worked tirelessly all day carrying boxes and furniture up to the third floor, and never once made me feel like a burden. As for how I felt, I was touched and slightly humbled, because I knew what he had given up. I think keeping promises, especially inconvenient ones, is a real test of character, and he passed it completely. His dependability deepened my trust in him enormously. Honestly, in a world where people break commitments so casually, someone who genuinely honours their word is rare and invaluable. That day taught me the kind of friend I want to be myself.

items.q: Do you always keep your promises?
items.text: I try very hard to. If I am not sure I can do something, I would rather not promise it at all. Breaking a promise, even a small one, can erode trust surprisingly quickly.

items.q: Did you ever do something similar for him?
items.text: Yes, last year I travelled to his town to help with his sister's wedding preparations, even though it was a busy time at work. It felt good to finally return the favour.

items.q: Describe a quiet person you know
items.text: I would like to talk about someone at work whom I completely misjudged at first. A quiet person I know well is a colleague of mine who rarely speaks unless he has something worth saying. He handles visa documents at the education consultancy where I work, and we have shared an office for about two years. At first I mistook his silence for coldness, but I soon realised he is simply reserved rather than unfriendly. As for what he is like, what I have come to appreciate is that when he does speak, people genuinely listen, because his words carry weight. He is an exceptional observer, noticing details in meetings that the more talkative people miss entirely. Once he spotted a small error in a student's visa application that the rest of us had missed for days, which saved the student a great deal of trouble and possibly a rejected visa. I think our culture tends to reward loud, outgoing personalities, so quiet people are often overlooked, which is a shame. Over time I have discovered that he is thoughtful, kind and surprisingly funny once you get to know him. His calm presence is actually quite soothing in a busy office, especially during the stressful application season. As for how I feel about him, I like and respect him enormously. Honestly, he has taught me that you do not have to be the loudest voice in the room to be respected, and I have a lot of time for him.

items.q: Would you describe yourself as quiet?
items.text: Somewhere in the middle, I think. I can be talkative with people I know well, but in new situations I prefer to listen and get the measure of people before saying much.

items.q: Do you think quiet people make good leaders?
items.text: Yes, they can be excellent leaders. They often listen carefully and think before acting, which leads to better decisions. Leadership is not only about speaking loudly; it is about earning respect.

items.q: Describe a person who has travelled a lot
items.text: I would like to talk about the most well-travelled person in my family. A person who has travelled extensively is an uncle of mine, my mother's elder brother, who spent much of his career working abroad as an engineer. He has lived on several continents and visited dozens of countries, from the Gulf to Malaysia, Germany and Canada, and his stories are genuinely captivating. He has recently moved back to Bangladesh and lives in Dhaka, so I see him whenever I visit my elder sister there. What I find most interesting is not the places themselves, but how travel has shaped his outlook; he is remarkably tolerant and open to different ways of life. He often says that seeing how others live cured him of taking anything for granted. He also learned to be patient and adaptable, because nothing abroad ever went quite according to plan, from missed trains to misunderstood menus. Listening to him is almost like receiving an informal education in geography and culture. I think people who travel widely tend to develop a certain wisdom that is hard to gain any other way. As for how I feel about his experiences, I am a little envious, to be honest, and his stories have made me determined to explore more of the world myself, starting, I hope, with studying abroad. Whenever I hear them, I feel a pang of wanderlust and a renewed appreciation for how vast and varied the world really is.

items.q: Would you like to travel as much as he has?
items.text: I would love to, although perhaps not for work. I would rather travel slowly, spending weeks in one place to properly soak up the culture, instead of rushing from city to city.

items.q: Which country would you most like to visit?
items.text: Probably Canada or the UK, partly because many of my students go there and I would like to see what their lives are like. I am also fascinated by Japan's mix of tradition and technology.

items.q: Describe a person who is a good listener
items.text: I would like to talk about the person I go to whenever I need to talk something through. The best listener I know is a close friend of mine, and it is a quality I value in her enormously. We met at university, where we were in the same tutorial group, and she now teaches at a school in Sirajganj, so we still meet regularly. In an age when most people are just waiting for their turn to speak, she gives you her complete, undivided attention. She puts her phone away, makes eye contact and never glances around the room while you are talking. When I talk to her about a problem, she never rushes to offer solutions; instead she lets me express myself fully first, which is surprisingly rare. She asks thoughtful questions that show she has genuinely been paying attention. What makes her such a good listener is her natural empathy; she seems to feel what you are feeling. As for how I feel about her, I always come away from our conversations feeling lighter, as though a weight has been shared. Last year, when I was unsure whether to apply for a master's degree abroad, she listened to me for an entire evening without once telling me what to do. I think being truly listened to is one of the most comforting experiences a person can have. Honestly, her ability to listen without judgement is a genuine gift, and it is a big part of why she is so treasured by everyone who knows her.

items.q: Are you a good listener yourself?
items.text: I am getting better. My job has taught me to listen carefully, because students often reveal their real worries only if you give them time. But I still sometimes jump in too quickly when I get excited.

items.q: Why do you think some people are poor listeners?
items.text: Often because they are distracted, particularly by their phones, or because they are more interested in sharing their own opinions. Listening properly takes patience and genuine interest in the other person.

items.q: Describe a city you have visited
items.text: I would like to talk about a trip I made to Kolkata, in India, a couple of years ago, which left a lasting impression on me. I went during the winter with two friends from university, and we spent about five days there. It is an old, historic city, and what struck me immediately was its wonderful sense of character. The streets were bustling with activity, full of markets, trams and street food that smelled incredible. What I loved most was the blend of old and new; grand colonial buildings stood alongside modern shops, creating a genuinely atmospheric feel. I spent my days exploring museums and wandering through the older neighbourhoods, which felt almost timeless. We also rode one of the old trams, which rattled along at a wonderfully slow pace. We visited the Victoria Memorial, and I spent a whole afternoon on College Street, which is lined with second-hand bookshops, so as a keen reader I was completely in my element. The people were remarkably friendly and always happy to point me in the right direction, and since so many of them speak Bengali, I never felt like a complete outsider. Of course, it was crowded and chaotic at times, but that energy was part of its charm. Honestly, I found the whole experience genuinely invigorating, and it gave me a real appreciation for the city's rich cultural heritage. In a way it also felt strangely familiar, because we share so much history, language and food. I would go back without hesitation, ideally for longer next time.

items.q: Would you like to go back to Kolkata?
items.text: Yes, definitely. Next time I would like to stay longer and explore some of the smaller neighbourhoods and old cafés. I would also love to go during Durga Puja, when the whole city is beautifully lit up.

items.q: Do you prefer visiting cities or the countryside?
items.text: It depends on my mood, really. Cities are exciting for a few days, but I get tired of the noise quite quickly, so for a proper rest I would usually choose the countryside.

items.q: Describe a place near water that you like
items.text: The place I would like to describe is the riverside near my home in Sirajganj, beside the Jamuna river, which has always been a favourite spot of mine. It is only a short rickshaw ride from our flat, along the embankment on the edge of town. I try to go there two or three times a week, usually in the early evening once I have finished work. There is something deeply calming about sitting by the water and watching the sun set over it. The gentle sound of the current is wonderfully soothing, and it seems to wash away the stress of daily life. I usually go for a slow walk along the bank, or simply sit with a cup of tea from one of the little stalls and let my mind wander. Sometimes I watch the fishing boats coming in, or children playing near the water's edge. What I love most is how tranquil it is compared to the noise of the town centre. There is often a cool breeze coming off the water, which is a blessing in the heat, especially in the sticky weeks before the monsoon. Of course, the river has another side too; in the rainy season it swells enormously, and riverbank erosion has cost many local families their land over the years. Perhaps that is why I respect it as much as I love it. Honestly, being near water has a therapeutic effect on me that is hard to explain. It is my favourite place to think, and I always leave feeling refreshed.

items.q: Do many people go there?
items.text: Yes, quite a lot, especially in the evenings and on holidays. Families come to enjoy the breeze and young people gather to chat, but if you walk a little further along the bank it becomes much quieter.

items.q: Has the riverside changed since you were a child?
items.text: Yes, a fair bit. The embankment has been strengthened, and there are more tea stalls and lights now. It is busier than before, but the view across the water is exactly the same.

items.q: Describe a quiet place you like to spend time in
items.text: A quiet place I really treasure is a small reading corner in the public library in our town, just a ten-minute walk from our flat. I stumbled upon it by chance a few years ago, when I was looking for somewhere to prepare for my university exams, and I have been going ever since. Tucked away near the back, behind the tall shelves of old newspapers, it is a secluded little spot that most people seem to overlook. I usually go there to read or study, because the silence helps me concentrate in a way that is impossible at home, where my younger sister is often revising and the television is on in the next room. These days I mostly go on a free afternoon with a novel or a book about business. There is something wonderfully peaceful about being surrounded by books, with only the occasional turning of a page to break the quiet. In our increasingly noisy world, finding somewhere so genuinely serene feels like a small luxury. I often lose track of time there, completely absorbed in whatever I am reading. Honestly, it has become a kind of sanctuary for me, a place to escape the constant distractions of modern life, and I deliberately leave my phone on silent at the bottom of my bag. I always feel calmer and more focused after spending an afternoon there, and I think everyone deserves a corner like that somewhere in their life.

items.q: Do you prefer studying at home or in a library?
items.text: Definitely in a library. At home there are too many distractions, like the television, my phone and family conversations, whereas in a library everyone around me is focused, which makes it much easier to concentrate.

items.q: Do many young people in your town use the library?
items.text: Fewer than before, I think. A lot of students now study online or at coaching centres, but during exam season the library still fills up with young people looking for a quiet place to revise.

items.q: Describe a historical place you have visited
items.text: A historical place that genuinely moved me was the Sixty Dome Mosque in Bagerhat, in the south-west of Bangladesh, which I visited during a trip to Khulna about three years ago. It dates back to the fifteenth century, and stepping inside felt like travelling back in time. The architecture was absolutely magnificent, with thick brick walls and long rows of slender stone pillars supporting dozens of small, rounded domes. What struck me most was the sense of history embedded in the walls; you could almost feel the countless generations who had passed through. A local guide explained its significance, telling us that it was built in the time of Khan Jahan Ali and that the whole area is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, which made the experience far richer than simply looking at old stones. I also wandered around the grounds and the large pond beside it, and I was surprised to learn that the mosque is still used for prayers today, so it is a living place rather than just a monument. I found myself genuinely awestruck by the craftsmanship of an era without modern machinery. Places like this are an important reminder of our heritage, and I think it is vital that we preserve them, especially as damp and salt are a real threat to old brickwork in that region. Honestly, I came away with a deeper appreciation of the past and how much skill and devotion went into these monuments. It was easily one of the most memorable trips I have taken.

items.q: Would you recommend it to foreign visitors?
items.text: Absolutely. It is one of the most important historical sites in Bangladesh, and combining it with a trip to the Sundarbans makes perfect sense, because both are in the same part of the country.

items.q: Did you learn about it at school?
items.text: Yes, briefly, in our history lessons, but reading about it in a textbook is nothing compared to standing inside. Seeing it in person made the history feel real rather than just facts to memorise.

items.q: Describe a place you would like to visit in the future
items.text: A place I have long dreamed of visiting is Switzerland, particularly the Alpine region. I first became captivated by it through photographs and documentaries, which made the scenery look almost unreal, and more recently through my job, because I work at an education consultancy and a few of our students have gone there to study hospitality. When they send photos back, I must admit I feel a little envious. The idea of snow-capped mountains, crystal-clear lakes and charming villages is incredibly appealing to me, especially as someone who has never actually seen snow. If I ever go, I would love to take the scenic train routes that wind through the mountains, which are said to be breathtaking. I would also like to go hiking beside one of the lakes and perhaps visit a small village where cheese is still made in the traditional way. I imagine the air there is wonderfully fresh, a world away from the dust and traffic I am used to. What draws me most is the promise of such pristine natural beauty, which is increasingly rare. I would also love to experience the local culture and food, of course. Honestly, it is at the very top of my bucket list, and I am determined to get there one day, even though it is famously expensive. I think some places are worth saving up for, and this is definitely one of them, so I have quietly started putting a little money aside each month.

items.q: Would you prefer to go alone or with others?
items.text: With others, ideally my family or a couple of close friends. Beautiful places are more enjoyable when you can share them, and I think my parents would be amazed to see snow for the first time.

items.q: How long would you like to stay there?
items.text: At least two weeks, if I could afford it. I would not want to rush from one place to another; I would rather travel slowly and actually enjoy each place properly.

items.q: Describe a park or garden you like
items.text: The place I would like to describe is a public park not far from where I live, which is a real green oasis in the middle of our town. It is only about ten minutes' walk from our flat, so it is very easy to reach. I try to visit at least once a week, usually on Friday afternoons, and more often in winter when the weather is pleasant. It is beautifully landscaped, with wide lawns, tall shady trees and a small pond in the middle, surrounded by flower beds that are at their best in early spring. There is also a walking track around the edge and a little play area for children. Sirajganj is getting more built up every year, so having such a lush green space nearby is genuinely precious. I usually go there to walk, read or simply sit on a bench and watch the world go by. What I love most is how it brings the community together; families picnic, children play cricket on the grass and elderly men sit chatting for hours. The atmosphere is always laid-back and cheerful, and nobody seems to be in a hurry. Honestly, spending time surrounded by greenery has a noticeably restorative effect on me, especially after a stressful week at work. Sometimes I take my four-year-old nephew there when my elder sister visits from Dhaka, and watching him run around is a joy in itself. I think every town needs places like this, and I feel lucky to have one so close.

items.q: Do you think your town needs more parks?
items.text: Yes, definitely. The town is growing quickly and new buildings are going up everywhere, so green spaces are shrinking. More parks would give children somewhere safe to play and give everyone a place to breathe.

items.q: What do you usually do there at the weekend?
items.text: Mostly I walk a few laps of the track and then sit under a tree with a book. Sometimes I meet a friend there, and we buy roasted peanuts from a vendor and chat for an hour.

items.q: Describe a place where you like to relax
items.text: The place where I relax most completely is actually the rooftop of our building, which offers a surprisingly lovely view over the town. We live on the third floor, so it is just a short climb up the stairs, and on a clear evening you can see the rooftops stretching out towards the river. I go up there most evenings, especially after a long or stressful day at the office. There is something wonderfully liberating about being up high, away from the noise and crowds below. I usually take a cup of tea, put on some quiet music and simply watch the sky change colour as the sun goes down. Some of our neighbours grow plants in pots up there, so it feels almost like a small garden. The gentle breeze is genuinely refreshing, and it seems to clear my head. What makes it so relaxing is the sense of solitude; it is my own little escape where no one bothers me. I often do my best thinking there, or sometimes just switch off entirely. During the monsoon I stand under the shelter of the stairwell and watch the rain sweep across the town, which is strangely calming. My job involves a lot of talking and problem-solving, so I need a moment to unwind before dinner with my family. Honestly, having a spot like this has been invaluable for my mental wellbeing. It costs nothing, yet it does more for my mood than almost anything else.

items.q: Do you ever go up there with other people?
items.text: Occasionally. My younger sister sometimes comes up after she finishes studying, and during Eid the whole family goes up in the evening. Mostly, though, I prefer to keep it as my own quiet time.

items.q: Is it easy to find places to relax in your town?
items.text: Not always. Sirajganj is fairly calm compared with Dhaka, but it is still getting busier, and most public places are quite noisy. That is why a private spot like our rooftop is so valuable.

items.q: Describe a building you find interesting
items.text: A building I find genuinely fascinating is the National Parliament House in Dhaka, known in Bengali as the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban, which is considered an architectural masterpiece. It stands in the Sher-e-Bangla Nagar area of the capital, surrounded by an artificial lake and wide lawns. Designed by the American architect Louis Kahn, it is unlike anything else in the country. What makes it so striking is its bold, geometric design, using simple shapes like circles and triangles cut into vast concrete walls. Despite its size, it has a strange sense of lightness and elegance, especially when the whole building is reflected in the still water around it. I find it interesting because it manages to be both avant-garde and timeless at the same time, even though it was completed in the early 1980s. The way natural light filters through the openings is genuinely ingenious, changing the whole feel of the interior throughout the day. It serves as the seat of our government, so it carries real symbolic importance too. I have mostly seen the interior in photographs, but I once walked around the grounds while visiting my sister, and the scale of it was quite overwhelming up close. Honestly, every time I see it I notice some new detail I had missed before. I think great architecture like this is a form of art, and it is something the country can rightly be proud of. I would love to see inside properly one day.

items.q: Would you like to see inside it?
items.text: Very much. I have seen photographs of the interior, with light pouring through the huge openings, and I would love to experience that in person if I ever get the chance to go inside.

items.q: Do you think modern buildings in Bangladesh are well designed?
items.text: Some are, but many new buildings are rather plain concrete blocks put up in a hurry. I think architects should learn from buildings like this one, which are practical but also genuinely beautiful.

items.q: Describe a place you visited on holiday
items.text: I would like to talk about a holiday I took to Cox's Bazar, home to one of the longest natural sea beaches in the world. I went there last winter with a few close friends from university, and it turned out to be one of the most memorable trips of my life. We took an overnight bus from Dhaka, which was tiring, but the excitement kept us going. The beach itself was absolutely stunning, stretching as far as the eye could see. We spent our days swimming, walking along the shore and watching the most spectacular sunsets I have ever seen. One morning we hired a jeep and drove along the Marine Drive towards Inani beach, with green hills on one side and the sea on the other, which was unforgettable. We also stopped at Himchari, where a small waterfall runs down the hillside, although it was only a trickle in the dry season. In the evenings we sampled fresh seafood, which was delectable, especially the grilled fish from the little stalls near the beach. What made it special was the combination of natural beauty and good company, which is a hard thing to beat. We laughed constantly and stayed up late talking, just like in our student days. Being by the sea was genuinely rejuvenating after months of office life. Honestly, there is something about the vastness of the ocean that puts your everyday worries into perspective. I came home feeling completely recharged, and it left me with cherished memories that I still look back on fondly.

items.q: Would you go back to Cox's Bazar?
items.text: Yes, without a doubt. Next time I would like to take my parents, because my mother has never seen the sea properly, and I think watching the sunset there together would be very special.

items.q: Do you prefer holidays with friends or with family?
items.text: Both have their charms. With friends, trips are more spontaneous and adventurous, while family holidays are calmer and more comfortable. At my age, I probably enjoy the energy of travelling with friends slightly more.

items.q: Describe a place that was full of noise
items.text: A place I remember as being incredibly noisy was Chawkbazar, a large wholesale market in Old Dhaka. I went there one morning last year, while I was staying with my elder sister, to help my brother-in-law buy things in bulk for a family wedding, and the sheer volume of sound was overwhelming from the moment we stepped out of the rickshaw. The lanes are extremely narrow, and every inch is filled with shops, porters carrying huge loads on their heads and handcarts squeezing past. Traders were shouting out their prices, customers were haggling loudly, and the constant honking of vehicles added to the chaos. It was genuinely deafening at times, and I struggled to hear the person next to me. Yet there was an undeniable energy to it all; the noise felt alive rather than unpleasant. I found the whole scene strangely exhilarating, even if I would not want to be there every day. After a couple of hours, though, I was desperate for some quiet, as the constant din became exhausting, and I had a slight headache by the time we left. Coming from Sirajganj, which is relatively calm, I was amazed that people work in that environment every single day. Honestly, it gave me a real appreciation for peace and quiet, which I usually take for granted. It was a fascinating, if overwhelming, glimpse of everyday commerce, and I felt I had seen the real heartbeat of the capital.

items.q: Do you mind noisy places in general?
items.text: I can tolerate them for a short while, especially if there is a good reason to be there, but I definitely prefer quiet places. After a long day, noise wears me out far more quickly than hard work.

items.q: Is your hometown noisy?
items.text: Not really, compared with Dhaka. There is traffic and plenty of rickshaw bells in the town centre, but the residential area where we live is fairly quiet, especially in the evenings.

items.q: Describe a café or restaurant you like
items.text: A café I am particularly fond of is a small, cosy place tucked away on a quiet street near my office in Sirajganj. I discovered it by accident about a year ago, when I ducked inside to escape a sudden monsoon downpour, and I have been a regular ever since. What makes it special is not just the tea, though their milk tea with a hint of cardamom is excellent, but the wonderfully inviting atmosphere. It has soft lighting, comfortable seating and quiet music, which makes it perfect for unwinding. There are only about eight tables, and the walls are decorated with old photographs of the town and the river. The staff are genuinely friendly and remember my usual order, which gives it a lovely personal touch. I usually have a cup of tea with a plate of singara, or a chicken sandwich if I have skipped lunch. I often go there to read or catch up with a friend, and I never feel rushed to leave. In a town where most places to eat are loud and crowded, finding somewhere so intimate feels like a real treat. The food is simple but consistently good, which is all I really want. Sometimes I even meet students from the consultancy there for an informal chat about their applications, because it is much more relaxed than the office. Honestly, it has become a bit of a second home, and I think a good café is worth its weight in gold for how welcoming it can be.

items.q: Do you prefer going to cafés alone or with friends?
items.text: It depends on my mood. If I want to read or think, I go alone, but most of the time I go with a friend, because a café is really about good conversation as much as the tea.

items.q: Are cafés popular in your town?
items.text: They are becoming more popular, especially among young people. Traditionally, people gathered at roadside tea stalls, which are still everywhere, but a few modern cafés have opened recently and they are usually quite busy.

items.q: Describe a place in your hometown that you like
items.text: A place in my hometown that I have always loved is the old square in the centre of Sirajganj, which is really the heart of the town. It sits at a busy crossroads not far from the main bazaar, and almost every rickshaw in town seems to pass through it at some point. It has been there for generations, and it holds a lot of nostalgia for me. As a child I would play there, and even now I find myself drawn back to it most weekends. My father used to take me there on the back of his bicycle to buy sweets, and I still go to the same sweet shop today. The square is surrounded by old shops, some with faded signboards that must be decades old, giving it a wonderfully quaint character. In the evenings it comes alive, with families strolling, vendors selling snacks and friends gathering to chat. I usually meet a couple of old school friends there, and we sit at a tea stall and talk about cricket or work for an hour or so. What I love most is that it has remained largely unchanged over the years, which is comforting in a fast-moving world. It feels like a place where the whole community naturally comes together, whatever their age or background. Honestly, being there always fills me with a warm sense of belonging. It is a simple place, but it means a great deal to me and to everyone who grew up there, and I hope it is never torn down in the name of development.

items.q: Has the square changed much since you were a child?
items.text: A little. Some of the old shops have been replaced by mobile phone shops, and there is more traffic now. But the basic layout and the evening atmosphere are exactly as I remember them.

items.q: Would you take a visitor there?
items.text: Yes, definitely. If someone wanted to understand everyday life in Sirajganj, I would take them there in the evening, buy them some sweets and just let them watch the town go by.

items.q: Describe a natural place you have visited (mountain or forest)
items.text: A natural place that took my breath away was Lawachara National Park, a hilly, forested area near Sreemangal in the north-east of the country. I went there with my family about two years ago, during a short winter holiday, hoping to escape our usual routine for a few days. The moment we arrived, I was struck by how lush and green everything was, with rolling tea gardens stretching across the hills on the way in. Walking through the forest, surrounded by tall trees and birdsong, was a genuinely humbling experience. At one point our guide pointed out a family of gibbons high up in the branches, and we all stood completely still, hardly daring to breathe. The air was wonderfully clean, and the whole landscape felt untouched by the chaos of modern life. We spent our days hiking along the forest trails and simply admiring the views, which were spectacular. We even crossed the railway line that runs straight through the forest, which felt like a scene from an old film. What struck me most was the profound sense of peace; being in such pristine nature made all my worries seem trivial. My grandfather, who could not join us, made me describe every detail on our next visit to the village. Honestly, I came away with a renewed appreciation for the natural world and a determination to protect it. It reminded me how important it is to disconnect and reconnect with nature.

items.q: Do you often visit natural places like this?
items.text: Not as often as I would like. Work keeps me busy, so I usually manage one proper trip a year. In between, walking by the Jamuna is my way of staying connected to nature.

items.q: What could be done to protect places like this?
items.text: I think visitor numbers should be controlled, and people should be taught not to leave litter or make noise. Local communities should also benefit from tourism, so they have a reason to protect the forest.

items.q: Describe a place where you would like to live
items.text: If I could live anywhere, I would choose a quiet coastal town, somewhere that balances natural beauty with a sense of community. I am thinking of somewhere like the area around Inani, south of Cox's Bazar, where green hills come right down towards the beach. I have always been drawn to the sea, so waking up to the sound of waves would be genuinely idyllic for me. I imagine a place that is peaceful but not isolated, with friendly neighbours, a small market and a slower pace of life. What appeals to me most is the idea of escaping the relentless hustle and bustle of big cities like Dhaka, which I find exhausting whenever I visit. I would love to spend my mornings walking along the shore and my evenings watching the sunset. During the day I could work remotely, advising students online, which is becoming quite possible in my field. At the weekends I might learn to fish or simply read on a balcony facing the sea. I think such an environment would be far more conducive to a healthy, balanced lifestyle. Of course, I would still want decent amenities nearby, such as a hospital and good internet, so it would need to be reasonably well connected, and close enough for my parents to visit. Honestly, the thought of such a calm, wholesome existence is very appealing. Perhaps one day, when my career allows it, I will make that dream a reality.

items.q: Do you think you will actually live there one day?
items.text: Perhaps, though probably not for many years. For now my family and my career are here, but it is a dream I keep at the back of my mind, maybe for later in life.

items.q: Would your family be happy if you moved away?
items.text: My parents would probably worry at first, as they like having us close. But if I were within a day's journey and visited often, I think they would gradually come round to the idea.

items.q: Describe a place where you like to shop
items.text: A place I really enjoy shopping is Jamuna Future Park, a huge, modern shopping mall in Dhaka, which I usually visit when I am staying with my elder sister. It is one of the biggest shopping centres in the country, so you could easily spend a whole day there. I mostly buy clothes, especially new shirts and a panjabi before Eid, and sometimes books or small gifts for my younger sister. I go there perhaps every two or three months, depending on how often I travel to Dhaka. What I like about it is that everything is under one roof, which makes it wonderfully convenient. It has a vast array of shops, from local brands to international ones, so I can compare prices without walking from market to market in the heat. Beyond the shopping itself, it is a pleasant place to spend a few hours; it is clean, air-conditioned and has good places to eat. I often go with my sister and her husband, and my nephew loves the play area, so it doubles as a family outing. What makes it enjoyable is the lively but comfortable atmosphere, which is never too overwhelming, except perhaps in the last few days before Eid. Honestly, even when I do not buy much, I enjoy just browsing and window-shopping. I think a good shopping centre is designed to be an experience, not just a transaction, and this one gets that balance right. Back home, I still prefer local shops for everyday things, but for special purchases this is my favourite place.

items.q: Do you prefer shopping in malls or in local markets?
items.text: For clothes and special purchases, I prefer malls because of the choice and fixed prices. For everyday things like fruit and vegetables, I always go to the local market, where everything is fresher and cheaper.

items.q: Do you ever shop online?
items.text: Yes, more and more, mainly for books and small electronics. It is convenient, but I still like to see and touch clothes before buying them, so for those I usually go to a shop.

items.q: Describe a place you visit often
items.text: A place I visit almost every day is a small gym near my home, which has become an important part of my routine. It is on the ground floor of a building just two streets away from our flat, so I can walk there in five minutes. I started going a couple of years ago to improve my health, after I realised that sitting at a desk all day was giving me back pain, and it quickly became a habit I genuinely look forward to. It is nothing fancy, but it is clean, well-equipped and rarely too crowded. I usually go straight after work and spend about an hour there, doing a mix of weights and running on the treadmill, followed by some stretching. It is one of the few times my mind switches off completely. What keeps me coming back is how energising a workout is after a long day at a desk. There is also a real sense of camaraderie among the regulars, which makes it feel welcoming rather than intimidating; we encourage each other and sometimes argue about cricket between sets. The trainer knows everyone by name, and he has been very patient with me. Beyond the physical benefits, it has become a valuable outlet for stress. Honestly, going there consistently has been genuinely transformative for both my body and my mood, and even my mother says I seem more cheerful these days. I think having a place that keeps you disciplined and healthy is worth its weight in gold.

items.q: Do you prefer exercising alone or with others?
items.text: I actually like a mix. I do my workout on my own, but having other people around keeps me motivated, and it is always easier to push yourself when someone is cheering you on.

items.q: Are gyms popular where you live?
items.text: They have become much more popular in recent years. When I was younger, hardly anyone in Sirajganj went to a gym, but now several have opened, and they are mostly full of young people.

items.q: Describe a tourist attraction you have visited
items.text: A tourist attraction that genuinely impressed me was the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest, which stretches across the south-west of Bangladesh and into India. I visited it about two years ago on a three-day boat tour that started from Khulna. It is a vast, remote wilderness, famous for being home to the Royal Bengal Tiger. Gliding through the narrow waterways surrounded by dense forest was an unforgettable experience. The mangrove trees themselves were fascinating, with their roots sticking up out of the mud like hundreds of little spikes, which helps them breathe when the tide comes in. We slept on the boat, and at night the silence was broken only by the calls of birds and the sound of the water. What made it so special was how untamed everything felt; this was nature completely on its own terms. During the day we took smaller boats into the creeks and walked along wooden trails with armed forest guards. We spotted deer, monkeys, exotic birds and even crocodiles, though sadly no tigers. The whole trip was genuinely exhilarating, partly because of the slight sense of danger. Our guide explained how ecologically important the area is, especially as a natural barrier that protects the coast from cyclones, which deepened my appreciation. I found the sheer scale and biodiversity of the place utterly captivating. Honestly, it is one of the few tourist attractions that fully lived up to the hype. It also made me realise how vital it is to protect such fragile natural wonders before they disappear, especially as rising sea levels are already putting the forest under pressure.

items.q: Would you go back to the Sundarbans?
items.text: Yes, I would love to, ideally in a different season to see how it changes. And of course I am still hoping that one day I will be lucky enough to catch a glimpse of a tiger.

items.q: Is it popular with foreign tourists?
items.text: It attracts some foreign visitors, but I think it is still underrated internationally. Most tourists there are Bangladeshis, which is a pity, because it is genuinely one of the most remarkable places in the region.

items.q: Describe a place where you studied
items.text: The place I would like to describe is my university campus, where I spent some of the most formative years of my life. It was a large, leafy campus on the outskirts of the city, with old buildings, a big central field and plenty of open green space. I studied there for four years, doing a BBA with a focus on management, and I graduated a few years ago. What I loved was how vibrant the atmosphere was; there was always something happening, from lectures and presentations to club activities and cultural programmes. I joined the debating club, which did wonders for my confidence and my English. The library in particular became a second home, a wonderfully studious environment that made it easy to focus, especially before exams. Beyond the academics, the campus was where I made lifelong friendships and grew as a person, partly because it was my first time living away from my family. Looking back, those years were genuinely pivotal in shaping who I am today, and even the skills I use at work now, like advising students and giving presentations, started there. There was a real sense of community, and everyone seemed to be striving towards something together. I still remember the long conversations over cheap tea at the canteen after classes. Honestly, I feel a strong sense of nostalgia whenever I think about it. I think a good campus offers far more than an education, and mine certainly did.

items.q: Do you still visit your university?
items.text: Only occasionally, when I have work nearby or there is an alumni event. It always feels a little strange, because the faces are all new, but walking across the field still brings back lots of memories.

items.q: What did you like least about studying there?
items.text: Probably the stressful exam periods, when the library was so full you could hardly find a seat, and missing home cooking. Still, those challenges were part of the experience, and they taught me independence.

items.q: Describe a library you have visited
items.text: A library I am very fond of is the public library in Sirajganj, a modest but well-kept building not far from the town centre. It is not grand, but it has a quiet dignity about it, with rows of tall wooden shelves and long reading tables. I try to go a couple of times a month, usually on a free afternoon when I need to study or simply want some quiet. The moment you step inside, you are enveloped in a wonderfully hushed atmosphere that immediately calms the mind. It has a decent collection of Bengali literature as well as some English books, so I can always find something interesting to read. I usually borrow novels, but I also read the daily newspapers there and occasionally look through books on business and management. What I love most is the sense of reverence people seem to have there; everyone respects the silence, which is increasingly rare. I usually sit at the same desk in a quiet corner near the back, which is my favourite spot. There is something deeply gratifying about being surrounded by so many books and knowing I will never run out of things to discover. Many students from less well-off families also rely on it for exam preparation, which makes it even more valuable to the town. Honestly, in an age of screens and constant noise, a library feels almost like a sanctuary. I think these places are precious, and I hope they never disappear.

items.q: Do you think libraries will still exist in the future?
items.text: I think so, but they will need to change. They will probably offer more digital resources and study spaces, but people will always need quiet places where they can read and think.

items.q: Do you prefer printed books or e-books?
items.text: Printed books, without doubt. I read on my phone when I am travelling, but I love the feel of a real book, and I remember what I read much better on paper.

items.q: Describe a beautiful place you have been to
items.text: One of the most beautiful places I have ever been to is Sreemangal, in the tea-growing region of Sylhet, which is often called the tea capital of Bangladesh. I had been once before with my family, but I went again last winter with a couple of friends from work, and winter is the ideal time, so the scenery was absolutely breathtaking. Endless rolling hills covered in neat rows of tea bushes stretched out in every direction, glowing green in the sunlight, with tall shade trees dotted between them. In the early morning, a thin mist hung over the valleys, giving the whole place an almost ethereal quality. I remember simply standing and staring, completely spellbound by the view. Later in the day we watched the tea pickers at work, moving along the rows with baskets on their backs, and we tried the famous seven-layer tea at a little shop in town, which was as colourful as it was strange. What made it so beautiful was the untouched, serene nature of it all, so far from the traffic and dust of the roads back home. I took countless photos, but honestly none of them captured how magical it felt in person. Being in such a beautiful place had a genuinely uplifting effect on my mood, and I felt almost at one with my surroundings. It is a memory I return to whenever I need a moment of calm, and I would happily go back every winter if I could.

items.q: Would you like to go back there?
items.text: Yes, definitely. Next time I would like to stay in one of the cottages near the forest and spend more time walking, rather than rushing around trying to see everything in a couple of days.

items.q: Do you prefer hills or beaches?
items.text: It is a difficult choice, but probably hills. Beaches are wonderful, but places like Sreemangal feel calmer and cooler, and I love the endless shades of green and the quiet of the early morning.

items.q: Describe a crowded place you have been to
items.text: A remarkably crowded place I remember was the Eid fair held on an open ground in the centre of our town last year, on the day after Eid-ul-Fitr. After Eid prayers at the mosque and visits to relatives the day before, I went with some old school friends to soak up the atmosphere, and the sheer number of people was staggering. It was so crowded because families from all the surrounding villages come into town for the fair, everyone has a few days off work, and children have new clothes and Eid money to spend. The ground and the streets around it were absolutely packed, with families, vendors and performers filling every inch of space. There were stalls selling toys, bangles and sweets, a small Ferris wheel and even a group of folk singers. At times it was genuinely difficult to move, and the crowd felt almost overwhelming. Yet despite the crush, there was an infectious sense of joy in the air that was hard to resist. The whole place was buzzing with energy, music and the smell of street food. While I would not want to deal with such crowds every day, on that occasion it felt like part of the celebration. I did lose my friends for about twenty minutes, and we only found each other again by shouting. Honestly, being swept along with so many happy people was strangely uplifting. It reminded me how such shared events bring an entire community together, even if you do lose a bit of personal space in the process.

items.q: Do you usually enjoy crowds?
items.text: Not really. I find them tiring in everyday situations, such as busy markets or traffic. But at festivals it is different, because everyone shares the same happy mood and the crowd becomes part of the fun.

items.q: How do people in your town celebrate Eid?
items.text: The day starts with prayers at the mosque, then people visit relatives, share special food like semai and give money to children. Over the next few days, many families go to fairs or visit friends.

items.q: Describe a place with beautiful views
items.text: A place with truly beautiful views that I will never forget was the top of a hill in Bandarban, in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, which I hiked up during a trip with friends about three years ago. We travelled by bus to Bandarban town, then took a jeep along winding mountain roads to a small village, and from there we climbed on foot for about three hours with a local guide. The climb was fairly demanding, especially in the heat, but the reward at the summit was more than worth the effort. The final stretch was so steep that we had to use our hands in places, and I was drenched in sweat by the time we reached the top. From the summit, the view was absolutely panoramic, stretching across valleys, forests and the Sangu river winding through the landscape far below. Layer after layer of green hills faded into the blue distance, and clouds were drifting past almost at eye level. I remember feeling a genuine sense of elation as I caught my breath and took it all in. The scale of the scenery was humbling, making me feel wonderfully small against such a vast backdrop. We stayed up there for nearly an hour, simply admiring the view, sharing some biscuits and taking photographs. There is something special about a view you have earned through effort, which makes it feel all the more rewarding. Honestly, it was one of those rare moments when the natural world takes your breath away. I still picture that view whenever I need a moment of calm.

items.q: Do you enjoy hiking?
items.text: Yes, although I do not get many chances, because there are no hills near Sirajganj. When I travel, though, I always try to include a walk or a hike, because it is the best way to see a place properly.

items.q: Did you take a lot of photos there?
items.text: Plenty, but none of them really did the view justice. Nowadays I try to take a few photos and then put my phone away, so I can actually enjoy the moment.

items.q: Describe a place where you learned something new
items.text: A place where I learned something genuinely new was a small pottery studio in Dhaka, where I took a one-day weekend workshop while I was staying with my elder sister last year. I had always been curious about working with clay, partly because Bengal has such a long tradition of terracotta and clay pots, so when my sister showed me an advert online, I signed up on a whim. What I learned was the basics of shaping clay on a potter's wheel, from centring the lump of clay to slowly pulling up the walls of a bowl. From the moment I sat at the wheel, I realised how much more demanding the craft is than it looks. My first few attempts collapsed hopelessly, which was humbling but oddly enjoyable. The instructor was wonderfully patient, guiding us step by step, sometimes placing her hands over ours so we could feel the right pressure, until I finally shaped something recognisable. There were only six of us, so we got plenty of individual attention and learned a lot from each other's mistakes as well. What I found most valuable was learning to be patient with myself; the process required real perseverance. There was something deeply satisfying about creating something with my own hands, away from screens. By the end of the day I had made a slightly wobbly bowl that I was absurdly proud of, and it now sits on my desk at home. Honestly, the experience was surprisingly therapeutic, and it reminded me how rewarding it is to step outside your comfort zone.

items.q: Have you done pottery since then?
items.text: Not yet, unfortunately, because there is no studio near Sirajganj. But I have been looking for another workshop in Dhaka, and I would love to try again and hopefully make something less wobbly.

items.q: Do you think adults should keep learning new skills?
items.text: Absolutely. Learning something new keeps your mind active and stops life from becoming routine. It does not have to be useful for work; even a hobby like pottery can teach you patience and confidence.

items.q: Describe a public place that was recently built or renovated
items.text: A public place that was recently renovated in my town is the riverside walkway along the Jamuna, which has been beautifully transformed over the last couple of years. It runs along the embankment on the edge of Sirajganj, not far from where I live. It used to be quite neglected and run-down, with broken paving, rubbish piling up and hardly any lights, so most people avoided it after dark, and the change has been remarkable. Now it features a wide walking path, proper lighting, rows of young trees and plenty of seating, making it far more accessible to everyone, including elderly people and families with small children. The whole area feels clean, modern and genuinely welcoming, which it never did before. On any given evening it is now full of people walking, jogging or simply relaxing by the water, and a few tea stalls have opened nearby. What I appreciate most is how the renovation has revitalised a part of the town that was previously ignored. It has become a real gathering point for the community, and I often bump into neighbours and old classmates there. My parents now walk there most evenings, which is good for my father now that he has retired. Honestly, I think this kind of investment in public spaces is commendable, because it improves everyone's quality of life. My only concern is that it must be properly maintained, or it could fall into disrepair again. It has quickly become one of my favourite places to unwind, and it shows what good urban planning can achieve.

items.q: Do you think more public places should be improved?
items.text: Definitely. There are several parks and fields in our town that are in poor condition, and improving them would benefit everyone, especially children and elderly people who have few other places to go.

items.q: Who should pay for improvements like this?
items.text: Mainly the local government, as it is a public space. But I think local businesses could also contribute, because a pleasant area attracts more visitors, which is good for their trade as well.

items.q: Describe a place away from home where you stayed
items.text: A place away from home where I once stayed was a small guesthouse in the hills near Rangamati, during a short break with my family last year. We stayed there because my father had just retired, and we wanted to mark the occasion with a few quiet days somewhere away from the usual tourist crowds. A friend of my father's recommended it, so we booked it without really knowing what to expect. It turned out to be a wonderfully charming little place, run by a warm local family. The rooms were simple but immaculately clean, and the view from the balcony, looking out over the hills and the blue water of Kaptai Lake, was spectacular. What made the stay so memorable was the genuine hospitality of the hosts, who treated us like old friends and cooked delicious home-style meals, including fresh fish from the lake. In the afternoons we took a boat out on the lake, and in the evenings we sat on the veranda drinking tea and chatting until late. Waking up to birdsong and fresh hill air was a world away from my usual office routine. I felt completely relaxed there in a way that hotels rarely achieve, and it was lovely to see my parents so happy and rested. Honestly, the whole experience was thoroughly refreshing, and it reminded me that the best trips are often about atmosphere rather than luxury. I would happily go back and stay there again.

items.q: Do you prefer guesthouses or hotels?
items.text: For a relaxing break, I prefer guesthouses, because they feel more personal and you meet local people. For a work trip, though, a hotel is more practical, as everything is organised and predictable.

items.q: Would you recommend the area to others?
items.text: Definitely. Rangamati is beautiful, especially around the lake, and it feels quite different from the rest of Bangladesh. I would just advise people to avoid the peak holiday season, when it gets much busier.

items.q: Describe a market you have visited
items.text: A market I find genuinely fascinating is the old bazaar in the centre of Sirajganj, which has been trading for as long as anyone can remember. I love wandering through it whenever I get the chance, usually on a weekend morning. It is a wonderfully vibrant place, with narrow lanes crammed with stalls selling everything from fresh vegetables, fish and spices to fabrics and handicrafts. Because our district is well known for handloom weaving, there are also shops piled high with colourful saris, lungis and gamchas, many of them made by weavers in nearby villages. The colours, smells and sounds combine to create an atmosphere that is completely immersive. What I enjoy most is the lively art of haggling, which is expected and almost a game between buyer and seller. I usually go there to buy fresh produce for my mother or small gifts, though half the fun is simply browsing. Before Eid I always buy a new lungi there for my grandfather, because he insists that local cloth is better than anything from Dhaka. The market has a raw, authentic character that modern shopping malls completely lack. Honestly, there is something special about a place where commerce has happened the same way for generations. Of course, it can be muddy and chaotic during the monsoon, but I have learnt to take that in my stride. It feels genuinely alive, and I always come away with a small treasure and a real sense of having experienced something quintessentially local.

items.q: Do you think traditional markets will survive?
items.text: I hope so, and I think they will, at least in towns like mine. Many people still prefer fresh food and a personal relationship with sellers, although supermarkets and online shopping are slowly attracting younger customers.

items.q: Are you good at bargaining?
items.text: Not as good as my mother, who is an expert. I usually start too high and give in too quickly, so when I need something important, I take her with me.

items.q: Describe a place you go to be alone
items.text: A place I go to be completely alone is a quiet stretch of the riverbank a short walk from my home, well beyond the busy part of the embankment where people gather in the evenings. To reach it, you follow a narrow path past a few fields and a clump of bamboo, and then the river suddenly opens up in front of you. I tend to go there once or twice a week, and more often whenever I feel overwhelmed and need to clear my head. It is a secluded spot that few people seem to know about, which is exactly why I love it. I usually just sit on the grass under an old tree, watch the water and let my thoughts settle. Occasionally I bring a book, but more often I do nothing at all, which I rarely get to do these days. There is something deeply restorative about being alone in nature, with no phone buzzing and no one demanding my attention. I go alone because at home and at work I am constantly surrounded by people, and although I love them, I also need time to recharge my batteries. I find that a bit of solitude helps me process my feelings and make sense of whatever is bothering me. Far from feeling lonely, I feel more like myself there than almost anywhere else. Honestly, in a world that never seems to stop, having a private place to simply be is a rare luxury. I always return home feeling calmer and more centred.

items.q: Do you think it is important to spend time alone?
items.text: Yes, I do. Time alone gives you space to reflect and understand your own feelings. Without it, I think people can become stressed and lose touch with what really matters to them.

items.q: Does your family know about this place?
items.text: My younger sister does, and she teases me about my secret hideout. My parents know I go for walks by the river, but I do not think they know exactly where I go.

items.q: Describe a famous place in your country
