items.text: A famous place in my country that I think everyone should see is the National Martyrs' Memorial, which honours those who died in our war of independence in 1971. It is located in Savar, on the outskirts of Dhaka, about an hour's drive from the city centre depending on the traffic. It is a deeply poignant and symbolic site, and it holds enormous significance for the nation. The memorial itself is architecturally striking, with seven triangular structures of different heights rising towards the sky, and I have read that they represent the key stages of our struggle for independence. It is famous not only for its design but also because every year, on Independence Day and Victory Day, huge crowds come to lay wreaths there, led by the country's leaders. I first visited it on a school trip and went again a few years ago with my younger sister. Visiting it is a genuinely moving experience, as it commemorates such an important chapter of our history. What makes it so meaningful is that it represents the sacrifice and courage of ordinary people, farmers, students and workers alike. I think it is important for younger generations to visit and understand their heritage. The surrounding grounds are peaceful and beautifully maintained, with a lake and mass graves nearby, which adds to the solemn atmosphere. Honestly, I would recommend it to any visitor, ideally early in the morning, because it offers real insight into what shaped our country. It is a place that inspires both reflection and a quiet sense of patriotism.

items.q: Do schools in Bangladesh take students there?
items.text: Yes, many schools organise trips there, especially around Victory Day and Independence Day. I think it is a valuable experience, because it helps young people connect emotionally with the history they read about.

items.q: Are there other monuments like this in your country?
items.text: Yes, the Central Shaheed Minar in Dhaka commemorates the Language Movement of 1952. On the twenty-first of February, huge numbers of people walk there barefoot at dawn to lay flowers.

items.q: Describe a place you enjoyed visiting as a child
items.text: A place I absolutely loved visiting as a child was my grandparents' village home, not far from Sirajganj, where they still live today. Although it is not a long journey, as a small boy it felt like travelling to another world. I went there with my parents and my two sisters, usually during the school holidays and always for Eid, and those visits are among my happiest childhood memories. Often my cousins came too, so the house would be full of noise and laughter. The house was surrounded by open fields and ponds, which felt like a boundless playground to a small child. I would spend whole days climbing mango trees, fishing with my grandfather and running around barefoot with my cousins. In the monsoon we would jump into the pond from the bank, and my grandmother would scold us and then feed us hot rice and fish. Everything felt wonderfully carefree, far from the rules and routines of school and town life. What made it so special was the sense of freedom and the warmth of the whole extended family gathered together. The pace of life there was so gentle and unhurried. Honestly, looking back, those visits filled me with a deep sense of belonging that I still treasure. We still visit often, and my mother helps look after my grandparents, but the village has changed a lot since then, with more concrete houses and fewer open fields. Even so, the memories remain vivid and precious to me.

items.q: Do children today still enjoy visiting villages?
items.text: Some do, but many are so used to screens that they get bored without the internet. My nephew loves it, though, especially chasing the chickens, so I think it depends on how children are introduced to it.

items.q: Do you still enjoy going there now?
items.text: Very much, though for different reasons. Now I enjoy sitting with my grandparents, listening to their stories and helping them out, rather than climbing trees. It feels calm and grounding compared with work.

items.q: Describe a sports venue or stadium you have visited
items.text: A sports venue I visited that left a strong impression on me was the Sher-e-Bangla National Cricket Stadium in Mirpur, Dhaka, which is the main home ground of the Bangladesh team. I went there a couple of years ago with my brother-in-law to watch a one-day international, and it was my first time watching live cricket at that level. Cricket is almost a religion in my country, so the atmosphere was electric long before the game even started; people were queuing outside hours in advance, with their faces painted red and green. The stadium was absolutely packed to the rafters, with thousands of fans singing, blowing horns and waving flags. When our team hit a boundary or took a wicket, the roar of the crowd was genuinely thunderous, and I could feel the energy in my chest. What made it so memorable was the incredible sense of unity; complete strangers were hugging and celebrating together as one. Watching a match on television simply cannot compare to being there in person. The whole experience was thrilling and completely immersive. We bought snacks from the vendors walking up and down the stands and stayed until the very last ball. Honestly, by the end I had lost my voice from cheering, but I did not care in the slightest, especially as we won comfortably. It was one of the most exciting days of my life, and I would jump at the chance to go again.

items.q: Do you prefer watching sports live or on TV?
items.text: Live, definitely, for the atmosphere, although I watch most matches on television because tickets are hard to get and the stadium is far from Sirajganj. At home, at least, you get the replays and commentary.

items.q: Do you play cricket yourself?
items.text: Only casually now. As a boy I played every afternoon with friends in the field near our house, but these days I prefer watching, and I occasionally join a friendly match during the holidays.

items.q: Describe a place you would like to visit again
items.text: A place I would love to visit again is Darjeeling, a small hill town in India, which I went to a few years ago and which completely charmed me. I first went there with two friends from university just after our final exams, crossing the border by land and taking a shared jeep up the winding mountain roads. I only stayed a few days, which was nowhere near long enough to appreciate it fully. The town was wonderfully picturesque, with steep lanes, old colonial buildings and tea gardens clinging to the hillsides, and on clear mornings we could see the snowy Himalayan peaks in the distance. On that first visit I explored the local trails, rode the famous toy train for a short stretch and sampled the regional food, especially the momos, but I feel I only scratched the surface. What draws me back is the incredibly tranquil pace of life there, which was a world away from my hectic routine. There is a certain magnetic quality to some places that stays with you long after you leave, and this town has it. I have often found myself daydreaming about returning and staying longer next time, perhaps in spring when the views are clearer. I would also like to take my parents, because my father loves tea and would enjoy visiting a proper tea estate. Honestly, some destinations simply leave you wanting more, and revisiting it would be a genuine delight. I hope to make it happen soon.

items.q: What would you do differently next time?
items.text: I would stay much longer, at least a week, and go in spring when the views are clearer. I would also like to stay in a small family-run guesthouse rather than a hotel.

items.q: Do you prefer visiting new places or returning to familiar ones?
items.text: Generally I prefer new places, because I love discovering something different. But a few special places, like Darjeeling, are worth returning to, because you notice things you missed the first time.

items.q: Describe a peaceful place you know
items.text: A place I associate with real peace is an old, quiet mosque near my grandparents' home in our ancestral village, which I have known since childhood. It sits at the edge of a pond, shaded by a huge old banyan tree, and it is small, with whitewashed walls and a single dome. I first went there as a little boy, holding my grandfather's hand for Friday prayers, and I still go with him whenever we visit, even though he walks much more slowly now. It is not grand or famous, but it has a wonderfully tranquil atmosphere that I have never found elsewhere. Whenever I visit, I am struck by the deep sense of calm the moment I step inside. The thick walls seem to shut out the noise of the world completely, leaving only silence and the occasional sound of birds outside. Inside, the floor is cool and the light is soft, because the windows are small. Even for a few minutes, sitting there is genuinely meditative, and it helps me clear my mind of everyday worries. What makes it so peaceful is not just the quiet, but the sense of stillness and reflection it encourages, and perhaps also the memories of my grandfather teaching me there. In our fast-paced, noisy lives, such places feel increasingly rare and valuable. Honestly, I always leave feeling lighter and more centred. I think everyone needs a place like this, somewhere they can retreat to and simply be at peace for a while.

items.q: Do you go there often?
items.text: Whenever we visit my grandparents, which is quite often, usually for Friday prayers with my grandfather. Even when I am busy, I try to stop there for a few minutes before we head back to town.

items.q: Is it easy to find peaceful places nowadays?
items.text: It is getting harder, especially in towns and cities, where noise and crowds are everywhere. That is why places like this feel so precious, and why I think we should protect them.

items.q: Describe a hotel you have stayed in
items.text: A hotel that genuinely exceeded my expectations was a resort in Cox's Bazar where I stayed during a family holiday by the sea, about a year after I started working. It was the first holiday I had helped to pay for, so it felt quite special, and the whole family came, including my elder sister, her husband and their two children. We stayed for four nights in December, when the weather is cool and dry. From the moment we arrived, the service was impeccable, and the staff went out of their way to make us feel welcome, even arranging a small cake when they found out it was my mother's birthday. The room was spacious and immaculately clean, with a balcony overlooking the ocean, which was breathtaking at sunrise. What impressed me most was the attention to detail; everything felt thoughtfully designed and genuinely luxurious without being pretentious. The food was excellent, especially the seafood at dinner, and the whole atmosphere was wonderfully relaxing. I remember spending hours by the pool with my nephew, feeling completely at ease, while my parents walked on the beach. Of course, it was not cheap, but the experience felt worth every penny. Honestly, a well-run hotel can make or break a holiday, and this one made ours truly special. It set a standard that has been hard to match since. I still remember that stay as one of the most comfortable of my life.

items.q: Do you usually stay in hotels when you travel?
items.text: Not usually. On most trips I stay with relatives or in cheaper guesthouses to save money, so that resort was a real treat. It was worth it once, but I could not afford that every time.

items.q: What do you think makes a good hotel?
items.text: Friendly, attentive staff most of all, followed by cleanliness and comfort. A beautiful building helps, but if the staff are rude or careless, even the most luxurious hotel will not feel welcoming.

items.q: Describe a place with clean and fresh air
items.text: A place I associate with wonderfully clean air is a tea estate in the hills near Sylhet, which I visited a couple of years ago during the winter. I had just spent a few days in Dhaka, so the difference in air quality was immediately noticeable and genuinely refreshing. The moment I stepped off the bus, I could not stop taking deep breaths of the cool, crisp air. It felt as though my lungs were being cleaned out after days of breathing in the capital's smog and dust. I spent my days walking through the tea gardens and chatting with some of the workers, and in the mornings I climbed a small hill to watch the sunrise over the rows of tea bushes. The fresh air made even simple activities feel invigorating, and I slept better than I had in months. What made it so pleasant was the complete absence of heavy traffic, brick kilns and factories; the environment felt truly unpolluted. The endless trees and bushes all around must have helped too, and the dew on the leaves in the early morning made everything smell wonderfully green. Honestly, the experience made me realise that clean air is something we take for granted, and how badly urban pollution affects us, especially children and older people like my grandparents. I came away not only feeling healthier but also more conscious of environmental issues, and now I try to walk short distances instead of taking an auto-rickshaw. It is a place I would return to just to breathe properly again.

items.q: Is air pollution a problem where you live?
items.text: In Sirajganj it is not as bad as in Dhaka, but it is getting worse, mainly because of dust, traffic and brick kilns in the dry season. During the monsoon the air is much cleaner.

items.q: Would you like to live somewhere like that?
items.text: For a while, yes, but perhaps not permanently. The tea gardens are quite remote, and I would miss my family and the convenience of town. A long holiday there every year would be ideal.

items.q: Describe a museum or art gallery you have visited
items.text: A museum I found genuinely fascinating was the Bangladesh National Museum in Shahbag, Dhaka, which I first visited on a school trip years ago and again more recently with my younger sister. Although it is quite a long journey from Sirajganj, both visits were well worth the effort. It houses an impressive collection spanning our country's history, from ancient artefacts to modern art, spread over several floors. What I found most captivating was the section on ancient Bengal, with terracotta plaques, stone sculptures and old coins, some of them more than a thousand years old, beautifully preserved behind glass. Walking through the galleries felt like stepping through different eras, which was genuinely enlightening. I also spent a long time in the Liberation War gallery, where there are photographs, letters and personal belongings of people who fought in 1971, and that part was very emotional. My sister was particularly interested in the paintings by Zainul Abedin, one of our most celebrated artists. I have always believed that museums are an underrated way to learn, far more vivid than any textbook. Seeing real historical objects gave me a much deeper appreciation of the past, and it made the stories my grandfather tells feel more real. The building itself was grand and well maintained, adding to the sense of occasion. Honestly, I could easily have spent an entire day there without getting bored. I think places like this are invaluable, because they keep our history alive for future generations to discover and appreciate.

items.q: Do you often go to museums?
items.text: Not as often as I would like, as there are few museums near Sirajganj. Whenever I visit Dhaka for more than a couple of days, though, I try to spend an afternoon in a museum or gallery.

items.q: Should museums be free?
items.text: I think entry should be free or very cheap, especially for students, because museums are educational. If people have to think twice about the price, the ones who would benefit most will simply stay away.

items.q: Describe a place that is important to your family
items.text: A place that holds deep importance for my family is our ancestral home in the village, not far from Sirajganj, which has been in the family for generations. It is surrounded by rice fields, with a pond at the back and a big courtyard in the middle. Although we now live in a flat in town, this house remains a powerful symbol of our roots. My grandparents still live there, and my mother often goes to help look after them, so we are back and forth all the time. Every major family occasion, from weddings to Eid, seems to bring us all back there, and my elder sister travels from Dhaka with her children for the big celebrations. The house itself is old and simple, with a tin roof and wooden beams, but it is filled with sentimental value that no amount of money could replace. My father grew up there, and his old wooden school desk is still in one of the rooms. Walking through those rooms fills me with a strong sense of continuity and belonging. What makes it so important is that it connects the whole extended family across the generations, and my grandfather loves telling stories about the people who lived there before him. In a fast-changing world, having such an enduring anchor feels genuinely precious. Honestly, I hope we manage to keep it in the family for many years to come, even though some relatives have talked about selling part of the land. It is far more than a building; it is the cornerstone of our family's identity, and I feel deeply attached to it.

items.q: Do you think your family will keep the house?
items.text: I really hope so. There is some talk about the land, but my father feels strongly that the house should stay in the family, and I think most of us agree with him.

items.q: Do young people in Bangladesh still care about their ancestral homes?
items.text: Many do, especially at Eid, when huge numbers of people travel back to their villages. But as more young people settle in cities or abroad, those ties are becoming weaker, which I find a little sad.

items.q: Describe a place with interesting architecture
items.text: A place with genuinely interesting architecture that comes to mind is Ahsan Manzil, an old palace in Old Dhaka, right on the bank of the Buriganga river. It was built in the nineteenth century as the residence of the Nawabs of Dhaka, and today it is a museum, which I visited while staying with my sister last year. People often call it the Pink Palace because of its colour, and it is a striking example of the Indo-Saracenic style, which mixes European and Mughal influences. What fascinated me was the craftsmanship; the arches, pillars and balconies are full of detail, and a grand staircase at the front leads up to the large dome at the centre of the building. The building is ornate without feeling excessive, and it blends beauty with clever practical design, such as high ceilings and wide verandas that keep the rooms cool in the heat. I found it remarkable how sophisticated the design was, considering it was built long before air conditioning. Inside, the rooms display furniture, portraits and household objects from the period, which give you a sense of how the family lived. Standing inside, I felt a real sense of admiration for the skill of the people who created it. Honestly, modern buildings, for all their convenience, rarely have this kind of soul. I think architecture like this tells us a great deal about the culture and values of the past, which is exactly what makes it so compelling to me. It also reminds me how important it is to conserve such buildings in a city that is changing so fast.

items.q: Do you prefer old or modern buildings?
items.text: For beauty and character, I definitely prefer old buildings. Modern buildings are more comfortable and practical, of course, but they often look the same, whereas old buildings tell you something about the place and its history.

items.q: Was it crowded when you visited?
items.text: Yes, fairly crowded, as it is one of the most popular sights in Old Dhaka. There were school groups and families everywhere, but it was still possible to find quieter corners to look around.

items.q: Describe a village or countryside area you have visited
items.text: A countryside area I visited that I still think about fondly is a small farming village in Bogura district, about two hours from Sirajganj by road. I went there last year during the harvest season to visit a university friend's family, and although I know village life well from my grandparents' home, this place felt even more remote and peaceful. The village was surrounded by endless green paddy fields, and everything moved at a wonderfully leisurely pace. Most families there grow rice and vegetables, and many keep a few cows and chickens, so the day starts very early. What struck me most was how genuinely content the people seemed, despite having far fewer material comforts than people in towns and cities. My friend's mother cooked for us on a clay stove, and the food, fresh from their own fields and pond, was some of the best I have ever eaten. We spent our days walking along the narrow paths between the fields, and I even tried my hand at cutting rice, which was far harder than it looked. In the evenings we sat talking under a sky absolutely full of stars. The air was clean and the atmosphere was completely unhurried. Honestly, the experience gave me a real appreciation for a simpler way of life. It made me question how much of our constant rush is actually necessary. I came away feeling calm and strangely rejuvenated, and I would love to spend more time somewhere like that, away from it all.

items.q: Would you like to live in a village like that?
items.text: For a few months, perhaps, but probably not permanently. I love the peace, but my work depends on good internet and being near clients, and I would miss the conveniences of town life.

items.q: Are villages in Bangladesh changing?
items.text: Yes, quite rapidly. Most villages now have electricity, mobile phones and better roads, and many young people move away for work. Life is more comfortable, but some of the traditional community spirit is fading.

items.q: Describe a place where you like to walk
items.text: A place I love to walk is a tree-lined avenue in the park near my home, which runs along one side of the park beneath tall rain trees and a few old mango trees. It is only about ten minutes from our flat, so it is very easy to fit into my day. I try to go there most evenings after work, and on Friday mornings I sometimes go early, before the heat builds up. Usually I go alone, but occasionally I go with a friend, and now that my father has retired he sometimes joins me, which has become a nice chance for us to talk. What makes it perfect for walking is the shade from the mature trees and the wide, well-kept paths. It is far enough from the main roads that the noise fades away, leaving a wonderfully calm atmosphere. I find that walking there is not just good exercise but also genuinely meditative; it is when I do some of my best thinking. The changing light in the evening, as the sun filters through the leaves, makes the whole place feel serene. Sometimes I listen to music or a podcast, and other times I simply enjoy the sound of birds settling down for the night. When I walk with my father, he tells me how the town looked when he was young, which I find fascinating. Honestly, this simple daily walk has become one of the most rejuvenating parts of my routine. It clears my head, lifts my spirits and gives me a small pocket of calm in an otherwise busy day.

items.q: Do you think walking is a good form of exercise?
items.text: Yes, it is probably the most underrated one. It is free, anyone can do it and it is gentle on the body, yet it still keeps you fit, especially if you walk briskly every day.

items.q: Do many people walk there?
items.text: Quite a lot, particularly in the early morning and the evening. You see older people walking for their health, families strolling with children and a few serious joggers who overtake everyone.

items.q: Describe your ideal home
items.text: If I could design my ideal home, it would be a comfortable two-storey house on the edge of a quiet town, balancing modern convenience with a connection to nature. It would not need to be huge or extravagant; I value comfort and warmth far more than showing off. I picture large windows that let in plenty of natural light, making the whole space feel open and airy, and a wide veranda where the family could sit together in the evenings with tea. Ideally, it would be somewhere near Sirajganj, perhaps within sight of the Jamuna, so that I could stay close to my parents and grandparents. As for features, a small garden would be essential, somewhere I could grow a few vegetables, plant a mango tree and relax outdoors. Inside, I would want a cosy reading corner with shelves full of books and a proper kitchen, since those are the rooms where I spend most of my time. A spare bedroom would also be important, so that my elder sister and her children could stay whenever they visit from Dhaka. The house would need to be built with the monsoon in mind, raised slightly off the ground so that it never floods. What matters most to me is that it feels genuinely welcoming, both to family and to guests. I would also love it to be in a peaceful area with clean air and friendly neighbours. Honestly, my idea of an ideal home is less about luxury and more about creating a sanctuary where I can truly relax and feel at peace.

items.q: Is your current home similar to your ideal home?
items.text: In some ways. Our flat is comfortable and in a quiet area, but it has no garden and not much natural light. The biggest similarity is that it is full of family, which matters most.

items.q: Would you prefer to live in a house or a flat?
items.text: A house, ideally, because of the space and the possibility of having a garden. Flats are more practical and secure in towns, though, so for now I am perfectly happy where I am.

items.q: Describe a difficult decision you once made
items.text: I'd like to talk about a decision that honestly kept me awake at night for weeks. One of the hardest decisions I have faced was turning down a stable job to pursue something more uncertain but closer to what I actually wanted. This was about two years ago, just after I had been offered a comfortable position with good pay at a bank, only a few months after finishing my BBA. At the same time, a small education consultancy offered me a role helping students apply to study abroad, which paid less but felt far more meaningful. On paper the bank was the sensible choice, which is exactly what made walking away so agonising. In my town, a bank job is seen as a real achievement, so I knew people would question my judgement. I spent weeks weighing it up, going back and forth, because the secure option felt safe while the other was a genuine gamble. What ultimately tipped the balance was realising I would probably bitterly regret not taking the risk far more than any short-term setback. Telling my family was nerve-wracking, since they naturally worried, but they came round once they saw how determined I was. As for how I felt, I was anxious for a long time, but also strangely liberated. Looking back, it was a real turning point, and although the following months were rocky, it taught me that the most rewarding paths are rarely the most comfortable. I still feel it was the right call.

items.q: Did your family agree with your decision in the end?
items.text: Yes, eventually. My father was the first to support me, probably because he ran his own business for over thirty years and understood taking a chance. My mother took a little longer to feel comfortable.

items.q: Do you find it easy to make decisions in general?
items.text: Not really, to be honest. For small things I'm quick, but with big decisions I tend to overthink. These days I try to set myself a deadline so I don't go round in circles forever.

items.q: Describe a time you helped someone
items.text: I'd like to describe a time I helped a new colleague at the education consultancy where I work. A time I clearly remember helping someone was when a younger colleague was struggling badly with a project and close to panicking. It was during our busiest season last year, and he had been asked to prepare several students' university applications with very tight deadlines. He was new and clearly overwhelmed, afraid to admit he was falling behind. I noticed he seemed stressed, so I quietly offered to sit with him after work and go through it together. Over a couple of evenings, we broke the task into manageable steps and slowly untangled the problem. I also showed him the checklist I use for each application and how to deal with the most urgent deadlines first. What I found most rewarding was watching his confidence gradually return as things started to make sense. He was incredibly grateful, though honestly, helping him did not feel like a chore at all. I think we underestimate how much a small act of generosity can mean to someone at a low point. It also reminded me of the times people had helped me when I was new and lost. Honestly, that experience left me feeling genuinely fulfilled, and it strengthened our working relationship enormously. These days he is one of the most dependable people in our office, and I like to think those evenings played a small part in that.

items.q: Do you often help your colleagues?
items.text: Fairly often, yes. Our office is quite small, so we depend on each other a lot. If someone is stuck, it is usually quicker for everyone if we pitch in rather than let the problem grow.

items.q: Did he ever return the favour?
items.text: He did, actually. A few months later I was buried in visa paperwork before a holiday, and he stayed late to help me finish. It felt good to know the support went both ways.

items.q: Describe a time when you were very busy
items.text: The busiest time I can remember was about a year ago, and I still feel slightly tired just thinking about it. A period when I was extraordinarily busy was during the final weeks before a major deadline at work, which happened to coincide with a family event. At the consultancy, it was the peak of the application season, when lots of students were trying to submit their university applications at once, and at the same time my cousin was getting married in our ancestral village. I found myself juggling long working hours with preparations at home, and there simply were not enough hours in the day. My schedule was absolutely relentless; I would wake early, work through lunch and often continue late into the night. Then at weekends I travelled to the village to help with the arrangements for the wedding. At times it felt genuinely overwhelming, and I worried I might drop the ball on something important. What got me through was staying organised, making detailed lists and prioritising ruthlessly. Somehow I managed to meet the deadline and see the family event through successfully. As for how I felt, I was exhausted but also quietly proud. Looking back, it taught me a great deal about managing pressure, and I discovered I was more capable under stress than I had thought. Honestly, while I would not want to repeat it too often, it was a valuable lesson in resilience and time management.

items.q: How do you usually relax after a busy period?
items.text: I like to take a long walk by the Jamuna in the evening, or just sit at home with a cup of tea and a book. After that busy month, I mostly caught up on sleep.

items.q: Do you think people are busier now than in the past?
items.text: I think so. My father worked hard, but his work mostly stayed at the shop. Now phones mean work follows us home, so it is much harder to switch off completely.

items.q: Describe a time you received good news
items.text: I'd like to talk about the day I found out I had got my current job, because it was a real turning point for me. A moment of wonderful news that I will never forget was when I found out I had been accepted for a position I had desperately wanted. It was a role at an education consultancy, helping students apply to study abroad, which suited both my BBA and my own interest in international education. I had applied weeks earlier and had almost given up hope, so the email from the director caught me completely off guard. I was actually sitting at a tea stall with a friend when my phone buzzed, and I assumed it was another rejection. I remember reading it several times, hardly able to believe it, feeling utterly elated. My first instinct was to call my family, who had supported me throughout the stressful application process. My mother answered, and I could hear her telling my father and sister in the background before I had even finished. Their reaction was just as overjoyed as mine, which made the moment even sweeter. What made the news so meaningful was how hard I had worked and how uncertain the outcome had felt. The relief was almost as strong as the happiness; it was genuinely euphoric. That evening we celebrated together over my mother's cooking, and I felt an immense sense of accomplishment. Honestly, it remains one of the happiest days of my life, and it reminded me that persistence really can pay off.

items.q: Who is usually the first person you share good news with?
items.text: Usually my mother, because she worries about me the most, so good news means a lot to her. My younger sister is a close second, since she tends to find out everything anyway.

items.q: Do you prefer to receive news by phone or in person?
items.text: In person, if possible. You can see someone's face and share the moment properly. That said, for something like a job offer, an email is fine, because you can read it again and again.

items.q: Describe a time you learned a new skill
items.text: A skill I taught myself during my university years was cooking, which I had always avoided out of sheer laziness. At home, my mother has always done the cooking, so I never really had to lift a finger in the kitchen. That changed when I moved to Dhaka for my BBA and started sharing a small flat with three other students. Living away from home, I got tired of eating out and decided it was time to become self-sufficient. I started with simple recipes from online videos, and my early attempts were genuinely disastrous. There was a real learning curve, and I burned more meals than I care to admit, which was quite discouraging at first. I also rang my mother constantly, asking how much turmeric to add or how long to cook the lentils. But I persevered, and gradually things started to improve. What I found most rewarding was the moment I cooked a proper chicken curry that actually tasted good, and my flatmates asked for more. Beyond the practical benefit, cooking turned out to be surprisingly relaxing, almost therapeutic after a stressful day. I also realised how much work my mother had been doing for years without a word of complaint. It gave me a real sense of independence and pride. Honestly, learning this skill changed my daily life for the better, and it reminded me that most things become manageable if you are willing to fail a few times first. Now that I am back home, I even cook for the family occasionally.

items.q: Do you still cook now?
items.text: Now and then. My mother still rules the kitchen, but on Fridays I sometimes make a simple curry or fried rice for everyone. My younger sister is my harshest critic, which keeps me honest.

items.q: What skill would you like to learn next?
items.text: I'd love to learn to play the guitar properly. I listen to a lot of music, and being able to play a few songs for friends and family would be really satisfying.

items.q: Describe a memorable journey you have taken
items.text: I'd like to describe a train journey I took a couple of years ago, because my friends and I still talk about it. A journey that stands out vividly in my memory was a long train ride I took through the countryside with a group of close friends. We were travelling from Dhaka to Sylhet to see the tea gardens, but honestly the journey itself turned out to be the highlight. There were four of us, all old university friends, and we had managed to get seats together in the same carriage. We set off early in the morning with bags of snacks and far too much luggage. The train wound slowly through picturesque landscapes of green paddy fields, rivers and small villages, and later past gentle hills covered in tea. We spent hours chatting, playing cards and simply watching the ever-changing scenery, which was wonderfully soothing. At almost every station, vendors came on board selling tea and snacks, which only added to the fun. What made it so memorable was not the destination but the shared experience and the sense of freedom. There was something almost nostalgic about the slow rhythm of train travel, so different from the rush of flying. We laughed until our sides ached and made memories I still treasure. Honestly, that journey taught me that travel is often about the moments in between rather than just arriving. It remains one of my most cherished trips, precisely because it was so unhurried and full of good company. By the time we arrived, we were tired, but none of us wanted it to end.

items.q: Would you like to make that journey again?
items.text: Definitely. I'd love to do it again, maybe with my younger sister this time, since she has never been to Sylhet. Though I suspect it would not feel quite the same without my friends.

items.q: Do you prefer travelling by train or by bus?
items.text: By train, without a doubt. Buses in Bangladesh can be quite cramped and the roads are often jammed, whereas on a train you can stretch your legs and actually enjoy the view.

items.q: Describe a time you were late for something
items.text: I'd like to talk about a morning I would honestly rather forget. A time I was embarrassingly late was for an important job interview a few years ago, just after I had finished university. The interview was in Dhaka, so I stayed the night before at my elder sister's flat, thinking that would give me plenty of time. I had planned everything carefully, but on the day, the traffic was absolutely horrendous due to an unexpected road closure. I sat helplessly in a CNG auto-rickshaw, watching the minutes tick away, growing more jittery by the second. I kept checking my watch every thirty seconds, as if that would somehow make the traffic move. I called ahead to apologise, which was mortifying, and eventually arrived nearly half an hour late, flustered and sweating. To my relief, the interviewers were surprisingly understanding, and the interview went reasonably well despite my terrible start. One of them even joked that being stuck in Dhaka traffic was practically a local tradition, which helped me relax a little. As for how I felt, I was ashamed at first and then hugely relieved. However, the whole experience taught me a valuable lesson about leaving a proper buffer for the unexpected. Since then I have become almost obsessive about arriving early for anything important. Honestly, the stress of that day was enough to change my habits for good. I now always plan for delays, because I never want to feel that particular kind of panic again. It was a bad day, but I am oddly grateful for it now.

items.q: Did you get the job in the end?
items.text: No, I didn't, though I don't think it was only because I was late. Luckily, a few weeks later I was offered my current job at the consultancy, which suits me much better anyway.

items.q: Are people in your country usually on time?
items.text: Honestly, not always. Traffic in the cities is so unpredictable that people tend to be quite relaxed about being a little late. For formal things like interviews, though, punctuality really matters.

items.q: Describe a time you solved a difficult problem
items.text: I'd like to talk about a problem at work that had nothing to do with paperwork and everything to do with people. A difficult problem I once solved involved a serious misunderstanding between two members of a team I was working with at the consultancy. One of them handled students' documents and the other handled visa files, and each felt the other was causing delays. Their disagreement had escalated to the point where it was affecting everyone's work. At first I was reluctant to get involved, because it was not really my responsibility, but I could see the whole office was suffering. Rather than taking sides, I decided to sit down with each of them separately to understand their perspectives. It quickly became clear that the whole conflict stemmed from poor communication rather than any real malice. I then arranged a calm conversation between them over tea, acting as a neutral mediator. It was a delicate situation that required a lot of tact, but eventually they cleared the air. We also agreed on a simple shared checklist, so nobody would be left guessing about who was doing what. What I found most rewarding was seeing them work together productively again afterwards. Honestly, resolving that tension felt like a genuine achievement, and it taught me the value of listening carefully before jumping to conclusions. It made me realise that many difficult problems are really just communication failures in disguise, and patience is often the best tool. I still feel quite proud of how that turned out.

items.q: Do the two colleagues get on well now?
items.text: Surprisingly well, yes. They still tease each other now and then, but it is friendly. They even sit together at lunch, which nobody in the office would have predicted a year ago.

items.q: Do you enjoy solving problems like this?
items.text: I do, as long as they don't happen too often. I find it satisfying to untangle a situation and see people relax again, although it can be quite draining while it is going on.

items.q: Describe an achievement you are proud of
items.text: There are a few things I am proud of, but one stands out above the rest. An achievement I am genuinely proud of was completing a challenging professional qualification while working full time. It was a certificate course in international student counselling, which I finished last year to become better at my job. Balancing study with a demanding job was far harder than I had anticipated. For nearly a year, I sacrificed most of my evenings and weekends, which required real discipline. I would come home from the office, have dinner with my family and then burn the midnight oil at my desk, often with a cup of tea going cold beside me. There were moments when I felt like giving up, especially when the material seemed impossibly difficult. On those nights, a quick walk by the river usually helped me clear my head and start again. What kept me going was a stubborn determination to finish what I had started. When I finally passed the final exam, the sense of relief and pride was overwhelming. My father was so delighted that he bought sweets for half the neighbourhood. What made it so meaningful was that I had earned it entirely through my own effort and persistence. Honestly, that accomplishment gave me a huge confidence boost and proved to myself that I could handle serious challenges. It remains one of my proudest moments, not because of the qualification itself, but because of the resilience it took to get there. It taught me I am capable of far more than I thought.

items.q: Has the qualification helped you in your job?
items.text: Yes, quite a lot. I feel more confident advising students now, especially about choosing courses and preparing for interviews, and my manager has started giving me some of the more complicated cases.

items.q: How did your family support you during that time?
items.text: They were very patient. My mother kept bringing me tea late at night, and my younger sister, who is a serious student herself, often studied beside me, which kept both of us motivated.

items.q: Describe a time you tried something for the first time
items.text: I'd like to talk about the first time I spoke in front of a large audience, because it was a genuine milestone for me. A memorable first for me was trying public speaking at a fairly large event, something I had always dreaded. It happened about a year ago, when our consultancy organised a study abroad seminar for students and parents in a hall in Sirajganj. My manager asked me to give a short presentation, and my instinct was to refuse, but I forced myself to accept, partly because I knew I could not avoid it forever. In the days leading up to it, I was genuinely terrified, rehearsing constantly and imagining every possible disaster. I even practised in front of my younger sister, who turned out to be a surprisingly tough audience. When the moment came, my heart was pounding and my mouth was dry. But once I started speaking, something surprising happened; I gradually became more composed, and the words began to flow. By the end, I actually felt a rush of exhilaration. It was far from perfect, but I had done it, and the sense of achievement was immense. A few parents even came up afterwards with questions, which told me I had made sense. I was still shaking a little, but I was smiling from ear to ear. Honestly, pushing through that fear was genuinely liberating, and it taught me that we are often far more capable than our anxiety suggests. Since then I have been much more willing to step outside my comfort zone.

items.q: Have you given any presentations since then?
items.text: Yes, several. We now hold seminars every few months, and I usually present the section on applications. I still get a few butterflies beforehand, but nothing like that first time.

items.q: Would you like to try any other new things in the future?
items.text: I'd really like to study abroad myself one day. After helping so many students do it, I think experiencing it first-hand would be both challenging and incredibly worthwhile.

items.q: Describe a time you felt nervous
items.text: I'd like to talk about my first day at the education consultancy where I still work. A time I felt intensely nervous was on my first day at a new job, walking into an office full of complete strangers. It was only a few months after I had finished my BBA, and it was my first proper full-time job. I had really wanted the role, which somehow made me even more apprehensive about making a bad impression. The night before, I barely slept, and I think I ironed my shirt at least twice. I even left home forty minutes early, just in case the rickshaw got stuck in traffic. My mind was racing with worries about whether I would fit in or make some embarrassing mistake. I remember my hands were slightly shaking as I introduced myself. To my relief, my new colleagues were warm and welcoming, which gradually put me at ease. One senior colleague took me out for tea and explained how everything worked, which made a huge difference. By lunchtime, most of my nerves had melted away, and I began to feel genuinely optimistic about the job. Looking back, I realise that my anxiety had been almost entirely in my head. What I learned was that nervousness before something important is completely natural, and it usually fades once you actually begin. That experience taught me to trust that things generally turn out far better than my worried mind predicts. When I got home that evening, my family were waiting to hear every detail over dinner.

items.q: Do you still feel nervous at work sometimes?
items.text: Occasionally, mostly before meeting parents who are very worried about sending their child abroad. But it is a useful kind of nervousness now, because it makes me prepare properly.

items.q: What do you usually do to calm your nerves?
items.text: I take a few slow breaths and remind myself that I have prepared. If I have time, a short walk and a cup of tea usually help me feel settled again.

items.q: Describe a time you gave advice to someone
items.text: I'd like to talk about some advice I gave to one of my oldest friends from university. A time I gave advice that actually made a difference was when this close friend was agonising over whether to change careers. He had been working in a bank for two years and was deeply unhappy in his job, because what he really wanted was to teach, but he was terrified of the uncertainty of starting over. He came to me feeling completely stuck, and I could see he just needed someone to help him think clearly. We met at our usual tea stall by the river and talked for hours. Rather than telling him what to do, I encouraged him to weigh up what he truly valued in the long term. I shared my own experience of taking a similar risk when I chose my current job, which seemed to reassure him. I also suggested he speak to a few teachers first, to see what the job was really like day to day. My main advice was that regret over never trying is usually worse than the fear of failing. It was a genuinely delicate conversation, because I did not want to push him into anything. In the end, he made the change and is now far happier teaching at a college. He told me recently that our conversation was the push he needed. Honestly, seeing him thrive was incredibly gratifying, and it reminded me that sometimes the best help is simply helping someone find their own answer.

items.q: Do people often come to you for advice?
items.text: Quite often, actually, probably because of my job. Students and their parents ask me about studying abroad every day, and friends seem to assume I am good with big decisions too.

items.q: Is there anyone whose advice you always trust?
items.text: My grandfather. He is in his eighties but still remarkably sharp, and he has a way of cutting through a problem with one simple question. I always come away seeing things more clearly.

items.q: Describe a time you worked as part of a team
items.text: I'd like to describe a group project from my BBA, because it taught me a lot about working with other people. A memorable experience of teamwork was a group project during my university years, where we had to deliver a major presentation in just two weeks. The task was to design a complete marketing plan for a small local business and then present it to our lecturers. Our team was made up of five people with very different personalities and strengths. One was brilliant with numbers, another was a confident speaker, and one was very creative with design. At first, coordinating everyone was genuinely challenging, and there were a few clashes over how to approach things. My role naturally became that of the organiser, keeping track of deadlines and making sure everyone stayed on the same page. What made it work in the end was our willingness to compromise and play to each other's strengths. We met almost every evening in the library, often staying until it closed. As we got closer, the atmosphere became genuinely collaborative, and the project came together beautifully. On the day itself, everyone played their part, and it felt like a genuine team effort. We ended up receiving one of the highest marks in the class. Honestly, the experience taught me more about cooperation than any lecture could, and I felt really proud of what we had built together. It showed me that a good team is far more than the sum of its parts, provided everyone is committed to the same goal.

items.q: Are you still in touch with the people from that team?
items.text: With most of them, yes. We have a group chat that is still surprisingly active, and whenever a couple of us are in Dhaka at the same time, we try to meet up for dinner.

items.q: Do you prefer working alone or in a team?
items.text: It depends on the task. For detailed paperwork I like to work alone and concentrate, but for planning or solving problems, I think a team usually comes up with far better ideas.

items.q: Describe a time you complained about something
items.text: I'd like to talk about a complaint I made last year, which turned out much better than I expected. A time I had to make a complaint was over a faulty product I had bought online, which stopped working within days. It was a pair of wireless headphones that I used for listening to music on my evening walks by the river. I was quite frustrated, as it had been fairly expensive and I felt genuinely let down. I contacted the company's customer service, determined to stay calm and polite rather than lose my temper, which I find rarely helps. I explained the situation clearly and provided all the necessary evidence, including photos and my order details. When I had heard nothing after two days, I phoned their helpline and patiently explained it all again. To my surprise, the representative was genuinely apologetic and handled the matter far better than I expected. They arranged a full refund and even offered a discount on a future purchase, which I thought was a gracious gesture. The whole thing was sorted out in less than a week. What I learned from the experience was that complaining effectively is really about being clear and reasonable rather than angry. Honestly, the whole thing was resolved far more amicably than I had feared, and I felt quite satisfied afterwards. It also made me realise that most companies genuinely want to keep their customers happy. It reminded me that a firm but respectful approach usually gets the best results, and I have used the same approach several times since.

items.q: Do you often complain when something goes wrong?
items.text: Not very often. I only complain when it really matters, like when I have paid good money for something. For small things, I usually decide it is not worth the time and energy.

items.q: Do you still shop online after that experience?
items.text: Yes, I do, but I am more careful now. I read the reviews properly and check the return policy before buying anything expensive, which I never used to bother with.

items.q: Describe a time you helped a stranger
items.text: I'd like to describe a small moment of kindness that happened in the main market in Sirajganj a few months ago. A time I helped a stranger was when I came across an elderly man who had stumbled and dropped his shopping on a busy street. There were vegetables and a bag of rice spread across the road, and rickshaws were weaving around him. Most people simply walked past, which I found rather disheartening. I stopped to help him gather his things and made sure he was not hurt. Luckily, apart from a small scrape on his hand, he was fine. He seemed a little shaken, so I stayed with him for a few minutes and offered to walk him to a nearby bench outside a tea stall. He was incredibly grateful, and we ended up having a lovely short chat; it turned out he was a retired schoolteacher who now lived alone, since his children had moved to Dhaka for work. What struck me was how such a small gesture clearly meant a great deal to him. Honestly, it took only a couple of minutes of my time, yet it felt genuinely meaningful. It reminded me that we often overlook small chances to be kind because we are so caught up in our own lives. That brief encounter left me feeling heartened for the rest of the day, and it made me more attentive to people around me who might need help. I still see him in the market sometimes, and he always waves.

items.q: Do you think people help strangers less than in the past?
items.text: In big cities, perhaps. Everyone is in a hurry and slightly wary of strangers. In smaller towns like mine, people still tend to stop, although even here I notice it happening less.

items.q: Has anyone ever helped you when you were a stranger somewhere?
items.text: Yes, when I got lost in Chattogram once, a shopkeeper drew me a little map and pointed me in the right direction. I have never forgotten how kind he was.

items.q: Describe a time you changed your plan
items.text: I'd like to talk about a trip that did not go to plan at all, but still turned out well. A time I had to change my plans quite suddenly was when a long-awaited trip with friends fell through at the last minute due to bad weather. The original plan was to spend three days in Cox's Bazar, but a cyclone warning was issued the day before we were due to leave, and our bus was cancelled. I had been looking forward to it for weeks, so the cancellation was initially a crushing disappointment. Rather than sulking about it, though, we decided to be flexible and make the best of the situation. We ended up organising a day trip to a char, one of the sandy river islands in the Jamuna, something none of us had planned. We hired a small boat, packed a picnic and spent the afternoon walking on the sandbanks and watching the fishermen bring in their nets. To our surprise, it turned out to be a wonderful day, arguably better than the original plan. What I took from it was that rigidity often leads to frustration, whereas being adaptable opens up unexpected opportunities. It was a good reminder that plans falling apart is not always a bad thing. Honestly, some of my best experiences have come from spontaneous changes like that, and I remember feeling surprisingly content on the boat home as the sun went down. I now try to hold my plans a little more loosely and stay open to whatever comes.

items.q: Did you manage to go to Cox's Bazar later?
items.text: Yes, about three months later, once the weather had settled. It was lovely, but funnily enough, when we talk about that year, it is usually the day on the char that we remember.

items.q: Do you usually plan your trips carefully?
items.text: I plan the essentials, like transport and where to stay, but I leave the rest fairly open. Too much planning makes a trip feel like work, and the unexpected moments are often the best.

items.q: Describe a time you got lost somewhere
items.text: I'd like to talk about the time I got lost in Chattogram, a city I had never visited before. It was about three years ago, when I went there with some university friends on a short study tour. A time I got hopelessly lost was during that trip, when I wandered off from my group one afternoon to explore the older part of the city near the port. Before long I realised I had no idea where I was, and to make matters worse, my phone battery had died. I felt a growing sense of panic as the narrow lanes all started to look the same, and I was completely disoriented. Rather than making it worse by rushing, I forced myself to keep a level head and think logically. I asked a friendly shopkeeper for directions, and although his local dialect was quite hard for me to follow, he was very patient and even drew me a little map on a scrap of paper. Eventually I found my way back to a landmark I recognised and reunited with my relieved group, who had been searching for me for nearly an hour. I felt rather sheepish, and my friends teased me about it for the rest of the trip. Looking back, although it was stressful at the time, it turned into a strangely memorable escapade. It taught me to pay more attention to my surroundings and always memorise a few key landmarks. Honestly, getting lost made me a more careful traveller.

items.q: Do you usually rely on your phone for directions?
items.text: Yes, far too much, if I am honest. Since that day, though, I always make sure my phone is charged, and I try to notice a couple of landmarks wherever I go.

items.q: Have you been back to Chattogram since then?
items.text: Once, for work, to attend an education fair. This time I stayed close to the venue, but I did recognise the lane where the kind shopkeeper had helped me, which made me smile.

items.q: Describe a time you celebrated a special occasion
items.text: I'd like to describe a celebration that my whole family still talks about. A special occasion I celebrated with real joy was my parents' wedding anniversary, which my sisters and I organised as a surprise last year. We had been planning it secretly for weeks, which made the anticipation even more exciting, and keeping it from my mother was not easy, because she notices everything. My elder sister came from Dhaka with her husband and their two children, and my grandparents travelled in from the village. We decorated the house, invited close relatives and arranged all their favourite food, including the biryani my father loves. My younger sister was in charge of the cake, and I handled the guest list. The look of genuine surprise and delight on my parents' faces was absolutely priceless. It was a wonderfully heartwarming evening, full of laughter, old stories and a few happy tears. My grandmother even told us how my parents first met, which none of us had heard before. What made it so special was seeing the whole family come together to honour them. In our increasingly busy lives, these gatherings feel few and far between, and so all the more precious. My four-year-old nephew kept trying to blow out the candles before anyone else, which had everyone in fits of laughter. I remember feeling an overwhelming sense of gratitude and love that evening. Honestly, occasions like this remind me of what truly matters. The whole event was thoroughly unforgettable, and I think it meant just as much to us as it did to my parents. It is a night I will always treasure.

items.q: Do you often celebrate special occasions with your family?
items.text: Yes, especially Eid, when everyone tries to be together. We are a close-knit family, so even smaller occasions like birthdays usually end with a big dinner at home.

items.q: What did your parents say about the surprise?
items.text: My father was lost for words, which is rare for him. My mother cried a little and then immediately started worrying whether there was enough food for everyone, which made us all laugh.

items.q: Describe a time you had to wait for something
items.text: I'd like to talk about a wait that felt far longer than it really was. A time I had to wait anxiously was for the results of an important exam, which took several weeks to arrive. It was my HSC exam, the final exam at the end of college, and my university plans depended on it. That waiting period was genuinely agonising, because so much depended on the outcome, and there was absolutely nothing I could do to change it. I waited about two months in total. Every day felt longer than the last, and I found myself constantly checking for updates. To distract myself, I tried to stay busy with hobbies and spending time with friends, which helped a little. I read a lot of novels, played cricket in the evenings and took long walks by the river with my father. Still, the suspense was always there, lurking in the back of my mind. I remember trying to prepare myself mentally for both possible outcomes, which was difficult. On the day they were published online, my whole family crowded round the computer with me. When the results finally came and turned out to be positive, the relief was immense, and my mother immediately handed out sweets to the neighbours. What that experience taught me was how to cope with uncertainty, which is a genuinely useful skill. Honestly, learning to sit with that discomfort rather than let it consume me was invaluable. I now handle waiting far better than I used to, knowing that worrying rarely changes the result.

items.q: Are you usually a patient person?
items.text: More than I used to be. I can wait calmly for most things now, but I still find traffic jams and slow internet surprisingly hard to tolerate, so there is room for improvement.

items.q: What do you usually do while waiting for something?
items.text: I normally read. I always keep a book or an e-book on my phone, so if I am stuck waiting somewhere, the time passes far more pleasantly and I don't feel it is wasted.

items.q: Describe a time you made a promise to someone
items.text: I'd like to talk about a promise I made to my younger sister, who means a great deal to me. A promise I made and worked hard to keep was when I assured her I would help her prepare for her exams. It was about a year ago, before her HSC exams, and she was struggling with accounting, which happens to be one of my stronger subjects from my BBA. At the time I was extremely busy at work, so it was a fairly bold commitment. She was quite anxious and had started to lose confidence, which worried all of us. As the weeks went on, keeping that promise became genuinely demanding, because my own workload kept piling up. There were evenings when I was exhausted and tempted to cancel, but I felt a strong sense of obligation not to let her down. So I pushed through, spending several evenings a week going over her subjects with her at the dining table after dinner. I also made her a simple timetable so she could see her progress week by week. My mother kept us going with endless cups of tea. When she eventually did well, the pride I felt was immense, and our bond grew even stronger. Keeping that promise meant missing a few cricket matches with friends, but I never regretted it for a moment. What I learned was that keeping a promise, especially an inconvenient one, is a real measure of character. Honestly, seeing how much my help meant to her made every tiring evening worthwhile. It reinforced my belief that your word should always mean something.

items.q: Do you think it is important to keep promises?
items.text: Absolutely. If you break promises often, people stop trusting you, and that trust is very hard to win back. So I try not to promise anything unless I am sure I can deliver.

items.q: Does your sister still ask you for help with her studies?
items.text: Sometimes, but less and less. She is at university now and very hard-working, so these days she is more likely to correct my mistakes than ask me to explain anything.

items.q: Describe a time you were pleasantly surprised
items.text: I'd like to talk about a birthday that started badly and ended as one of my favourite days. A time I was pleasantly surprised was on my birthday a couple of years ago, when I was convinced everyone had forgotten. It was a working day, nobody at the office said a word, and even my family seemed unusually quiet at breakfast. The day had passed quietly, and honestly I felt a little dejected, assuming no one had remembered. When I got home in the evening, tired and expecting a quiet dinner, my friends and family jumped out and surprised me with a party. I was completely taken aback; I genuinely had no idea they had been planning it. It turned out my younger sister had organised the whole thing and had sworn everyone to secrecy. My friends had apparently been hiding in my room for almost an hour. The whole thing was wonderfully thoughtful, with my favourite food, decorations and even a homemade cake. What moved me most was realising how much effort they had gone to in secret. That moment turned a gloomy day into one of the happiest I can remember, and I felt a real lump in my throat. What surprised me most was how convincingly everyone had kept a straight face all day. Honestly, the surprise meant far more to me than any expensive gift could have. Even my grandparents called from the village later that night to wish me well. It was a powerful reminder of how fortunate I am to have such caring people in my life.

items.q: Do you like surprises in general?
items.text: Pleasant ones, yes. I am not keen on surprises at work, like a sudden deadline, but a surprise like that party is wonderful, because it shows someone was thinking about you.

items.q: Have you ever organised a surprise for someone else?
items.text: Yes, for my father when he retired. I gathered his old friends and relatives for a small celebration, and seeing his face was worth all the secret planning.

items.q: Describe a time you had a disagreement with someone
items.text: I'd like to talk about a disagreement with one of my closest friends, Rafi, whom I have known since school. A disagreement that I remember clearly was with him over how to handle a shared responsibility during a group trip to Sylhet last year. The two of us were in charge of the money and the plans, but we had quite different ideas about budgeting and planning, and the discussion became rather heated. We are both quite stubborn, and for a moment it felt as if the whole trip might be spoiled. He wanted to book comfortable hotels and see as much as possible, while I wanted to keep costs down so everyone could afford it. At the time, I felt genuinely frustrated because I was sure my approach was more sensible. However, once we both calmed down, we realised the argument was largely down to poor communication. We sat down and each explained our reasoning properly, which helped enormously. In the end we reached a compromise that combined the best of both ideas: simple guesthouses, but a couple of special day trips. What I learned was the importance of listening rather than simply trying to win the argument. Honestly, resolving it amicably actually strengthened our friendship rather than damaging it. It taught me that disagreements are a normal part of any close relationship, and how you handle them matters far more than the disagreement itself. I now try to stay far more open-minded during such moments, and to bite my tongue before saying something I might regret.

items.q: Do you often disagree with your friends?
items.text: Not often, and usually about small things like where to eat or which cricket team is better. Serious disagreements are rare, and when they happen, we try to talk them through calmly.

items.q: How did the trip go in the end?
items.text: It went really well. The guesthouses were simple but clean, and the day trip to the tea gardens was the highlight. Rafi even admitted that my budget left us more money for good food.

items.q: Describe a time you saw something interesting in the sky
items.text: I'd like to describe something I saw in the night sky a few years ago, which I still think about. Something genuinely interesting I once saw in the sky was a spectacular meteor shower during a stay at my grandparents' home in our ancestral village. The village is far from any city lights, which made the night sky incredibly clear. My cousin, who follows these things online, told me the shower was expected, so a group of us, including my younger sister, stayed up late and lay on a mat in the courtyard to watch. It was a cool, clear night in December, just after the rice harvest. When the first streaks of light shot across the sky, we were all completely mesmerised. It was a genuinely awe-inspiring sight, and the sheer scale of the universe suddenly felt very real. We lay there for over an hour, gasping each time a bright meteor appeared. Even my grandfather came out to join us for a while and told us about the stars he used to navigate by as a young man. What made it so special was the shared sense of wonder among us. Some of the younger cousins fell asleep on the mat, but I stayed awake until the very end. Honestly, in towns and cities we forget how magnificent the night sky can be. That experience left me feeling small in the best possible way, and it sparked a lasting fascination with astronomy. It is a memory I will always find genuinely humbling, and it made me appreciate the unspoilt darkness of the countryside.

items.q: Do you often look at the stars?
items.text: Not as often as I would like. In Sirajganj there is a bit too much light at night, but whenever we visit the village, I make a point of stepping outside after dinner to look up.

items.q: Would you like to learn more about astronomy?
items.text: Yes, I would. I have started reading about it a little, and one day I would love to look through a proper telescope and see the rings of Saturn with my own eyes.

items.q: Describe a time technology helped you solve a problem
items.text: I'd like to talk about a time technology got me out of a tricky situation abroad. A time technology genuinely saved me was when I was travelling in Nepal with two friends and struggled with a serious language barrier. It was my first proper trip abroad, so I was already slightly on edge. We had just arrived in Kathmandu late in the evening, and I found myself unable to communicate with a taxi driver, which was becoming quite nerve-racking. He spoke almost no English, and our few words of Nepali were not enough to explain where our guesthouse was. Then I remembered a translation app on my phone, which turned out to be a lifesaver. I simply typed what I wanted to say, and it translated it instantly, allowing us to understand each other. It even read the sentence out loud, and the driver laughed and nodded. It felt almost miraculous that a small device could bridge such a gap so easily. What impressed me most was how seamless and quick the whole process was. Without it, I honestly do not know how I would have managed. The experience really opened my eyes to how indispensable technology has become in daily life. While I sometimes worry that we rely on it too heavily, moments like that remind me of its genuine value. It turned a potentially frustrating situation into a smooth one, and I was extremely grateful for it. In the end we reached the guesthouse safely, and the driver even recommended a good place for breakfast. We ended up using that app for the rest of the trip.

items.q: Do you use translation apps in your daily life?
items.text: Occasionally at work, when a student sends me a document in a language I don't know. But for English I prefer to rely on myself, because I want to keep improving my own skills.

items.q: Do you think technology makes travelling easier?
items.text: Definitely. Maps, booking apps and translation tools remove a lot of the stress. The only downside is that people sometimes stare at their screens instead of enjoying where they are.

items.q: Describe a time you spent in nature
items.text: I'd like to talk about a few days I spent deep in the Sundarbans, the huge mangrove forest in the south of Bangladesh. A time I spent immersed in nature that I remember fondly was a three-day boat trip there with a few friends, about two winters ago. We had grown tired of busy streets and craved a proper escape into the wild. From the moment we arrived, the change was striking; the air was fresh, and the only sounds were birdsong, rustling leaves and the water lapping against the boat. We spent the days gliding along narrow channels, spotting deer, monkeys and even crocodiles on the muddy banks, although sadly no tigers. We slept in small cabins on the boat, and the crew cooked fresh fish for us every evening. Early one morning we walked along a wooden trail through the forest, and the silence was almost eerie. In the evenings we sat on the deck under a sky full of stars. Being so completely disconnected from screens was genuinely refreshing, almost like a reset for my mind, because there was hardly any phone signal. What I found most rejuvenating was the simple, slow pace of it all. There is something deeply grounding about being surrounded by nature with none of the usual distractions. Honestly, I returned home feeling calmer and more clear-headed than I had in months. The experience made me realise how much modern life disconnects us from the natural world, and how restorative it is to reconnect. I would love to go back one day and take my younger sister with me.

items.q: Do you often spend time in nature?
items.text: Not as much as I'd like, but I do walk by the Jamuna most evenings. It is not a forest, of course, but watching the river and the open sky helps me unwind after work.

items.q: Were you worried about seeing a tiger?
items.text: A little, to be honest, although the guides were very experienced and we mostly stayed on the boat. Part of me was actually disappointed not to catch even a glimpse of one.

items.q: Describe a time you missed an important event
items.text: I'd like to talk about an event I still feel a little sad about missing. A time I sadly missed an important event was a close friend's wedding, which I had genuinely been looking forward to. He was one of my best friends from university, and the wedding was in Rajshahi about two years ago. Unfortunately, I came down with a high fever just a day before and was simply too unwell to travel. It was supposed to be the first time our whole university group had been together in years. I was absolutely devastated, because I had promised to be there and had even helped with some of the preparations. Lying at home while the celebration went on without me was deeply frustrating, especially when photos and videos kept arriving on my phone. I remember feeling guilty, even though the situation was entirely out of my control. My mother insisted I stay in bed, and of course she was right. My friend was incredibly understanding, which only made me feel worse about missing it. To make up for it, I visited them as soon as I recovered and gave them a heartfelt gift, a framed photo of our old university group. Honestly, the experience taught me how unpredictable life can be and how we cannot always control our circumstances. It also showed me the value of a forgiving friend. Although I still regret missing it, I have made peace with the fact that some things are simply beyond our control. My friend and his wife still joke that I owe them a dance.

items.q: Do you often go to weddings?
items.text: Quite often, actually. Weddings in Bangladesh are big occasions, and between relatives, neighbours and friends, there always seems to be one coming up, especially in the winter season.

items.q: How did your friend react when you told him you couldn't come?
items.text: He was very kind about it. He told me to rest and not to worry, and he even called me during the reception so I could say a few words to everyone.

items.q: Describe a time you were proud of a family member
items.text: I'd like to talk about my younger sister, who is probably the most hard-working person I know. A time I felt enormously proud of a family member was when she finished at the top of her year in her HSC exams and received an award at her college's prize-giving ceremony last year. I had watched her study relentlessly for two years, often sacrificing her social life, so her success felt thoroughly well-deserved. The whole family went to the ceremony, and my parents were dressed in their best clothes. In our family, education has always been treated as something precious, so this meant a great deal to my parents. Sitting in the audience, I felt a lump in my throat as her name was called out for the special award. It was a genuinely emotional moment for the whole family, and my mother could not stop wiping her eyes. What made me so proud was not just the achievement itself, but the perseverance and discipline she had shown to get there. I remembered all the times she had doubted herself and kept going anyway, sometimes studying until two in the morning. Honestly, seeing her hard work pay off so publicly was one of the most uplifting experiences I have had. Afterwards, we went out for sweets and tea, and she could not stop smiling. I told her how proud I was, and I meant every word. It was a powerful reminder that dedication truly does pay off in the end, and it made me want to push myself harder too.

items.q: Do you and your sister get on well?
items.text: Very well. We tease each other constantly, as siblings do, but she is also the person I talk to when something is bothering me. She gives surprisingly wise advice for her age.

items.q: How did your family celebrate her success?
