items.text: We had a special dinner at home, and my mother cooked all her favourite dishes. My father also phoned my grandparents in the village, who were absolutely delighted to hear the news.

items.q: Describe a time you spent money on something special
items.text: I'd like to talk about the first really expensive thing I ever bought for myself. A time I spent money on something genuinely special was when I bought my first proper laptop with money I had saved myself. It was during my second year at university, and I paid for it with the money I earned from private tuition, teaching two schoolchildren in the evenings. It took me months of careful budgeting, as it was a significant amount for me at the time. I had to be quite frugal, cutting back on unnecessary spending to reach my goal. I kept a small notebook where I wrote down every taka I saved. I stopped eating out, walked instead of taking rickshaws, and said no to a few trips with friends. When I finally had enough and walked into the shop to buy it, the feeling was incredibly satisfying. It was a mid-range model, nothing fancy, but to me it felt like the most valuable thing in the world. What made it so special was that I had earned it entirely through my own effort and patience, without asking my father for anything. It was not just a purchase; it felt like a genuine accomplishment. The laptop went on to become essential for my studies and work, so it turned out to be a wise investment too. Honestly, buying something you have saved hard for feels far more rewarding than a casual, impulsive purchase. That experience taught me the value of patience and delayed gratification, a lesson I still carry with me.

items.q: Do you still have that laptop?
items.text: I do, although it is quite slow now. My younger sister used it for her studies for a while, and these days it mostly sits on my desk at home for watching cricket highlights.

items.q: Are you good at saving money now?
items.text: Reasonably good, yes. I put a little aside every month, partly because I would like to study abroad one day, and that goal makes it much easier to resist unnecessary spending.

items.q: Describe a time you overcame a fear or challenge
items.text: I'd like to talk about a fear that followed me for most of my life. A significant fear I managed to overcome was my long-standing fear of water, which had followed me since childhood, when I slipped into a pond and swallowed a lot of water before someone pulled me out. Growing up beside the Jamuna, not being able to swim was both limiting and slightly embarrassing. For years I avoided swimming entirely, and I would always find an excuse when my friends went to the river. Eventually, about two years ago, I decided enough was enough, and my cousin in the village, who is a strong swimmer, offered to teach me in the pond behind my grandparents' house. The first few sessions were genuinely terrifying, and I nearly gave up several times. My cousin, however, was incredibly patient and encouraging, which made all the difference. Every weekend we travelled to the village, and he would stand beside me in the water, holding me up until I found my balance. Slowly but surely, my confidence began to grow, and I became less petrified of deep water. The moment I finally swam from one side of the pond to the other unaided was absolutely exhilarating, and my grandfather clapped from the bank. Overcoming that fear gave me a huge sense of achievement that went far beyond swimming itself. Honestly, it taught me that most fears shrink once you confront them head-on rather than avoiding them. It was a genuinely empowering experience, and it made me braver about tackling other things I had been putting off out of fear.

items.q: Do you swim regularly now?
items.text: Not regularly, but whenever we visit my grandparents in summer, I go into the pond with my cousins. I am still not a strong swimmer, but I am no longer afraid, which is what matters.

items.q: Do you think children should learn to swim?
items.text: Absolutely, especially in a country with so many rivers and ponds like Bangladesh. It is a basic safety skill, and it is much easier to learn as a child than as an adult.

items.q: Describe a time something made you very happy
items.text: I'd like to describe a day that made me happier than I had felt in a long time. A moment that filled me with genuine happiness was a spontaneous reunion with old friends I had not seen in years. We had all drifted apart after finishing our BBA, scattered by work and life, some in Dhaka, some in Chattogram and a couple abroad. Then, quite unexpectedly, one of them organised a get-together last winter, and almost everyone managed to come. I was so excited that I took the early morning bus from Sirajganj and arrived far too early. We met at a small restaurant near our old university campus in Dhaka. The moment we all saw each other again was absolutely heartwarming; it felt as though no time had passed at all. We spent hours reminiscing, laughing about old memories and catching up on each other's lives. We even walked past our old classrooms and the tea stall where we used to spend far too much time. What made it so special was the effortless, genuine warmth between us. In our busy adult lives, such carefree gatherings have become increasingly rare. I remember feeling completely content, surrounded by people who knew the real me. Honestly, that day reminded me how important old friendships are, and how easily we let them slip away. The whole reunion was thoroughly joyful, and it left me determined to make more effort to stay in touch. We stayed so long that the restaurant staff eventually had to ask us, very politely, to leave. Since then, we have tried to meet at least once a year.

items.q: Do you find it hard to stay in touch with old friends?
items.text: Sometimes, yes. Everyone is busy with work and family now. But a quick message or a phone call now and then keeps the connection alive, even if we can't meet often.

items.q: What else usually makes you happy?
items.text: Simple things, mostly. A good dinner with my family, a cricket match on television, or a quiet walk by the river in the evening. I don't think happiness needs to be complicated.

items.q: Describe a time you stayed calm in a difficult situation
items.text: I'd like to talk about a moment when I surprised myself by staying calm. A time I managed to stay calm under real pressure was during a minor emergency at a family gathering, when my grandfather suddenly felt faint. It happened last Eid at my grandparents' village home, where the whole family had gathered for lunch. It was a very hot afternoon, and he had been busy greeting guests all morning. There was an immediate sense of alarm among everyone, and the atmosphere quickly became chaotic, with people shouting advice from every direction. For some reason, I felt a strange sense of clarity and knew someone had to take charge. I calmly helped him sit down in the shade, brought water, and reassured everyone while we decided whether to call the local doctor. I also asked the children to step back and give him some air. My younger sister ran to fetch a hand fan, which helped a lot. Staying composed was not easy, because I love him dearly, but I knew that adding to the panic would only make things worse. Thankfully, he recovered within a few minutes, and it turned out he was simply tired and dehydrated. Afterwards, several relatives told me how reassuring my calmness had been, which surprised me. Honestly, I had not known I was capable of keeping such a level head. That experience taught me that staying rational in a crisis is a genuinely valuable ability, and it gave me more confidence in myself. My grandmother still mentions it whenever the family gets together.

items.q: Is your grandfather well now?
items.text: Yes, thankfully. He is in his eighties but still remarkably sharp and active. Since that day, though, we make sure he rests more and drinks plenty of water, especially during the hot months.

items.q: Do you think staying calm can be learned?
items.text: I think so, at least partly. Some people are naturally calmer, but practice and experience help a lot. The more difficult situations you face, the less likely you are to panic.

items.q: Describe a time you received help from someone
items.text: I'd like to talk about someone who made a big difference to me when I first moved to Dhaka. A time I received invaluable help was when I was moving to the capital to start university and felt completely overwhelmed by everything. I had never lived away from home before, and the size and noise of the city frightened me a little. I remember my mother packing enough food for a week, as if Dhaka had no restaurants. A senior student from my hometown, who was already in his third year, went out of his way to help me settle in. My father had got his number from a family friend, and he met me at the bus station on my very first day. He helped me find accommodation, showed me around, and introduced me to people, which was incredibly generous of him. He even taught me which buses to take and where to find cheap but decent food near campus. Without his support, those first few weeks would have been far more daunting and lonely. What struck me was that he expected absolutely nothing in return; his kindness was completely selfless. I remember feeling deeply indebted to him, especially since we had barely known each other before. His help made an enormous difference to how quickly I adjusted. Honestly, the experience reminded me how much a small act of kindness can mean to someone in a vulnerable situation. It also inspired me to be equally supportive when I later saw first-year students struggling to settle in. I still remember his generosity fondly.

items.q: Are you still in contact with him?
items.text: Yes, we still message each other now and then. He works in Dhaka now, and whenever I visit my elder sister there, I try to meet him for a cup of tea.

items.q: Do you think people help each other more in small towns or big cities?
items.text: In small towns, I think. People know each other, so helping feels natural. In big cities, people are kind too, but they are often too rushed to notice when someone is struggling.

items.q: Describe a time you taught something to someone
items.text: I'd like to talk about the time I taught my mother to use a smartphone, which was more of a challenge than I expected. A time I taught something to someone was when I helped her learn the basics about two years ago, because she had always found smartphones intimidating. She was keen to stay in touch with my elder sister in Dhaka and see her grandchildren more often, but felt hopelessly lost with the technology. I decided to teach her step by step, and I quickly realised how much patience it required. I had to slow right down and explain things I take for granted, like swiping, typing a message or finding the camera. I wrote the steps in Bengali on a small card, which she kept beside her phone for months. There were moments of frustration on both sides, but she kept pressing the wrong buttons and then apologising, which made us both laugh. We persevered, usually with a cup of tea in the evenings. What made it so rewarding was watching her confidence grow, until she could video-call her grandchildren all by herself. Her delight was genuinely touching, and it made every patient hour worthwhile. Honestly, the experience taught me as much as it taught her; it made me far more empathetic towards people who struggle with technology. It reminded me that teaching is really about seeing things through someone else's eyes. Seeing how much it improved her daily life was deeply satisfying. Now she sends me more messages than anyone else I know.

items.q: Do you enjoy teaching people things?
items.text: I do, as long as the person is keen to learn. In my job I explain application processes to students every day, so I suppose teaching has become a natural part of my life.

items.q: What else would you like to teach your mother?
items.text: Maybe online banking, so she doesn't have to queue at the bank. She is a little nervous about using money on her phone, though, so I will take it very slowly.

items.q: Describe a time you had an interesting conversation
items.text: I'd like to describe a conversation with a complete stranger that I still think about. An interesting conversation I remember well was with an elderly man I happened to sit next to during a long train journey from Dhaka back to Sirajganj. It was about a year ago, and the train was delayed, so we had plenty of time. What began as polite small talk gradually turned into a genuinely fascinating discussion. He was a retired schoolteacher who had lived through decades of enormous change and shared stories that were both moving and eye-opening. He told me how, before the Jamuna bridge was built, crossing the river meant a long and unpredictable ferry journey, sometimes taking half a day. I found his perspective on life incredibly insightful, shaped by experiences so different from my own. Time seemed to fly by as we talked about history, family and how much the world had changed. He was also curious about my work and asked me lots of questions about why so many young people want to study abroad. What made it so thought-provoking was how open and reflective he was with a complete stranger. By the end of the journey, I felt as though I had learned more than I would from any book. Honestly, that conversation reminded me how much wisdom ordinary people carry, if only we take the time to listen. It was a wonderfully enriching encounter, and it made me more willing to strike up conversations with people I do not know.

items.q: Do you often talk to strangers?
items.text: More than I used to. On trains and buses I sometimes start a conversation if the other person seems friendly. Not everyone wants to chat, of course, so I try to read the situation first.

items.q: Who do you usually enjoy talking to the most?
items.text: My grandfather, probably. He has a story for everything and a very dry sense of humour. Whenever we visit the village, I end up sitting with him for hours.

items.q: Describe a time you took a risk
items.text: I'd like to talk about the biggest professional risk I have taken so far. A significant risk I once took was leaving a secure position to join a small, unproven education consultancy that had only just opened. I had been working in the accounts office of a large company for a few months after my BBA, which was safe but, honestly, quite dull. It was a genuinely daunting decision, because the new company had no guarantee of success and I was giving up stability. Everyone around me thought I was being reckless, which made me doubt myself at times. My mother kept asking whether I was sure, almost every evening at dinner. However, I felt a strong pull towards the opportunity, because I genuinely wanted to help students study abroad, and I decided to trust my instincts. The early months were certainly turbulent; we had very few clients, and there were moments when I feared I had made a terrible mistake. Gradually, though, the company found its feet, and the experience turned out to be one of the most rewarding of my career so far. What I gained in skills and confidence was immeasurable. Honestly, taking that leap taught me that calculated risks are sometimes necessary for real growth. It reinforced my belief that playing it safe is not always the wisest choice. Looking back, I am genuinely glad I was bold enough to follow my instincts, and I feel a quiet pride whenever I see how far the company has come. Today it is a busy office with a steady stream of students.

items.q: Are you generally someone who likes taking risks?
items.text: Not really. I am quite careful by nature, and I like to think things through. But I have learned that a well-considered risk can be worth taking, especially when you are young.

items.q: How did your parents feel about the risk?
items.text: They were worried at first, naturally. My father, having run his own business for over thirty years, understood the idea of starting small, and his support gave me a lot of confidence.

items.q: Describe a time you got up very early
items.text: I'd like to talk about a morning when I got up far earlier than I ever normally would. A time I got up unusually early was to watch the sunrise from a hilltop during a short trip to Bandarban with friends, about two years ago. We had to wake at around four in the morning, which was genuinely brutal, especially as none of us are naturally early risers. The reason was simple: people had told us that the sunrise over the hills, with clouds drifting below you, was something you had to see at least once. Half asleep, we made the climb in the dark, questioning why we had agreed to it, with only our phone torches to guide us. Our guesthouse owner had kindly woken us with hot tea before we set off. It was surprisingly cold, and I remember wishing I had brought a thicker jacket. But the moment the sun began to rise over the horizon, all the tiredness melted away. The view was absolutely breathtaking, with the sky shifting through shades of orange and pink, and a sea of clouds stretching out beneath us. It was a genuinely serene moment, and we stood there in near silence, simply taking it in. What made it so worthwhile was that we had earned that view through real effort. Honestly, that early start turned out to be the crowning moment of the whole trip. It taught me that sometimes the best moments require sacrificing a bit of comfort, and I would happily do it again.

items.q: Are you usually an early riser?
items.text: Not naturally. On working days I get up around seven, which is early enough for me. At the weekend I try to sleep in a little, although the call to prayer usually wakes me anyway.

items.q: Do you think getting up early is good for people?
items.text: For many people, yes. The morning is quiet and you can get a lot done before the day becomes busy. But I think it depends on the person, since some people genuinely work better at night.

items.q: Describe a time you failed at something and learned from it
items.text: I'd like to talk about a failure that I am actually quite grateful for now. A failure that ultimately taught me a great deal was when I performed poorly in an important exam early in my studies. It was a financial accounting exam in the first year of my BBA, and I came very close to failing it. I had been overconfident and had not prepared nearly as thoroughly as I should have. I had done well at college, so I assumed university would be just as easy, and I spent far too much time with friends. My classmates were surprised, because I had always seemed so relaxed about studying. When the results came out, I was genuinely crestfallen, and it was a humbling experience. I remember phoning my father and struggling to tell him. At first I felt quite demoralised, but after some reflection I realised the failure was entirely my own doing. Rather than dwelling on it, I decided to treat it as a wake-up call. I completely changed my study habits, becoming far more disciplined and organised, and I started reviewing my notes every evening instead of cramming at the last minute. The next time around, my results improved dramatically, which proved the lesson had sunk in. Honestly, that early failure was one of the most instructive experiences of my life. It taught me that setbacks are not the end of the world but valuable opportunities to grow. I now genuinely believe that how you respond to failure matters far more than the failure itself.

items.q: How did your father react when you told him?
items.text: Much more calmly than I expected. He told me that his business had failed more than once in the early years, and that what matters is getting back up. That conversation really helped.

items.q: Do you think failure is important for young people?
items.text: Yes, in small doses. Failing early, when the stakes are low, teaches you humility and resilience. People who never fail can struggle badly when something finally goes wrong later in life.

items.q: Describe a time you were excited about an upcoming event
items.text: I'd like to describe the build-up to my first trip abroad, because I don't think I have ever been so excited. An event I was intensely excited about was a long-planned holiday to Nepal, my first proper trip outside Bangladesh. It was last winter, and I was going with two close friends from university after we had been saving for almost a year. For weeks beforehand I was almost unable to think about anything else, and the anticipation was overwhelming. I spent hours researching places to visit and imagining what it would be like to see the Himalayas with my own eyes. Helping students travel abroad is my job, but this time it was finally my turn, which made it even more special. The night before departure I was so restless that I barely slept, and I checked my passport at least five times. My younger sister made me promise to bring her back a souvenir. When the day finally arrived and the plane took off, I felt a rush of pure exhilaration. The trip itself lived up to every expectation, filled with new sights, foods and experiences, especially the view of snow-capped mountains from Pokhara. What made the excitement so special was that it was building towards something I had dreamed about for years. Honestly, the joy of looking forward to it was almost as good as the trip itself. That experience taught me that anticipation is a wonderful part of any adventure. It remains one of the most unforgettable and genuinely thrilling experiences of my life.

items.q: Where would you like to travel next?
items.text: I'd love to visit somewhere in Europe, perhaps the UK, since so many of my students go there. Ideally I would go as a student myself, which is something I really hope to do one day.

items.q: Do you enjoy planning trips?
items.text: Very much. Reading about a place, choosing where to stay and making a rough plan is half the fun for me. My friends usually leave the planning to me, which I don't mind at all.

items.q: Describe a special meal you had
items.text: I'd like to talk about a meal that, for me, sums up what Eid is really about. A special meal that stands out in my memory was a large family feast during Eid last year, prepared mostly by my mother and grandmother. We celebrated at my grandparents' home in our ancestral village, and the whole extended family gathered there, which is increasingly rare these days. My elder sister came from Dhaka with her husband and children, and my uncles and cousins came too. My job was to help my grandfather greet the guests and make sure everyone had a seat. The table was laden with traditional dishes, like beef curry, chicken roast, polao and several kinds of sweets, and the aromas alone were mouthwatering. What made the meal so special was not just the food, though it was absolutely delicious, but the sense of togetherness. We spent hours eating, talking and laughing, with several generations gathered around one table, from my grandfather in his eighties to my four-year-old nephew. There is something deeply comforting about a home-cooked meal shared with people you love. In our busy lives, such unhurried gatherings feel genuinely precious. I remember feeling completely content, surrounded by family and good food. After lunch, the older men sat in the courtyard drinking tea while the children played. Honestly, meals like that are about far more than eating; they are about connection and belonging. It is a treasured memory, and it reminds me that the best meals are the ones shared with the people who matter most. I am already looking forward to the next Eid.

items.q: Can you cook any of those dishes yourself?
items.text: Only a simple chicken curry, I am afraid. The Eid dishes take real skill and a lot of time, so I leave them to my mother and grandmother and happily do the washing up instead.

items.q: Do you prefer eating at home or in restaurants?
items.text: At home, definitely. Restaurants are nice for a change, but nothing compares to my mother's cooking, and eating together at home feels far more relaxed and personal.

items.q: Describe a time you visited a place for the first time
items.text: I'd like to talk about my first visit to Dhaka, which made a lasting impression on me. A first visit that I still remember vividly was my trip to the capital when I was about seventeen, which was surprising since it is only a few hours from Sirajganj by road. I went there with my father for a short admission coaching course, and everything about it felt new and slightly overwhelming at first. The city was enormous, fast-paced and far busier than my quiet hometown, with endless traffic, crowds and noise. We stayed with a relative in Mirpur, and I remember standing on the roof at night, amazed by how many lights there were. Once I got my bearings, though, I found it genuinely exhilarating. I spent my free time exploring historical sites, markets and museums, soaking it all in, often with a cousin who lived there as my guide. I especially loved the old part of the city, with its narrow lanes, rickshaws and centuries-old buildings. What struck me most was the sheer diversity of people and experiences packed into one place. I found the whole experience thoroughly eye-opening, and it broadened my horizons considerably. Honestly, visiting somewhere completely unfamiliar reminded me how much there is to discover beyond your own small world. Although it was a little daunting at times, I came away feeling more self-assured and independent. It made me eager to explore even more new places, and a couple of years later I went back there to study.

items.q: How often do you go to Dhaka now?
items.text: Fairly often, maybe once every month or two. My elder sister lives there with her family, and I also go for work sometimes, to attend education fairs or meet university representatives.

items.q: Would you prefer to live in Dhaka or in your hometown?
items.text: My hometown, at least for now. Dhaka has more opportunities, but it is exhausting and crowded. In Sirajganj life is calmer, and I can walk by the river whenever I like.

items.q: Describe a time you did something to make someone happy
items.text: I'd like to talk about something I did for my father, who has always put his family first. A time I went out of my way to make someone happy was when I organised a small surprise for him on his retirement last year. He had run a small business for over thirty years, often putting the family's needs before his own, so I wanted to do something meaningful. He is quite a modest man, and I knew he would never ask for any kind of celebration himself. With help from my mother and sisters, I secretly gathered old friends, relatives and a few of his long-time customers, and arranged a modest gathering at home to honour him. My mother cooked his favourite dishes, and my younger sister made a small album of old photos from his shop. The look of genuine surprise and joy on his face was absolutely priceless. He was clearly touched that so many people had come to celebrate him, and at one point his voice broke as he thanked everyone. What made it so special was seeing someone who rarely asks for anything finally being appreciated. Honestly, the whole thing was as rewarding for me as it was for him. There is a unique kind of happiness that comes from making someone else feel valued. It reminded me that thoughtful gestures often mean far more than expensive gifts. Seeing him so at peace that evening is a memory I will always treasure, and it deepened our bond.

items.q: How does your father spend his time now that he has retired?
items.text: He reads the newspaper for hours, visits his friends at the local tea stall and spends a lot of time in the village with my grandparents. He seems more relaxed than I have ever seen him.

items.q: Do you often do things to make your family happy?
items.text: I try to. Usually it is small things, like bringing home sweets or taking my mother to visit her parents. I think those little gestures matter more than big occasions.

items.q: Describe a time you reached an agreement after a disagreement
items.text: I'd like to talk about a disagreement during my BBA that ended far better than I expected. A time I reached a hard-won agreement was during a group project when a classmate and I had fundamentally different visions for the final result. We were designing a business plan for a small café, and I wanted to focus on low prices for students, while he wanted a more upmarket place with a stylish design. Initially, neither of us was willing to budge, and the disagreement threatened to derail the entire project. The tension was uncomfortable, and progress ground to a halt, which was frustrating for the rest of the group. Eventually I suggested we step back and actually listen to each other's reasoning properly, so we met one evening over tea to talk it through. The rest of the group were clearly relieved to see us talking calmly again. Once we did, I realised his idea had genuine merit that I had dismissed too quickly. Through calm discussion, we managed to blend both approaches into something better than either original plan: affordable food in a comfortable, attractive setting. Reaching that compromise required real humility on both sides, but it was worth it. What I learned was that being stubborn rarely helps, whereas being flexible often leads to a superior outcome. Honestly, the final result was far stronger for having combined our ideas, and I felt relieved and quite proud. It taught me that the best solutions often emerge from disagreement, provided both people are willing to be level-headed and open-minded.

items.q: Are you still friends with that classmate?
items.text: Yes, we actually became good friends after that project. He now works for a bank in Dhaka, and we still joke about our imaginary café whenever we meet up.

items.q: Do you find it easy to change your mind?
items.text: Easier than I used to. When someone gives me a good reason, I am happy to change my view. What I find harder is admitting it straight away, but I am working on that.

items.q: Describe a time you were impressed by something
items.text: I'd like to talk about a performance that completely changed how I think about music. A time I was genuinely impressed was when I went to a large classical music festival in Dhaka with my elder sister and her husband a few years ago. I had always enjoyed music, but I had never experienced anything on that scale in person. The festival ran through the night in a huge open-air venue, with thousands of people sitting on the ground and listening in near silence. We had brought a thin mat and a flask of tea, like most of the people around us. From the moment the performance began, I was completely captivated. The sheer skill of the musicians, a sitar player and a tabla player responding to each other in perfect harmony, was absolutely remarkable. What impressed me most was the emotion they managed to convey purely through their instruments, with no words at all. The sound was so rich and powerful that I felt it resonate in my chest. It was a genuinely mesmerising experience, quite unlike listening to a recording on my phone. I came away with a whole new appreciation for the years of discipline behind such a performance, since musicians like that often train from childhood. Honestly, it left me feeling deeply moved, and it reminded me of the extraordinary things humans can achieve through dedication. By the time we left, the sun was coming up, and I was tired but completely inspired. I have been eager to attend more live performances ever since.

items.q: What kind of music do you usually listen to?
items.text: Mostly Bengali songs, both old classics and some modern bands, and a bit of English pop. I listen while walking by the river in the evening, which is probably my favourite time for music.

items.q: Have you ever wanted to learn a musical instrument?
items.text: Yes, the tabla, after that festival. I never actually started, though, because I didn't have the time. Perhaps one day, when life is a little less busy, I will finally give it a try.

items.q: Describe an adventurous thing you have done
items.text: I'd like to talk about the most adventurous thing I have ever done, which was a trek in the hills of Bandarban. An adventurous thing I did that pushed me well outside my comfort zone was going on a fairly challenging trek to Keokradong, one of the highest peaks in Bangladesh, with a group of four friends from university. It was about two years ago, in the dry season, when the paths are safer. I am not the most outdoorsy person, so agreeing to it was already a stretch for me. The trail was steep and gruelling in places, and at several points I genuinely wondered whether I could make it. My legs ached and my lungs burned, but my friends kept egging me on. We stopped in small villages along the way, where local people offered us water and bananas, which was incredibly kind. We spent the night in a simple guesthouse beside a lake on the way. Reaching the summit after hours of effort was absolutely exhilarating, and the panoramic view of endless green hills was more than worth it. What made it so rewarding was proving to myself that I was tougher than I had believed. Honestly, I surprised myself with how much I enjoyed the challenge, despite the discomfort. That experience gave me a real taste for adventure and a newfound confidence in my own resilience. It taught me that stepping outside your comfort zone, while difficult, is often where the most memorable experiences are found. My mother, of course, was relieved to see me home in one piece.

items.q: Would you do something like that again?
items.text: Yes, I think so, although I would train a bit beforehand this time. My friends have been talking about a trek in Nepal, and I would love to join them if work allows.

items.q: Do you think young people today are adventurous enough?
items.text: Some are very adventurous, but many spend most of their free time on screens. I think a little adventure, even something small, builds confidence in a way that nothing online can.

items.q: Describe a time you kept trying although it was difficult
items.text: I'd like to talk about learning to drive, which tested my patience more than almost anything else. A time I had to keep pushing through real difficulty was while learning to drive about two years ago, which I found far harder than I had expected. I wanted to learn because my father had recently retired and was no longer comfortable driving long distances, so someone in the family needed to take the car to the village. The roads here are full of rickshaws, buses and people crossing without warning, so even a short drive felt stressful. I struggled with confidence behind the wheel and failed my first test, which was genuinely disheartening. Part of me was tempted to give up entirely and rely on buses and rickshaws instead. However, I knew driving would be a valuable skill, so I forced myself to persevere. I booked more lessons, practised early in the mornings when the roads were quiet and slowly chipped away at my nervousness. Progress was frustratingly slow at times, and it required a lot of patience. When I finally passed on my second attempt, the sense of accomplishment was immense, precisely because it had not come easily. Honestly, that experience taught me the value of persistence more than almost anything else. It proved that giving up at the first setback would have cost me a skill I now use regularly. My grandparents are always delighted when I drive my parents to visit them, and I have carried that lesson into other challenges ever since.

items.q: Do you enjoy driving now?
items.text: On quiet roads, yes, especially the drive to my grandparents' village, which passes through lovely green fields. In busy town traffic, though, I still find it more tiring than enjoyable.

items.q: Do you think it is important for young people to learn to drive?
items.text: It is useful, but not essential for everyone. In big cities, public transport or ride-sharing can be easier. In smaller towns, though, being able to drive gives you a lot more independence.

items.q: Describe a gift you received that was important to you
items.text: I'd like to talk about something small that I keep on my desk at home. A gift that means a great deal to me is a fountain pen my father gave me when I finished my studies. That was when I completed my BBA, just before I started my job at an education consultancy. It is not particularly expensive, but its sentimental value is enormous. It has a dark blue body with a thin silver clip, and it writes beautifully. He handed it to me with a short note saying he hoped I would use it to sign many important documents in my career. I remember reading the note twice with a lump in my throat. What made it so special was the thoughtfulness behind it, rather than the object itself. My father ran a small business for over thirty years, and I think he knew better than anyone how much a signature can carry. My father is not a man of many words, so this gesture was genuinely touching. I keep it safely on my desk and use it only on special occasions. In fact, I used it to sign my first employment contract, which felt like keeping a small promise to him. Every time I hold it, I am reminded of his quiet faith in me. Honestly, it is the kind of gift that grows more precious with time. I think the best presents are those that carry meaning and memory, not just a high price tag. This pen is something I intend to keep for the rest of my life and perhaps pass on one day.

items.q: Do you still use the pen?
items.text: Yes, but only for important things, like signing contracts or writing Eid cards. I'm quite careful with it, because refilling a fountain pen and cleaning it properly takes a bit of patience.

items.q: Have you ever given your father a gift like that?
items.text: Not quite like that, but when he retired, my sisters and I gave him a good-quality watch. He insisted it was unnecessary, but he has worn it every single day since.

items.q: Describe a gift you gave to someone
items.text: I'd like to describe a present I made for someone rather than bought, because it is the one I'm proudest of. A gift I was particularly pleased with was a photo album I put together for my mother's birthday. My mother has spent her whole life looking after all of us, and I felt she deserved something that celebrated that. Rather than buying something generic, I wanted to give her something genuinely meaningful. I chose an album because I knew she would never ask for anything for herself, and memories matter far more to her than possessions. I spent weeks gathering old family photographs and arranging them chronologically, adding little notes beside each one. Some of them I found in a dusty trunk at my grandparents' village home, including a faded picture of her wedding day, and my elder sister secretly sent me a few from Dhaka as well. It was surprisingly time-consuming, but the effort felt worthwhile. When she opened it, her reaction was absolutely priceless; she was moved to tears as she flicked through the memories. She kept stopping at certain pages to tell us the story behind each picture, and we ended up sitting around the dining table for hours. What made it so special was that it cost very little money but a great deal of care. She told me it was the most heartfelt gift she had ever received, which meant the world to me. Honestly, seeing her so delighted was far more rewarding than giving an expensive present ever could be. That experience confirmed my belief that the best gifts are personal ones that show you truly know the person. It is something she still treasures and shows to visitors.

items.q: Do you enjoy choosing gifts for people?
items.text: Yes, very much, although it takes me a long time. I like noticing what people mention in passing, so that the gift feels personalised rather than something picked up at the last minute.

items.q: Would you make a homemade gift again?
items.text: Definitely. I'm actually planning one for my grandparents, a small booklet of old family stories and photos, because I think they would value that far more than anything from a shop.

items.q: Describe a useful object in your home
items.text: I'd like to talk about something very ordinary that sits on our kitchen counter. A genuinely useful object in my home is my electric kettle, which I honestly could not do without. It is a simple steel one that my younger sister and I bought for the family a couple of years ago. It might sound trivial, but as someone who drinks tea several times a day, it is completely indispensable. I use it mainly to boil water for tea, but my mother also uses it when she needs hot water for cooking, and my sister makes instant noodles with it during late-night study sessions. I use it first thing in the morning, throughout the day, and last thing at night. On a typical day it must be switched on six or seven times, especially when guests drop by, which happens a lot in our household. What makes it so useful is how quickly and efficiently it boils water, saving me a lot of time. Before I had it, using the stove felt slow and cumbersome by comparison. It is also wonderfully convenient, with an automatic switch-off that means I never have to watch it. Such a simple appliance has become woven into my daily routine without my even noticing. Honestly, it is a perfect example of how the most ordinary objects are often the most useful. I think we tend to overlook these everyday items, yet they quietly make life far more manageable. If it broke tomorrow, I would replace it immediately without a second thought.

items.q: Who else in your family uses the kettle?
items.text: Pretty much everyone. My mother uses it while cooking, my younger sister relies on it during late-night study sessions, and my father makes his afternoon tea with it now that he's retired.

items.q: Is there anything about it you would improve?
items.text: Perhaps the size. When relatives visit, we have to boil water two or three times for everyone's tea, so a slightly larger one would be more practical for a household like ours.

items.q: Describe a piece of technology you find useful
items.text: I'd like to talk about the piece of technology I reach for more often than anything else. A piece of technology I find genuinely useful is my smartphone, which has become an extension of my daily life. I know that is a fairly obvious choice, but its sheer versatility is remarkable. It functions as my alarm, camera, map, bank and library all in one device. At work, I use it constantly to reply to students' messages, check university deadlines and join video calls with admissions officers abroad. In the evenings, I use it to read e-books, listen to music or video-call my elder sister and her children in Dhaka. I learned to use it intuitively, simply by exploring its features over time. Nobody really taught me; I just experimented, made a few mistakes and occasionally watched a short tutorial when I got stuck. Funnily enough, I've now become the person my parents turn to whenever their own phones misbehave. What makes it so useful is how it consolidates dozens of tasks that once required separate tools. It has made my life significantly more efficient, allowing me to work, communicate and organise on the move. Of course, I am aware there is a downside; it can be quite addictive if you are not careful. Still, used sensibly, it is an incredibly powerful tool. Honestly, it is hard to imagine how people managed everyday tasks before smartphones existed. I think it is a perfect example of how technology has become deeply embedded in modern life, for better or worse, and I would struggle to function without mine.

items.q: Do you think you use your smartphone too much?
items.text: Probably, yes, especially in the evenings. I've started leaving it in another room while I read, which helps me switch off properly and makes that time feel far more restful.

items.q: Is there any other technology you find useful?
items.text: My laptop, definitely. For long documents and university applications at work, a phone just isn't enough, so the two complement each other rather well and I use both every day.

items.q: Describe something you bought that was expensive
items.text: I'd like to talk about the most expensive thing I've ever bought for myself. Something expensive I bought after much deliberation was a good-quality laptop for my work and studies. It was a significant purchase for me, so I did not take the decision lightly. I needed it because my old one was painfully slow, and in my job at an education consultancy I'm constantly preparing documents and applications for students. I also wanted something reliable for the online courses I take in the evenings, since I'm hoping to study abroad myself one day. I researched extensively for weeks, comparing models to make sure I was making a sensible choice. I had saved for it gradually, which made me appreciate its value even more. I put aside a portion of my salary every month for almost a year, and in the end I paid for it in full, because I didn't want to be paying it off in instalments. When I finally bought it, I felt a mixture of excitement and slight apprehension at spending so much. However, it quickly proved to be a genuinely worthwhile investment, as I use it every single day. Its speed and reliability have made my work far more productive. Honestly, although the price was high, the value it has provided over the years has been immense. It taught me that spending more on something you use constantly is often smarter than buying a cheaper version that disappoints. I have never once regretted the purchase, and I think it was one of my wiser financial decisions.

items.q: Have you bought anything expensive since then?
items.text: Nothing on that scale. I tend to be quite careful with money, and I'd rather save towards bigger goals, such as studying abroad, than make impulse purchases that I might regret later.

items.q: Do you prefer to save up or to buy things on credit?
items.text: I definitely prefer to save up first. My father ran his business for over thirty years without borrowing more than he needed, and I suppose I've inherited that cautious attitude.

items.q: Describe a photograph you like
items.text: I'd like to describe a photograph that I look at almost every day. A photograph I treasure is one of my entire extended family gathered together at a reunion several years ago. It was taken during Eid in the courtyard of my grandparents' home in the village, with everyone squeezed onto a few plastic chairs and a mat on the ground. My grandparents are sitting in the middle, surrounded by their children and grandchildren, and a couple of neighbours who wandered in at the last minute. It captures a rare moment when everyone, across three generations, was in the same place at the same time. It was taken by my cousin, who had just bought his first proper camera and insisted on setting a timer so he could run into the frame himself. In fact, you can just about see him mid-jump, still trying to reach his spot. What makes it so precious is that some of the older relatives in it, like my great-uncle, have since passed away. Whenever I look at it, I am filled with a warm sense of nostalgia. The photo is not technically perfect; it is slightly blurry and someone is looking the wrong way, but that only adds to its charm. What I love is how it froze a genuinely happy, fleeting moment forever. It reminds me of the importance of family and how quickly time passes. Honestly, no professionally staged photograph could ever mean as much to me. I keep a printed copy framed on my wall, and it never fails to make me smile. It is a powerful reminder of how irreplaceable these moments and people are.

items.q: Do you take many photographs yourself?
items.text: Quite a few, but mostly on my phone, and I rarely print them. I'd like to change that, because a printed photo somehow feels more permanent than thousands of images buried in a phone gallery.

items.q: Would you like to take a similar photo in the future?
items.text: Yes, very much. I'd love to organise another family photo at my grandparents' home next Eid, especially now that my sister's children are old enough to sit still, or at least try.

items.q: Describe a book you have recently read and enjoyed
items.text: I'd like to talk about a book that I finished a few weeks ago and still find myself thinking about. A book I recently read and thoroughly enjoyed was a work of non-fiction about human psychology and decision-making. It was about the mental shortcuts we all take, and the way our emotions and habits push us towards choices that are not always logical. The book explained, in a remarkably accessible way, why people so often behave irrationally. A friend had recommended it, and I was immediately intrigued by the subject. Part of the reason I picked it up was my job, because at the education consultancy I watch students make huge decisions about their futures, sometimes for surprisingly emotional reasons, and I wanted to understand that better. What I found most compelling was how it used real experiments to illustrate its points, which made the ideas stick. I read it far more quickly than I expected, because it was genuinely gripping despite being educational. Most evenings I would sit down to read one chapter with a cup of tea and end up reading three. It completely changed how I think about my own choices and biases. Honestly, a good non-fiction book that leaves you seeing the world differently is a real treasure. Since finishing it, I have found myself noticing these psychological patterns in everyday life, even in the way I shop or argue with my sister. I think the best books are the ones that stay with you long after the final page, and this one certainly did. I have already recommended it to several friends, calling it one of the most enlightening books I have read in years.

items.q: Do you usually prefer fiction or non-fiction?
items.text: These days I lean towards non-fiction, because I like learning something useful. That said, I still enjoy a good Bengali novel now and then, especially on long bus journeys or rainy monsoon afternoons.

items.q: Do you prefer printed books or e-books?
items.text: Printed books, without a doubt. I like the feel of the pages and being able to scribble notes in the margins, although e-books are admittedly handy when I'm travelling.

items.q: Describe a piece of clothing you like to wear
items.text: I'd like to talk about a jacket that I probably wear more than anything else I own. A piece of clothing I am particularly fond of is a simple, well-made jacket I bought a few years ago. It's a plain navy one with a soft lining and a couple of deep inside pockets. It is nothing flashy, but it has become a real staple of my wardrobe. I wear it mostly in winter, because the mornings in the north of Bangladesh can get surprisingly chilly, and it's perfect for my early walks by the river. What I love about it is how versatile it is; I can wear it to work, to a casual outing or even a semi-formal event. I bought it in Dhaka while I was visiting my elder sister, and she helped me choose it after I'd spent ages hesitating between two colours, so it also carries a nice memory. It fits me perfectly and is remarkably comfortable, which matters far more to me than following trends. Despite years of regular use, it has proved incredibly durable and still looks good. Honestly, I have come to appreciate quality over quantity when it comes to clothes. A single well-chosen item like this is worth more than a dozen cheap ones. It has become something of a signature piece for me, and I always feel confident wearing it. I suspect I will keep wearing it until it finally falls apart.

items.q: Do you usually wear traditional or Western clothes?
items.text: Mostly Western clothes for work, like shirts and trousers. But for Eid, weddings and Friday prayers I prefer a panjabi, which feels more comfortable and more in keeping with the occasion.

items.q: Do you enjoy shopping for clothes?
items.text: Not particularly, to be honest. I tend to put it off until I really need something, and I'd rather buy one good item than spend hours browsing through shops full of things I don't need.

items.q: Describe something you would like to own in the future
items.text: I'd like to talk about something that is still a long way off for me, but which I think about quite often. Something I would genuinely love to own one day is a house of my own, ideally with a small garden. I picture a modest two-storey house on the edge of Sirajganj, not far from the river, with a few mango trees and space for my mother to grow vegetables. Right now it feels like a distant dream, but it is one I am steadily working towards. The main reason I want it is the sense of security and permanence that comes with owning your own home. We live in a comfortable flat on the third floor, but I've always longed for a patch of land of our own, something I only really enjoy when we visit my grandparents in the village. A home of my own would be a real sanctuary, and a place where my father could enjoy his retirement surrounded by greenery. As for how I'd get it, I plan to save carefully over the coming years, which will require patience and discipline. I'll probably need a home loan as well, and I hope that gaining more experience, perhaps even studying abroad, will eventually improve my earnings. I imagine the feeling of finally getting the keys would be absolutely exhilarating, a real milestone. It represents stability, achievement and a place to build a future. Honestly, I think there is something deeply satisfying about having a space that is truly yours. While I know it is a long-term goal that will take considerable effort, it is one I am determined to reach. It keeps me motivated to work hard and save wisely.

items.q: Do you think you will achieve this goal?
items.text: I hope so, although realistically it will take quite a few years. As long as I stay disciplined with my savings and keep progressing in my career, I think it's an attainable goal.

items.q: Would you prefer to live in a house or a flat?
items.text: A house, ideally. Flats are practical and secure, but I've always loved open space, fresh air and the idea of stepping out into my own garden with a morning cup of tea.

items.q: Describe something you made yourself
items.text: I'd like to talk about the first thing I ever built with my own hands. Something I once made myself that I am quite proud of was a small wooden shelf for my room. I had never really done any woodwork before, so it was genuinely ambitious for a complete beginner. I watched a few online tutorials, gathered some basic tools and set to work, expecting disaster. I bought a few planks from a carpenter's workshop near our local market and borrowed a saw and a drill from my father, who still keeps a box of tools from his business days. I measured everything on our balcony floor, cut the pieces, screwed them together and sanded the edges. The process was far more challenging than I anticipated, involving plenty of mistakes and a couple of bruised fingers. It was very much a case of trial and error. But I persevered, and after a weekend of effort, I had a shelf that actually stood up straight. I made it mainly because my books had outgrown the space on my desk, and I liked the idea of building something myself for once. The sense of satisfaction I felt was surprisingly intense, far greater than simply buying one. What made it special was that I had created something functional with my own two hands. Honestly, there is a unique pride that comes from making something yourself. It now sits in my room holding my books, and every time I look at it, I feel a little glow of accomplishment. It gave me a real appreciation for the value of craftsmanship.

items.q: Have you made anything else since then?
items.text: Only small things, like a wooden stand for my phone and a simple frame for a family photo. Nothing ambitious, but each project has made me a little more confident with tools.

items.q: Do you think people make fewer things by hand nowadays?
items.text: I think so. Everything is so cheap and easy to order online that making things yourself can seem pointless, although I think it's a dying art that is well worth reviving.

items.q: Describe an object that has sentimental value to you
items.text: I'd like to talk about something small that I keep in a drawer beside my bed. An object with deep sentimental value to me is an old wristwatch that belonged to my grandfather. He wore it for decades, and a few years ago, when the small dial became hard for him to read, he took it off his wrist and gave it to me. He lives in our ancestral village not far from Sirajganj, and I still remember him pressing it into my hand during one of our visits and telling me to look after it better than he had. So I've had it for about four years now. The watch itself is fairly worn and no longer even keeps perfect time, yet I would not trade it for anything. The leather strap is cracked and the glass has a tiny scratch across it, but I've deliberately never had it polished. What makes it so precious is the memories it carries; I remember him glancing at it constantly throughout my childhood. Holding it now brings back a flood of warm, nostalgic feelings. It is a tangible connection to a man I love and admire deeply. He is in his eighties now but still remarkably sharp, and he always asks whether I'm taking care of it. I keep it safely stored and only take it out occasionally, almost like a relic. Honestly, its emotional worth is completely disconnected from its monetary value. I think objects like this become irreplaceable precisely because of the people and memories attached to them. One day I hope to pass it on to my own children, along with the stories of the wonderful man who gave it to me.

items.q: Do you ever wear the watch?
items.text: Only occasionally, usually when I visit my grandfather. He always notices straight away and smiles, which makes it feel like a small, shared ritual between the two of us.

items.q: Do you think young people value old things as much as older people do?
items.text: Perhaps not always. Many young people prefer new things, but I think we come to appreciate old objects later in life, once we understand the memories and stories behind them.

items.q: Describe something you lost that was important to you
items.text: I'd like to talk about something I lost a couple of years ago, which still bothers me a little when I think about it. Something important I once lost was a small notebook in which I had jotted down ideas and personal reflections for over a year. It was a plain brown notebook, but it held everything from favourite quotations to plans for my career and thoughts about studying abroad. I must have left it somewhere while travelling, and by the time I realised, it was gone. I was coming back from Dhaka on a crowded bus after visiting my sister, and I think it slipped out of my bag when I dozed off. I was genuinely distraught, because its contents were irreplaceable and deeply personal. I retraced my steps and asked around, but sadly it never turned up. I even phoned the bus company and went back to the ticket counter the next day, but nobody had handed anything in. For days I felt a real sense of loss, almost as though I had lost a part of myself. What upset me most was that no amount of money could recover what was written inside. Eventually I had to come to terms with the fact that it was gone and try to move on. The experience taught me a valuable lesson about backing things up and being more careful with things that matter. These days I keep my notes on my laptop as well as on paper. Honestly, it still stings a little when I think about it. It made me realise how attached we can become to seemingly ordinary objects, simply because of what they represent to us.

items.q: Are you generally a careful person with your belongings?
items.text: Much more careful now than I used to be. After losing that notebook, I always double-check my bag before getting off a bus, and I keep important things in one zipped pocket.

items.q: Have you ever found something that someone else lost?
items.text: Yes, once I found a wallet on a rickshaw seat. I tracked the owner down using a card inside it, and he was so relieved that he insisted on buying me a cup of tea.

items.q: Describe a piece of furniture you like
items.text: I'd like to talk about a piece of furniture that most visitors wouldn't even notice. A piece of furniture I am genuinely fond of is a large, comfortable armchair in the corner of my room. It is old and a little worn, but it is easily my favourite spot in the entire flat. It used to sit in our living room when I was a child, and when my parents bought a new sofa set, I rescued it before it could be given away. I positioned it right beside a window, so I get plenty of natural light and a pleasant view of the quiet street below our third-floor flat. I use it mainly for reading, and it has become my personal little retreat. After a long day at the consultancy, I often sit there with a book, or simply listen to music with my eyes closed. My younger sister occasionally borrows it to revise for her exams, though she always gives it back rather reluctantly. What I love about it is how wonderfully comfortable it is; I can sink into it for hours without any discomfort. There is something deeply cosy about having a dedicated chair just for relaxing and reading. Honestly, some of my most peaceful moments have been spent in that chair with a good book and a cup of tea. It might not be the most stylish piece of furniture, but its comfort makes it invaluable to me. I think everyone needs a favourite spot like this, and that chair is undoubtedly mine.

items.q: Would you ever replace the chair?
items.text: Not unless it completely falls apart. It has been reupholstered once already, and I'd happily do that again rather than buy a new one, because a new chair simply wouldn't feel the same.

items.q: Do you prefer modern or traditional furniture?
items.text: I prefer traditional wooden furniture, the kind that lasts for generations. My grandparents still have a carved wooden bed in the village that's older than my father, and it's still perfectly solid.

items.q: Describe a traditional or handmade item you own
items.text: I'd like to talk about something I own that is closely connected to where I come from. A traditional handmade item I own and treasure is a beautifully woven shawl made by artisans in a rural part of my country. In fact, it was woven on a handloom in a village near Sirajganj, an area well known for its weaving. It was given to me by my grandmother, who bought it from a weaver she has known for years, and it is a wonderful example of local craftsmanship. What makes it special is that it was made entirely by hand, using techniques passed down through generations. The intricate patterns and vivid colours are genuinely exquisite, and no two pieces are ever exactly alike. Mine is a deep maroon with a fine cream border, and if you look closely you can see tiny irregularities that show a human being made it. I use it mainly during the cooler months, and it always draws compliments. I wrap it around my shoulders on foggy winter mornings, and I also wear it to weddings and family gatherings, because it looks smart over a panjabi. Beyond its practical use, I value it because it represents a fading heritage that deserves to be preserved. In a world dominated by mass-produced goods, owning something so authentic feels increasingly meaningful. Honestly, I feel a sense of responsibility to look after it well. It connects me to my culture, to my grandmother and to the skilled hands that created it. I think items like this are far more valuable than anything churned out by a factory.

items.q: Do many young people in Bangladesh wear handmade clothes?
items.text: Fewer than before, sadly, although handloom fabrics are becoming fashionable again among some young people. Social media has helped, because small weavers can now sell directly to customers.

items.q: Would you buy another handmade item?
items.text: Definitely. Next time I visit my grandparents, I'd like to buy a couple of handwoven gamchhas from the local weavers, both to use and to support their livelihoods.

items.q: Describe a gadget you find helpful in daily life
items.text: I'd like to talk about a small gadget that I carry with me almost everywhere. A gadget I find genuinely helpful in daily life is a pair of wireless earphones I bought a while ago. They might seem like a small thing, but they have become surprisingly indispensable. They connect to my phone by Bluetooth as soon as I take them out of their little charging case, and a single tap on either earbud lets me pause music or answer a call. The case recharges them whenever I put them back, so one full charge usually lasts me several days. I use them constantly, whether I am commuting, exercising or simply trying to concentrate on work. I'd say I wear them for at least two or three hours every day, including on my evening walks by the river. What makes them so useful is the freedom they offer; without any wires, I can move around completely unhindered. They also block out background noise, which is a real blessing on our busy streets, where rickshaw bells and horns never seem to stop. I honestly appreciate how such a compact device can make everyday tasks so much more pleasant. Listening to music or podcasts during my commute has transformed what used to be a tedious part of my day. It is a perfect example of a small piece of technology that is genuinely practical rather than just a gimmick. Honestly, I would replace them immediately if they broke. I think the best gadgets are the ones you barely notice using, because they have become so seamlessly woven into your routine.

items.q: Do you ever worry about using earphones too much?
items.text: A little, yes. I try to keep the volume moderate and take them out when I'm walking along busy roads, because it's important to stay aware of rickshaws and traffic around me.

items.q: What other gadget would you like to buy?
items.text: Perhaps an e-reader. I read a lot, and it would be handy on long bus journeys to Dhaka, since carrying several books at once is rather cumbersome.

items.q: Describe a toy you enjoyed playing with as a child
items.text: I'd like to talk about a toy that kept me busy for most of my early childhood. A toy I absolutely adored as a child was a set of building blocks my parents gave me one birthday. They were bright plastic pieces in red, yellow and blue, packed into a bucket that seemed enormous to me at the time. My father brought them back from a trip to Dhaka, which made them feel even more special, since toys like that were hard to find in our town back then. It might sound simple, but it kept me endlessly entertained for years. I would spend hours constructing houses, towers and imaginary cities, completely lost in my own little world. Sometimes I tried to copy the bridge over the Jamuna, and it collapsed more times than I can count. What I loved was how the blocks allowed for endless creativity; I could build almost anything I could imagine. When my younger sister was old enough, I let her join in, and we built whole villages together on the living room floor. Looking back, I think that toy quietly nurtured my imagination and problem-solving skills. It was wonderfully engaging in a way that required real involvement, unlike the passive screens children have today. I have very fond, nostalgic memories of sitting on the floor surrounded by my creations. Honestly, I think the best toys are the ones that let children invent and build rather than just watch. That simple set taught me patience and creativity without my ever realising it. It remains one of the toys I remember most warmly from my childhood, and I would happily give one to a child today.

items.q: Do children today still play with toys like that?
items.text: Some do, but many prefer tablets and phones. My four-year-old nephew in Dhaka absolutely loves building blocks, though, so perhaps they haven't completely lost their appeal after all.

items.q: Did you have any other favourite toys?
items.text: I also loved a small plastic cricket bat that I used in endless matches with the neighbourhood children, usually until someone hit the ball over a wall and we had to go and apologise.

items.q: Describe something you bought recently that you are happy with
items.text: I'd like to talk about a fairly modest purchase that has turned out to be surprisingly useful. Something I bought recently that I am delighted with is a good-quality water bottle designed to keep drinks cold for hours. It's an insulated steel bottle in dark green, just the right size to fit in the side pocket of my bag. I bought it from an online shop after comparing a few options, and it arrived at our flat within a couple of days. I bought it because I had been trying to drink more water and stay healthier. I used to go through half the working day without drinking anything, and I'd often come home in the evening feeling tired and dehydrated, especially in summer. It sounds trivial, but it has genuinely improved my daily routine. What makes me so happy with it is how well it actually works; my water stays refreshingly cold even in the intense heat. During the hottest months, when the afternoons are almost unbearable, that makes a real difference. It has proved far more practical than I expected. The build quality is excellent, so it feels durable and worth the money. Beyond the practical benefit, it has genuinely encouraged me to develop a healthier habit, which is an unexpected bonus. Honestly, it is one of those small, sensible purchases that quietly makes life a little better. I now carry it everywhere I go. I think the most satisfying purchases are often the modest, useful ones rather than the flashy, expensive ones. It has quickly become an essential part of my daily kit.

items.q: Do you usually think carefully before buying things?
items.text: Yes, usually. I compare a few options, read reviews and ask myself whether I'll actually use it. That habit has saved me from quite a few impulsive purchases over the years.

items.q: Do you prefer shopping online or in person?
items.text: It depends. For practical items like this bottle, online is quicker and often cheaper, but for clothes or anything I want to touch and try, I still prefer going to a shop.

items.q: Describe a musical instrument you would like to learn
items.text: I'd like to talk about an instrument I've wanted to play for as long as I can remember. A musical instrument I have long wanted to learn is the piano, which I have always found genuinely captivating. There is something about its rich, versatile sound that appeals to me enormously. It can sound gentle and calm one moment and powerful the next, and I think that range is what draws me to it. The main reason I want to learn it is that I have always regretted never pursuing music as a child. Music has always been a big part of my life; I listen to it on my way to work and while I read, but I've only ever been a listener, never a player. I imagine learning it would be both challenging and deeply rewarding. As for how I'd learn, I would probably start with online lessons and gradually move to a proper teacher, since patience and consistency are essential. Pianos are quite rare in my town, so I'd begin with a small digital keyboard in my room and practise for half an hour each evening. I know progress would be slow at first, requiring real perseverance. Still, the thought of one day being able to play a piece I love is genuinely exciting. I think playing an instrument would also be a wonderful way to relax and express myself. I can even imagine playing simple tunes for my little nephew when my elder sister visits from Dhaka. Honestly, I believe it would be a hugely fulfilling hobby that I could enjoy for the rest of my life. It is definitely something I intend to make time for once my schedule allows.

items.q: Did you learn any music at school?
items.text: Very little, apart from singing the national anthem and a few songs for cultural programmes. Music wasn't really treated as a serious subject, which I think was a missed opportunity.

items.q: Is there any other instrument you'd like to learn?
items.text: Perhaps the harmonium, because it's so central to traditional Bengali music. My grandmother loves old songs played on it, so learning it would let me play for her in the village.

items.q: Describe a piece of art you like
items.text: I'd like to talk about a painting I came across almost by accident. A piece of art that has stayed with me is a large landscape painting I saw at an art exhibition in Dhaka a while ago. I was visiting my elder sister, and her husband suggested we spend an afternoon at a gallery, which isn't something I would normally do. It depicted a rural scene at sunset, with rich, warm colours that seemed to glow. There was a wide river in the foreground with a small wooden boat, a line of palm trees along the bank, and a few farmers walking home across the fields. I am no art expert, but something about it was genuinely captivating. The artist's use of light was remarkably skilful, making the whole scene feel alive. The sky was painted in layers of orange and gold, and the water reflected every shade of it. What drew me in was the incredible sense of peace it conveyed; I could almost feel the calm of that imaginary evening. I stood in front of it for far longer than I expected, completely absorbed. What I appreciate about art like this is its ability to stir genuine emotion without a single word. Honestly, it reminded me of the quiet countryside around my grandparents' village, and of evening walks along the Jamuna, which made it feel personal. I think a truly good piece of art creates a lasting impression, and that painting certainly did. I still think about it, and I would love to see it again.

items.q: Do you often go to art galleries?
items.text: Not very often, to be honest, since there aren't many in my town. But whenever I'm in Dhaka, I try to visit an exhibition, because it's a refreshing change from my usual routine.

items.q: Have you ever tried painting yourself?
items.text: Only at school, and the results were quite underwhelming. I enjoy looking at art far more than creating it, although I'd like to try sketching one day, just to relax.

items.q: Describe an object you use every day
items.text: I'd like to talk about something I pick up every single morning before I leave home. An object I genuinely use every single day is my backpack, which has become an essential part of my routine. It's a plain black one made of tough, water-resistant material, which is very handy during the monsoon. It carries everything I need for the day, from my laptop and documents to my water bottle and other essentials. What makes it so useful is how practical and well-organised it is, with plenty of compartments. I keep students' files in the main section, my laptop in a padded sleeve, and small things like keys, pens and a charger in the front pocket, so I never waste time searching for anything. It is comfortable to carry even when heavily loaded, which is genuinely invaluable during long commutes. I have had it for several years now, and it has proved remarkably durable despite constant use. My elder sister gave it to me when I started my final year at university, so it has been with me through exams, job interviews and my first years at the consultancy. Honestly, I rely on it so much that I would feel completely lost without it. It might seem like an ordinary object, but it plays a surprisingly important role in keeping my day organised. Over the years it has become a bit worn, but I have grown quite attached to it. I think it is a perfect example of how the most mundane objects often turn out to be the most useful ones in daily life.

items.q: Would you buy a new backpack soon?
items.text: Not unless it breaks. One of the zips is starting to stick, but I'd rather get it repaired, because it still does its job perfectly and I know exactly where everything goes.

items.q: Do you usually carry a lot with you?
items.text: Probably more than I need. Between my laptop, student files, a charger and my water bottle, it gets quite heavy, so I'm trying to travel lighter and keep more documents digitally.

items.q: Describe a vehicle you would like to own
items.text: I'd like to talk about something I hope to own in the next few years. A vehicle I would love to own one day is a reliable, fuel-efficient car, ideally something practical rather than flashy. I'm thinking of a small family car with enough room for my parents and my younger sister. Even in a modest town like Sirajganj, having my own car would make daily life significantly more convenient. The main reason I want one is the freedom it offers; I would no longer depend on crowded public transport or unreliable schedules. At the moment, getting anywhere means haggling with rickshaw drivers or squeezing onto packed buses, especially on the long journey to Dhaka. I imagine using it for my daily commute and for weekend trips out of town, which I rarely manage now. Above all, I'd use it to drive my parents to my grandparents' village home, which we visit often, and to see my elder sister and her children in Dhaka whenever we like. What appeals to me most is the sense of independence it would bring. I would probably choose something environmentally friendly, since fuel efficiency matters to me. Owning a car would feel like a real milestone, a sign of stability and progress. I think my father, who worked so hard for so many years, would be especially proud to sit in the passenger seat. Honestly, though it is a considerable expense, I think it would genuinely improve my quality of life. It is a goal I am steadily working towards, and I know the sense of freedom would make it thoroughly worthwhile.

items.q: Can you drive at the moment?
items.text: Not very well, honestly. I've had a few lessons from a cousin, but I'd need proper training before driving on our roads, because traffic can be quite unpredictable, especially on the highways.

items.q: Would you prefer an electric car?
items.text: Ideally, yes, because it would be better for the environment. But charging points are still rare outside the big cities here, so for now a fuel-efficient car seems far more realistic.

items.q: Describe something you borrowed from someone
items.text: I'd like to talk about something I borrowed last year that turned out to be a great help. Something I once borrowed that proved incredibly useful was a professional camera I borrowed from a close friend for a family event. The event was a small gathering we held at home when my father retired after running his business for over thirty years. My elder sister came from Dhaka with her family, and my grandparents travelled in from the village, so I knew it was a day worth remembering.
