I had wanted to capture the occasion properly but could not justify buying an expensive camera for a single day. My friend, who is a keen photographer, generously offered to lend me his, which was very considerate of him. I was slightly nervous about handling such a valuable and delicate piece of equipment. He kindly gave me a quick lesson on how to use it, which I really appreciated. The photos it produced were of a quality I could never have achieved with my phone, so I was genuinely grateful. My favourite is a shot of my father laughing with my grandfather, which now sits framed in our living room. I made sure to return it promptly and in perfect condition, as I did not want to betray his trust. I also printed a few of the best photos for him as a small thank-you. Honestly, the whole experience reminded me how valuable it is to have generous friends. It also made me consider eventually investing in a decent camera of my own.

items.q: Do you often borrow things from others?
items.text: Not often. I don't like troubling people, so I only borrow when it's really necessary, and I always make sure I return things quickly and in the same condition.

items.q: Do you lend your own things to friends?
items.text: Yes, usually books. I'm happy to lend them, although I've learnt to write my name inside the cover, because a few have mysteriously vanished over the years.

items.q: Describe a piece of jewellery or accessory you own
items.text: I'd like to talk about the only piece of jewellery I really own. A piece of jewellery that is special to me is a simple silver ring that my grandmother gave me. It originally belonged to her father, and she had kept it wrapped in a cloth in a small tin box for decades. She gave it to me when I got my first job, during one of our visits to the village, and I have treasured it ever since. It is not particularly valuable in monetary terms, but its sentimental worth is immeasurable. The ring is quite plain and old-fashioned, yet that simplicity is part of its charm. I wear it on special occasions, such as Eid, weddings and family gatherings, and doing so makes me feel closely connected to her. My grandmother has very little formal education, but she is one of the wisest people I know, and when she gave it to me, she simply said that honest work deserved something honest to wear. Every time I put it on, it brings back warm memories of that afternoon on her veranda. What makes it so meaningful is that it is a tangible link to my family's past. Honestly, it is one of my most cherished possessions, precisely because of the memories attached to it rather than its appearance. I intend to look after it carefully and one day pass it on within the family. Items like this become genuinely irreplaceable, carrying stories that no new purchase ever could.

items.q: Do men in Bangladesh often wear jewellery?
items.text: Not much, generally. A simple silver ring or a watch is quite common, but most men keep it modest. Women, on the other hand, often wear beautiful gold jewellery at weddings and festivals.

items.q: Would you ever sell it?
items.text: Never, no matter how much someone offered. It's not about the money at all; selling it would feel like giving away a piece of my family's history, and my grandmother would be heartbroken.

items.q: Describe something that saves you time
items.text: I'd like to talk about an app on my phone that has changed the way our family handles everyday errands. Something that saves me a remarkable amount of time is a food-delivery and grocery app on my phone. As someone with a busy schedule, it has become genuinely invaluable. I mostly use it to order groceries for the household, things like rice, lentils, cooking oil and vegetables, and occasionally a takeaway on evenings when my mother deserves a break from cooking. I simply choose the items, pay through my mobile wallet and pick a delivery time that suits us. Instead of spending hours travelling to shops and queuing, I can order everything I need in a few minutes. What makes it so useful is how efficient the whole process is; the items arrive at my door within hours. It also means my mother no longer has to carry heavy bags back from the bazaar in the heat. This frees up time I can then spend on work or relaxation, which matters enormously to me. Honestly, it has completely transformed how I manage my errands. I am aware there is a slight risk of becoming overly reliant on such conveniences, but used sensibly it is a genuine time-saver. I still enjoy going to the local market now and then, because there is something about haggling with the vegetable sellers that no app can replace. In a fast-paced world where time is arguably our most precious resource, tools like this are extremely welcome. It is a perfect example of how technology, at its best, can make everyday life more manageable. I honestly do not know how I coped before it existed.

items.q: Do older people in your family use apps like this?
items.text: My parents are gradually getting used to it. My father now browses the app himself, although he still likes to phone me before ordering anything, just to check he's pressing the right button.

items.q: Is there anything you dislike about the app?
items.text: Sometimes the vegetables aren't as fresh as the ones from the market, and deliveries can be delayed during heavy monsoon rain. But overall, the benefits far outweigh those small frustrations.

items.q: Describe a magazine or newspaper you like to read
items.text: I'd like to talk about something I read every week without fail. A publication I genuinely enjoy reading is a weekly current-affairs magazine that covers global news and analysis. It's an English-language magazine that deals with politics, economics, science and culture from around the world, along with longer features and book reviews. I read it regularly, usually at the weekend when I have time to digest it properly. I normally go through it on my laptop on Friday mornings with a cup of tea, and then return to a couple of the longer articles on Saturday evening. What I appreciate most is the depth of its reporting; unlike quick news headlines, it offers thoughtful, in-depth analysis. It helps me understand the context behind major events, which I find genuinely enlightening. That is especially useful in my job, because students often ask me about the situation in the countries they hope to study in. The writing is intelligent without being pretentious, which makes even complex topics accessible. Reading it keeps me well informed about the world in a way that scrolling social media never could. Honestly, in an age of shallow, rapid news consumption, I value having a source that encourages proper reflection. It has also noticeably improved my vocabulary and general knowledge over time. I think it is important to consume some substantial content rather than just quick, fragmented updates. It has become a genuinely enjoyable weekend ritual that leaves me feeling both informed and intellectually stimulated.

items.q: Do you ever read local newspapers too?
items.text: Yes, I skim a Bengali daily newspaper most mornings over breakfast, mainly for national news. The magazine is for deeper reading, whereas the newspaper keeps me up to date with what's happening at home.

items.q: Do you prefer reading news in print or online?
items.text: Online, mostly, because it's quicker and more convenient. That said, my father still insists on a printed newspaper every morning, and I do enjoy sharing it with him over tea.

items.q: Describe something you have kept for a long time
items.text: I'd like to talk about something I've held onto since I was about ten years old. Something I have kept for many years is a childhood diary that I started writing when I was quite young. It's a thick notebook with a faded cartoon cover, full of my untidy handwriting, little drawings and even a few pressed flowers. I have held onto it for well over a decade now, moving it carefully from one flat to another whenever my family moved. These days it lives in a drawer in my desk. It contains my youthful thoughts, dreams and daily events, which are often amusing to read back now. There's one entry where I announced very seriously that I would become a famous cricketer, and another describing an argument with my younger sister over the last piece of a mango. I have kept it because it is a genuine time capsule of who I once was. Whenever I flick through it, I feel a wave of nostalgia for a simpler time in my life. What makes it so precious is that no amount of money could recreate those honest, unfiltered memories. It is fascinating, and occasionally embarrassing, to see how much my perspective has changed. Honestly, I think keeping such personal records is genuinely valuable. It reminds me of how far I have come and grounds me in my own history. I fully intend to keep it for the rest of my life; it is far too meaningful to ever throw away.

items.q: Do you still keep a diary now?
items.text: Not a daily one, sadly. Life got busier, but I still jot down my thoughts in a notebook now and then, especially after important events, because I know I'll enjoy looking back on them later.

items.q: Would you let anyone read your old diary?
items.text: Only my younger sister, and only certain pages. Some entries are far too embarrassing, although we had a good laugh when she found the one about our argument over the mango.

items.q: Describe a collection you have or would like to have
items.text: I'd like to talk about a collection that takes up more and more space in my room every year. A collection I have gradually built up over the years is my collection of books, which has grown into something I am genuinely proud of. I now have a couple of hundred books, mostly novels and history, plus a few on business and psychology, in both Bengali and English. It started fairly innocently, with a few titles I loved, but it has since become a bit of an obsession. The very first ones were old storybooks my father bought me from a street stall when I was about twelve, and I still have every one of them. I add to it whenever I travel or come across an interesting title, so it keeps expanding steadily. My favourite time to buy is the big book fair in Dhaka every February, where I usually come home with a bag far heavier than I planned. My friends also know that a book is the safest gift for me. What I enjoy most is that each book represents a different idea, story or period of my life. There is something deeply satisfying about being surrounded by a personal library. Unlike many collections, mine is not just for display; I actually read and reread them. Honestly, my books have become almost like old friends, each with its own significance. I find the act of collecting them, and the memories attached to them, thoroughly rewarding. I think a good collection reflects who you are and what you value. I hope to keep growing mine for many years to come.

items.q: Where do you keep all your books?
items.text: Mostly on the shelves in my room, including one I built myself. They've started spilling over onto my desk and even the floor, so I'll need more space quite soon.

items.q: Do you ever lend books from your collection?
items.text: Yes, to close friends and my younger sister. I like sharing them, because discussing a book afterwards is half the pleasure, although I do keep a careful mental note of who has what.

items.q: Describe a device you would find hard to live without
items.text: I'd like to talk about the device I'd miss most if it suddenly disappeared. A device I would genuinely struggle to live without is my mobile phone, which has become deeply woven into every part of my day. I rely on it for communication, work, navigation, banking and entertainment, all in one place. In the morning it wakes me up, at work I use it to answer students' questions and track application deadlines, and in the evening I video-call my elder sister in Dhaka so my parents can chat with their grandchildren. I also pay most of my bills through a mobile banking app. What makes it so indispensable is the sheer number of tasks it handles that once required separate tools. It is not just the convenience but the fact that so much of my daily life is organised through it. Most of my contacts, work files and appointments exist only on that phone. I am aware this level of dependence is not entirely healthy, and I do sometimes worry about it. Honestly, if I lost it, I think I would feel quite disoriented, at least for the first few days. If I had to cope without it, I imagine I would eventually adapt, as people did for generations before. I'd probably go back to writing things down in a notebook, keeping important numbers on paper and visiting people in person more often, which might not be such a bad thing. Still, in the short term it would be genuinely disruptive. It is a striking reminder of how quickly these devices have become essential rather than optional in modern life.

items.q: Have you ever tried a day without your phone?
items.text: Once, during a visit to my grandparents' village, where the signal was very weak. It was frustrating at first, but by the evening it felt surprisingly liberating to simply sit and talk.

items.q: Do your parents rely on their phones as much?
items.text: Not nearly as much. My father mainly uses his for calls and the news, and my mother uses hers to video-call my elder sister. They're far less attached than my generation.

items.q: Describe an object that is important in your culture
items.text: I'd like to talk about something you can see at almost every celebration in Bangladesh. An object of real cultural importance in my country is the traditional handloom sari, which carries deep significance. It is far more than a piece of clothing; it is a symbol of our heritage and identity. Woven by skilled artisans, each one is a genuine work of craftsmanship, often taking days or even weeks to complete. The finest example is probably the jamdani, a delicate, almost transparent cotton sari whose weaving tradition has been recognised internationally. Women wear handloom saris at weddings, at Eid and especially at Pohela Boishakh, when the streets are full of red and white. They are also given as gifts at important family moments. I have known about it my whole life, having seen the women in my family wear them at every important occasion. My mother keeps a few folded carefully in her cupboard for special days, and since Sirajganj has a long tradition of handloom weaving, I've often seen weavers at work in nearby villages. What makes it so important is that it represents a centuries-old tradition that is sadly under threat from mass production. Wearing one on special days feels like honouring our ancestry. The intricate designs are genuinely exquisite, and no two are ever identical. Honestly, I think it is vital that we protect such traditional crafts before they disappear. They connect us to our roots in a tangible way. I feel a real sense of pride whenever I see this beautiful item being worn and celebrated.

items.q: Have you ever bought a sari for someone?
items.text: Yes, I bought a handloom sari for my mother last Eid. Choosing one was surprisingly difficult, because there were so many beautiful designs, but she loved the colour I picked.

items.q: Do young women in Bangladesh still wear saris?
items.text: Yes, especially on special occasions like Pohela Boishakh and weddings. For everyday life, many prefer the salwar kameez, which is more practical, but the sari is still deeply cherished.

items.q: Describe something you own that you repaired or fixed
items.text: I'd like to talk about something I brought back to life last year. Something I managed to repair myself was an old bicycle that had been sitting unused for years because of a series of faults. It was the bike I used to ride to school, and it had been gathering dust in a corner of our building's parking area ever since. The tyres were flat, the chain was rusted and the brakes barely worked. One of the pedals was also loose, so it made an awful clicking sound whenever anyone tried to ride it. Rather than throwing it away or paying for repairs, I decided to attempt to fix it myself, which was rather ambitious given my limited skills. I watched several tutorials, bought a few basic parts and set about it patiently over a weekend. I patched the inner tubes, scrubbed the rust off the chain and oiled it, then replaced the brake pads and tightened everything I could find. The bicycle mechanic near our local market kindly lent me a special tool when I got stuck. The process was more fiddly than I expected, and there were moments of real frustration. But gradually, piece by piece, the bicycle came back to life. When I finally took it for a ride along the river, the sense of accomplishment was genuinely satisfying. What pleased me most was that I had saved money and rescued something from the scrap heap. Honestly, repairing it myself was far more rewarding than simply buying a new one. It gave me a real appreciation for fixing things rather than discarding them.

items.q: Do you still ride the bicycle?
items.text: Yes, mostly for short trips around town and for evening rides along the river. It's also a nice way to get some exercise without having to go to a gym.

items.q: Do you usually repair things or replace them?
items.text: I try to repair them where possible. It's cheaper, less wasteful and more satisfying, although with modern electronics that's getting harder, because many simply aren't designed to be repairable.

items.q: Describe a hobby you enjoy
items.text: The hobby I'd like to talk about is reading, which has been a part of my life since childhood. It started when my parents gave me story books, and I quickly became hooked. I still remember my father bringing home Bengali adventure stories from the market, and I would read them again and again until the pages were falling out. These days I read almost every evening before bed, mostly non-fiction and the occasional novel, and on Fridays I sometimes manage a couple of hours with a cup of tea. What I love about it is how it allows me to escape into different worlds and broaden my knowledge at the same time. Reading is also wonderfully therapeutic; after a stressful day, losing myself in a good book helps me unwind completely. I tend to switch between history, biographies and books about psychology, so there is always something new to look forward to. Beyond entertainment, it has noticeably improved my vocabulary and the way I express myself, which really helps in my job, since I spend a lot of time writing to students and universities. Honestly, in an age dominated by screens, I think reading is an increasingly underrated pleasure. It costs very little yet offers enormous rewards. I always keep a book on my bedside table, and I feel slightly restless if I go too long without one. Looking back, those simple story books were a truly formative influence on me, and reading is a hobby I hope to keep for the rest of my life.

items.q: Do you prefer printed books or e-books?
items.text: Printed books, without a doubt. I like the feel of the paper and being able to scribble notes in the margins. I do read on my phone when travelling, but it never feels quite the same.

items.q: Would you like your family to read more?
items.text: My younger sister already reads a lot, so she doesn't need encouragement. I'd love my nephew in Dhaka to develop the habit, though, so I always bring him a colourful picture book when I visit.

items.q: Describe a skill you would like to learn
items.text: A skill I would really love to learn is public speaking, something I have always found rather daunting. I can talk comfortably to one student at a time, but standing in front of a room full of people is a completely different story. I want to learn it because being able to speak confidently in front of others is genuinely valuable, both professionally and personally. At the moment, the thought of addressing a large audience makes me quite nervous, and I would love to overcome that. In fact, my consultancy sometimes holds information sessions for students and parents, and I usually let my colleagues do the talking. I would probably start by joining a speaking club, where I could practise regularly in a supportive environment. There are a few groups like that in Dhaka, and some even meet online, which would suit someone living outside the capital like me. I might also record myself and watch it back, which sounds painful but would show me exactly what to improve. I know it would require stepping well outside my comfort zone and a good deal of perseverance. Still, I believe the reward would be immense. Being an effective communicator could open up all sorts of opportunities in my career, and it would make me far more articulate in meetings. Honestly, I think it is one of the most empowering skills a person can develop. It would also boost my confidence in everyday situations. It is definitely near the top of my list of things to work on once I have the time to commit to it properly.

items.q: Have you ever had to give a speech?
items.text: Yes, once at my university farewell programme. I had to say a few words on behalf of my batch, and although my hands were shaking, everyone was kind, and I felt quite proud afterwards.

items.q: Do you think public speaking can be taught?
items.text: I think so. Some people are naturally confident, but most good speakers have simply practised a lot. With honest feedback and regular practice, even a fairly reserved person can become comfortable in front of an audience.

items.q: Describe a goal you hope to achieve in the future
items.text: A goal I am genuinely determined to achieve is to build a successful career in a field I am passionate about, rather than simply working for a salary. For me, that field is education, and more specifically helping students from small towns like Sirajganj get into good universities abroad. This matters to me because I believe finding your work meaningful is essential to a happy life. In my experience, a single good piece of advice at the right moment can change the direction of someone's life. I see many bright young people around me who have the ability but lack the right guidance, and I would love to help fill that gap. To achieve it, I am steadily developing my skills and gaining as much relevant experience as possible at the consultancy where I work. I also hope to do a master's degree abroad myself, so that I understand the whole journey first-hand. I know it will require patience and a lot of persistence, as such things rarely happen overnight. I try to set myself small, attainable targets along the way to stay motivated. Honestly, the thought of one day doing work that I find genuinely fulfilling is incredibly motivating. If I achieved it, I think I would feel an enormous sense of pride and satisfaction, especially seeing former students thrive. It is not about wealth or status for me, but about purpose. I am fully aware the road will be arduous, but I am prepared to put in the effort, because I believe it will be thoroughly worth it in the end.

items.q: Have you told your family about this goal?
items.text: Yes, and they are very supportive. My father ran his own business for over thirty years, so he understands better than anyone what it takes to build something slowly and steadily.

items.q: Do you think your goal might change in the future?
items.text: The details might change, for example where I work or what my exact role is. But I think the core idea of helping young people make good decisions about their education will stay with me.

items.q: Describe a healthy habit you have
items.text: A healthy habit I have developed over the past couple of years is going for a brisk walk every evening. I usually head down to the embankment along the Jamuna, not far from our flat, and walk for about forty minutes as the sun goes down. I started it during a stressful period when I needed a way to clear my head, and it quickly became a daily ritual. At the time, I was working long hours and hardly moving at all, and I could feel it affecting both my energy and my mood. What I love about it is that it is so simple yet genuinely beneficial, both physically and mentally. After a long day at a desk, the fresh air and movement are wonderfully refreshing. It has noticeably improved my mood and helps me sleep far better at night. Sometimes my younger sister joins me, and we end up having the kind of relaxed conversations we rarely have at home. Honestly, this small habit has had a surprisingly profound effect on my overall wellbeing. I think habits like this are important because they are sustainable; unlike intense workouts, a daily walk is something you can sustain for years. It requires no equipment or gym membership, just a bit of consistency. I would genuinely recommend it to anyone. It has become one of the most valuable parts of my daily routine, and I would find it hard to give up now, especially on calm evenings when the river looks so tranquil.

items.q: Do you still walk during the monsoon?
items.text: Not always. When it is pouring, I sometimes walk up and down the stairs of our building instead, which my neighbours find rather amusing. But I try not to let the weather become an excuse.

items.q: Do you prefer walking alone or with someone?
items.text: Mostly alone, because it gives me time to think things through. That said, walks with my sister or a friend are lovely too; they are just more about conversation than quiet reflection.

items.q: Describe a sport or activity you would like to try
items.text: A sport I have always wanted to try is scuba diving, which has fascinated me for as long as I can remember. The idea of exploring the underwater world, with its vibrant coral and marine life, is genuinely captivating. Growing up beside the Jamuna, I spent a lot of time in and around water, but I have only seen the sea a couple of times, at Cox's Bazar. I want to try it because I love the ocean and I am drawn to the sense of adventure it offers. I would most like to do it at Saint Martin's Island, which is the only coral island in Bangladesh. To prepare, I would need to take a proper certified course, since safety is paramount in an activity like this. I can swim, as I learned in my grandparents' village pond as a boy, but I would need to build up my stamina and get used to breathing through the equipment. I imagine my first dive would be both terrifying and exhilarating in equal measure. I have watched countless videos of divers gliding past shoals of fish, and I always find myself wishing I were there. There is something about entering a completely different environment that appeals to my sense of curiosity. Honestly, I think it would be an unforgettable experience, quite unlike anything I have done before. Of course, it requires overcoming a certain amount of fear, but I think that is part of the appeal. It is firmly on my list of things to do, and I am resolved to try it one day.

items.q: Would you go diving alone or with friends?
items.text: Definitely with friends, and of course with a qualified instructor. Sharing something that nerve-racking with people you know makes it less frightening, and it gives you a story to laugh about together afterwards.

items.q: Is scuba diving popular in your country?
items.text: Not really, although it is slowly growing. Most people here see the sea as somewhere to walk along the beach, so diving is still a fairly niche activity, mainly for adventurous young people.

items.q: Describe a positive change you would like to make in your life
items.text: A positive change I genuinely want to make is to spend less time on my phone and social media. I have noticed that I waste far too many hours scrolling mindlessly, which leaves me feeling drained rather than refreshed. It usually starts innocently, checking one message, and suddenly forty minutes have disappeared. I want to make this change because I believe that time could be far better spent on hobbies, exercise or real relationships. Even at the dinner table, which is a special time in my family, I sometimes catch myself glancing at the screen, and I don't like that about myself. To do it, I plan to set strict limits on certain apps and keep my phone out of reach during meals and before bed. I also want to replace the habit with something better, such as reading a few pages instead of reaching for my phone. I know breaking such an ingrained habit will require real discipline. Honestly, I think reducing screen time would have a hugely beneficial effect on my focus and mental wellbeing. It would allow me to be more fully present instead of constantly distracted. I have already started making small changes, such as turning off notifications for most apps, and I have noticed a difference. I seem to get through my work faster, and I actually finish the books I start. I think in our hyper-connected world, consciously stepping back from technology is one of the healthiest changes a person can make.

items.q: Has anyone in your family commented on your phone use?
items.text: Yes, my mother, many times! She jokes that the phone is my second sister. She means it kindly, but it did make me realise how much of our time together I was wasting.

items.q: Do you think you will succeed in making this change?
items.text: I think so, as long as I am realistic. I don't plan to give up my phone completely, since I need it for work, but cutting down gradually feels achievable.

items.q: Describe a subject you would like to study in the future
items.text: A subject I would love to study in the future is psychology, which I find endlessly fascinating. I have always been curious about why people think and behave the way they do. I became interested in it after reading a few popular books on the topic, which completely captivated me. My job has made that interest even stronger, because I meet many students who are anxious about their future, and I often wish I understood their worries better. I would ideally study it formally, perhaps through a postgraduate course, as I feel it deserves proper, in-depth study. Since my background is in business administration, I might first take a short introductory course online to see whether I can cope with the scientific side of it. What appeals to me most is how applicable it is to everyday life; understanding human behaviour is useful in almost any profession. I think it would help me become more empathetic and a better communicator, both personally and professionally. In my line of work, being able to read people and put them at ease is half the job. Honestly, I believe it is one of those subjects that genuinely changes how you see the world. You start noticing patterns in your own behaviour, and you become a little more patient with others. It bridges science and human experience in a way I find deeply appealing. It is definitely something I hope to pursue once my circumstances allow, because I think it would enrich both my career and my understanding of the people around me.

items.q: Would you like to work as a psychologist?
items.text: Probably not as a full-time psychologist. I'd rather use what I learn in education and counselling, helping students manage stress and make confident decisions about their studies and careers.

items.q: Is psychology a popular subject in your country?
items.text: It is becoming more popular, especially in Dhaka. A generation ago, people rarely talked about mental health, but young people now are much more open, so interest in the subject has grown considerably.

items.q: Describe a plan you have for the near future
items.text: A plan I have for the near future is to pursue further studies abroad, which has been a long-held ambition of mine. Ideally, I would like to do a master's in management, probably in the UK or Australia. I made this decision fairly recently, after realising that international experience would greatly benefit my career. Ironically, it was helping other students with their applications every day that finally convinced me to take the step myself. To carry it out, I have been researching universities, preparing for the required exams and saving diligently, since it is quite an ambitious undertaking. At the moment, I am working on my IELTS, practising a little every evening after work. The process is genuinely demanding, but I am approaching it in a methodical, step-by-step way. My younger sister has been a great help too, quizzing me on vocabulary over dinner. This plan is important to me because I believe studying in a different country would be a hugely enriching experience, both academically and personally. It would push me out of my comfort zone and expose me to new perspectives. Honestly, the thought of it is both exciting and slightly nerve-wracking, especially the idea of being so far from my family. I know there will be challenges along the way, but I am fully committed to seeing it through. It represents a significant investment in my future, and I am determined to make it a reality, so that I can come back with skills that are genuinely transferable.

items.q: How does your family feel about your plan?
items.text: They are proud but a little emotional about it. My mother worries about me living alone, while my father keeps reminding me that opportunities like this don't come twice, so I should grab it.

items.q: Would you come back to Bangladesh afterwards?
items.text: Yes, I think so. My family is here, and I would like to use what I learn to help young people from towns like mine. Gaining experience abroad first would be a real bonus, though.

items.q: Describe a way you like to relax
items.text: A way I love to relax is by listening to music while doing absolutely nothing else. It might sound simple, but in our busy lives, giving yourself permission to just be still is something of a rarity. I usually do this in the evening, after we have had dinner as a family, lying on my bed or sitting on the rooftop of our building with a cup of tea. The rooftop is my favourite spot, because it is quiet up there and on clear nights you can feel a gentle breeze coming off the river. What makes it so relaxing is that it lets my mind completely unwind after a hectic day. Depending on my mood, I choose calming acoustic tracks or something more uplifting. I never use music as background noise at these times; I give it my full attention, which is what makes the difference. Quite often I end up listening to old Bengali songs that my parents used to play, which feel like home to me. There is something almost meditative about focusing purely on the music and letting my thoughts settle. Honestly, this small ritual has become essential for my mental wellbeing. In a world that constantly demands our attention, having a way to properly decompress is genuinely valuable. It costs nothing and asks nothing of me, which is exactly why I love it. I always feel noticeably calmer and more centred afterwards, ready to face whatever comes next, and I think everyone deserves a little sanctuary like that.

items.q: Do you use headphones or play the music aloud?
items.text: Usually headphones, because I don't want to disturb my sister while she's studying. On the rooftop, though, I sometimes play it quietly through my phone, which feels more relaxed and natural.

items.q: Have your ways of relaxing changed since you were a child?
items.text: Quite a lot. As a child I relaxed by running around outside with my cousins. Now I need calm rather than excitement, which I suppose is a natural part of growing older.

items.q: Describe a daily routine that is good for you
items.text: A daily routine that has genuinely benefited me is waking up early and having a calm, unhurried start to my day. I get up around six, well before I need to, which gives me time for myself before the world wakes up. Our neighbourhood is very quiet at that hour, apart from the birds and the odd rickshaw bell, and I really value that peace. I use this quiet period to plan my day, read a little and enjoy a proper breakfast rather than rushing. My mother is usually up too, so we often share the first cup of tea together before the rest of the family is awake. What makes it so valuable is that it sets a productive, positive tone for everything that follows. I keep it up by going to bed at a reasonable hour, since discipline at night makes the mornings easier. I also leave my phone in another room, so I am not tempted to stay up late scrolling. Honestly, starting the day calmly rather than in a panic has had a remarkable effect on my mood and focus. It gives me a sense of control that lasts throughout the day, and I rarely feel that I am chasing my own schedule. When I have skipped it, perhaps after a late wedding or a long journey, I can really feel the difference. I think how you begin your morning genuinely shapes the rest of it. This routine has become one of the most beneficial habits I have ever developed, and I would recommend it to anyone who feels perpetually rushed.

items.q: Is it hard to keep this routine at the weekend?
items.text: A little. On Fridays I sometimes allow myself an extra hour in bed, but I try not to change my sleep pattern too much, because Saturday mornings then feel much harder.

items.q: Were you an early riser as a child?
items.text: Not at all. My mother practically had to drag me out of bed for school. It is funny how things change; now I am often the first one awake in our flat.

items.q: Describe a tradition in your country
items.text: A tradition I love in my country is the celebration of Pohela Boishakh, the Bengali New Year. It takes place in mid-April and marks the beginning of the year according to our traditional calendar. It is a public holiday, so almost everyone is free to join in, whatever their background. On this day, people dress in traditional clothes, usually red and white, and the streets come alive with colourful processions, music and fairs. In Sirajganj, there is a big fair, or mela, where you can buy clay toys, handmade crafts and sweets, and children walk around with their faces painted. Many families start the morning with panta bhat, which is soaked rice, served with fried hilsa fish. What I find so special is how it brings the entire community together in a spirit of joy and renewal. Families gather to share traditional food, and there is a wonderful sense of festivity everywhere. It is important because it celebrates our cultural identity and heritage, which I think is vital to preserve. Unlike religious festivals, it belongs to every Bengali, which makes it wonderfully inclusive. In an increasingly globalised world, traditions like this help keep our roots alive. Honestly, the atmosphere on that day is genuinely uplifting, and it fills people with optimism for the year ahead. Every year I go to the fair with my younger sister, and even though we buy the same sweets and wander past the same stalls, it never loses its charm. I think it is a beautiful example of how a shared tradition can strengthen a whole community's sense of belonging.

items.q: Has the way people celebrate it changed?
items.text: Somewhat. It has become more commercial, with shops running special offers and people posting endless photos online. But the heart of it, dressing up and spending the day together outdoors, has stayed the same.

items.q: Do young people still care about this tradition?
items.text: Very much, in my experience. If anything, young people are the most enthusiastic, because it is colourful, joyful and a chance to show off traditional outfits with friends.

items.q: Describe a festival you enjoy celebrating
items.text: A festival I thoroughly enjoy celebrating is Eid, which is one of the most important occasions in my culture. There are actually two Eids each year, but the one after Ramadan is my favourite, because it follows a month of fasting and reflection. The day begins with special prayers at the Eidgah, the open prayer ground, followed by visiting relatives, exchanging gifts and, of course, an enormous feast. The atmosphere is wonderfully joyous, with everyone dressed in their finest clothes and children excitedly collecting small gifts of money, which we call salami. I celebrate it with my entire extended family, which is a big part of why I love it so much. We usually spend it at my grandparents' village home, and my elder sister travels up from Dhaka with her husband and children, so the house is full of noise and laughter. My four-year-old nephew always comes straight to me for his salami. What I enjoy most is the strong sense of togetherness it creates; in our busy lives, it is one of the few times the whole family gathers. The food, prepared over several days by my mother and grandmother, is absolutely delectable. Honestly, the warmth and generosity that fill the day are genuinely heartwarming. It is far more than a religious occasion; it is a celebration of family, gratitude and community, and many people share food with neighbours and those less fortunate. I always look forward to it, and it leaves me feeling deeply content and grateful for the people in my life.

items.q: What is your favourite Eid dish?
items.text: Definitely my mother's shemai, a sweet vermicelli dish cooked with milk and sugar. Eid morning doesn't feel complete until I have had a bowl of it, usually before we even leave for prayers.

items.q: Is Eid celebrated differently in cities and villages?
items.text: A little. In Dhaka it can feel quieter, because so many people travel back to their home districts. In villages it is more communal, with the whole neighbourhood visiting each other's houses throughout the day.

items.q: Describe a piece of advice you would give a young person
items.text: A piece of advice I would give to any young person is not to be afraid of failure, but to see it as part of learning. It sounds like a cliché, but I think very few people actually live by it. I think this is genuinely important because so many young people are paralysed by the fear of getting things wrong. In my country especially, exam results are treated as a matter of family honour, so failing can feel like a disaster rather than a lesson. I would give this advice to my younger cousins, who sometimes hesitate to try new things in case they fail. I would also share it with the students I meet at work, many of whom are too scared to apply to good universities in case they are rejected. I would tell them that every successful person has failed countless times, and that setbacks are often the most instructive experiences of all. The key is to be resilient and to keep going. A rejection letter or a poor mark is simply information about what to improve next time, not a judgement on who you are. I believe this mindset could help them enormously, freeing them to take risks and pursue their dreams. Honestly, I wish someone had drilled this into me when I was younger, because I wasted opportunities out of fear. I think teaching young people to embrace failure rather than dread it is one of the most invaluable lessons we can offer them. It builds courage and confidence for life, and it makes the journey far less nerve-racking.

items.q: Who gave you the best advice when you were younger?
items.text: Probably my grandmother. She had little formal education, but she used to say that a tree that bends in the storm doesn't break. It took me years to appreciate how profound that was.

items.q: Do young people usually listen to advice?
items.text: Not always, especially if it sounds like a lecture. I think they listen more when advice comes with a personal story, so they can see that you have actually been through it yourself.

items.q: Describe a rule at school or work that you agree with
items.text: A rule at my workplace that I genuinely agree with is the policy of allowing flexible working hours. I work at an education consultancy, where the workload goes up and down with application deadlines, so this rule makes a real difference. Rather than forcing everyone to arrive at a fixed time, we are allowed to start and finish within a reasonable window. This rule exists because the company recognises that people work best at different times and have different personal commitments. One of my colleagues, for example, drops her children at school every morning, and another prefers to start early and leave before evening. What I appreciate is that it treats employees as responsible adults, rather than having them constantly micromanaged. People follow it responsibly, ensuring their work still gets done, and in my experience it has made everyone more productive. We simply agree on core hours for meetings and keep each other updated. I agree with it strongly because it has noticeably improved morale and reduced unnecessary stress, such as sitting in rush-hour traffic. Honestly, I think it is a genuinely progressive and sensible approach. It has made me far more loyal to the company, and I think it helps us keep good staff, who might otherwise be tempted by bigger firms in Dhaka. I believe rules like this, which trust employees and prioritise results over rigid attendance, are the future of work. They create a healthier and more balanced working environment for everyone, and I think other employers would be wise to follow suit.

items.q: Has anyone ever taken advantage of this rule?
items.text: Once or twice, someone started arriving very late and missing meetings. Our manager had a quiet word with them, and it was sorted out quickly. On the whole, people respect the trust they are given.

items.q: Is there a rule at work you disagree with?
items.text: Not strongly, but I find the dress code a little formal for days when we don't meet clients. Still, I understand why it exists, since first impressions matter in our line of work.

items.q: Describe a film that made a strong impression on you
items.text: A film that made a lasting impression on me was a drama I watched a couple of years ago about a family overcoming hardship. The story followed a father who loses his livelihood and struggles to keep his children in school, while trying to hide his worries from them. On the surface it was a simple story, but it dealt with its themes in a genuinely profound way. I watched it at home on a quiet evening with my parents, expecting light entertainment, and ended up completely absorbed. What impressed me most was how realistic and emotionally honest it was; the characters felt like real people rather than actors. The acting was wonderfully understated, with no dramatic speeches, just small looks and silences that said everything. There was one scene where the father quietly skips his own meal so the children can eat, and the whole room went silent. By the end, I was genuinely moved, and I found myself thinking about it for days afterwards. My father, who ran a small business for many years, went unusually quiet, and I think it reminded him of some difficult times of his own. It explored ideas about resilience and family in a way that really resonated with me. Honestly, I think the mark of a great film is that it stays with you long after the credits roll, and this one certainly did. It was far more than mere entertainment; it offered a real insight into the human condition. I have recommended it to many friends since, and it remains one of my favourite films.

items.q: Would you watch it again?
items.text: Yes, but not too soon. It is quite emotionally heavy, so I would save it for the right mood. I suspect I would notice even more details the second time around.

items.q: Do you prefer watching films at home or in the cinema?
items.text: Mostly at home, partly because Sirajganj has limited cinema options. Watching with my family also means we can pause and talk about it, which I actually enjoy more than a silent cinema hall.

items.q: Describe a song or piece of music that is important to you
items.text: A song that holds real significance for me is a particular folk melody that was often played in my home when I was a child. It is a bhatiali song, a traditional kind of boatman's song from our river region, slow and full of longing. I first heard it as a young boy, and it is deeply tied to memories of my grandparents. My grandfather used to hum it while we sat on the veranda of their village home, watching the boats move slowly along the river in the evening. Whenever I hear it now, it instantly transports me back to those carefree childhood days. What makes it so important is not the song itself but the powerful nostalgia it evokes. The gentle melody and heartfelt lyrics have a wonderfully soothing quality that I find comforting. It is amazing how a single piece of music can carry such emotional weight and instantly bring back a whole era of your life. Honestly, I think this is the true power of music; it becomes intertwined with our memories. My grandfather is in his eighties now, and he still hums it sometimes when we visit, which makes it feel even more precious to me. Listening to it now sometimes brings a tear to my eye, in the best possible way. It is a cherished reminder of my roots and the people I love, and I hope to pass it on one day, perhaps starting with my little nephew, so that it lives on in our family.

items.q: Do young people in your country still listen to folk music?
items.text: Fewer than before, but it has had a revival recently. Some young bands mix folk songs with modern instruments, which has introduced them to a whole new audience, especially online.

items.q: Can you play or sing this song yourself?
items.text: I can sing a few lines, though not very well! I once tried learning it on a harmonium, but I didn't have the patience. Maybe I will try again with proper guidance.

items.q: Describe a website or app you find useful
items.text: A website I find genuinely useful is an online learning platform that offers courses on almost any subject imaginable. I use it regularly to develop new skills related to my work and personal interests. Over the past year, for instance, I have done a course on digital marketing, which helps with promoting our consultancy, and another on advanced spreadsheets. I usually log on three or four evenings a week, for about an hour, and a bit longer on Fridays. What makes it so useful is how accessible it makes education; I can learn from experts around the world without leaving my home. That matters a lot when you live in a smaller town like Sirajganj, where specialist training is hard to find. I have taken several courses on it, and the quality of instruction has been genuinely impressive, with clear videos, short quizzes and forums where you can ask questions and get answers from other learners. It fits perfectly around my busy schedule, since I can learn at my own pace whenever I have free time. Honestly, I think platforms like this are revolutionising the way people learn. They democratise knowledge that was once available only to a privileged few. I find it incredibly empowering to be able to keep learning and improving myself so easily. In a rapidly changing world where continuous learning is essential, I think tools like this are invaluable. It has genuinely helped me grow both professionally and personally, and I recommend it to everyone, especially students preparing to study abroad.

items.q: Have you ever paid for an online course?
items.text: Yes, a couple of times, when I needed a proper certificate. Most of what I learn is free, but paying for a course actually makes me more committed, because I don't want to waste the money.

items.q: Is online learning as good as learning in a classroom?
items.text: For practical skills, I think it is almost as good. But a classroom gives you spontaneous discussion and a teacher who notices when you are confused, which is hard to replicate online.

items.q: Describe an interesting idea you have heard about
items.text: An interesting idea I came across recently is the concept of a four-day working week, which I find genuinely intriguing. I heard about it through an article discussing trials carried out by various companies in Europe. A colleague shared it in our office group chat, and it sparked quite a lively debate over lunch. The basic idea is that people work fewer days but remain just as productive, if not more so. What I find so fascinating is the claim that working less can actually make people more efficient, because they are better rested and more focused. It completely challenges the traditional assumption that longer hours mean more output. In Bangladesh, many people work six days a week, so for us the idea sounds almost like science fiction. Honestly, I think it is a genuinely revolutionary idea that could transform work-life balance. Of course, there are practical challenges, and it would not suit every industry. Hospitals, shops and farming, for example, simply cannot stop for three days, so it would probably need a rota system. Still, the early results suggesting improved wellbeing and unchanged productivity are quite compelling. Personally, I feel cautiously optimistic; I would love an extra day for my family and hobbies, but I think it would need to be introduced gradually. I think ideas like this are important because they force us to question long-held assumptions about how we live and work. It is definitely a concept I would love to see explored more widely, and I suspect it will gain momentum in the future.

items.q: What would you do with an extra day off?
items.text: I would probably visit my grandparents in the village more often and spend more time reading. I might also finally start that public speaking course I keep putting off.

items.q: Do you think your employer would try it?
items.text: Perhaps not straight away, because our busiest periods revolve around university deadlines. But a trial during quieter months could be feasible, and I think my manager would at least be open to discussing it.

items.q: Describe a habit you would like to give up
items.text: A habit I would genuinely like to give up is my tendency to procrastinate, especially with tasks I find unpleasant. Paperwork is the worst example; I will happily reply to twenty student messages to avoid filling in one boring form. It started, I think, as a way of avoiding stress, but over time it has become quite ingrained. At university I often left assignments until the night before, and because I usually got away with it, I never learned to change. I want to give it up because it often leaves me rushing at the last minute, which is both stressful and counterproductive. I know that if I tackled things sooner, my life would be far calmer and more organised. It also isn't fair on my colleagues when they have to wait for my part of the work. To break the habit, I have started using to-do lists and breaking large tasks into smaller, more manageable steps. I have also tried the technique of simply starting a task for five minutes, which often removes the initial reluctance. Once I begin, I usually realise the task is not nearly as bad as I had imagined. I have also started tackling the task I dread most first thing in the morning, while my energy is high. Honestly, procrastination is a surprisingly stubborn habit to break, and I have to remain constantly vigilant. Still, I have made real progress, and I feel much better when I stay on top of things. It is a work in progress, but one I am fully committed to.

items.q: Do other people in your family procrastinate?
items.text: Not really, which makes it more embarrassing! My younger sister is incredibly disciplined and finishes her work days early. She often teases me about it, which is actually good motivation.

items.q: Is procrastination always a bad thing?
items.text: Mostly, yes, but occasionally a little delay helps, because ideas have time to develop. The problem is when it becomes a chronic pattern and you are always working under pressure.

items.q: Describe a personal quality that is important for success
items.text: A personal quality I believe is essential for success is perseverance, the ability to keep going despite setbacks. In my view, talent alone is rarely enough; it is persistence that ultimately makes the difference. I think this is important because the path to any worthwhile goal is inevitably filled with obstacles and failures. Anyone who expects a smooth journey is likely to give up the first time things go wrong. A close friend of mine embodies this quality perfectly; he failed several times before finally building a successful business, but he never gave up. His first venture, a small clothing shop, closed within a year, and his second barely covered its costs. What I admire is his refusal to be discouraged by temporary defeats. Each time, he studied what had gone wrong and tried again, and today he runs a thriving online shop. I have seen the same quality in my father, who kept his small business going for over thirty years through floods, price rises and difficult seasons. I genuinely believe that this kind of resilience is what separates those who succeed from those who quit. Honestly, in a world that often celebrates instant success, we forget how much quiet, stubborn effort lies behind most achievements. Perseverance keeps you moving forward when motivation fades, and motivation always fades at some point, however excited you were at the start. I think it is one of the most underrated qualities a person can have, and it is something I consciously try to cultivate in myself.

items.q: Do you think perseverance can be learned?
items.text: I think so, mostly through experience. Every time you push through a difficulty and see the result, you become a bit more confident that you can do it again next time.

items.q: Is there a time you showed perseverance yourself?
items.text: Getting my first job was one. I had several rejections after graduating, which was disheartening, but I kept improving my CV and interview skills until the consultancy finally offered me a position.

items.q: Describe something you do to help the environment
items.text: Something I make a conscious effort to do for the environment is reduce my use of single-use plastic. I started a couple of years ago, after seeing some genuinely alarming documentaries about ocean pollution. Around the same time, I noticed how much plastic was piling up along the banks of the Jamuna near my home, and it really hit me that this was not just a distant problem. Now I carry a reusable water bottle and cloth shopping bags everywhere, and I avoid plastic packaging wherever I can. Jute bags are easy to find in Bangladesh, so there is really no excuse. I have even persuaded my mother to take a basket to the market instead of coming home with a dozen polythene bags. I do it because I feel we all have a personal responsibility to protect the planet, however small our individual contribution. I am under no illusion that my efforts alone will solve the problem, but I believe change starts with individuals. Honestly, I think it is easy to feel helpless about huge issues like climate change, but taking small actions gives me a sense of agency. It also makes me more mindful of my consumption in general, and I think twice before buying things I don't really need. I feel genuinely good about doing my part, however modest. I think if enough people adopt these sustainable habits, the collective impact could be significant. It is a small change, but it lets me live with a clear conscience.

items.q: Do your friends do the same?
items.text: A few of them do, and some started after teasing me about my cloth bag. Most still use plastic without thinking, though, so I try to set an example rather than lecture anyone.

items.q: What else would you like to do for the environment?
items.text: I would like to join a riverbank clean-up group, as some young people organise them in our area. Planting a few trees on my grandparents' land in the village would also be a worthwhile project.

items.q: Describe a way you keep fit and healthy
items.text: A way I keep fit and healthy is by going to the gym a few times a week, which has become an important part of my lifestyle. There is a small gym about ten minutes from our flat, and I usually go on Saturday, Monday and Wednesday evenings after work, for roughly an hour each time. I started a couple of years ago, initially just to lose a little weight, but it soon became something I genuinely enjoy. At first I felt quite self-conscious, because everyone else seemed to know exactly what they were doing, but one of the trainers kindly showed me the basics. What works for me is having a set routine, which keeps me accountable and stops me making excuses. Beyond the obvious physical benefits, I find exercise incredibly therapeutic for my mental health. After a stressful day, a good workout is the perfect outlet for releasing tension. On the days I don't go, I still take a walk by the river, so I am rarely completely inactive, even during the busiest weeks. Honestly, the sense of discipline it has given me has spilled over into other areas of my life. I feel more energetic, sleep better and generally more positive. It required real commitment to make it a habit, but now I would feel restless without it. I think finding a form of exercise you actually enjoy is the key to sustaining it long term, and for me, the gym is exactly that, a routine I would find very hard to abandon.

items.q: Do you ever go to the gym with a friend?
items.text: Sometimes, with a university friend who lives nearby. Having a partner helps on days when I feel lazy, because I don't want to let him down, although we do end up chatting more than training.

items.q: Is going to the gym popular where you live?
items.text: It is becoming more popular among young people, even in a modest town like Sirajganj. A few years ago there were hardly any gyms, but now several have opened, which shows how attitudes are changing.

items.q: Describe a course or class you would like to take
items.text: A course I would genuinely love to take is one in creative writing, something I have long been curious about. I have always enjoyed writing, but I feel my skills are quite rudimentary and could benefit from proper guidance. I have a notebook full of half-finished short stories, mostly about village life and my grandparents' generation, but I never quite know how to shape them. I want to take it because writing well is such a valuable and versatile skill, useful in almost any field. In my job, for example, I often help students with their personal statements, and I can see how much a well-told story can strengthen an application. I would probably take it online, so I could fit it around my work, though a face-to-face class with feedback would be ideal. There are occasional workshops in Dhaka, so I might try to attend one when I visit my elder sister. What appeals to me most is the chance to learn techniques from experienced writers and to receive constructive criticism. Honestly, I think a good course could help me express my ideas far more clearly and creatively. It would also give me a productive and fulfilling hobby outside of work. I believe learning should be a lifelong pursuit, and this is one course I am determined to take eventually. It is exactly the kind of skill that could enrich both my professional and personal life, and who knows, perhaps one day I will finally finish one of those stories and see it in print.

items.q: Would you write in English or Bengali?
items.text: Probably both. Bengali feels more natural for stories about village life, because some expressions simply don't translate. But writing in English would help my work and reach a wider audience.

items.q: Have you ever shown your writing to anyone?
items.text: Only to my younger sister, who is a very honest critic. She once told me a story was far too long and rather repetitive, which hurt a little, but she was absolutely right.

items.q: Describe an ambition you have had for a long time
items.text: An ambition I have held for many years is to one day start my own business. I first had this dream as a teenager, watching my father run his small enterprise with such dedication. He ran that business for over thirty years before retiring recently, and I saw both the freedom and the worry it brought him. What has always appealed to me is the idea of building something of my own and being self-reliant. More specifically, I would love to open my own education consultancy in Sirajganj, so that students here would not have to travel to Dhaka for reliable advice. Towards this goal, I have been gaining relevant work experience and quietly saving whatever I can. My current job has taught me how the whole process works, from counselling students to dealing with universities and visa requirements. I am also constantly learning about how businesses operate, since I know success requires far more than just a good idea. This ambition matters to me because it represents freedom, creativity and the chance to make a real impact. Honestly, I find the idea both thrilling and slightly daunting, given the risks involved. Still, I believe the potential rewards, both financial and personal, are worth it. My father always says that a business is like a child, needing constant care, and I think he is right. I know it will require enormous perseverance, but it is a dream I refuse to let go of. With my father's hard-earned advice and enough preparation, I am confident that one day I will make it happen and prove myself as a genuinely entrepreneurial person.

items.q: Would you ask your father to help with your business?
items.text: Definitely, at least as an adviser. He knows a great deal about managing money, dealing with customers and surviving difficult years, which is exactly the kind of practical wisdom no textbook can give you.

items.q: Do many young people in your country want to start a business?
items.text: More and more, I think. Many young graduates are frustrated by limited job opportunities, so they start small online businesses. Social media has made it much easier to get started with very little capital.

items.q: Describe a game or sport you enjoy playing or watching
items.text: A sport I absolutely love is cricket, which is almost a national obsession in my country. These days I mostly watch it, but I played a great deal when I was younger. I got into it as a child, playing casual games in the street with the neighbourhood kids, using a taped tennis ball and a bat my father bought me from the local market. What I love about it is the wonderful blend of strategy, skill and teamwork. As a spectator, I find major matches genuinely thrilling, especially when the national team is playing. I watch almost every international match Bangladesh plays, usually at home with my father, who analyses every shot as if he were the coach. The atmosphere during a big game is electric, and the whole country seems to come to a standstill. Honestly, there is a special sense of unity that cricket brings, uniting people across all backgrounds. I still join a friendly game with old friends now and then during the holidays, as it is a fun way to stay active. What makes it so captivating is its unpredictability; a match can turn completely in a single moment. Some of the most nail-biting evenings of my life have been spent in front of the television, waiting for the final ball. I think its enduring popularity here is thoroughly deserved. For me, cricket is far more than a game; it is a shared passion that connects millions of people and brings my family together in front of the screen.

items.q: Have you ever watched a match in a stadium?
items.text: Only once, in Dhaka, when I was staying with my elder sister. The noise and the sea of red and green shirts were unforgettable, although honestly you see the action more clearly on television.

items.q: Do women in your family enjoy cricket too?
items.text: Yes, my younger sister is just as passionate as I am, and even my mother keeps an eye on the score during big matches. Cricket really is a family affair in our household.

items.q: Describe a way you have changed in the last few years
items.text: A significant way I have changed over the last few years is that I have become far more patient and self-assured. In my younger days, I was quite impulsive and would get frustrated easily when things did not go my way. At university, I would argue with friends over the smallest things and make hasty decisions I later regretted. I think this change came about through a combination of life experience and facing a few genuine challenges. Starting work played a big part, because dealing with worried students and demanding deadlines forced me to stay calm. Around the same time, my father retired, and I found myself taking on more responsibility at home. Overcoming difficulties taught me that most problems are temporary and that panicking rarely helps. As a result, I now approach setbacks far more calmly and rationally. This shift has affected me profoundly; I feel more grounded and less anxious than I used to. It has also improved my relationships, as I listen more and react less. Honestly, I am genuinely pleased with this change, because it has made me a more balanced person. I think personal growth like this is one of the quiet rewards of getting older. I no longer sweat the small things the way I once did. My mother says I have become more like my grandfather, which I take as the highest compliment. It is a change I am proud of, and it is genuinely liberating to feel this much calmer, as though a weight has been lifted from my shoulders.

items.q: Did anyone help you make this change?
items.text: My grandfather, in a quiet way. Whenever I got worked up, he would just smile and tell me that no problem lasts forever. Seeing how calm he stays, even in his eighties, taught me a lot.

items.q: Is there anything about your younger self you miss?
items.text: Perhaps a little of the fearlessness. When I was younger, I would try things without overthinking. Now I am more cautious, which is sensible, but occasionally I wish I were more spontaneous.

items.q: Describe something you would like to be better at
items.text: Something I would genuinely like to be better at is managing my time more effectively. While I am fairly organised, I often find myself struggling to fit everything in, which leaves me feeling stretched. Between work, my IELTS preparation, family commitments and trying to keep up my reading, there never seem to be enough hours in the day. I am constantly juggling different things and rarely feel I am giving any of them my full attention. I want to improve because I believe better time management would reduce my stress and make me far more productive. To improve, I have started using planning tools and trying to prioritise my tasks more ruthlessly, focusing on what truly matters. Every Friday evening I sit down and plan the week ahead, which already helps, because I start Saturday knowing exactly what needs doing first. I am also learning to say no to commitments that are not worth my time, which is surprisingly hard in a culture where refusing an invitation can seem rude. Honestly, I think time is our most precious resource, and using it wisely is one of the most valuable skills a person can develop. If I mastered it, I believe I could achieve far more while feeling less overwhelmed. It would give me more time for the things I actually enjoy, like evening walks and dinner with my family, which is the whole point. It is an ongoing effort, but even small improvements have already made a noticeable and tangible difference to my daily life.

items.q: Who in your family manages time best?
items.text: My younger sister, without question. She plans her study schedule weeks in advance and actually sticks to it. I have started borrowing some of her methods, although I would never admit that to her.

items.q: Do you think people were better at managing time in the past?
items.text: Perhaps they had fewer distractions. My father's generation didn't have phones constantly buzzing, so it was easier to focus. Today the challenge is less about time and more about attention.

items.q: Describe a skill you think everyone should have
items.text: A skill I firmly believe everyone should have is basic cooking. In my view, it is a genuinely essential life skill that far too many people neglect. In Bangladesh, many young men grow up never having to cook, because mothers usually take care of the kitchen, and I was exactly the same until a few years ago. It is important because it directly affects your health, your finances and your independence. Relying entirely on takeaways and processed food is both expensive and unhealthy, whereas cooking allows you to eat well and affordably. This is especially relevant for students going abroad, and I always tell the students I advise to learn a few dishes before they leave. People can learn it easily these days, with countless free tutorials available online, so there really is no excuse. Honestly, I think learning to cook is one of the most practical and empowering things a person can do. It gives you control over what you put into your body, and it means you are never stuck when you end up living on your own. Beyond the health benefits, I find cooking to be a surprisingly therapeutic and creative activity. I learned a few years ago, when my mother spent several weeks in the village looking after my grandparents, and she taught me the basics over the phone. Those weeks of burnt rice and oversalted dal were humbling, but they transformed my daily life for the better. I genuinely believe that if everyone learned to cook a few simple meals, both public health and personal wellbeing would improve considerably.

items.q: What dish can you cook best?
items.text: Probably chicken curry with rice. It took me many attempts to get the spices right, but now even my mother says it is quite good, which is high praise from her.

items.q: Should cooking be taught in schools?
items.text: I think so, at least the basics. It would help both boys and girls become more independent, and it could also challenge the old idea that cooking is only a woman's responsibility.

items.q: Describe a way technology has changed the way we live
items.text: A way technology has profoundly changed our lives is in how we communicate with one another. The rise of smartphones and social media has made staying in touch almost instantaneous, regardless of distance. This happened incredibly quickly; within about a decade, cheap smartphones and mobile internet reached almost every corner of Bangladesh, even villages like my grandparents'. In the past, keeping in contact with faraway friends and family relied on letters or expensive phone calls, which now seems almost unimaginable. My father still remembers queuing at a shop in town to make a short, crackly call to a relative in Dhaka, and letters took over a week to arrive. Today, a video call across continents is effortless and free, which is genuinely remarkable. I speak to my elder sister in Dhaka almost every day, and my nephew loves showing me his toys on the screen. On the whole, I think this change has been overwhelmingly positive, keeping relationships alive that might otherwise have faded. However, I do have some reservations; I feel it has sometimes replaced deeper, face-to-face interaction with shallower digital contact. There is a certain irony that we are more connected than ever yet arguably lonelier. At family gatherings, I sometimes notice everyone staring at their phones instead of talking to the people sitting right next to them. Honestly, like most technology, I think it is a double-edged sword. Used mindfully, it is an incredible tool, but it requires a degree of discipline. Overall, though, I am grateful for how it has shrunk the world and brought distant people closer.

items.q: Do your grandparents use video calls?
items.text: My grandfather does, surprisingly well for someone in his eighties. My grandmother prefers ordinary calls, because she finds it strange to see her own face on the screen, which always makes us laugh.

items.q: Do you still write letters or cards?
items.text: Almost never, sadly. I do sometimes write a card for Eid or a birthday, and people seem to treasure them far more than a message, precisely because they are so rare now.

items.q: Describe a cultural event you would like to attend
items.text: A cultural event I would love to attend is the Lalon festival, a large traditional music gathering held every year in Kushtia, in the west of Bangladesh. It celebrates Lalon, a nineteenth-century mystic poet and songwriter whose songs are still sung all over the country. Although I have seen it on television, I have never experienced it in person, which I would genuinely love to change. It takes place over several days at his shrine and showcases performers from all over the region, especially Baul singers, the wandering minstrels in their saffron robes. Kushtia is not too far from Sirajganj, so it would be quite easy to get there by bus, and I could stay for a couple of nights. I want to attend because I believe experiencing such an event live would be far more immersive and moving than watching a screen. What draws me to it is the celebration of our rich cultural heritage, which I think is increasingly important to preserve. Lalon's songs are about humanity and questioning divisions between people, and I find that message still feels timeless. I imagine the atmosphere would be absolutely electric, surrounded by thousands of people sharing the same appreciation for the art. Honestly, I think events like this are vital for keeping traditions alive and passing them to younger generations. It would be a wonderfully enriching experience, deepening my connection to my own culture. It is definitely on my list of things to do, and I hope to attend it next year with a couple of friends.

items.q: Would you take your family with you?
items.text: Probably not the first time, as it gets very crowded and the music goes on late into the night. I would go with friends first, and perhaps take my younger sister another year.

items.q: Are cultural events like this popular with young people?
items.text: More than you might expect. Many young people find Baul music refreshingly authentic compared with commercial pop, and some modern bands have even recorded new versions of Lalon's songs.

items.q: Describe a challenge that young people face today
items.text: A significant challenge facing young people today is the immense pressure created by social media. In my view, constant exposure to carefully curated, idealised versions of other people's lives has become genuinely detrimental to mental health. Everyone seems to be on holiday, getting engaged or landing a dream job, and it is easy to forget that these are just the highlights. This exists because platforms are designed to be addictive, encouraging endless comparison. The more time we spend scrolling, the more money these companies make, so they have little reason to change. It affects almost all young people, who often feel inadequate when measuring their real lives against these unrealistic highlights. I see it in my younger sister's friends, who worry about how many likes a photo gets, and in some of the students I advise, who compare themselves with classmates who have already gone abroad. I think it can lead to serious anxiety and a distorted sense of self-worth.
