To tackle it, I believe we need better education about using social media mindfully, along with a cultural shift towards valuing authenticity over appearances. Parents and teachers also need to talk about it openly, rather than simply banning phones. Honestly, I think the platforms themselves should also bear some responsibility for their design. It is a complex issue without a simple solution. Having grown up alongside this technology, I have felt its effects personally. I think raising awareness is the crucial first step, helping young people understand that what they see online is rarely the full, honest picture, and that real life is far more nuanced.

items.q: Do you think this problem is worse for girls or boys?
items.text: It affects both, but perhaps differently. Girls often face more pressure about appearance, while boys feel pressure to look successful or wealthy. Neither is healthy, and both deserve more attention.

items.q: Would you ever give up social media completely?
items.text: Probably not, because I use it to stay in touch with family and for work. But I have become far more selective, unfollowing accounts that make me feel worse rather than better.

items.q: Describe an important decision about your future you need to make
items.text: An important decision I currently need to make about my future is whether to pursue further studies abroad or continue building my career at home. It is a genuinely pivotal choice that will shape the next several years of my life. I need to make it because application deadlines for next year's intake are approaching, and universities will not wait for me to make up my mind. On one hand, studying abroad would offer invaluable experience and open new doors, but it is expensive and involves leaving my family. My father has recently retired, and my mother often travels to the village to look after my grandparents, so I feel a certain responsibility to be around. On the other hand, staying would mean steady progress but perhaps fewer opportunities for growth. I have a good position at my consultancy, and my manager has hinted that more responsibility may come my way soon. I need to make this decision soon, which makes it feel quite pressing. Honestly, I keep going back and forth, weighing the potential rewards against the risks and sacrifices. It is a rather daunting choice, precisely because both paths have real merit. I have been seeking advice from people I trust, including my father and my elder sister, and trying to think about what truly matters to me in the long run. Whatever I decide, I want it to be a well-considered choice rather than an impulsive one. I am confident I will eventually reach a sensible conclusion, and that I will have no regrets.

items.q: What does your family advise you to do?
items.text: My father encourages me to go, saying that he and my sister can manage things at home. My mother is more hesitant, although she would never stop me. Their support makes the decision a little easier.

items.q: How do you usually make big decisions?
items.text: I write down the pros and cons, talk to a few people I trust, and then give myself a few days. Rushing never works for me; I need time for things to sink in.

items.q: Describe a useful habit for managing money
items.text: A useful habit I have developed for managing money is setting aside a fixed amount of savings every single month, before spending on anything else. I developed this habit a few years ago, after realising I was spending rather carelessly and never managing to save. When I got my first salary, I spent it on eating out and new gadgets, and by the end of the month there was nothing left. My father, who ran a small business for over thirty years, sat me down and explained how he had always put something aside, even in difficult years. Now, as soon as I receive my salary, I transfer a set portion into a separate savings account. What makes it so effective is that it removes the temptation to spend that money, since it is out of sight. This habit has given me a genuine sense of financial security and a safety net for emergencies. It is also how I am funding my plans to study abroad, which would be impossible otherwise. Honestly, it has been one of the most beneficial financial decisions I have ever made. I would strongly recommend it to anyone, because it makes saving automatic rather than an afterthought. The key is to treat savings as a non-negotiable expense, just like any other bill. Over time, even small, consistent amounts add up considerably. It has taught me the value of discipline and delayed gratification, which are invaluable lessons in life, and I am grateful my father taught me early.

items.q: Do young people in your country usually save money?
items.text: Many try, but it is not easy with rising prices and the pressure to keep up with friends. Mobile banking has made saving simpler, though, and I think financial awareness is gradually improving.

items.q: Have you taught this habit to anyone else?
items.text: Yes, my younger sister. I encouraged her to save a small part of her pocket money every month, and she was delighted when she could buy her own books without asking our parents.

items.q: Describe a social problem you care about
items.text: A social problem I care deeply about is the lack of quality education available to children from poorer backgrounds. In my country, a child's future is too often determined by the wealth of their family, which I find genuinely unjust. Wealthier families can pay for private tutors and good schools, while poorer children often sit in overcrowded classrooms with too few teachers. This matters to me because I believe education is the most powerful tool for breaking the cycle of poverty. I also see it every day in my work, where the students who reach us are usually the lucky ones who had support from the start. It affects millions of talented children who never get the chance to fulfil their potential simply due to their circumstances. Near my hometown, for example, there are children living on the char lands, the river islands of the Jamuna, who have to cross the river by boat just to reach school, and many simply drop out. I think this is a tragic waste of human potential. To address it, I believe there needs to be far greater investment in public schools and more scholarship opportunities for the disadvantaged. Better pay for rural teachers would also help attract talented people. Honestly, I think providing equal access to good education is one of the most important things any society can do. It is an issue I feel strongly about, and I try to support relevant charities where I can. I genuinely believe that giving every child a fair start would create a more equitable and prosperous society for everyone.

items.q: Have you ever volunteered to help with this problem?
items.text: A little. During university, I taught basic English to children in my grandparents' village during the holidays. It was only a few weeks, but seeing their enthusiasm was incredibly rewarding.

items.q: Do you think the situation is improving?
items.text: Slowly, yes. More girls are in school now than a generation ago, and mobile phones give some access to online lessons. But the gap in quality between rich and poor areas is still very wide.

items.q: Describe an outdoor activity you enjoy
items.text: An outdoor activity I thoroughly enjoy is hiking, particularly in the hill areas of Sylhet and Bandarban. Sirajganj itself is completely flat, so I usually go on a trip once or twice a year, often during the cooler winter months when the trails are dry. I usually go with a small group of close friends from university, which makes it even more enjoyable. We share the planning, travel overnight by bus and stay in simple guesthouses, which is all part of the adventure. What I love about it is the wonderful combination of exercise, fresh air and stunning scenery. After months of office work and busy roads, spending a few days in nature is genuinely rejuvenating. There is something deeply satisfying about reaching the top of a trail after a challenging climb and being rewarded with a breathtaking view. In Bandarban, you can sometimes stand above the clouds in the early morning, which I will never forget. Honestly, I find hiking to be both physically and mentally restorative; it clears my head like nothing else. It is also a great way to bond with friends, away from the distractions of daily life, as the phone signal is often weak anyway. I think spending time in nature is something modern life sorely lacks, and hiking is my favourite way to reconnect with it. Between trips, I make do with long walks along the river at home. I always return home feeling tired but genuinely content. It is easily one of my favourite ways to spend a holiday, and I am already counting down to our next excursion.

items.q: Does your family worry when you go hiking?
items.text: My mother certainly does. She makes me promise to call her every evening and to avoid dangerous trails in the rainy season. It is a small price to pay for her peace of mind.

items.q: Would you like to hike in another country?
items.text: Very much. I would love to trek in Nepal one day, perhaps on one of the shorter routes in the Himalayas. The scenery there must be even more awe-inspiring than anything we have here.

items.q: Describe a new activity you have started recently
items.text: A new activity I have taken up recently is journaling, or writing down my thoughts each day. I started it a few months ago, after reading about its benefits for mental clarity and wellbeing. I bought a simple notebook from a stationery shop near my office, and I write in a mixture of Bengali and English, depending on what feels more natural. I began it because I often felt my mind was cluttered and I wanted a way to process my thoughts. Work had been particularly busy, and I was also thinking a lot about my future and whether to study abroad, so my head was full of unfinished worries. What I have discovered is that putting things down on paper is surprisingly therapeutic; it helps me make sense of my feelings. Each evening I spend a few minutes reflecting on my day, which has become a calming ritual. I usually write after dinner, when the house is quiet, sitting at my desk with a cup of tea. Honestly, I have found it far more beneficial than I expected. It has helped me become more self-aware and has noticeably reduced my stress. I also enjoy being able to look back and see how my thoughts have evolved over time; problems that felt huge a few months ago now seem quite small. I think it is a wonderfully simple yet rewarding practice. I intend to keep it up, as it has quickly become one of the most valuable parts of my daily routine.

items.q: Would you let anyone read your journal?
items.text: Definitely not! It is completely private, which is exactly why I can be honest in it. My younger sister once tried to peek, and I have hidden it more carefully ever since.

items.q: Do you think journaling suits everyone?
items.text: Not necessarily. Some people prefer talking things through or exercising to clear their minds. But I think anyone who tends to overthink would benefit from trying it for a few weeks.

items.q: Describe how you like to spend your weekends
items.text: I like to spend my weekends striking a balance between relaxation and being productive. In Bangladesh, the weekend is Friday and Saturday, so it has a slightly different rhythm from the West. After a demanding week, my priority is usually to properly unwind and recharge. I often start by catching up on sleep, which I sacrifice during the week. On Friday, I go to the mosque with my father for the midday prayer, and afterwards the whole family has a big lunch together, which is the highlight of my week. I then like to meet friends or family, perhaps for a meal or a simple outing, since spending time with loved ones is genuinely restorative. Once or twice a month, we take the bus to my grandparents' village home, where I sit with my grandfather and listen to his stories. I also try to fit in some of my hobbies, like reading or walking along the Jamuna, which I never have time for during the week. On Saturday evenings, I often meet a couple of old friends at a tea stall near the river. What I enjoy most is the freedom and lack of a rigid schedule; I can be spontaneous and do whatever I feel like. Honestly, I think weekends are essential for maintaining a healthy work-life balance. Without that break, the weeks would blur into one exhausting stretch. I make a conscious effort not to let work spill into them. A good weekend leaves me feeling refreshed and genuinely reinvigorated, ready to face the week ahead with renewed energy and a clear sense of perspective.

items.q: Do you ever work at the weekend?
items.text: Occasionally, when application deadlines are close and students need urgent help. I don't mind now and then, but I try hard not to let it become a habit.

items.q: Were your weekends different when you were a child?
items.text: Completely. As a child, I spent weekends playing cricket in the street from morning till evening. Now I value rest and conversation far more, which I suppose is a sign of growing up.

items.q: Describe an important lesson you have learned in life
items.text: An important lesson I have learned in life is that failure is not something to be feared, but a valuable teacher. I learned this the hard way, after failing at something I had worked hard for and initially feeling completely demoralised. After school, I prepared for months for the admission test of a well-known public university, but I missed out on a place by a small margin. For weeks, I barely wanted to leave the house, and I felt I had let my parents down. In time, however, I came to see that the setback taught me far more than easy success ever could. I went on to study business administration at another university, worked hard and discovered a field I truly enjoy. This lesson is important because the fear of failure holds so many people back from even trying. Once I embraced the idea that mistakes are simply part of growth, I became far more resilient and willing to take risks. Honestly, this shift in mindset has been genuinely transformative. I now approach challenges with curiosity rather than dread. It has affected every area of my life, from my career to my personal relationships. At work, I now share this story with students who receive rejection letters, and it seems to reassure them. I think it is one of the most liberating realisations a person can have. Understanding that failing is part of succeeding has given me the courage to pursue things I once would have avoided entirely, including my plan to study abroad.

items.q: How did your parents react when you failed that test?
items.text: Much better than I expected. My father told me he had faced many losses in business and still recovered, and my mother simply cooked my favourite food. Their calm reaction really helped me move on.

items.q: Do you think schools should teach this lesson?
items.text: Yes, definitely. Schools here focus so heavily on results that children see failure as shameful. Teachers could normalise mistakes by showing how every expert once struggled as a beginner.

items.q: Describe a hobby that is popular in your country
items.text: A hobby that is enormously popular in my country is playing and watching cricket. It is genuinely a national passion, cutting across all ages and social backgrounds. You will find children playing it in narrow alleys and open fields all over the country, using whatever equipment they can find. Boys have always dominated, but more and more girls are joining in too, partly inspired by the success of our women's team. Even older men, like my father, follow every ball on television and discuss matches at the tea stall for days afterwards. It is popular partly because it requires very little to get started, making it wonderfully accessible to everyone. A tennis ball, some tape and a plank of wood are really all you need. I think its popularity also stems from the sense of unity and pride it brings, especially when the national team performs well. During major matches, the whole country seems to come to a standstill, which is quite remarkable. Honestly, I think it is a wonderful thing for a nation to share such a common passion. It brings people together in a way few other things can. I am very fond of it myself, mostly as a spectator these days, though I played constantly as a boy. My only slight concern is that cricket overshadows other sports, like football, which receive far less attention and investment. Still, I believe this shared enthusiasm is a genuinely unifying force, and it is a lovely part of our national identity.

items.q: Is cricket more popular than football in your country?
items.text: Nowadays, yes, although football was once hugely popular too. During the World Cup, people still fly Argentina and Brazil flags from their rooftops, so football hasn't disappeared, it just comes in waves.

items.q: Do you think this hobby will stay popular in the future?
items.text: I am fairly sure it will. It is so deeply rooted in our culture, and every new generation grows up playing it in the street. It is hard to imagine Bangladesh without cricket.

items.q: Describe a way people can lead a healthier lifestyle
items.text: A simple but effective way people can lead a healthier lifestyle is by incorporating more physical activity into their daily routine, without needing a gym. In my view, small changes like walking instead of driving for short trips, or taking the stairs, can be genuinely transformative over time. In Bangladesh, for example, many people take a rickshaw even for a five-minute journey, when walking would be just as quick and far healthier. This works because it does not require a huge, intimidating commitment; it simply builds movement into everyday life. You don't need special clothes, money or even extra time, which removes most of the usual excuses. Almost anyone could benefit from this, particularly people with sedentary, desk-based jobs like mine. Older people could benefit too; since my father retired, he has started walking to the market every morning, and he says he feels years younger. I think the reason many people fail to get fit is that they set unrealistic goals and quickly become discouraged. A gentler, more sustainable approach is far more likely to stick. Honestly, I feel strongly that health is our most precious asset, yet we take it for granted until something goes wrong. Combining a little more movement with a balanced diet is a genuinely practical path to better health. It is something I try to practise myself, with my evening walks by the river, and I would encourage everyone to do the same. Small, consistent steps really do add up.

items.q: Is it easy to walk in your town?
items.text: In quieter areas, yes, but the main roads can be crowded and there aren't always proper footpaths. The river embankment is ideal, though, which is why it is always busy in the evenings.

items.q: Do you think your family lives a healthy lifestyle?
items.text: Mostly, yes. We eat home-cooked food and rarely have takeaways. The weak point is probably our love of sweets and oily snacks, especially during festivals, which is hard to resist.

items.q: Describe a person who taught you something useful
items.text: I'd like to talk about my uncle on my father's side, who taught me how to fix a bicycle puncture when I was about ten. He's a motor mechanic by trade — a big, gruff man who doesn't say much, and to be honest I was slightly scared of him as a child. He had this small workshop at the end of our lane, and I'd sometimes hang around watching him work, mostly because of the smell of rubber glue and engine oil, which I found oddly appealing. One afternoon my bicycle got a flat tyre, and I went to him expecting him to fix it. Instead, he handed me the tools and said, "You do it." He talked me through it step by step — finding the hole by dipping the tube in a bucket of water and watching for bubbles, roughing up the rubber, applying the patch — but he never once touched the bike himself. When I put the tyre back on the wrong way, he just raised an eyebrow and waited until I noticed. It took me nearly an hour to do something he could have done in five minutes. Looking back, the puncture itself wasn't really the lesson. What he actually taught me was that I could figure things out if someone just refused to do them for me. That attitude has been far more useful than the skill — whether it's a broken laptop or a maths problem, my first instinct now is to try before asking for help. So I'd say he gave me a way of thinking rather than just a repair job, and I'm still grateful for it.

items.q: Describe a place you visited that was very different from where you live
items.text: The place I'd like to describe is a small village in the hill districts in the south-east of the country, which I visited last December with three friends from university. We stayed two nights in a wooden house on stilts, owned by a family from one of the indigenous communities there. It was about a two-hour drive up winding roads from the nearest town, and by the time we arrived it was dark and the driver had to use a torch to show us the steps. Almost everything was different from my city life, but the biggest thing was the silence. I'm so used to a constant background of horns and generators that the first night I genuinely couldn't sleep — the quiet felt loud, if that makes sense. Then at five in the morning the roosters started, and that was the alarm clock for the whole village. The houses were all wood and bamboo, raised off the ground, with the kitchen fire in the middle. The food was different too — a lot of bamboo shoot and fresh herbs, very little oil, nothing like the heavy curries I grew up on. And people moved at a completely different pace; nobody was rushing anywhere, because there was nowhere to rush to. How I felt about it changed over the two days. At first I was disoriented, almost anxious — I kept reaching for my phone and there was no signal. By the second day I'd started to feel slightly ashamed of how much noise we city people make, how loudly we talk, how fast we eat. By the time we left I felt calmer than I had in months, and I remember the sound of the first horn when we got back to town like a slap. So it was a small trip, but it made me realise that what I think of as normal is really just one way of living among many.

items.q: Describe a place where you like to study or work
items.text: The place I'd like to describe is a particular corner of my university library — the third floor, at the back, by the window that looks out onto a mango tree. The library itself is an old building, and that floor hasn't been renovated, which is exactly why I like it. The desks are heavy wooden ones with initials carved into them by students from decades ago, and each has a green-shaded lamp. It smells of old paper and floor polish. The librarian on that floor is a small, silent woman who enforces the no-talking rule with a glare that could stop traffic, and I'm genuinely a little frightened of her. During term time I go four or five days a week, usually from nine until about one. That corner is popular, so I've learned to arrive early; by ten it's gone. Why it works for me comes down to three things. First — and this was an accident — there's almost no phone signal in that corner, so the biggest distraction in my life simply doesn't function there. Second, the silence is real, not the polite silence of a café where someone's always on a call. And third, being surrounded by other people working creates a kind of pressure I can't generate at home. When the person across from me has been writing for an hour, I feel I can't be the one scrolling. I've tried working at home and in cafés, and my output is maybe half of what it is in that corner. Some of that is the place, some is the routine, but honestly I think a lot of it is the mango tree — looking at something green every few minutes seems to reset my brain. So it's my most productive place, and I'm slightly worried about what happens when I graduate and lose it.

items.q: Describe something you bought that you were not happy with
items.text: I'd like to talk about a bag I bought online last year, which turned out to be one of the more embarrassing purchases of my life. I needed a proper bag for job interviews — something that looked professional — and I saw an advert on social media for a leather laptop bag at a very reasonable price, from a page with about fifty thousand followers and glowing reviews. The photos looked great: dark brown, brass fittings, that sort of thing. I ordered it and paid on delivery, about three and a half thousand taka. What arrived was not leather. It was some kind of plastic that had been embossed to look like leather, in a colour closer to orange than brown, and it smelled strongly of chemicals for about a week. I told myself it would be fine. Then, on the second week, on the way to an actual interview, the strap snapped on the stairs of the office building, and my laptop and papers went everywhere in front of the receptionist. I got the job anyway, but I don't think it was because of my entrance. What I did about it was, at first, the sensible thing: I messaged the page, politely, with photos. No reply. I messaged again — six times over two weeks. Eventually they blocked me. There was no phone number, no address, no company name. The fifty thousand followers, I later worked out, were mostly fake. So in the end what I did was learn an expensive lesson. I went to a real shop, touched a real bag, and paid twice as much, and it's still fine two years on. Now if I can't find a physical address for a seller, I don't buy. And I've become the annoying friend who asks "Did you check the page?" before anyone orders anything.

items.q: Describe a sporting event you watched or took part in
items.text: The sporting event I'd like to talk about wasn't anything official — it was the final of our neighbourhood cricket tournament, about three years ago, between the team from our lane and the team from the next lane over. It was played on the local school field on a winter afternoon, with a tape-ball — a tennis ball wrapped in electrical tape, which is how most cricket in this country is actually played. The rivalry between the two lanes goes back decades; our fathers played each other. So even though it was, objectively, twenty-two amateurs on a bumpy field, about two hundred people turned up. Kids sat along the boundary wall, old men brought radios and did their own commentary louder than the actual match, and someone's mother sold tea from a flask. The reason I remember it, unfortunately, is that I dropped the catch that decided it. Last over, they needed three runs, the batsman skied one straight to me at mid-off, and I could hear the entire crowd go "ooooh" as it went up. I had time to think. That was the problem. It hit my hands and went through, and they got the two runs, and we lost by two. I expected to be blamed for weeks. What actually happened was the opposite. My teammates were laughing before I'd even picked the ball up; one of them put his arm around me and said something like, "Now you're a real cricketer, you've dropped a final." And then both teams sat together on the field until dark, drinking tea from the same flask, going over every ball. The rivalry, it turned out, was the excuse for the friendship rather than the other way round. So I remember it for the drop, yes, but mostly for what the drop taught me about the people I live among.

items.q: Describe a time when the weather changed your plans
items.text: I'd like to talk about a day last summer when a storm cancelled a trip that eight of us had been planning for weeks — and accidentally gave us a better day. The plan was a day trip to a small river island a couple of hours from the city. We'd booked a boat, arranged food, and everyone had taken the day off work, which in my group of friends is a small miracle. We were supposed to leave at seven in the morning. At six, my phone lit up with a storm warning. By eight the sky was completely black — that heavy, greenish dark you get before a real monsoon storm — and the boatman called to say the river was far too rough. Then the rain came, the kind where you can't see the building across the road. The trip was clearly off. What we did instead started as a consolation. Since everyone was already up and dressed and had nothing to do, they all came to my flat. Nine people in a two-bedroom apartment. We cooked a huge pot of khichuri, which is what you're supposed to eat when it rains, and I mean huge — my mother's biggest pot, with eggs and whatever vegetables were in the fridge. Then the power went out, so we played cards by candlelight, shouting over the rain hammering on the tin roof next door. Somebody found an old guitar. It went on until nearly midnight, when the rain finally stopped and they could get home. How I felt went through stages. First, genuinely annoyed — I'd organised the trip, and I felt the whole day had been wasted before it began. By lunchtime I'd stopped thinking about the island. By evening I'd realised that the trip would have been pleasant but this was something else: nobody was taking photos, nobody was checking their phone because the signal had gone, and we just talked, properly, for twelve hours. So the change felt like a loss for about two hours and like a gift ever since. Some of the best plans, it turns out, are cancelled ones.

items.q: Describe a job you would like to do in the future
items.text: The job I'd like to do in the future is urban planning — deciding how a city grows, where the roads and parks and drains go, before the buildings arrive and make it too late. What it involves, as far as I understand it, is a mix of the technical and the political. On the technical side, zoning maps, transport modelling, drainage and flood planning — which in my country is not a minor detail. On the political side, it means sitting in rooms with residents who don't want a road, developers who want three more floors, and officials who want the problem to go away. A planner is the person who has to say "no" to powerful people and "wait" to impatient ones, and back it up with evidence. The skills I'd need are a slightly odd combination: enough maths to model traffic, enough drawing to communicate an idea on paper, and enough diplomacy to survive a public meeting. I'd say I have one of the three — the maths — and I'm working on the drawing. The diplomacy I'll have to learn the hard way. Formally, it means a master's degree in the subject, which is part of why I'm sitting this exam. Why I want it goes back to the town I grew up in. When I was a child there was an open field behind our house where the whole neighbourhood played and, in the monsoon, where the water went. Now it's a car park, and the water goes into people's ground floors instead. Nobody planned that. It just happened, plot by plot, permission by permission, with nobody looking at the whole. My father complains about it every single day. I'd like to be the person whose job is to look at the whole — so that the next field gets kept on purpose rather than lost by accident. It's not a glamorous ambition, and I'll probably lose most of the arguments. But I'd rather lose them than not be in the room.
